generated_by: flashcard-authoring workflow (Opus 5); grounded in 2027 CFA L3 curriculum volumes 1-6

cards.front: Capital market expectations are expectations about what, exactly — and what are the seven steps of the framework for developing them, in order?
cards.back:
• CME = expectations for the RISK AND RETURN PROSPECTS OF ASSET CLASSES (however broadly or narrowly the investor defines them) — an essential input to STRATEGIC asset allocation, and acted on tactically via short-term expectations as well; not expectations for individual securities (though CME work feeds security selection)
• 1. Specify the set of expectations needed, including the time horizon(s) to which they apply
• 2. Research the historical record — and the factors that drive each asset class's returns
• 3. Specify the method(s)/model(s) to be used and their information requirements
• 4. Determine the best sources for those information needs
• 5. Interpret the current investment environment, applying experience and judgment
• 6. Provide the expectations and document the conclusions (reasoning and assumptions)
• 7. Monitor actual outcomes vs expectations and feed back to improve the process
• Priority: do NOT over-emphasize precision on any single asset class — cross-sectional consistency (across asset classes) and intertemporal consistency (across horizons) matter far more
• Good forecasts are unbiased/objective/well researched, efficient (small forecast errors), and internally consistent
cards.mnemonic: Steps 1-4 build the foundation; 5-6 are the heart ("do the work, then defend it"); 7 is the feedback loop.

cards.front: An analyst measures equity risk over a five-year window that happened to be a strong bull market and concludes equities are low risk. Name the error — and state its mirror image.
cards.back:
• Ex post (realized) risk is a biased measure of ex ante risk; compounded here by time-period bias
• "Peso problem" version: prices embedded fear of a severe event that never materialized → looking backward we UNDERSTATE ex ante risk and OVERSTATE ex ante expected return (high realized returns were compensation for a risk that did not show up)
• Mirror image: if the sample happens to contain one rare disaster, its observed frequency far exceeds its true probability → risk measures that use only worst-case outcomes (VaR) OVERSTATE the danger. Curriculum example: 22 trading days in March 2020 implied a 13.4% daily 5% VaR on that stock, a loss it did not repeat for 19 months
• Fix: condition the estimate on current prices/valuations; never quote trailing volatility as forward risk right after a big move

cards.front: An analyst forecasts an asset class with the CAPM. Beta is 0.8 in expansion and 1.2 in recession; the market returns 12% in expansion and 4% in recession; Rf = 2%; the two states are equally likely. Compute the unconditional expected return correctly, then show what averaging the inputs first would give — and name the error.
cards.back:
• Error: failure to account for conditioning information — risk and return characteristics vary with the regime, and unconditional forecasts dilute that by averaging over environments
• Setup: beta 0.8 in expansion, 1.2 in recession; market return 12% in expansion, 4% in recession; Rf = 2%; states equally likely
• CORRECT (condition first, then weight): 2% + 0.8 × (12% − 2%) = 10%; 2% + 1.2 × (4% − 2%) = 4.4% → unconditional = (0.5 × 10%) + (0.5 × 4.4%) = 7.2%
• WRONG (average the inputs): beta 1.0, market 8% → 2% + 1.0 × (8% − 2%) = 8.0% — an overestimate
• Exam tell: quoting a full-cycle average (e.g., a long-run ERP) at an extreme point in the cycle

cards.front: Distinguish data-mining bias from time-period bias, and give the curriculum's test for detecting each.
cards.back:
• Data-mining (data snooping): repeatedly searching a dataset until a statistically significant pattern appears. Warning sign is the absence of an economic rationale — "no story, no future." Tests: demand an a priori economic rationale; check the relationship out of sample
• Trap: inventing the story AFTER discovering the relationship is still data mining (and correlation is not causation)
• Time-period bias: the finding is specific to the chosen start and end dates. Test: re-run over different windows
• Curriculum's time-period example — US small-cap vs large-cap: +0.43%/yr from 1926-1974, but +3.49%/yr if you start in 1932 (skipping the Depression); +4.5%/yr 2000-2010 vs −2.8%/yr 2010-2020
• Both are "biases in analysts' methods," separate from data limitations and psychological biases

cards.front: Decompose trend (potential) growth into its four building blocks, then compute it from: labor-force growth 0.5%, participation +0.1%, capital deepening 0.8%, TFP 1.1%.
cards.back:
• Labor input = growth in POTENTIAL LABOR FORCE SIZE (demographics, net migration, workplace norms such as length of work week) + growth in ACTUAL LABOR FORCE PARTICIPATION (labor-vs-leisure choices, real wages, social norms, policy)
• Labor productivity = CAPITAL DEEPENING (more capital per worker) + TOTAL FACTOR PRODUCTIVITY (broadly technology and efficiency; measured historically as a residual)
• Work: labor input = 0.5 + 0.1 = 0.6%; productivity = 0.8 + 1.1 = 1.9%; trend growth = 0.6 + 1.9 = 2.5%
• Units: all terms are annual percentage growth rates and simply add
• Use it as the anchor for long-horizon forecasts; extrapolate past components, then adjust for observable changes (bigger adjustments for less developed economies undergoing structural change)
• Classic error: treating a cyclical acceleration as a change in trend — the cycle fluctuates AROUND the trend; only a shock shifts the trend
cards.formula: Trend growth = growth in labor input + growth in labor productivity; labor input = potential labor force growth + participation growth; labor productivity = capital deepening + total factor productivity

cards.front: Name the six sources of exogenous shocks to trend growth, and the three ways a financial crisis can hit output.
cards.back:
• Sources: (1) policy changes, (2) new products and technologies, (3) geopolitics, (4) natural disasters, (5) natural resources / critical inputs, (6) financial crises
• Pro-growth policy elements: sound fiscal policy, minimal intrusion on the private sector, encouraging competition, support for infrastructure and human capital, sound tax policy
• Financial-crisis types: Type 1 = persistent decline in the LEVEL of output, trend growth unchanged; Type 2 = no persistent level decline but a REDUCED trend growth rate; Type 3 = both (the eurozone after the global financial crisis)
• Direction varies: a natural disaster destroys capacity and cuts growth short run, but may RAISE long-run growth if old capacity is replaced with more efficient facilities; geopolitical tension diverts resources yet can spur growth-enhancing innovation
• Key exam point: a truly exogenous shock is not built into asset prices in advance (only the risk of such events is), is impossible to foresee, and constitutes a regime change

cards.front: Write the identity linking the aggregate market value of equity to GDP, and explain why it forces long-run equity appreciation to track GDP growth.
cards.back:
• Ve = aggregate market value of equity; GDP = level of NOMINAL GDP; Sk = capital's share of income (earnings/GDP); P/E = the multiple applied to those earnings
• Over long periods neither Sk nor the P/E multiple can rise or fall forever, so in the long run the growth rate of Ve is pinned to the growth rate of nominal GDP (long-run aggregate earnings growth ≈ nominal GDP growth)
• Over FINITE horizons, expected changes in Sk and P/E do affect the forecast — that is where a valuation drag or boost comes from
• The identity covers only the CAPITAL APPRECIATION component. For income: dividend yield = payout ratio ÷ profit multiple — set any two of the three ratios and infer the third
• Classic error: assuming the identity delivers total return, or projecting a permanently rising P/E. Curriculum's US example (1946–2020): rising P/E added 0.9%/yr of "extra" return for 74 years — 67% cumulative, leaving the market roughly 95% (= exp[0.67]) above "fair value"
cards.formula: Ve = GDP × Sk × (P/E), where Sk = earnings ÷ GDP; and dividend yield = dividend payout ratio ÷ profit multiple

cards.front: Do countries with higher economic growth reliably deliver higher equity returns? Give the evidence, the two explanations, and state what trend growth DOES anchor.
cards.back:
• No. Studies (Klement 2015, 44 countries) show countries with higher economic growth rates do NOT reliably generate higher equity market returns
• Explanation 1: the higher growth is likely already reflected in market prices
• Explanation 2: stock returns ultimately reflect the return on invested capital — a rapidly growing capital stock drives that return down (so either GDP growth slows or profits fall as a share of GDP)
• A high-growth country is attractive only to the extent the growth is NOT already priced in
• What trend growth does anchor: (a) the average level of real (nominal) default-free bond yields — faster trend growth implies higher average real yields, and yields are pulled toward that level over time; (b) long-run aggregate earnings/equity appreciation; (c) how fast actual growth can run before accelerating inflation becomes a concern (key for projecting policy and bond yields)
• Intertemporal consistency requires factoring this anchor even into shorter-horizon forecasts

cards.front: Compare econometric models, leading indicators, and the checklist approach — key strengths, key weaknesses, and the one weakness the exam loves.
cards.back:
• ECONOMETRIC MODELS: robust, many factors; new data generates output quickly; quantifies the impact of exogenous variables; imposes discipline and consistency. Weaknesses: complex and time-consuming; input variables themselves must be forecast; relationships are not static and the model may be mis-specified; FALSE SENSE OF PRECISION; and the favorite fact — they RARELY FORECAST TURNING POINTS (recessions) WELL
• LEADING INDICATORS: intuitive and simple, focused on identifying turning points, available off the shelf and easy to track. Weaknesses: false signals; the entire history may be revised each month ("look-ahead" bias makes past fit look better than it was); overfitted in sample; may give little more than binary up/down guidance
• CHECKLIST: limited complexity; flexible — structural changes and new items easily incorporated, any source usable; broad. Weaknesses: subjective, arbitrary, judgmental; time-consuming; manual process limits depth; no consistency across items or over time
• Related detail: a diffusion index measures how many indicators point up vs down (7 of 10 up → economy likely accelerating); the OECD composite LEI uses 5-9 variables that turn 6-9 months early; "nowcasting" (GDPNow) forecasts only the CURRENT quarter's BEA advance estimate
• The three approaches are not mutually exclusive — thorough analysis uses elements of all three

cards.front: Walk the five phases of the business cycle in order, giving for each the direction of short rates, the yield curve, and the assets that perform best.
cards.back:
• INITIAL RECOVERY (short, from the trough): confidence rising, stimulus still in place, large negative output gap, inflation decelerating. Short rates and bond yields LOW, yields bottoming; curve STEEP; stocks may rise briskly; cyclical/riskier assets win — small stocks, high yield, EM equities and bonds
• EARLY EXPANSION: momentum building, unemployment falling but output gap still negative, profits rising fast. Short rates MOVING UP as stimulus is withdrawn; long yields stable to slightly rising; curve FLATTENING; stocks trend upward
• LATE EXPANSION: output gap closed, boom mentality, low unemployment, wages and inflation rising, capacity pressure. Policy becoming restrictive; bond yields rise more slowly than short rates so the curve FLATTENS further; pressure on credit markets; stocks often rise but volatile; cyclical assets underperform, INFLATION HEDGES outperform
• SLOWDOWN: economy decelerating toward the peak, especially vulnerable to a shock; inflation often still rising. Short rates high and peaking; bond yields TOP OUT and may fall sharply; curve may INVERT; credit spreads widen (weaker credits most); stocks may fall — interest-sensitive (utilities) and "quality" stable-earnings stocks do best
• CONTRACTION (recessions typically 12-18 months): investment spending leads the decline, profits drop, unemployment rises quickly, central bank eases once recession is confirmed. Short rates and bond yields DROP; curve STEEPENS substantially; spreads widen and stay elevated until a trough is evident; stocks fall early but usually start rising well BEFORE the recovery emerges

cards.front: Over what forecast horizon is business-cycle information most valuable, and what three factors complicate converting cycle analysis into returns?
cards.back:
• Signal-to-noise is highest over horizons within the range of likely expansion/contraction phases — roughly ONE TO THREE YEARS
• Shorter horizons: returns are driven mainly by market reactions to transitory developments, undermining the cycle's predictive value
• Much longer horizons: the period spans one or more turning points, so returns increasingly reflect AVERAGING over the cycle — information about the current cyclical state has NO predictive value over very long horizons (there, use the trend-growth anchor)
• Three complications: (1) phases vary in length and amplitude (a weak phase may be only a "growth recession"); (2) cyclical and secular forces are hard to separate — post-GFC rates and inflation stayed far lower, far longer than a cyclical view implied; (3) how, when, and by how much markets respond to the cycle is as uncertain as the cycle itself, perhaps more so
• Context (NBER): 34 complete US cycles since 1854, averaging 59 months peak to peak; contractions average 17 months, expansions 42

cards.front: Contrast how cash, nominal bonds, equities, and real estate respond to inflation ABOVE the expected range versus DEFLATION.
cards.back:
• CASH (short-term interest-bearing instruments): essentially a zero-duration, inflation-protected asset earning a floating real rate. Relatively ATTRACTIVE in a rising-rate environment (yields reset up), unattractive when rates decline. Deflation makes cash particularly attractive if the zero lower bound binds the nominal rate
• NOMINAL BONDS: cash flows are fixed, so the entire effect runs through discount rates. Rising inflation → capital LOSSES; falling inflation → gains. Within the expected cyclical range, short yields move more but with less price impact (shorter duration); if inflation moves OUTSIDE the range, LONG yields move more sharply as investors reprice the long-run average inflation rate. Persistent deflation benefits the HIGHEST-QUALITY bonds (greater purchasing power of the cash flows) but impairs the creditworthiness of lower-quality debt
• EQUITIES: little net effect while inflation stays within the expected range (cash flows and discount rates move together). Unexpectedly high/rising inflation signals central bank tightening ahead; very low/falling inflation or deflation threatens recession and falling asset prices. Winners under higher inflation: firms able to pass costs through. Deflation is especially damaging to asset-intensive, commodity-producing, and highly leveraged firms
• REAL ESTATE: near-term cash flows are locked by existing leases. Higher-than-expected inflation usually coincides with strong demand, rents rising faster than general inflation, and rising property values (a hedge) — effect is idiosyncratic, depending on lease length and new supply. Unexpectedly low inflation or deflation pressures rental income and values, especially for less-than-prime properties
• Cycle placement: inflation is PRO-CYCLICAL and lags — accelerating in the later stages once the output gap has closed, decelerating in recession and the early years after

cards.front: State the Taylor rule, compute it for r_neutral = 2.25%, target inflation 2%, trend growth 2.5%, expected growth 3.5%, expected inflation 3% — and say what it implies if the actual policy rate is lower than the rule's rate.
cards.back:
• i* = target NOMINAL policy rate; r_neutral = the real policy rate targeted when growth is at trend and inflation on target; pi_e and pi_target = expected and target inflation; Y_e and Y_trend = expected and trend REAL GDP GROWTH RATES (growth rates, not an output-level gap)
• Work: 2.25% + 3% + 0.5 × (3.5% − 2.5%) + 0.5 × (3.0% − 2.0%) = 6.25% nominal, i.e. a 3.25% real policy rate
• Real form (move pi_e to the left): i* − pi_e = r_neutral + 0.5 × (growth gap) + 0.5 × (inflation gap) — the real rate deviates from neutral by HALF of each gap
• Reading the stance: rule rate ABOVE the actual policy rate → policy is EASY/stimulative (tightening likely); rule rate BELOW the actual rate → policy is TIGHT
• Use: assess the central bank's current stance and project how it will evolve
• Classic errors: forgetting to add expected inflation (that gives the real, not nominal, rate); using an output-LEVEL gap instead of the growth-rate gap; applying the weights as 1.0 rather than 0.5; and treating the rule as mechanical — none of its inputs is objectively observable, so judgment remains
cards.formula: i* = r_neutral + pi_e + 0.5 × (Y_e − Y_trend) + 0.5 × (pi_e − pi_target)

cards.front: Why is monetary policy the primary counter-cyclical lever, where does it lose traction, and what does fiscal policy actually contribute over the cycle?
cards.back:
• Monetary policy aims to be COUNTERCYCLICAL (mandates for price stability and/or growth consistent with potential), but its impact comes with "long and variable lags" and substantial uncertainty, so fine-tuning is limited and policy can exacerbate rather than moderate the cycle
• Asymmetry: restrictive policy is like PULLING on a string (it works); expansionary policy is like PUSHING on a string — it rarely suffices to turn a contraction into a strong recovery
• Risk of policy error is GREATEST AT THE TOP of the cycle: the bank may overestimate momentum and/or underestimate the potency of restrictive policy, triggering a contraction it cannot immediately counteract
• The "zero lower bound" proved not to bind: negative policy rates were sustainable because deposits and reserves carry a convenience/transaction value physical cash cannot replace. Quantitative easing (large-scale purchases of high-quality domestic bonds, funded by creating reserves) grew balance sheets and lowered sovereign yields, but proceeds often funded buybacks rather than capex — effectiveness of both QE and negative rates remains unclear
• Setting CME with negative rates: use the LONG-RUN EQUILIBRIUM short rate (the Taylor rule's r_neutral, adjusted for a modest spread) as the risk-free baseline, not the observed negative rate; historical data and quantitative models are even less reliable, and concurrent measures distort market relationships
• Fiscal policy: rarely used to fine-tune growth — the decision process is too slow and frequent large changes would disrupt government services — but AUTOMATIC STABILIZERS (progressive taxes making effective rates pro-cyclical, means-based transfers moving inversely) do mitigate fluctuations and should not be overlooked. A major structural change (e.g., a corporate tax overhaul) warrants attention at all horizons

cards.front: What two components determine the slope of the default-free yield curve, and how does the curve evolve across the business cycle as a growth predictor?
cards.back:
• Slope depends primarily on (1) the expected future path of SHORT-TERM RATES and (2) a risk/maturity premium compensating for the greater price volatility of longer-maturity bonds — that premium is why the term structure is NORMALLY UPWARD SLOPING
• Changes in slope (flattening/steepening) are driven mainly by the evolution of short-rate expectations, which in turn are driven by the business cycle and policy
• Cycle pattern: STEEP at the bottom of the cycle → flattens through the expansion → very flat or INVERTED at the peak → re-steepens during the contraction, likely steepest on the cusp of initial recovery
• As a predictor: the curve's shape (commonly the 10-year minus 3-month spread) is supported by both casual observation and formal econometric analysis, and it passes the "good model" test — there is a solid economic rationale for why it should predict growth, not just a fitted correlation
• Caveat to state on the exam: both the curve shape and growth are ENDOGENOUS — A may predict B this period and B predict A the next; interpret with care
• Also countercyclical: the horizon structure of inflation expectations is upward sloping at the trough and inverted at the peak (long-run expectations stay anchored if the target is credible), reinforcing the countercyclical curve slope

cards.front: Using the curriculum's four-box policy mix, give the effect of persistently loose/tight monetary and fiscal policy on real rates, expected inflation, and the LEVEL of nominal rates.
cards.back:
• Loose FISCAL (large deficits) → HIGH real rates (the domestic private sector must be induced to save more/invest less, and/or capital attracted from abroad); tight fiscal → LOW real rates
• Loose MONETARY → HIGH actual and expected inflation (holding nominal rates down is self-defeating and ultimately raises them); tight monetary → LOW expected inflation and therefore lower nominal rates
• Loose money + loose fiscal: high real rates + high expected inflation = HIGH nominal rates
• Tight money + tight fiscal: low real rates + low expected inflation = LOW nominal rates
• Either mixed case (loose money/tight fiscal, or tight money/loose fiscal): the two effects offset, so nominal rates are "MID" — the direction is ambiguous, though the split between real rates and expected inflation is still clear
• Trap: this grid describes the average LEVEL of rates, not the slope — slope changes come from short-rate expectations over the cycle (and possibly debt-maturity management)
• Related risk: with high and rising government debt, a central bank may be coerced into inflating the debt away; merely the risk of this steepens the curve, and if it happens it feeds an inflationary spiral

cards.front: State the national income identity linking net exports to private saving and the government balance, and use it to say what a tax cut with unchanged spending does to the current account.
cards.back:
• X − M = net exports (virtually always the dominant component of the current account); S = domestic private saving; I = domestic investment spending; T − G = the government surplus (negative when in deficit)
• Reading: net exports always equal NET PRIVATE SAVING plus the government surplus. Anything that changes net exports must change net private saving, the government surplus, or both
• Tax cut, spending unchanged: the government deficit widens → all else equal, a ONE-FOR-ONE increase in the current account deficit; if the cut also raises investment, net private saving falls and the deficit widens further; rising income lifts saving and offsets part of it
• Mirror image: a current account surplus must be matched by a capital account deficit, and vice versa — a capital account surplus is how a nation funds investment plus government spending in excess of saving plus taxes
• Four mechanisms keep the two accounts in balance: changes in income (GDP), relative prices, interest rates and asset prices, and exchange rates. In the SHORT run, rates, FX, and asset prices adjust because the current account evolves slowly
• Classic error: sign confusion — flip every sign when restating the identity in capital account terms

cards.front: State the policy trilemma, and the exact condition under which two countries share a single default-free yield curve.
cards.back:
• A country cannot simultaneously (1) allow unrestricted capital flows, (2) maintain a fixed exchange rate, and (3) pursue an independent monetary policy — it can have at most TWO. A country that pegs with open capital markets imports the anchor country's monetary policy
• Mechanism: push rates down → capital flows out → downward pressure on the currency → the central bank must buy its own currency → the expansionary policy is reversed (and the reverse for tightening)
• Shared yield curve requires BOTH: perfect capital mobility AND an exchange rate credibly fixed FOREVER. It is precisely the lack of credibly fixed exchange rates that lets default-free curves, and bond returns, be less than perfectly correlated across markets
• Peg without full credibility: yields in the weaker currency are nearly always higher (Greece/Italy/Spain vs Germany/France). With no imminent devaluation risk, the shortest maturities trade at comparatively narrow spreads; once devaluation looks imminent, spreads widen across the curve — MOST at the shortest maturities — and the curve almost certainly INVERTS, because a devaluation would collapse the currency-risk premium and generate larger capital gains on long bonds
• Floating rates: the link is expectational — to equalize risk-adjusted expected returns, rates must be HIGHER in a currency expected to DEPRECIATE; this can make the exchange rate "overshoot" so as to create the expectation of the opposite move
• Real rates need not be equal across countries, but global saving must equal global investment, so they tend to move together

cards.front: Write the building-block formula for the required return on a fixed-income asset class, and say what each block pays you for.
cards.back:
• Short-term default-free rate — the only (potentially) observable block; a frequently issued government bill (~3-month), tied to the policy rate
• Term premium — compensation for duration risk; positive, rises with maturity, roughly proportional to duration, varies over time
• Credit premium — compensation for bearing default risk, IN ADDITION to the expected level of default losses
• Liquidity premium — baseline estimate = yield spread between the highest-quality issuer (usually the sovereign) and the next-highest-quality large issuer (often a government agency), then adjust
• Units: annual %, added arithmetically. Use when no clean market yield exists, or for cyclical/policy-driven forecasts
• Classic error: treating the observed credit spread AS the credit premium. Spread = credit premium + expected default losses, so the premium cannot be read straight off the spread
• Second trap: with a negative policy rate, using the observed short rate unadjusted understates required return on risky assets — normalize it or raise the premiums
cards.formula: Required return = short-term default-free rate + term premium + credit premium + liquidity premium
cards.mnemonic: Short rate + T-C-L (Term, Credit, Liquidity)

cards.front: When do rising yields RAISE rather than lower a bond portfolio's realized return, and what horizon separates the two cases?
cards.back:
Two offsetting effects when rates change:
• Capital gain/loss — rising rates cause losses
• Reinvestment income — rising rates raise it
The dividing line is the Macaulay duration of the bond/portfolio:
• Horizon SHORTER than Macaulay duration → capital loss dominates → rising rates mean LOWER return
• Horizon LONGER than Macaulay duration → reinvestment dominates → rising rates mean HIGHER return
• Horizon EQUAL to Macaulay duration → the two roughly offset, realized return ≈ initial YTM
Conditions: exact only if (a) the yield curve is flat and (b) the rate change occurs immediately in a single step; otherwise an approximation
• Timing matters for reinvestment only, not for the capital gain/loss (which depends on beginning and ending values). A gradual rate rise pushes the balancing horizon out BEYOND Macaulay duration
• Practical rule: for long-horizon forecasts, split the horizon into subperiods matching when the largest rate moves are expected

cards.front: Recite the country-risk warning levels the curriculum gives for an emerging market sovereign, and name the single most closely watched ratio.
cards.back:
Most closely watched ratio: fiscal deficit ÷ GDP
• Fiscal deficit/GDP — persistently above 4% is a concern
• Debt/GDP — above 70%–80% signals vulnerability in an EM (only mild concern in a developed market)
• Real GDP growth — persistently below 4% means it is barely catching up; per capita income may even be falling (political stress)
• Current account deficit — persistently above 4% of GDP suggests a lack of competitiveness
• Foreign debt — above 50% of GDP, or above 200% of current account receipts, is a danger sign
• FX reserves ÷ short-term debt — below 100% is risky; above 200% is ample
• Also check: access to IMF/World Bank support, and the country's track record (past crises, defaults, restructurings, inflation/currency instability)
• Caveat the exam rewards: these numbers are merely suggestive of a need for further scrutiny, not bright-line rules

cards.front: Emerging market debt risk splits into ability to pay vs willingness to pay. Sort the risks into each bucket — and which bucket does sovereign immunity fall in?
cards.back:
ABILITY to pay = economic risks
• Concentrated wealth/income and a narrow tax base
• Dependence on specific, often cyclical industries (commodities, agriculture); no world pricing power
• Restrictions on trade, capital flows, currency conversion
• Poor fiscal controls and monetary discipline
• Less skilled workforce, weak infrastructure, low industrialization
• Reliance on foreign borrowing, often in hard currencies not their own
• Small/unsophisticated financial markets; susceptibility to capital flight

WILLINGNESS to pay = political and legal risks
• Weak property rights and weak contract enforcement; inability to enforce seniority among private claims
• SOVEREIGN IMMUNITY — belongs here; it makes forcing a sovereign to pay very difficult
• Confiscation, nationalization, corruption
• Fragile coalition governments and political instability
• Capital controls or conversion restrictions blocking repatriation

Exam cue: a bond issued under LOCAL law plus sovereign immunity is a willingness-to-pay red flag, regardless of how good the growth numbers look.
cards.mnemonic: Ability = Economics; Willingness = Law & Politics

cards.front: State the Grinold–Kroner model and break the expected equity return into its three named components.
cards.back:
Symbols (all annual percentages):
• D/P = dividend yield
• %ΔE = expected % change in TOTAL earnings (nominal, = inflation + real earnings growth)
• %ΔS = expected % change in shares outstanding (negative when there are net buybacks)
• %ΔP/E = expected % change in the price-to-earnings multiple
• (%ΔE − %ΔS) is earnings-per-share growth

Three components:
• Expected cash flow ("income") return = D/P − %ΔS
• Expected nominal earnings growth return = %ΔE
• Expected repricing return = %ΔP/E
• Capital gains = nominal earnings growth + repricing

Use it for forward-looking equity forecasts (the "supply" of returns) and for back-solving a missing input when E(Re) is given. Assumes an infinite horizon in principle.
Classic error: adding %ΔS instead of subtracting it. Net buybacks make %ΔS negative, so −%ΔS ADDS to return; net issuance (dilution) subtracts.
cards.formula: E(Re) ≈ D/P + (%ΔE − %ΔS) + %ΔP/E

cards.front: State the Singer–Terhaar risk premium for asset i, including how the segmented leg is built and what must be added at the end.
cards.back:
Symbols:
• RP_GM ÷ σ_GM = Sharpe ratio of the global market portfolio (risk premium per unit of global market risk)
• ρ(i,GM) = correlation of asset i with the global market; σ_i = asset i's volatility
• φ = degree of integration (0 = fully segmented, 1 = fully integrated)

Mechanics:
• Integrated leg is just CAPM: β(i,GM) × RP_GM, with β = ρ(i,GM) × σ_i ÷ σ_GM
• Segmented leg sets β = 1 AND ρ = 1 (the asset is its own market), leaving σ_i × its segmented Sharpe ratio
• Pragmatic simplification: assume the segmented Sharpe ratio equals the global Sharpe ratio
• Equilibrium models assume perfectly liquid markets, so ADD a liquidity premium after blending — especially for real estate and private assets

Starting values for φ: developed market equities and bonds 0.75–0.90; emerging market equities and bonds 0.50–0.75; real estate roughly on par with EM; commodities with deep futures markets higher.
Implication for allocation: more segmentation → higher required premium. As a market integrates, its required return FALLS, so prices rise and it delivers a higher return than previously expected — a reason to tilt toward integrating markets (usually DM → EM).
Classic errors: forgetting ρ = 1 in the segmented leg, and forgetting to add Rf at the end.
cards.formula: RP_i = φ × [ρ(i,GM) × σ_i × (RP_GM ÷ σ_GM)] + (1 − φ) × [σ_i × Sharpe_segmented];  E(R_i) = Rf + RP_i + liquidity premium

cards.front: An analyst reuses her 10-year Grinold–Kroner inputs as a "long-run" forecast. Why is that wrong, and what are the only long-run-consistent input values?
cards.back:
The only very-long-run consistent assumptions:
• %ΔE = nominal GDP growth
• %ΔS = 0
• %ΔP/E = 0
The longer the finite horizon, the less the projection should deviate from these.

Why the 10-year inputs break down:
• Earnings growing faster than GDP forever implies either an ever-rising economy-wide earnings/GDP ratio or non-index businesses shrinking to nothing
• Perpetual net buybacks would eventually eliminate all shares
• A perpetually rising P/E gives an arbitrarily high price per unit of EPS

P/E growth must also be tailored to the horizon. A P/E of 16.0 reverting to a stable 20 implies %ΔP/E of 4.56% over 5 years, 2.26% over 10 years, 0.75% over 30 years, and an arbitrarily small positive number in the true long run. Treating the 10-year 2.26% as the long-run figure implies a forever-rising P/E rather than convergence.
Exam form: "Are these assumptions plausible for the long run and for a 10-year horizon?" — answer separately for each horizon.

cards.front: What must an emerging market EQUITY investor analyze that an emerging market BOND investor does not, and why do country factors dominate industry factors in EM?
cards.back:
Bond investor focus: ability and willingness to pay a SPECIFIC obligation.
Equity investor focus: the many ways the value of the ownership claim can be expropriated, especially in macro/political distress —
• Corporate governance standards that let interested parties manipulate the capital structure and misuse business assets
• Accounting standards that let management and insiders hide or misstate information
• Weak disclosure rules that impede transparency and favor insiders
• Inadequate property rights laws, weak enforcement, and weak checks and balances on government — permitting seizure, nationalization, and prejudicial, unpredictable regulation
Plus the shared EM risks: fragile economies, lower informational efficiency, unstable political/policy frameworks, weaker legal protections.

Country vs industry: evidence is "vast and contradictory," but on balance country effects still dominate global industry effects — and especially so in EM, because emerging markets are less fully integrated into the global economy, so local economic and market factors exert greater influence.
Vignette cue: closely held listed firms with dominant shareholders, a 2-year financial history, and accounting standards set by the auditors themselves = governance/transparency answer.

cards.front: Give the cap rate definition and the finite-horizon expected return on commercial real estate. How does it differ from Grinold–Kroner?
cards.back:
• NOI = net operating income in the current period; all terms annual %
• Long-run/steady-state version drops the last term: E(Rre) = cap rate + NOI growth rate (a Gordon growth model applied to NOI)
• Long-run steady-state NOI growth for commercial real estate as a whole should be reasonably close to GDP growth
• Difference from Grinold–Kroner: identical structure but NO share-buyback term. %ΔCap rate plays the role of repricing — a RISING cap rate means falling values, so it enters with a minus sign
• Cap rates reflect long-term discount rates, so they move with long-term interest rates (pro-cyclical); countercyclical credit spreads mitigate that cyclicality; higher vacancy rates induce higher cap rates
• Pattern to know: higher cap rates for riskier property types (hotels vs apartments; skilled nursing vs medical office), lower-quality properties (low- vs high-productivity malls), and less attractive locations (secondary vs gateway city offices)
• Classic error: treating the cap rate as a cash flow yield. It is not — part of operating income is reinvested in the property (the gap may be on the order of 3 percentage points)
cards.formula: Cap rate = NOI ÷ property value;  E(Rre) = Cap rate + NOI growth rate − %ΔCap rate

cards.front: Build the required return on direct commercial real estate from risk premiums: which four apply, why, and where does the total land relative to bonds and equities?
cards.back:
• Term premium — real estate is very long-lived with relatively stable cash flows, so it has high effective duration and is sensitive to long-term rates
• Credit premium — a fixed-term lease is like a corporate bond issued by the tenant, secured by physical assets; demand what the average tenant would pay to issue such debt
• Equity premium — the owner bears property-value fluctuations (the most volatile component, strongly pro-cyclical) plus rent growth, lease rollover/termination, and vacancy risk
• Liquidity premium — property trades infrequently and is costly to transact

Total: combining bond-like components (term + credit) with a stock-like component puts the real estate risk premium SOMEWHERE BETWEEN corporate bonds and equities.
Liquidity premium sizing: think of illiquidity as being able to sell only at randomly spaced points in time. Estimates run ~0.60% for quarterly average liquidity, ~0.90% for annual, and 2%, 4%, 6% for trading opportunities every 2, 5, and 10 years. A 2%–4% liquidity premium is reasonable for commercial real estate.
Equilibrium caveats: de-smooth the data first, add the liquidity premium explicitly, and remember real estate is location specific — it may track LOCAL rather than global factors more than financial claims do.

cards.front: What does uncovered interest rate parity predict, what does the evidence actually show, and what problems do the resulting flows create for a central bank?
cards.back:
UIP prediction: the expected % change in the exchange rate equals the nominal short-term interest rate differential — only the first term of the capital-mobility building-block equation matters, so the high-rate currency should DEPRECIATE by the differential.
Evidence: it does not hold. Carry trades — borrowing low-rate currencies and lending high-rate currencies — earn meaningful profits on average. Burnside et al., Feb 1976–Jul 2009: rolling carry returned 4.31% p.a. after transaction costs vs the US dollar and 2.88% p.a. vs the British pound.
Why: profits are usually ascribed to a risk premium (the other premiums in the building-block equation DO matter), and the results may be capturing the overshooting phase of the response to rate differentials.

Hot money flows (vigorous capital movement chasing rate differentials) are problematic for central banks:
• They limit the ability to run an effective monetary policy (Mundell–Fleming with free capital flows)
• A flood of cheap short-term financing tempts firms to fund long-term needs short — setting up a crisis when it dries up
• The near-inevitable exchange rate overshoot disrupts non-financial businesses
Responses: intervene in the currency market, sterilize the liquidity impact by selling (or buying) government securities, and if that fails, impose capital controls. Most acute in emerging markets.

cards.front: Contrast the sample VCV matrix with a factor-model VCV matrix on bias, consistency, and capacity — then say what shrinkage estimation adds.
cards.back:
SAMPLE VCV
• Unbiased (correct on average) and consistent (converges to truth as sample grows)
• Cannot be used when the number of assets exceeds the number of observations — some portfolios would erroneously appear riskless
• Large sampling error at typical finance sample sizes; rule of thumb: observations should be at least 10 × the number of assets
• Imposes no cross-sectional consistency — each element estimated in isolation

FACTOR-MODEL VCV
• Handles many assets relative to observations, because covariances are fully determined by exposures to a few common factors while each variance keeps an asset-specific term
• Massive parameter reduction: N = 100 has 4,950 distinct covariances; K = 5 factors needs 500 sensitivities plus 15 factor-VCV elements — roughly a 90% cut
• Imposes cross-sectional structure and cuts estimation error
• But BIASED and INCONSISTENT unless the imposed structure is exactly right

Trade-off in one line: estimating something "not quite right" precisely versus the "right thing" with a lot of noise.
SHRINKAGE: a weighted average of the sample VCV and a target VCV (a factor-based matrix is a good target), with the SAME weights applied to every element. It is biased, but its mean-squared error (variance + bias squared) is generally lower, so the estimate is more efficient. Virtually any target improves efficiency; the more plausible the target, the bigger the gain.

cards.front: Private real estate data show low volatility and low correlation with equities. Why is that an artifact, what is the correction, and what does smoothing NOT distort?
cards.back:
Cause: observed returns are a weighted average of current and past TRUE (unobservable) returns, because valuations come from backward-looking appraisals rather than concurrent transactions. Same issue for private equity, private debt, and hedge funds.
Model: R_t = (1 − λ) × r_t + λ × R_(t−1), with 0 < λ < 1
Result: var(r) = [(1 + λ) ÷ (1 − λ)] × var(R) > var(R)
• Example: λ = 0.8 → true variance is 9 × the observed variance, so true standard deviation is 3 × the observed

What smoothing does:
• Understates true volatility
• Understates contemporaneous correlation with other market variables and spuriously induces a lead/lag correlation structure — which is why direct real estate LOOKS like a great diversifier
What it does NOT do: it does not, in general, bias the MEAN return. That is the half candidates get wrong.

Estimation: the true return is unobservable, so proxy it with an observable series — a REIT index for private real estate, an index of similar publicly traded equities for private equity.
Biggest trap: feeding raw SMOOTHED (appraisal-based, not yet de-smoothed) real estate data into an equilibrium model (e.g., Singer–Terhaar) distorts the results for ALL asset classes, not just real estate. The smoothing must be removed BEFORE the data enters the model.

cards.front: The economy is approaching the TROUGH of the business cycle. State the equity, bond-allocation, duration, yield-curve, and credit moves — and the causal chain for each.
cards.back:
• EQUITIES — buy. Near the trough, valuation multiples and expected earnings growth are low and set to rise; formalize the recommendation with Grinold–Kroner
• OVERALL BOND ALLOCATION — reduce, to fund the increased equity weight
• DURATION — reduce. Short-term rates are likely to start rising soon and the curve can be expected to flatten as the economy gains strength
• YIELD CURVE POSITION — cut intermediate maturities in favor of short (plus perhaps a small amount of long) to create a BARBELL at the desired duration
• CREDIT — increase exposure, a "down in quality" trade. At the trough the curve is steep, and a steep curve predicts BOTH a high term premium and a high credit premium (spreads are wide)
At or near the PEAK, reverse every one of these.

Cross-market version: if cycles are not synchronized, reallocate equities FROM markets nearest their peak TO markets nearest their trough, and do the opposite within the bond portfolio, adjusting duration, curve positioning, and credit within each market.
Grading anchors: name the specific move, give the causal chain, keep all the calls consistent with the SAME macro scenario — and finish by asking what is already reflected in asset prices, because valuations matter.

cards.front: Name the three levels of a typical institutional investment governance hierarchy and the six tasks an effective governance model performs.
cards.back:
Hierarchy (top down):
• Governing investment committee (often of the board)
• Investment staff (may be full in-house teams or a part-time CFO/treasurer)
• Third-party resources — managers, consultants, custodians, actuaries

Six elements of an effective governance model:
• Articulate the long- and short-term objectives of the investment program
• Allocate decision rights and responsibilities across the hierarchy, accounting for knowledge, capacity, time, and position in the hierarchy
• Specify processes for developing and approving the IPS
• Specify processes for developing and approving the strategic asset allocation
• Establish a reporting framework to monitor progress toward agreed goals
• Periodically undertake a governance audit

Governance = clarify mission, plan, review progress. Management = execution.
cards.mnemonic: O-R-I-S-R-A: Objectives, Rights, IPS, SAA, Reporting, Audit

cards.front: A sovereign fund's board spends most of its meeting time debating individual manager strategies and evaluating manager performance, with little time on asset allocation or risk. Why is this a governance failure, and what is the fix?
cards.back:
Why it fails:
• The SAA is the highest-impact decision and is what the committee should retain approval of (with staff/consultant input); it is being crowded out
• Manager selection and evaluation are implementation/execution decisions with heavy data-analysis content — they belong with staff and consultants, who have the expertise, capacity, and time
• Committee involvement at that depth signals weak checks and balances on the committee itself, and it opens the door to political or non-economic influence (e.g., picking local private equity)

Fix:
• Delegate manager research, selection, and monitoring to staff; committee keeps oversight
• Commission a governance audit by an independent third party to test whether policies, procedures, and structures actually work

Golden rule: each decision goes to whoever has the knowledge, capacity, and time to make it well. Good governance also guards against decision-reversal risk (abandoning a strategy at the point of maximum loss), key person risk, and blame avoidance.

cards.front: Write out the economic balance sheet identity and list the extended assets and liabilities that a conventional balance sheet leaves off.
cards.back:
• Symbols: economic (extended) assets and liabilities are all present values in the investor's currency; economic net worth is the plug that balances the statement
• Extended assets (individuals): human capital (PV of future earnings), PV of pension income, PV of expected inheritances. Institutions: underground mineral resources, PV of future IP royalties, PV of expected future contributions
• Extended liabilities: PV of future consumption (the "consumption liability"); for a foundation/endowment, PV of prospective payouts or future support (grants payable stay a conventional liability)
• Use it to: capture the whole picture before setting the financial portfolio's allocation — e.g., the Lee family (SGD 44m total, economic net worth SGD 18m, of which SGD 16m is human capital)
• Classic errors: omitting extended items entirely; including assets that belong to a related entity but not the investor (Auldberg University's own CAF$350m real estate is NOT on the endowment's balance sheet); ignoring that most net worth may be illiquid, non-tradable human capital
cards.formula: Economic net worth = (financial assets + human capital + PV of pension income + PV of expected inheritances) − (financial liabilities + PV of future consumption)

cards.front: How does the character of a client's human capital drive the financial portfolio's tilt, and what does research say about the average mix of human capital?
cards.back:
• Research: human capital is on average roughly 30% equity-like and 70% bond-like, with significant variation across industries
• Bond-like human capital (stable, secure salary — e.g., a tenured professor): the economic balance sheet is already bond-heavy, so tilt the FINANCIAL portfolio MORE to equity
• Equity-like human capital (variable, cyclical, commission or entrepreneurial income): tilt the financial portfolio MORE to bonds
• Life cycle: human capital dominates at age 25 and converts into earnings and financial capital, reaching ~zero by age 65. Holding total-wealth risk tolerance constant, the financial portfolio's bond weight must rise as human capital falls
• That is the logic of target-date/life-cycle balanced fund glide paths — one US family's path runs 85% equity / 15% bonds at age 25 to 49% / 51% at age 65
• Also check diversification against human capital: an early-stage life-sciences venture is a poor holding for a life-sciences entrepreneur

cards.front: For asset-only, liability-relative, and goals-based asset allocation: how does each relate to the economic balance sheet, what is its typical objective, and who typically uses it?
cards.back:
Asset only
• Does not explicitly model liabilities or goals
• Objective: maximize the Sharpe ratio for an acceptable level of volatility
• Users: some foundations and endowments, sovereign wealth funds, individual investors — when liabilities/goals are undefined or simplicity matters

Liability relative
• Models legal liabilities and quasi-liabilities
• Objective: fund the liabilities (pay them when due) and invest excess assets for growth
• Users: banks, defined benefit pensions, insurers — where the penalty for not meeting liabilities is high

Goals based
• Models goals; sub-portfolio per goal, each with its own time horizon and required probability of success; the sum of sub-portfolios is the total SAA (built bottom up)
• Objective: achieve goals with specified required probabilities of success
• Users: individual investors / private wealth

Trigger words: "maximize Sharpe, no liabilities" → asset only; "fund liabilities / surplus" → liability relative; "required probability of achieving a goal" → goals based.

cards.front: State the Sharpe ratio and explain why ranking candidate allocations on it alone is not enough for an asset-only investor.
cards.back:
• E(Rp) = expected (arithmetic) portfolio return; rf = risk-free rate (use the government bond rate given, e.g., 3%); σp = portfolio return standard deviation. Both in the same units and the same horizon (annual)
• Efficient portfolio test: among portfolios with the same return volatility, the efficient one has the highest Sharpe ratio
• Worked: GPFC Mix A → (8.25% − 3%) ÷ 14.24% = 0.369, versus 0.353 for the current mix
• Classic errors: (1) ranking on the Sharpe ratio alone — it ignores VaR, funded ratio, and cannot confirm that the ABSOLUTE level of risk sits inside the stated tolerance (e.g., volatility ≤ 17%, one-year 5% VaR no worse than −22%); (2) concluding that because one asset's stand-alone Sharpe ratio is higher (diversifying strategies 0.55 vs real estate 0.50) it should replace the other — that holds only if correlations and all else are equal, which they usually are not
cards.formula: Sharpe ratio = (E(Rp) − rf) ÷ σp

cards.front: Contrast the concept of risk — and the measures used — under asset-only, liability-relative, and goals-based approaches.
cards.back:
Asset only
• Risk = asset risk: volatility (standard deviation) of portfolio return, driven by asset class volatilities and correlations
• Can be augmented by tracking risk vs a benchmark and downside measures: semi-variance, peak-to-trough maximum drawdown, VaR; Monte Carlo simulation fills in stress and tail outcomes

Liability relative
• Risk = shortfall risk: having insufficient assets to pay obligations when due
• Also volatility of required contributions, surplus volatility, funded-ratio volatility
• Underpinned by asset-versus-liability differences: relative size, interest rate sensitivity, inflation sensitivity

Goals based
• Risk = the probability of failing to achieve a goal; the limit is stated as the maximum acceptable probability of NOT achieving it
• Overall portfolio risk is the weighted sum of the risks attached to each goal

Note: a given statistic can serve any approach — standard deviation measures portfolio volatility in asset-only work and surplus or funded-ratio volatility in liability-relative work.

cards.front: Define surplus and funded ratio, and show why an asset-only 65/35 allocation can threaten a 1.15-funded frozen DB plan.
cards.back:
• Assets = market value of plan assets; PV(liabilities) = present value of projected benefit payments. Funded ratio is a pure number (1.15 = 115% funded, slightly overfunded); surplus is in currency
• GPLE: assets $1.250bn, PV(liabilities) $1.087bn → funded ratio 1.15, surplus (buffer) $0.163bn
• Surplus optimization = mean–variance optimization run on surplus, with liabilities modeled as a short position in a bond or bonds matched to the PV and duration of the liabilities
• The trap: an asset-only recommendation of 65% equities puts 0.65 × $1.25bn = $0.8125bn in equities. A 20% equity decline wipes out the entire $0.163bn buffer and pushes the plan into underfunded status, creating contribution risk for the sponsor with no upside the sponsor or beneficiaries clearly need
• Liability-relative answer: a liability-hedging portfolio (here $1.125bn of duration-matched fixed income) plus a return-seeking portfolio ($0.125bn equities) — 90/10. It sits below the asset-only efficient frontier, and that is acceptable because risk is measured against liabilities, not assets
• Classic error: judging a pension allocation by asset-only volatility or Sharpe ratio instead of funded-ratio/surplus risk
cards.formula: Surplus = Assets − PV(liabilities)   •   Funded ratio = Assets ÷ PV(liabilities)

cards.front: List the five criteria for specifying asset classes for asset allocation, with the numeric threshold the curriculum attaches to one of them.
cards.back:
• Homogeneous — assets within a class have similar attributes (defining "equities" to include both real estate and common stock fails this)
• Mutually exclusive — no overlap. For a US investor holding domestic common equities, the second class should be world equities ex-US, not global equities
• Diversifying — no extremely high expected correlation with another class or with a linear combination of other classes; in general a pairwise correlation above 0.95 is undesirable (given enough observations to trust the estimate)
• As a group, make up a preponderance of world investable wealth — raises expected return for a given risk and widens the active opportunity set; regulatory limits on foreign investment can constrain this
• Have capacity to absorb a meaningful proportion of the investor's portfolio — liquidity and transaction costs both matter

Criteria 1–3 concern the assets themselves; criterion 5 (and partly 4) are investor-specific. Note also that "strategies" such as hedge funds are not asset classes — they apply strategies to asset classes and lack an inherent, non-skill-based expected return premium.
cards.mnemonic: Homogeneous, Mutually exclusive, Diversifying, Preponderance, Capacity

cards.front: Why can an asset pass a pairwise-correlation screen and still add zero diversification?
cards.back:
• Curriculum counterexample: let asset Z = aX + bY. Z is an exact weighted combination of X and Y, so it adds nothing to a portfolio of X and Y. Yet if the correlation between X and Y is −0.5, Z's correlation with X and with Y is only 0.5 — comfortably under the 0.95 screen
• Lesson: judge a candidate against ALL other assets as a group, not one by one; pairwise correlations can support limited or outright incorrect conclusions
• Second trap: full-sample correlations average across all market conditions. Examine return correlations during periods of financial market stress, which is when the diversification is actually needed
• Related granularity trap: the more sub-asset classes you define, the less distinctive they become — US large cap and US small cap share more risk sources than US and non-US equity do. Broad classes with fewer overlapping risk sources are better optimizer inputs, and their historical data are more reliable; sub-class choices belong at the implementation stage

cards.front: Risk factors are said not to be directly investable. Give the curriculum's five examples of how factor exposures are actually obtained.
cards.back:
• Risk factors are non-diversifiable (systematic) drivers associated with expected return premiums, but most are not directly investable — isolating them generally requires long and short (spread) positions or derivatives
• Inflation: long nominal Treasuries, short inflation-linked bonds
• Real interest rates: inflation-linked bonds serve as the proxy
• US volatility: VIX futures as a proxy for implied volatility
• Credit spread: long high-quality credit, short Treasuries/government bonds
• Duration: long 10+ year Treasuries, short 1–3 year Treasuries

Process: specify the factors and the desired exposure to each, describe asset classes by their sensitivities to those factors, build factor portfolios (long/short) to isolate each, then map the chosen exposures back to asset class space for implementation.

cards.front: How do risk factors relate to asset classes, what motivates a factor lens, and what is the key caveat about factor-based asset allocation?
cards.back:
• Asset classes bundle overlapping factor exposures — Exhibit 7 shows US equity and US corporate bonds sharing four factors: inflation, currency, volatility, and liquidity (equity alone carries GDP growth, real rates, value, momentum, size; corporate bonds alone carry capital structure, convexity, default risk, duration). Those overlaps are what explain the correlation of equity and credit assets
• Modeling with asset classes as the unit of analysis therefore obscures the portfolio's sensitivity to shared factors (inflation risk in that example), making risk control problematic
• Why investors adopt factors: to shape the allocation around goals asset classes cannot express (e.g., matching liability characteristics); an intense focus on risk in all dimensions plus commercial factor risk tools; recognition that highly correlated "asset classes" are better seen as sub-classes of one class (domestic and foreign equity within global public equity); recognition that equity risk can dominate even a seemingly well-diversified portfolio
• KEY CAVEAT: all else equal (including constraints such as no short selling), the set of achievable outcomes is not enlarged simply by changing the unit of analysis — adopting factor-based asset allocation does not by default produce superior investment outcomes

cards.front: Walk through the curriculum's sequence of steps for selecting a strategic asset allocation.
cards.back:
1. Determine and quantify the investor's objectives — what the pool of assets is for; what liabilities, needs, or goals must be recognized and how to model them
2. Determine risk tolerance and how risk should be expressed and measured (which risk measures, factor models, specific sensitivities)
3. Determine the investment horizon(s) over which objectives and risk tolerance are evaluated
4. Determine other constraints — tax status, ESG considerations, legal and regulatory factors, political sensitivities, IPS-imposed limits
5. Determine which approach to asset allocation suits the investor (asset-only, liability-relative, goals-based)
6. Specify asset classes and develop capital market expectations for them
7. Develop a range of candidate asset allocations, typically via optimization
8. Test robustness — simulations over the planning horizon, plus sensitivity of outcomes to changes in capital market expectations
9. Iterate back to Step 7 until an appropriate, agreed-on allocation is reached

Constructed-response tip: tie every element of the recommended allocation back to a specific stated objective or constraint — an unjustified number earns nothing.

cards.front: In the simplest asset allocation problem — one risky asset and one risk-free asset under mean–variance utility — what is the optimal weight in the risky asset?
cards.back:
• λ = the investor's degree of risk aversion; μ = expected return on the risky asset; rf = risk-free rate; σ² = VARIANCE of the risky asset's return. Work in decimals, not percentages
• Reading it: the allocation to the risky asset is inversely proportional to risk aversion and directly proportional to expected excess return per unit of risk, with risk measured by variance
• Context: this is the mean–variance utility special case of the general program — maximize E[U(W_T)] by choice of asset class weights w_i, subject to Σw_i = 1 plus any other constraints (duration or yield targets, weight limits). Power utility is the commonly used family; it has the convenient property that risk aversion does not depend on the level of wealth, and it can be approximated by mean–variance utility
• Classic errors: dividing by σ instead of σ²; entering returns as percentages (11 rather than 0.11), which scales the answer wildly; forgetting that the optimum maximizes expected utility of ENDING wealth at horizon T, not one-period return

cards.front: Why does theory recommend the global market portfolio as the baseline asset allocation, and what practical hurdles and common deviations arise?
cards.back:
Why it is the baseline:
• It sums all investable assets (global stocks, bonds, real estate, etc.) and reflects the balancing of supply and demand across world markets
• It minimizes diversifiable risk, which in principle is uncompensated, so it makes the most efficient use of the risk budget (two-fund separation: all investors hold the risk-free asset plus this optimal risky portfolio)
• It is a reference point for a highly diversified portfolio and disciplines biases such as home-country bias
• At a minimum it forces the investor to articulate a clear justification for moving away from global cap weights

Two phases: (1) allocate across global stocks, bonds, and real assets; (2) disaggregate each into regional, country, and security weights on capitalization weights, which the owner then accepts or alters.

Hurdles: estimating global asset class sizes is imprecise for non-publicly traded assets; residential real estate is largely in homeowners' hands; private commercial real estate and private equity are not divisible into accessible pieces — so proxies are built from traded assets such as ETFs, or alternative schemes (GDP or equal weighting) are used.

Common tilts: home country, value, size (small cap), emerging markets. Home bias example: Caflandia is 0.50% of global equity capitalization, yet GPFC's mixes hold 30%–50% domestic equity.

cards.front: Distinguish the two dimensions of the passive/active choice, and contrast tactical with dynamic asset allocation.
cards.back:
Two dimensions:
• Management of the strategic asset allocation itself — whether to deviate from it (TAA, DAA)
• Implementation within each asset class — where each allocation sits on the passive/active spectrum (manager structure for delegated assets)

Tactical asset allocation (TAA)
• Deliberate SHORT-TERM deviations from the SAA to exploit perceived deviations from equilibrium
• Signals: price momentum, perceived asset class valuation, stage of the business cycle
• May be stock/bond or stock/bond/cash only, or comprehensive (GTAA)
• Inherently involves market timing, but with smaller tilts than an invested-or-not strategy

Dynamic asset allocation (DAA)
• The label used when deviations are motivated by LONGER-TERM valuation signals or economic views

Both are active management at the asset class level and both are a source of risk versus the strategic mix: mandates are usually bounded by rebalancing ranges or active risk budgets, and any outperformance must be traded off against tracking error. Key barriers: monitoring and trading costs, plus higher short-term capital gains taxes for taxable investors. Evaluate through a cost–benefit lens against the cost of simply following a rebalancing policy.

cards.front: What factors determine where an asset owner places an allocation on the passive/active spectrum, and how is the degree of active management quantified?
cards.back:
Factors:
• Available investments — is there an investable, representative index to index to?
• Scalability of the active strategies considered — value added may fade above some asset level, and participation may be unavailable below some minimum
• Feasibility of investing passively while meeting client-specific constraints (e.g., particular ESG criteria may not match existing index products)
• Beliefs about market informational efficiency for the asset class — strong belief in efficiency orients toward passive
• Incremental expected benefits versus incremental costs and risks of active — management fees, trading costs, turnover-induced taxes, judged against lower-cost index alternatives (which vary by asset class)
• Tax status — taxable investors face a higher hurdle to profitable active management, and should generally hold active strategies in tax-advantaged accounts

Measures of the degree of active management: tracking risk (tracking error) and active share — both tend to rise moving toward the active end, but not in lockstep.

Also: indexing is generally the lowest-cost approach; cap-weighted indexing is self-rebalancing, while equal-weighted or other schemes and fixed-income indices require ongoing transactions. Passive and active elements can coexist — indexing to a value style index is passive in implementation but an active tilt in decision.

cards.front: What exactly counts as rebalancing, why is it described as contrarian, and what is its primary purpose?
cards.back:
• Definition: industry practice reserves "rebalancing" for portfolio adjustments triggered by PRICE CHANGES that pull weights away from the strategic target. Other adjustments, even systematic ones, are not rebalancing
• Why it is needed: assets with high forecast returns grow faster than the portfolio, and high-return assets are typically higher risk — so without rebalancing, overall portfolio risk rises and the mix of risks becomes more concentrated. Systematic rebalancing maintains the original strategic risk exposures
• Why contrarian: it is countercyclical — it sells the most recently best-performing holdings and buys the worst. Behavioral finance says this will feel uncomfortable, so it takes discipline
• PRIMARY PURPOSE: risk control, not return enhancement. Even though Willenbrock (2011) shows that in theory even zero-return assets can generate positive returns through rebalancing, the key takeaway is risk control
• Internet bubble illustration (60/40 with US large-cap growth): rebalanced and unrebalanced portfolios ended at similar wealth, but the rebalanced one carried far less risk (5th percentile drawdown)
• Two disciplines: calendar rebalancing (fixed schedule — simple, but the points are arbitrary) and percent-range rebalancing (tighter control of the mix). Rebalancing policy is documented in the IPS

cards.front: Set up a percent-range rebalancing policy: which questions must be answered, how are bands sized, and what makes a corridor wider or tighter?
cards.back:
Framework questions:
• How frequently is the portfolio valued? More frequent monitoring means greater precision; monthly or quarterly balances cost and benefit for most investors (governance and custodian resources matter)
• What size deviation triggers rebalancing? Trigger points around the target create a no-trade region — a 50% target with triggers at 45% and 55% is a 10 percentage point corridor; the portfolio is rebalanced when the weight first passes a trigger
• Is the deviation fully or partially corrected? Three practices: rebalance back to target, to the range edge, or halfway between the trigger point and the target

Band types: fixed width (±5% regardless of target size); proportional (width 0.20 of the target, so a 25% target runs 22.5%–27.5%, a 60% target ±6%, a 5% target ±0.5%); volatility-based; or cost–benefit derived.

Strategic considerations, all else equal:
• Higher transaction costs → WIDER ranges
• More risk-averse investors → TIGHTER ranges
• Less correlated assets → TIGHTER ranges (an asset highly correlated with the rest of the portfolio is nearly a substitute for it, so it merits a WIDER range)
• Belief in momentum → wider; belief in mean reversion → tighter
• Illiquid investments (hedge funds, private equity, direct real estate) → wide ranges, and they complicate rebalancing; exposure can be adjusted indirectly via a correlated liquid asset or derivatives, at the cost of basis risk (a reason allocations to illiquid assets are kept smaller)
• Taxes, being a large cost, discourage rebalancing and justify wider and ASYMMETRIC ranges (a 25% target might run 24%–28%, i.e., −1%/+3%, because loss harvesting saves tax while realizing gains triggers it)
• Derivatives permit synthetic rebalancing at lower cost, without disrupting separate accounts — but require more risk oversight
• Asset class volatility is also a consideration in range size

cards.front: State the asset-only mean–variance objective function used to choose the optimal asset mix, and say what its output number represents.
cards.back:
• U_m = investor's utility (value) of asset mix m
• E(R_m) = expected return of mix m; σ_m^2 = expected variance of mix m; λ = risk aversion coefficient
• Units: E(R) and σ stated in PERCENTAGES with % signs omitted; that is why the scalar is 0.005. If stated as decimals, use 0.5 instead
• Output = a certainty-equivalent return: the risk-free return the investor would value equally. Pick the efficient mix with the HIGHEST U
• λ = 0 is risk neutral (maximize E(R) only); most investors sit between 1 and 10; λ ≈ 4 is empirically a moderately risk-averse investor. Higher λ → bigger variance penalty → more conservative point on the frontier
• Classic error: plugging decimals into the 0.005 version (0.10 instead of 10), or squaring after multiplying — penalty uses variance, not standard deviation
cards.mnemonic: Utility = return minus "half lambda variance" — 0.005 only because the inputs are in percent.

cards.front: List the six curriculum criticisms of mean–variance optimization and name the remedy the reading pairs with each.
cards.back:
• Outputs highly sensitive to small changes in inputs → reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, constraints
• Allocations highly concentrated in a subset of asset classes → same fixes (constraints most directly)
• Investors care about more than mean and variance (skewness, kurtosis) → mean–semivariance, mean–CVaR, mean–variance-skewness(-kurtosis) optimization
• Allocations may look diversified across assets while the SOURCES of risk are not diversified → risk budgeting / risk parity / factor lens
• Most portfolios exist to pay a liability or consumption stream; MVO is not connected to it → liability-relative (surplus) or goals-based allocation
• Single-period framework ignoring trading/rebalancing costs and taxes → Monte Carlo simulation, multi-period models
• Note: input sensitivity is not unique to MVO — any optimizer fed uncertain forecasts has it, and it cannot be fully solved
• Weights are far more sensitive to expected-RETURN estimates than to volatilities and correlations, and returns are the hardest to estimate

cards.front: Black–Litterman vs resampled mean–variance optimization: what does each actually change, and what is the standard critique of resampling?
cards.back:
• Black–Litterman = better INPUTS. Starts from reverse-optimized excess returns (market-cap anchored) and blends in the investor's own views, stated either as an absolute forecast for a class or as a relative view (e.g., APAC ex Japan to beat Europe ex UK by 100 bps). It is a RETURN model, not an allocation model
• Effect on ALLOCATIONS: allocations to APAC ex Japan increase across the frontier and allocations to Europe ex UK decrease across the frontier, with very little impact on the other asset classes
• Effect on RETURNS: because the model accounts for the correlations between assets, EVERY class's return changes — and a class you did NOT express a view on can move nearly as much as one you did. Exhibit 13: APAC ex Japan +0.37%, emerging market equities +0.33% (correlation 0.94 with APAC ex Japan), Europe ex UK −0.18%, cash ~0.00%
• Resampling (Michaud) = better OPTIMIZER. Monte Carlo generates hundreds/thousands of alternative capital market assumptions, an MVO is run on each to give simulated frontiers, and the resulting weights are averaged; the averaged weights are plotted against the ORIGINAL assumptions to draw the resampled frontier
• Effect of resampling: smoother area graphs — smallest allocations get bigger, largest get smaller
• Criticisms of resampling: (1) some frontiers show concave "bumps" where expected return falls as risk rises, (2) the riskier mixes are over-diversified, (3) it still inherits the estimation error in the original inputs, (4) it lacks a foundation in theory
• The two are complements, not substitutes — the reading resamples using Black–Litterman returns

cards.front: On a long-only efficient frontier, what is a corner portfolio, and how do you construct an efficient mix with a required 8.0% return when adjacent corner portfolios return 9.0% and 7.0%?
cards.back:
• Corner portfolio = a point on the frontier where an asset class enters or leaves the efficient mix, or a constraint becomes (or stops being) binding. They show up as kinks in the slope line and as regime shifts in the area graph
• Every efficient mix BETWEEN two adjacent corner portfolios is a linear combination of them
• Solve w × 9.0 + (1 − w) × 7.0 = 8.0 → 2.0w = 1.0 → w = 0.50
• Hold 50% corner portfolio 1 / 50% corner portfolio 2; each asset-class weight is that same 50/50 blend of the two corner portfolios' weights
• If instead a nominally risk-free asset is distinguished, combine the TANGENCY (highest-Sharpe) portfolio with the risk-free asset: CFFA needed 6.50% with rf = 2.2% and Portfolio 4 at 7.24% → 6.50 = 7.24w + 2.2(1 − w) → w = 0.853, volatility = 0.853 × 11.65% = 9.94%, Sharpe preserved at 0.433
• Blending two RISKY corner portfolios (e.g., 4 and 5) to reach 6.5% would give a lower Sharpe ratio and would not lie on the linear efficient frontier

cards.front: A client with λ = 2 inherited €1,200,000 and will withdraw €60,000 in 12 months without invading the initial capital. Three allocations are proposed — A: E(R) 10.00%, σ 20%; B: 7.00%, 10%; C: 5.25%, 5%. A and B produce identical utility scores. What ratio breaks the tie, and which allocation wins?
cards.back:
• R_L = the threshold (minimum acceptable) return; here €60,000 ÷ €1,200,000 = 5.0%
• Higher ratio = higher probability of exceeding the threshold, assuming normally distributed returns (Roy's safety-first criterion)
• Goddard (λ = 2): U_A = 10.0 − 0.01(20^2) = 6.0; U_B = 7.0 − 0.01(10^2) = 6.0; U_C = 5.25 − 0.01(5^2) = 5.0 → indifferent between A and B on utility alone
• Ratios: A = (10 − 5) ÷ 20 = 0.25; B = (7 − 5) ÷ 10 = 0.20; C = (5.25 − 5) ÷ 5 = 0.05 → recommend A
• Use it whenever the client states a shortfall constraint (spending floor, no-invasion-of-capital, a required minimum) on top of a risk-aversion parameter
• Classic error: recommending on utility or expected return alone and ignoring the stated threshold — or setting R_L at zero instead of the required withdrawal rate
cards.formula: Safety-first ratio = [E(R_P) − R_L] ÷ σ_P

cards.front: How does adding human capital and non-traded assets to the balance sheet change the recommended FINANCIAL-portfolio allocation? Use the Emma Beel case.
cards.back:
• Traditional allocation looks only at the investment portfolio; the economic balance sheet adds extended assets — human capital, PV of pensions, non-traded real estate
• Bond-like human capital (stable, inflation-linked, long-duration cash flows) increases capacity to take risk in the financial portfolio; volatile, commission-based or equity-like human capital argues for a more conservative financial portfolio
• Beel: GBP 1,500,000 liquid (54.55%), GBP 750,000 London house (27.27%), human capital GBP 500,000 (18.18%) = GBP 2,750,000
• Human capital was MODELLED as a return composite: 70% UK long-duration inflation-linked bonds, 15% UK corporate bonds, 15% UK equities; the house was modelled on a de-smoothed London residential index
• Because the house and human capital are non-tradable, the optimizer was CONSTRAINED to hold them at their existing weights and optimize around them; with λ = 4 the optimum had about 8.2% volatility
• Result to remember: the liquid portfolio held NO UK equities and NO UK fixed income — each is highly correlated with her UK human capital or UK residential real estate
• The financial portfolio is the balancing item that shapes TOTAL economic risk

cards.front: How does reverse optimization turn the global market portfolio into expected returns, and what makes those returns a defensible starting point?
cards.back:
• Reverse optimization runs MVO backwards: it takes weights assumed optimal (normally observed market capitalizations), plus covariances and λ, and solves for the expected returns implied by them ("implied" or "imputed" returns)
• β(i,mkt) = beta of asset i against the working version of the global market portfolio built from the opportunity set; not against a domestic index
• UK example: rf = 2.5%, global market risk premium = 4%. US equities β = 1.33 → 2.5 + 1.33(4) = 7.84%; Global ex UK bonds β = 0.39 → 4.05%; cash β = 0 → 2.50%. Weighted-average return = 6.5% and weighted-average beta = 1.0
• Why it works: it forces a consistent relationship between each class's expected return and its systematic risk, so the optimizer finds no phantom bargains — this is why the base-case area graph stays well diversified with all 12 classes allocated over much of the frontier
• Use as the neutral baseline: holding market-cap weights requires no forecasting skill; every tilt away must be justified by liabilities, horizon, taxes, liquidity needs, or an explicit view (Black–Litterman)
• Classic error: assuming market-cap weights are the only permissible starting point — the mechanics work with any starting weights (existing policy portfolio, peer-group average, fundamental weights)
cards.formula: E(R_i) = r_f + β(i,mkt) × (Global market risk premium)

cards.front: Monte Carlo simulation vs scenario analysis: what does each produce, and when is Monte Carlo genuinely REQUIRED rather than merely nice to have?
cards.back:
• Monte Carlo: thousands of simulated paths → the full DISTRIBUTION of outcomes through time (percentile wealth paths, maximum drawdowns, probability of meeting a goal). It handles the multi-period problems MVO cannot: withdrawals, the interaction of rebalancing with taxes and trading costs, glide paths, annuities, human capital, non-normal multivariate returns
• Required only when terminal wealth is PATH DEPENDENT: with no cash flows, or with cash flows and i.i.d. returns, the sequence of returns is irrelevant and percentiles of terminal wealth can be obtained analytically. Saving into and spending out of the portfolio is what makes the path matter
