• Scenario analysis: a small number of specific, discrete events — a 100 bp parallel shift across all maturities, or a repeat of late 2008 — traced through both assets and PV(liabilities). These "what if" studies are the basis of regulator-required stress tests
• Classic prompt: a retiree drawing income (Ali withdrawing CAF$40,000 from CAF$1 million for 25 years) — Monte Carlo showed MEDIAN real wealth at age 90 below her CAF$1 million real bequest goal, so the allocation fails her objectives
• Present results in REAL terms whenever the goal is stated in today's purchasing power

cards.front: What two problems make direct real estate, infrastructure and private equity hard to put into an optimizer, and what are the three practical options the curriculum gives?
cards.back:
• Problem 1 — no accurate index: few indexes exist, rival indexes show noticeably different risk and return, the constituents cannot be diversified to remove idiosyncratic risk, and the indexes are widely believed not to reflect true volatility. So capital market assumptions are hard to make
• Problem 2 — even with a good index there is no low-cost passive vehicle to track it (unlike an ETF on a global equity index)
• Compounding issue: the actual VEHICLE differs from the asset class — a private equity fund's risk and return are dominated by company-specific risk, whereas the "asset class" means owning all private equity
• Three practical options: (1) exclude the illiquid classes from the allocation decision and treat the funds as implementation vehicles for the target allocation; (2) include them, modelling inputs to match the likely implementation VEHICLES; (3) include them, modelling inputs to match the highly diversified TRUE asset classes
• Watch out: using listed proxies (global REITs for global real estate, listed infrastructure, public-equity lookalikes for PE) violates the mutual-exclusivity recommendation for asset classes and raises cross-class correlations — which increases input sensitivity in the optimizer
• Illiquidity premium is available only to investors whose horizon and near-term liquidity needs allow it

cards.front: Write the marginal and absolute contribution-to-risk formulas and show the check that proves you used them correctly.
cards.back:
• β(i,P) = beta of asset class i with respect to the PORTFOLIO (not the market) — it captures both the asset's own volatility and its correlations with the other holdings
• σ_P = portfolio return volatility; w_i = the asset class's weight
• MCTR = the rate at which portfolio risk changes for a marginal change in the weight; ACTR = how much that class actually contributes to portfolio volatility
• Check: the ACTRs must SUM to σ_P. UK example — UK large cap: MCTR = 1.0289 × 10.876% = 11.19%; ACTR = 3.2% × 11.19% = 0.36%; %CTR = 0.36 ÷ 10.88 = 3.33%; all ACTRs total 10.88% = σ_P
• The lesson: capital weight ≠ risk weight. US equities at 34.4% of capital supplied 45.94% of the risk; a 54/46 equity/fixed-income split produced roughly 74% of risk from equities
• Classic errors: using beta versus a market index instead of versus the portfolio; multiplying MCTR by weight twice; forgetting that a smaller weight can dominate risk if its beta is high enough (asset B at half A's weight needs beta more than twice A's to contribute more)
cards.formula: MCTR_i = β(i,P) × σ_P ; ACTR_i = w_i × MCTR_i ; Σ ACTR_i = σ_P ; %CTR_i = ACTR_i ÷ σ_P

cards.front: State the condition that makes a risk budget OPTIMAL, and what the common value equals.
cards.back:
• Compute (expected return − risk-free rate) ÷ MCTR for every position; the budget is optimal when that ratio is the SAME for all assets
• That common ratio equals the Sharpe ratio of the tangency portfolio. In the UK example every class shows 0.368 — e.g. UK large cap (6.62% − 2.5%) ÷ 11.19% = 0.368 — so the reverse-optimized allocation is an optimal risk budget
• Decision rule: if one position's return per unit of risk CONTRIBUTION exceeds another's, shift risk toward it; the goal of risk budgeting is to spend risk efficiently in pursuit of return
• Active/relative analogue: expected active return ÷ marginal contribution to TRACKING ERROR equal across active positions; that common ratio is the information ratio — how a sponsor spreads a tracking-error budget over managers
• Units: numerator is an EXCESS return over the risk-free rate, not a total return
• Classic error: equalizing ACTRs across assets — that is risk parity, a different (and returns-blind) objective, not the optimality condition
cards.formula: [E(R_i) − r_f] ÷ MCTR_i = the same for all i = Sharpe ratio of the tangency portfolio

cards.front: Absolute vs relative risk budget: what risk is being allocated in each, at what stage of the process, and against what benchmark?
cards.back:
• Absolute risk budget: allocates TOTAL portfolio volatility (σ_P) across asset classes. It belongs to the asset allocation decision; measured with MCTR/ACTR against portfolio standard deviation; optimal when excess return ÷ MCTR is equal across classes
• Relative risk budget: allocates ACTIVE risk — tracking error versus a benchmark — across active positions or managers. It belongs to the IMPLEMENTATION decision; optimal when expected active return ÷ marginal contribution to tracking error is equal across positions
• Both rest on the same machinery: the marginal contribution to a type of risk is the partial derivative of that risk (total, active, or residual) with respect to the corresponding holdings (asset allocation, active, or residual holdings)
• Knowing a marginal contribution lets you (1) approximate the change in portfolio risk from changing one holding, (2) identify which positions are optimal, (3) build the risk budget
• Common framing: three parts to risk budgeting — the budget identifies total risk and allocates it to the parts; an OPTIMAL budget allocates it efficiently; the process of finding it is risk budgeting

cards.front: Beyond estimating λ, how are a client's stated needs and preferences about risk actually built into the allocation?
cards.back:
• Risk aversion cannot be estimated precisely: blend risk PREFERENCE (willingness — subjective, reaction to ups and downs, gauged by validated questionnaires such as Grable and Joo 2004) with risk CAPACITY (ability — objective: net worth, income, emergency fund versus consumption, savings rate)
• If λ is unavailable, work with what the client can express: a maximum tolerable volatility truncates the frontier (e.g. only mixes with σ ≤ 10% qualify), or a numerical return objective picks the mix (e.g. the allocation with 5% expected return)
• A stated shortfall concern becomes a threshold return and a safety-first test, not a change in λ
• Liquidity needs become an explicit cash allocation or an upper limit on illiquid classes (some advisers hold six months of expenses in cash)
• Preferences and policy limits enter as optimizer constraints: fixed weights for non-tradable assets, ranges for a class, relative constraints between classes, alternatives caps, and drawdown controls that address investors' asymmetric tolerance — upward volatility is much preferred to downward
• In goals-based settings, urgency differs by goal, so one client legitimately carries different required probabilities of success (and thus different risk levels) across sub-portfolios

cards.front: How is a factor-based opportunity set constructed, why are its correlations so low, and is it superior to an asset-class opportunity set?
cards.back:
• Typical factors: market (equity), size, valuation, momentum, liquidity, duration (term), credit, volatility — mostly return drivers identified as returns the CAPM did not explain
• Construction: apart from the market factor, each is a zero-dollar (self-financing) investment — short the underperforming attribute to fund a long in the other. Size factor return = small-cap return − large-cap return, so if large caps win, the realized size return is negative
• The offsetting short strips out most market exposure, which is why factors have low correlations with the market and with each other: average pairwise correlation 0.31 for the factor set versus 0.57 for the asset-class set in the curriculum's US data
• To optimize in familiar total-return space, add the assumed collateral return (3-month T-bills) to each factor return — necessary if factors and traditional asset classes appear in the same optimization; alternatively subtract cash from asset returns and work in excess-return space
• Idzorek and Kowara (2013): in a proper comparison neither approach is inherently superior — with access to similar exposures the two efficient frontiers nearly coincide, and the factor mixes mirror the asset-class mixes
• Choose the space in which you can best form capital market assumptions; adding any new weakly correlated factor OR asset class improves the risk–return trade-off
• Analytical use: decomposing an asset-class portfolio into factors exposes hidden concentrations

cards.front: List the seven liability characteristics that affect asset allocation, and say what they are used to determine.
cards.back:
• Fixed versus contingent cash flows (a fixed-coupon bond versus DB pension or insurance payouts that depend on retirement dates, longevity, or an insured event)
• Legal versus quasi-liabilities (a DB promise versus a university endowment's support of the operating budget, or an individual's spending needs)
• Duration and convexity of the liability cash flows
• Value of the liabilities compared with the size of the sponsoring organization
• Factors driving future liability cash flows: inflation, economic conditions, interest rates, risk premium
• Timing considerations, such as longevity risk
• Regulations affecting liability cash flow calculations
• What they drive: (1) the appropriate DISCOUNT RATE and therefore PV(liabilities), surplus and funded status; (2) the composition of the liability-hedging portfolio; (3) that portfolio's basis risk — the degree of mismatch between hedge and liabilities
• If the cash flows can be hedged perfectly by market-priced assets, the discount rate follows from those assets (a fixed liability with modified duration 5 → a five-year zero-coupon yield); ongoing plans depending on growth and inflation cannot be fully hedged
• Law of large numbers can make aggregate liabilities more certain (life insurance) but it does NOT eliminate longevity risk

cards.front: Compare the three liability-relative approaches on complexity, correlation assumption, risk level, required funded ratio, and number of periods — and name the institution each fits.
cards.back:
• Surplus optimization: simplicity; assumes LINEAR correlation between assets and PV(liabilities); works at all levels of risk; any funded ratio; single period. MVO run on surplus return, exploiting natural hedges through the expanded correlation matrix. Fits a plan whose liabilities can be approximated and correlated with assets
• Hedging/return-seeking (two-portfolio): simplicity; linear OR non-linear correlation; conservative level of risk; basic version needs a POSITIVE funded ratio; single period. Fund the liability hedge first (LOWTECH: US$2.261bn in long bonds), invest the surplus (US$0.239bn) for return. Fits conservative investors — insurers and overfunded/fully funded plans wanting to remove the risk of not paying liabilities
• Integrated asset–liability: increased complexity; linear or non-linear correlation; all levels of risk; any funded ratio; MULTIPLE periods. Jointly and dynamically optimizes the asset mix AND the composition of liabilities; called ALM at banks (Basel III stress scenarios) and dynamic financial analysis at insurers; also long–short hedge funds, where shorts are the liabilities
• Variants of the two-portfolio approach when there is no surplus: a partial hedge, or a dynamic liability glide path that raises the hedge as the funded ratio improves
• Only the multi-period integrated model can properly estimate the probability of meeting future obligations; the two single-period models struggle with it

cards.front: Write surplus, funding ratio, and the surplus objective function — then show how a change in discount rate alone flips a plan's status.
cards.back:
• Surplus = market value of assets − PV(liabilities); Funding ratio = market value of assets ÷ PV(liabilities). Fully funded = 1; above 1 overfunded; below 1 underfunded
• Surplus objective: U(LR,m) = E(R_s,m) − 0.005 × λ × σ^2(R_s,m), where surplus return R_s,m = (change in asset value − change in liability value) ÷ INITIAL ASSET VALUE, and liability return is the time value of money on the liabilities plus expected changes in the discount rate and future cash flows
• LOWTECH: assets US$2.500bn. At the 4% high-quality corporate rate (required by the US Pension Protection Act of 2006) PV = US$2.261bn → surplus +US$0.239bn, funding ratio 1.1057 (about 10.6% overfunded). At a 2% long government rate PV = US$3.039bn → surplus −US$0.539bn, funding ratio 0.8226 — underfunded, with nothing else changed
• Annual valuation steps: market-value the assets; project liability cash flows actuarially; choose the discount rate; compute PV(liabilities), surplus and funding ratio
• Classic error: treating the discount rate as a free choice — it is largely set by regulation and tradition, and high rates flatter the funded ratio and cut near-term contributions while low rates do the reverse
cards.formula: Surplus = MV(assets) − PV(liabilities) ; Funding ratio = MV(assets) ÷ PV(liabilities) ; U(LR,m) = E(R_s,m) − 0.005 × λ × σ^2(R_s,m)

cards.front: Walk through the goals-based process: how is a module chosen for a goal, how is required capital set, and how is the overall allocation obtained?
cards.back:
• Describe every goal: its cash flows, its time horizon, and the required minimum probability of success. Translate urgency into a probability using plain language — needs 90%–99%, wants, wishes, and dreams below 60% (mirror set for goals to avoid: nightmares, fears, worries, concerns)
• Select the module: in the row for that horizon and required probability, pick the module with the HIGHEST probability- and horizon-adjusted return. Highest adjusted return = lowest funding cost = least capital required today
• Allocate capital: discount the goal's expected cash flows at that adjusted return
• Smiths (US$25m): goal 1, need, 5 years, 95% → Module A at 2.3% → US$2,430k (9.7%); goal 2, want, 25 years, 85% → Module F at 6.1% → US$6,275k (25.1%); goal 3, need, 10 years, 90% → Module D at 4.1% → US$6,691k (26.8%); goal 4, wish, 20 years, 75% → Module F at 6.8% → US$2,683k (10.7%)
• The same module can serve more than one goal; leftover capital is a SURPLUS (here US$6,921k, 27.7%) parked in a middle module (C) as a labeled goal — "capital preservation"
• Overall portfolio = the weighted average of each module's asset-class weights, weights being each module's share of total financial assets; here E(R) 7.2%, σ 8.0%
• Rule of thumb: higher priority and shorter horizon → lower-risk module; lower priority and longer horizon → higher-risk module

cards.front: A goal-funding portfolio has a 7% expected return and 10% volatility; the goal must be met in 5 years with 90% confidence. Why is 7% the wrong discount rate, and what replaces it?
cards.back:
• The mistake is discounting the goal's cash flows at the module's AVERAGE (median) expected return. Individuals' risk measure is the probability of missing the goal, so the funding rate must be a probability- and horizon-adjusted MINIMUM EXPECTATION: the minimum return expected over that horizon at that required confidence
• Scaling over 5 years (i.i.d. assumption): return = 7% × 5 = 35%; volatility = 10% × √5 = 22.4%
• At 90% confidence the portfolio is expected to compound at only about 1.3% a year — far below 7%
• Consequence: use the lower rate, reserve MORE capital up front. Using 7% systematically underfunds the goal
• Two follow-on effects to know: because minimum expectations are conservative, in normal markets portfolios OUTPERFORM the discount rate, so funding can look excessive in hindsight and rebalancing is needed — and failing to rebalance lets the low-risk, short-horizon sub-portfolios creep up in weight, drifting the client DOWN the risk axis and taking less risk than they can bear
• Also: a stated horizon may be a placeholder — "the next five years" can still be five years a year later, especially when it reflects anticipated death

cards.front: Name the five heuristic/alternative allocation approaches and the single main limitation or identifying feature of each.
cards.back:
• "120 − age": equity % = 120 − age (cousins: 100 − age, 125 − age). A 25-year-old holds 95% equities. No theoretical basis, but the linear de-risking broadly matches target-date fund glide paths, which are often justified by the evolving ratio of human capital to financial capital
• 60/40 stocks/bonds: equities for long-term growth, bonds for risk reduction; roughly matches the estimated global financial market portfolio. The Norway model (Government Pension Fund Global) is the passive, ESG-screened, roughly 60/40 archetype — the opposite pole from Yale
• Endowment (Yale) model: heavy non-traditional and manager-skill-driven exposure, active management, and deliberate harvesting of illiquidity premiums (Yale June 2014: 33.0% private equity, 17.6% real estate, 17.4% absolute return, versus a US educational mean of 10.0% private equity). Needs scale, expertise and a long horizon; Swensen himself said most investors should not copy it
• Risk parity: each asset contributes equally to total risk, w_i × Cov(r_i, r_P) = σ_P^2 ÷ n, solved numerically; then lever up or hold cash to reach the desired risk. Its primary criticism is that it IGNORES expected returns — the mirror image of pre-Markowitz approaches that ignored risk. Results depend heavily on how the opportunity set is formed (7 equity and 3 fixed-income classes → about 70% of risk from equities)
• 1/N: equal weights across N assets, rebalanced on a calendar (often quarterly). Theory says optimizers should beat it; empirically it does well on Sharpe ratios and certainty equivalents precisely because it uses no estimates and so sidesteps estimation error

cards.front: Under percent-range rebalancing, which factors WIDEN and which NARROW an asset class's optimal corridor, and what do taxes and the choice of rebalancing target add?
cards.back:
• Positively related (higher factor → WIDER corridor): transaction costs (a high hurdle for rebalancing benefits to clear); risk tolerance (less sensitivity to divergence from target); the asset class's correlation with the rest of the portfolio (when classes move in sync, further divergence from target weights is less likely)
• Inversely related (higher → NARROWER corridor): the volatility of the REST of the portfolio, because large divergences become more likely
• Taxable investors: higher capital gains tax rates should also mean wider corridors; use portfolio cash flows to rebalance and cut transaction costs
• Why rebalance at all: divergence from an optimal strategic allocation is an expected utility loss; disciplined rebalancing has tended to reduce risk while adding return — interpreted as earning a diversification return, a return from being short volatility (equivalent to writing out-of-the-money puts and calls on the risky asset), and a return to supplying liquidity
• Calendar rebalancing has lower monitoring cost; percent-range is the more disciplined risk control because it responds to market moves
• Rebalance to target, to the corridor edge, or to inside the corridor: fixed transaction costs favor rebalancing all the way to TARGET weights; variable transaction costs favor going to the NEAREST corridor border, leaving the interior a no-trade zone — relevant for illiquid assets
• Optimal rebalancing in the multi-period, multi-asset case remains an unsolved problem

cards.front: "Higher volatility means a narrower rebalancing corridor" — when is that answer wrong?
cards.back:
• It is wrong when the volatility in question is the asset class's OWN volatility. For that factor, "holding all else equal" is not practically meaningful
• Absent transaction costs, higher own volatility WOULD narrow the corridor for a risk-averse investor, since a given drift is more likely to widen further. But a narrower corridor means more frequent trading and higher transaction costs, so the effect is a trade-off — and conclusions also depend on the assumed return dynamics
• In practice corridor width is usually set proportionally GREATER the higher the class's own volatility, focusing on transaction-cost control (volatility-based rebalancing; in equal-probability rebalancing each corridor is a common multiple of the class's own standard deviation, so every class is equally likely to trigger a trade)
• Do not confuse it with the volatility of the REST of the portfolio, which IS unambiguously inversely related to corridor width
• Example 12 test: domestic bonds are relatively illiquid and their volatility rises → WIDEN the band, because containing transaction costs outweighs the expected utility loss from a larger divergence
• Same exam trick with offsetting factors: international equity transaction costs up 20% (wider) but correlation with the rest of the portfolio falls (narrower) → the net effect is indeterminate

cards.front: Asset size constrains allocation in BOTH directions. What specifically blocks a very large asset owner, and what blocks a very small one?
cards.back:
Very large — diseconomies of scale:
• A mandate can exhaust an active manager's capacity: a US$25bn fund's 5% small-cap sleeve = US$1.25bn split across 3–4 managers = 23%–31% of each manager's AUM → operational risk for both sides
• Growth in AUM → larger trades, greater price impact, style drift, slower decisions
• Niche/small-cap positions are too small to move the needle; splitting a mandate across many managers yields an index-like result at active fees (bets cancel out)
• Offsetting advantage: governance resources and scale to access private equity, real estate, infrastructure, co-investments — large DB plans beat small ones by 45–50 bps/yr risk-adjusted (1990–2008); they often index developed equity
Very small (institutions < US$500M; private wealth < US$25M):
• High minimums and legal qualification rules block PE/HF/direct real estate (US qualified purchaser: natural person ≥ US$5M in investments; company or manager ≥ US$25M)
• Too few assets to diversify across managers; thin staff and due-diligence capacity
• Remedy: commingled vehicles, funds of funds, liquid-alt/ETF access channels, family limited partnerships
cards.mnemonic: Too big to fit, too small to get in.

cards.front: Trap: "A longer horizon diversifies risk away, so a long-horizon investor faces less equity risk." What does the curriculum actually say about time diversification?
cards.back:
• MVO assumes returns follow a random walk — Year X independent of Year X−1 — so under that baseline there is NO reduction in risk from a longer horizon
• Shortfall PROBABILITY may fall at longer horizons, but the dispersion of outcomes WIDENS → the magnitude of potential loss or shortfall is greater
• Curriculum illustration (US$100,000; 7.0% expected return, 15% σ, vs 1.5% risk-free): the 95% lower boundary is below the initial investment for every horizon under 10 years, and does not exceed risk-free ending wealth until 30 years; at 99% confidence it stays below the initial investment through 20 years
• Only an assumption of MEAN-REVERTING risky returns supports the conventional "fund long-term goals with risky assets and de-risk as the horizon shortens"
• Separately valid horizon logic: bond-like human capital declines with age → rising bond allocation; liabilities shift long → intermediate → cash-like as they approach

cards.front: State the decomposed after-tax expected return for an asset whose return is part income and part price appreciation, and compute it for an 8% pre-tax equity return that is 2% dividend / 6% appreciation with td = 25% and tcg = 25%.
cards.back:
Symbols (Equation 2): r_at = expected after-tax return; r_pt = expected pre-tax (gross) return; p_d = proportion of r_pt from dividend income; p_a = proportion from price appreciation (p_d + p_a = 1); t_d = dividend tax rate; t_cg = capital gains tax rate. All in decimal or % consistently, per period.
• Example: 0.25 × 8% × 0.75 + 0.75 × 8% × 0.75 = 1.5% + 4.5% = 6.0%
• Collapses to r_at = r_pt(1 − t) when one rate applies — a 3% coupon IG bond at a 40% interest tax rate → 3%(1 − 0.40) = 1.80%
• Use it to build after-tax capital market inputs BEFORE optimizing; interest income is usually taxed highest and annually, so interest-driven assets are the least tax efficient
• Classic errors: applying one blended rate to both components; taxing the whole return at the capital gains rate; running the optimizer on pre-tax inputs and "adjusting for tax afterwards" (explicitly suboptimal). It is an approximation — it ignores holding-period/deferral effects on the effective capital gains rate.
cards.formula: r_at = p_d × r_pt × (1 − t_d) + p_a × r_pt × (1 − t_cg)

cards.front: How do taxes change the standard deviation and correlation inputs for a taxable investor's optimization, and what does that do to the optimal mix?
cards.back:
Symbols (Equation 3): σ_at = expected after-tax standard deviation; σ_pt = expected pre-tax standard deviation; t = expected tax rate on that asset class.
• Why: taxes truncate BOTH tails — lower highs and higher lows. The investor is not taxed on losses but receives the economic benefit of the loss (realized losses offset gains; an unrealized loss makes future appreciation partly tax free)
• Correlations need NO adjustment — taxes are proportional to return, so after-tax co-movements equal pre-tax co-movements
• Curriculum inputs (interest 40%; dividends and gains 25%): IG bonds 3.0%/4.0% → 1.8%/2.4%; HY bonds 5.0%/10.0% → 3.0%/6.0%; equity 8.0%/20.0% → 6.0%/15.0%
• Result: the mid-risk after-tax portfolios (P25/P50/P75) cut HY bonds sharply — heaviest tax burden — while IG bonds survive for risk reduction (lower risk, 0.0 correlation with equity). P1 and P100 are essentially unchanged
• Traps: adjusting correlations too; taxing returns but leaving σ pre-tax (the bond sleeve then looks too attractive AND too risky — the errors do not cancel); concluding a tax-inefficient asset must be dropped — it can still earn a place on low correlations
cards.formula: σ_at = σ_pt × (1 − t)   (correlations unchanged)

cards.front: Give the taxable investor's equivalent rebalancing range, and convert a tax-exempt 50% equity target with a ±10% corridor at a 25% tax rate.
cards.back:
Symbols (Equation 4): R_at = after-tax (taxable investor's) rebalancing range; R_pt = the pre-tax / tax-exempt rebalancing range; t = tax rate on that asset class.
• Worked: 0.10 ÷ (1 − 0.25) = 13.3% → the tax-exempt 40%–60% corridor becomes 37%–63% for the taxable investor
• Why wider: after-tax volatility is lower (σ_at = σ_pt(1 − t)) and correlations are unchanged, so it takes LARGER asset class moves to materially alter the taxable portfolio's risk profile — and rebalancing is discretionary, so its tax cost is avoidable while the risk-control benefit is unchanged
• Effect: wider ranges → less frequent trading → fewer realized gains
• Classic error: multiplying by (1 − t), which narrows the band — the taxable band is always WIDER. Second error: rebalancing a taxable sleeve to target just because the tax-exempt sleeve was rebalanced
• Companion levers: rebalance with new cash flows and income distributions; tax-loss harvesting; strategic asset location — tax-INEFFICIENT assets (taxable/HY bonds, high-turnover and high-dividend strategies) into tax-deferred/exempt accounts, tax-EFFICIENT low-turnover equity in taxable accounts; exception — bonds funding near-term consumption stay in taxable accounts
cards.formula: R_at = R_pt ÷ (1 − t)

cards.front: How often should the SAA be re-examined, and what three families of change trigger an off-schedule review? Give examples of each.
cards.back:
Cadence: institutions typically run a formal asset allocation study at least every 5 years; ALL asset owners should affirm annually that the SAA remains appropriate.
Trigger 1 — GOALS: changed business conditions of the sponsoring organization and therefore expected cash flows (e.g. a disrupted revenue stream → less pension risk-taking); a change in personal circumstances altering risk appetite or risk capacity (marriage, children, disability, early retirement).
Trigger 2 — CONSTRAINTS (horizon, liquidity, asset size, regulatory): changed expected payments (endowment spending 5% → 4%); a significant cash inflow or unanticipated expenditure (a £100M gift to a £500M endowment); regulatory change (2006 US discount-rate rules → de-risking); a horizon change from adopting a lump-sum distribution option; asset size change from merging plans.
Trigger 3 — BELIEFS: a durable shift in capital market expectations (not a cyclical view); new trustees or committee members bringing different beliefs.
• A significant inflow should prompt a study, not simply be invested in parallel with existing assets
• Exception: pre-programmed changes already in the IPS — a glide path, or funded-status milestones — can be implemented without a new study
cards.mnemonic: Goals, Constraints, Beliefs.

cards.front: Discretionary vs systematic TAA: what is each based on, what signals does each use, and what benchmark judges both?
cards.back:
Common ground: short-term deviations from SAA targets, justified by cyclical variation within a secular trend or temporary price dislocations; asset-CLASS (or sector/factor) timing, never security selection; asset-only — liabilities and goals are not expressly considered; must stay inside IPS risk constraints (allowable range around each policy target, tracking-error budget, or predicted-volatility range).
• DISCRETIONARY: qualitative interpretation of political, economic and market conditions — predicated on manager skill; typically aims at an asymmetric payoff (hedge distressed markets, participate in rising ones). Inputs: valuations (P/E, P/B, dividend yield), term and credit spreads, central bank policy, GDP/earnings/inflation expectations, leading indicators; sentiment — consumer confidence, margin borrowing, short interest, and the volatility index (VIX, VDAX-NEW, V2X).
• SYSTEMATIC: rules-based quantitative signals capturing documented, persistent anomalies. Value/carry — Shiller earnings yield, dividend and cash-flow yield; FX carry via short-term rate differentials; commodity roll yield (backwardation vs contango); bond YTM and term premiums. Momentum/trend — trailing 12-month return, moving-average crossover.
• Benchmark for BOTH: the SAA policy portfolio. Evaluate by (1) TAA Sharpe ratio vs SAA Sharpe ratio, (2) information ratio or t-statistic of average excess return, (3) plotting realized TAA return/risk against the SAA efficient frontier — plus attribution of the over/underweights. Costs to clear: trading costs, taxes, and greater concentration of risk contributions.

cards.front: Name the six behavioral biases the curriculum flags as most relevant to asset allocation, the allocation behavior each produces, and the prescribed remedy.
cards.back:
• Loss aversion (emotional): risk judged against 0%, not the mean; can't hold the allocation through drawdowns; institutional herding to minimize reputation risk. Fix: frame risk as SHORTFALL PROBABILITY; fund high-priority goals with low-risk assets of similar duration, freeing other assets to take risk.
• Illusion of control (cognitive, amplified by overconfidence and hindsight): extreme TAA and all-in/all-out calls, excessive trading, leverage/shorting, retaining concentrated legacy stock, "extreme corner portfolios." Fix: start from the GLOBAL MARKET PORTFOLIO; formal process with long-term forecasts, constraints anchored on GMP weights, strict policy ranges; vet every deviation.
• Mental accounting: accounts treated in isolation (retirement vs education; ignoring vested options); with a concentrated legacy stock it is FURTHER REINFORCED by the endowment effect — ascribing more value to an asset already owned than to one bought to replace it. Fix: use the bias CONSTRUCTIVELY via goals-based investing — sub-portfolios on the same efficient frontier sum to an efficient whole; assign the concentrated stock to an aspirational goal (lower probability of success accepted; may also avoid capital gains tax if gifted).
• Representativeness/recency: return chasing; shifting toward the top of policy ranges after good performance. Fix: objective process, pre-specified allowable ranges, strong governance, long-term CME.
• Framing: the same risk answered differently depending on presentation; the first authoritative speaker anchors a committee. Fix: present multiple risk views — σ plus shortfall probability, VaR and CVaR, historical stress tests, Monte Carlo.
• Availability/familiarity: vivid recent events overweighted; HOME BIAS. Fix: GMP as the neutral anchor; stop comparing allocations and returns with peers.
• General antidote: acknowledging a bias exists already reduces its influence; formal process, governance and controls do the rest.

cards.front: What four roles do equities play in an overall portfolio, and what is the curriculum's stated limitation on the inflation-hedge role?
cards.back:
• Capital appreciation — the dominant driver of long-term equity return; 1900-2022 equities beat both bonds and bills in every region studied. Outperform in strong economic growth, underperform in weak periods.
• Dividend income — the most common income source; includes regular, special, and optional stock dividends plus preferred dividends. S&P 500 dividend yield has run 1%-3% since 1990, so dividends dominate total return in weak-price decades.
• Diversification with other asset classes — requires less-than-perfect correlation. Equity indexes correlate highly with each other but much less with Treasuries, IG bonds, and gold. Caveat: correlations are not constant and rise in crises, cutting the benefit exactly when needed.
• Hedge against inflation — firms that pass input costs to customers, and commodity producers, gain. But efficacy is mixed: positive correlation with inflation over the long run, yet in severe inflation (annual rate over 5%) real equity returns and inflation have been NEGATIVELY correlated — the hedge fails when most needed.
Equity inclusion and weight are driven by the IPS: risk objective, return objective, liquidity, time horizon, taxes, legal/regulatory, unique circumstances (including ESG).
cards.mnemonic: Roles = Growth, Income, Diversification, (weak) Inflation hedge — G-I-D-I

cards.front: Name the three ways an equity manager's investment universe is commonly segmented, and state the key drawback of each.
cards.back:
• Size and style (one combined approach) — size by market cap (large/mid/small); style value, growth, or blend/core, usually from a scored composite of P/B, P/E, earnings growth, dividend yield, and book value growth. Benefits: builds desired risk/return/income profile, diversifies across sectors, supports segment benchmarks, tracks a company's life-cycle drift (small-cap growth after IPO to large-cap value). Drawback: categories change over time and are defined differently by different investors/providers — guidelines, not a strict taxonomy.
• Geography — developed, emerging, frontier (MSCI uses economic development, size and liquidity, and accessibility criteria). Drawback: a country index may give lower-than-expected exposure to that economy (Nestlé, Roche, and Novartis are over half of MSCI Switzerland, yet Switzerland is under 2% of each company's sales), plus currency risk.
• Economic activity (sector/industry) — GICS (11 sectors, 24 industry groups, 68 industries, 157 sub-industries), ICB, TRBC, RGS. Drawback: large companies' business activities span more than one industry or sub-industry.
Indexes routinely combine the cuts (e.g., MSCI Europe Large Cap Growth).

cards.front: Explicit vs implicit trading costs in an equity portfolio: which items fall in each bucket, what drives the total, and which is actually disclosed to the investor?
cards.back:
• Explicit (observable, billed): brokerage commissions, taxes and stamp duties, stock exchange fees, and modest regulatory fees in many countries.
• Implicit (estimated, embedded in execution): bid-offer spread; market impact (price impact) — the effect of the trade itself on transaction prices; delay costs (slippage) — inability to complete trades immediately because of order size or lack of liquidity.
• Total trading cost is a function of three things: size of trades, frequency of trading, and the degree to which trades demand liquidity from the market.
• Disclosure trap: unlike management fees, total trading cost is generally NOT revealed to the investor — it is absorbed into the portfolio's reported total return.
• Strategy link: momentum strategies demand liquidity (buy what is rising) and cost more; deep value strategies tend to provide liquidity. Index funds trade less but bear a hidden predatory-trading cost when others front-run index additions/deletions. Borrowing stock also costs a lending fee.
Other cost lines: management fees (ad valorem), performance fees, administration (custody, depository, registration), and marketing/distribution (platform fees, sales commissions).
cards.mnemonic: Explicit = you get a bill; implicit = you get a worse price

cards.front: Walk through a stock-lending transaction: what the lender earns, what protects it, and what it gives up.
cards.back:
• Structure: a collateralized loan of shares, technically an assignment of title with a repurchase option. Collateral is cash or other high-quality securities. Loans are usually open-ended, but the borrower must return the shares on demand. Lending facilitates short sales.
• Income 1 — the lending fee: developed markets roughly 0.2%-0.5% annualized; emerging markets often 1%-2% for large caps; "specials" (high borrow demand) typically 5%-15%, and in extreme demand 25%-100% — but such fees do not persist long.
• Income 2 — reinvestment of cash collateral (favorable rates). The collateral is still exposed to market, credit, liquidity, and operational risk, and the program's administrative costs reduce this income.
• Dividends are "manufactured": the borrower compensates the lender for dividends it would have received.
• What is given up: voting rights transfer to the borrower. Recalling shares to vote a resolution forfeits lending revenue and risks reputation as a reliable lender. Borrowing shares purely to vote, with no capital at risk, is empty voting.
• Who lends: index funds are frequent lenders (large, long-term holdings and no concern that shorting depresses prices); large pensions/endowments also lend but care more about price effects — evidence on lending's price impact is mixed.

cards.front: Why is shareholder engagement "particularly relevant" for active managers but deprioritized by index-based managers, and what is the free-rider problem?
cards.back:
• Benefits to the company: a more effective corporate governance culture, which in turn can lead to better company performance for shareholders and other stakeholders.
• Benefit to the investor: more information about the company or its sector — strategy, culture, and the competitive environment within the industry. That information feeds ACTIVE decisions, so engagement is particularly relevant for active portfolio managers.
• Index-based managers are focused on tracking the benchmark while minimizing cost; any process that consumes management time and adds cost detracts from that primary goal. Less of an issue for VERY LARGE index portfolios, where engagement costs are spread over a sizable asset base.
• Free rider: a non-engaging holder of the same stock captures the price improvement won by another investor's costly engagement without bearing any of the cost.
• Engagement topics: strategy, allocation of capital, corporate governance and regulatory/political risk, remuneration, board composition.
• Disadvantages: time-consuming and costly; pressure to hit near-term share price or earnings targets at the expense of long-term decisions; selective disclosure that can create a material non-public information/insider-trading breach; conflicts of interest (e.g., a manager reluctant to oppose management at a company that is also a client).

cards.front: List the considerations that determine where an equity portfolio is positioned along the active-management spectrum.
cards.back:
Index-based vs active is a spectrum, not an either/or. Considerations:
• Confidence to outperform — needs understanding of the investment universe, competitive analysis of rival managers in it, and resources (research staff, information access).
• Client preference — will the strategy attract enough assets, and does the client believe alpha exists? In widely covered segments (large-cap developed) information is efficiently reflected, so perceived alpha is small.
• Suitable benchmark — active mandates need benchmarks with sufficient liquidity in the underlying securities (reasonable trading cost) and enough securities to generate alpha; this is why many single-country or single-sector strategies are index based.
• Client-specific mandates — ESG/exclusionary screens require ongoing monitoring of direct and indirect involvement, so they are typically managed actively (though index-based ESG vehicles are growing).
• Risks/costs of active management — more expensive to implement, plus "key person" (star manager) risk.
• Taxes — index-based strategies have lower turnover and a higher proportion of long-term gains.
Also know: a "closet index" is advertised as active but is essentially an index fund; the fee differential is the most significant and enduring advantage of index-based management.

cards.front: State the constituent weight in an equally weighted index, and give the traits and hidden costs that follow from it.
cards.back:
• w_i = weight of constituent i; n = number of stocks in the index; weights are set to 1/n at each rebalance date (pure numbers summing to 1.0).
• Produces the LEAST concentrated portfolio: its HHI equals 1/n, so the effective number of stocks equals n.
• Considered naive/factor-indifferent — it shows no preference for any stock and randomizes factor mispricing (Zeng and Luo).
• Imparts a small-cap bias, and therefore HIGHER volatility than cap weighting. Deviation from market weights is most dramatic for large-cap indexes containing mega-caps; constrained ranges such as mid-cap indexes already have fairly uniform weights.
• Requires regular rebalancing — weights stop being equal as soon as trading resumes. The S&P 500 equal weight rebalances quarterly, so over a 91-day quarter the index is not equally weighted 90/91 = 99% of the time.
• Limited capacity from illiquid small constituents: estimated capacity S&P 100 EW USD176bn, S&P 500 EW USD82bn, S&P 400 EW USD8bn, S&P 600 EW USD2bn.
• Qin and Singal: the mispricing advantage over cap weighting largely vanishes once taxes and transaction costs are counted; tax-exempt investors may still benefit.
Classic error: calling equal weighting "lower risk because it is diversified" — it raises volatility, turnover, and cost.
cards.formula: w_i = 1/n

cards.front: Give the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index for a portfolio or index, its range, and how to read it.
cards.back:
• w_i = the weight of stock i in the portfolio, expressed as a decimal; sum over all n holdings, so the weights must total 1.0. HHI is a pure number (no units).
• Range: 1/n at the low end (an equally weighted portfolio) up to 1.0 (everything in a single security). Higher HHI = greater stock-concentration risk / less diversification.
• Use: assess how concentrated a candidate benchmark or portfolio is before adopting it — a valid measure of stock-concentration risk (Woerheide and Persson; used by practitioners per Hannam and Jamet).
• Classic errors: squaring the SUM of the weights instead of summing the SQUARES; entering weights as percentages (8.9) rather than decimals (0.089), which inflates the result by 10,000.
cards.formula: HHI = Σ(i=1 to n) w_i²

cards.front: How do you convert an index's concentration into an "effective number of stocks," and what does the answer mean?
cards.back:
• Effective number of stocks = the reciprocal of the HHI, where w_i is stock i's decimal weight.
• Meaning: the number of EQUALLY WEIGHTED stocks that would mimic the concentration level of the index. It is always less than or equal to the actual number of constituents, and equals n only for an equally weighted portfolio.
• Worked curriculum example: a 50-stock cap-weighted index with squared weights summing to 0.03889 gives 1 ÷ 0.03889 = 25.71, so roughly 26 effective stocks, not 50.
• Cap-weighted indexes have surprisingly low effective numbers (Malevergne, Santa-Clara, and Sornette): for the NASDAQ 100 in May 2017 the squared weights summed to 0.0404, so 1 ÷ 0.0404 = 24.75 — 100 stocks concentrated like about 25. Top five weights were about 38% of the index; largest-to-smallest weight ratio was 77:1.
• Classic errors: quoting the HHI itself as the effective number, and assuming a large constituent count means a diversified benchmark.
cards.formula: Effective number of stocks = 1 ÷ HHI = 1 ÷ Σ w_i²

cards.front: A candidate accepts a famous index as the basis for an index-based strategy because it is widely quoted. What three requirements must an index meet first, and which well-known indexes fail?
cards.back:
An index must be RULES BASED, TRANSPARENT, and INVESTABLE.
• Rules based — objective, consistent, predictable rules for constituent inclusion and for how often weights are rebalanced (unlike an active manager's process, which others cannot replicate).
• Transparent — arguably the most important: the provider discloses rules and constituents with no black-box methodology, assuring investors the index will keep representing the intended strategy.
• Investable — performance can actually be replicated in the market. The FTSE 100 qualifies; hedge fund-of-funds indexes (the HFRI series) do not, because the constituent funds cannot be bought; the Value Line Geometric Index does not, because it is a multiplicative average of prices that cannot be replicated.
• Security-level investability screens: free-float adjustment (exclude shares held by founders, governments, affiliates) and minimum float/average-volume thresholds — low-float or thinly traded stocks move disproportionately when traded.
• The trap: visibility is not suitability. Benchmark choice starts from the IPS-driven desired factor exposures (geography, size, style, other risk factors), then construction method, weighting scheme, and rebalancing/reconstitution policy.
Related: buffering (ranges around size breakpoints) and packeting (moving a position in parts) limit migration turnover; transparent reconstitution invites front-running but Petajisto concluded transparency is still a virtue.

cards.front: Name the three roles fixed-income securities play in a portfolio, and the two broad categories of fixed-income mandates with the approaches that sit under each.
cards.back:
Roles:
• Diversification — generally low or negative correlation with equities and with real estate/commodities
• Regular cash flows — fund known future obligations; bonds can be "dedicated" to a liability stream
• Inflation hedging — floating-rate coupons (interest income only; principal unadjusted) and inflation-linked bonds (coupon and principal linked to a consumer price index)

Mandates:
• Liability based (ALM / LDI) — cash flow matching, duration matching, derivatives overlay, contingent immunization (immunization plus active management while assets exceed the PV of liabilities)
• Total return (vs a market-weighted index such as the Global Aggregate) — pure indexing, enhanced indexing, active management

Both types share the goal of the highest risk-adjusted return under constraints; the objectives differ (cover liabilities vs beat/track an index).
cards.mnemonic: Roles = D-R-I (Diversify, Regular cash flow, Inflation). Mandates = Liabilities or Index.

cards.front: Pure indexing vs enhanced indexing vs active management: target outperformance, active risk, duration match, and turnover for each — and which single statistic best identifies an active fund?
cards.back:
Pure indexing (full replication)
• Target active return and active risk both zero; aims to match risk factors exactly
• Turnover similar to the benchmark
• In practice the realized return is almost always BELOW the index because of trading costs and fees

Enhanced indexing
• Modest outperformance, generally 20–30 bps; active risk kept low, typically around 50 bps or lower
• Small deviations in holdings; primary risk factors — especially duration — closely matched; minor sector/quality bets allowed
• Turnover slightly higher than the benchmark

Active management
• Higher outperformance, generally around 50 bps or more, with higher active risk
• Large risk-factor deviations, most notably portfolio duration; turnover considerably higher; higher fees

The tell: a sizeable MODIFIED DURATION mismatch versus the index is the strongest single evidence of active management (e.g., 6.16 vs an index 5.22).
cards.mnemonic: 20–30 bps / 50 bps tracking = enhanced; 50+ bps and a duration bet = active.

cards.front: Match the measure to the job: which fixed-income risk statistic do you use for (i) cash flows contingent on interest rates, (ii) curve reshaping, (iii) credit spread moves, (iv) spread moves that are proportional rather than equal in basis points, (v) expressing price sensitivity as a money amount per basis point — and how is a portfolio's duration computed?
cards.back:
(i) Effective duration and effective convexity — bonds with embedded options, MBS, and any liability with uncertain amount/timing. EffDur = (PV− − PV+) ÷ [2 × ΔCurve × PV0]
(ii) Key rate (partial) durations — sensitivity at a specific maturity point; captures "shaping risk" (steepening, flattening, curvature)
(iii) Spread duration — approximate % price rise (fall) for a 1% decrease (increase) in credit spread
(iv) Duration times spread (DTS) = spread duration × current credit spread — spreads move proportionally, not in equal bp
(v) Money duration (dollar duration) and PVBP/DV01 — money gained or lost per 1 bp; BPV = money duration × 0.0001

Portfolio statistics are MARKET-VALUE weighted: AvgModDur = Σ ModDur_j × (MV_j ÷ MV); same weighting for convexity, spread duration and DTS.
Dispersion = weighted VARIANCE of the times to receipt of cash flows around the duration; higher dispersion means HIGHER convexity.
Macaulay duration is the weighted average time to receipt; modified duration = MacDur ÷ (1 + yield per period).
cards.mnemonic: Options → effective; curve twists → key rate; credit → spread duration/DTS; hedging money → PVBP.

cards.front: Describe the correlation characteristics of fixed income: versus equities by credit quality, between rates and spreads, across markets, and what a flight to quality does to those correlations.
cards.back:
• High-quality government and investment-grade bonds in developed markets move mostly with sovereign rate changes. Over the 20 years to December 2019 versus the S&P 500: 10-year US Treasury −0.30, US Aggregate −0.09, US TIPS 0.02, Global Aggregate 0.15, US Corporate 0.20.
• Below-investment-grade bonds are driven more by spread than by the general level of rates and correlate far more with equities: US High Yield 0.63, EM (USD) 0.51 — both asset classes are linked to issuer fundamentals.
• Rates and spreads are often NEGATIVELY correlated: as the economy weakens, rates fall while spreads widen; the reverse when it improves.
• Correlations between sectors WITHIN a market exceed those ACROSS markets (country-specific policy, growth, inflation); global government correlations are also driven by exchange rates. Excess-return correlations isolate the credit component from the rate component.
• Flight to quality: investors buy government bonds and sell equities and high yield, so government-vs-equity and government-vs-high-yield correlations FALL while equity-vs-high-yield correlations RISE.
• Correlations and volatilities are not constant — a long-run average need not hold in any given period.
cards.mnemonic: Rates drive the safe stuff, spreads drive the risky stuff — and spreads act like equity.

cards.front: Rank bond market sub-sectors and issues from most to least liquid, and state what the illiquid holder earns plus two ways liquidity shapes portfolio management.
cards.back:
Ranking (most to least liquid)
• On-the-run sovereign of a high-credit-quality government (large issue size, benchmark status, accepted repo collateral)
• Off-the-run sovereign of that same government — less liquid even if issued only one or two months earlier, because dealer inventory has moved to buy-and-hold investors
• High-credit-quality corporate
• Low-credit-quality corporate
Structured/securitized issues (e.g., asset-backed securities) and bonds with non-standard or complex features such as embedded options also sit at the illiquid end: bid–ask spreads on government bonds are generally lower than on corporate bonds or structured financial instruments, and plain vanilla corporates have lower spreads than complex ones.

More liquid issue = larger issue size, larger total issuance outstanding, recently issued, higher credit quality, shorter maturity, plain vanilla structure, frequent issuer.

Illiquidity is paid for with a LIQUIDITY PREMIUM — incremental yield to maturity compensating search costs and the bid–ask spread.

Effects on management:
• Pricing — many bonds trade rarely, so last traded prices are stale; use matrix pricing off liquid benchmark yields and spreads of comparable maturity, quality and sector
• Construction — the yield/liquidity trade-off: buy-and-hold investors harvest the premium in less liquid bonds; investors anticipating cash needs give up yield for liquidity. Wide spreads make active trading costly: a 10 bp bid–ask on a 15-duration bond costs about 1.50% (0.0010 × 15 × 100), so managers use mutual funds, ETFs, futures, and total return swaps instead of the cash bond.
cards.mnemonic: Big, new, safe, simple = liquid.

cards.front: Write the expected-return decomposition for a bond position and define every component, including how each view term is computed.
cards.back:
• Coupon income = Annual coupon payment ÷ Current bond price, plus reinvestment income; with no reinvestment it is the current yield
• Rolldown return = (Price at end of horizon − Price at start) ÷ Price at start, revaluing the bond on an UNCHANGED yield curve with zero rate volatility (pull to par)
• Rolling yield = coupon income + rolldown return
• Benchmark yield view = (−ModDur × ΔYield) + [½ × Convexity × (ΔYield)²]
• Spread view = (−ModSpreadDur × ΔSpread) + [½ × Convexity × (ΔSpread)²]; a narrowing spread is a negative ΔSpread and adds return
• Currency view applies only to bonds not in the home currency: R_DC = (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX) − 1

Units: enter Δ in decimals (0.26% = 0.0026); components are annualized percentages that are simply summed.
Use it whenever a strategy must be judged on expected return rather than yield to maturity.
Classic errors: quoting YTM as the expected return; using ModDur/convexity for a bond with embedded options (effective duration and effective convexity are required); double-counting the expected curve move inside rolldown; watch the vendor's convexity scaling.
It is only an approximation — it ignores taxes, assumes reinvestment at the YTM, and omits local richness/cheapness and repo financing advantages.
cards.formula: E(R) ≈ Coupon income + Rolldown return ± E(ΔPrice from benchmark yield view) ± E(ΔPrice from yield spread view) ± E(ΔPrice from currency view)
cards.mnemonic: Rolling yield, then your three views (rates, spread, FX).

cards.front: A fund's bonds average a price of $117.00 today and an expected $114.00 in one year on an UNCHANGED curve, with an average annual coupon of $3.63. Its rolling yield is only 0.54% — what mistake does that number catch?
cards.back:
Coupon income = $3.63 ÷ $117.00 = 3.10%
Rolldown = ($114.00 − $117.00) ÷ $117.00 = −2.56%  (NEGATIVE)
Rolling yield = 3.10% − 2.56% = 0.54%

The trap: assuming rolldown return is always positive.
• Bonds trading at a PREMIUM are pulled to par and so realize capital losses over their remaining life; bonds at a DISCOUNT realize capital gains.
• Rolldown is measured on an unchanged curve — any expected change in yields or spreads belongs in the separate view terms, never in rolldown.
• A high coupon does not mean a high expected return; yield to maturity alone is an incomplete measure of expected return.
cards.mnemonic: High price, high coupon, negative roll.

cards.front: Write the levered portfolio return decomposition, define every term, and state when leverage subtracts from return.
cards.back:
• r_P = return on the levered portfolio (return per unit of EQUITY)
• r_I = return on invested funds, earned on total assets V_E + V_B
• V_E = value of the portfolio's equity; V_B = borrowed funds; V_B ÷ V_E = leverage ratio
• r_B = borrowing rate (cost of borrowing)
Equivalent long form: r_P = [r_I × (V_E + V_B) − (V_B × r_B)] ÷ V_E

If r_I > r_B the second term is positive and leverage adds return; if r_I < r_B it is negative and leverage REDUCES return. The size of the effect is proportional to V_B ÷ V_E and to the spread r_I − r_B, in both directions.
Worked: r_I = 6.20%, r_B = 2.80%, V_B = $42.00 million, V_E = $94.33 million → 6.20% + (42.00 ÷ 94.33) × (6.20% − 2.80%) = 7.71%.
Classic errors: dividing by total assets instead of equity, and using V_B ÷ (V_E + V_B) as the leverage ratio.
cards.formula: r_P = r_I + (V_B ÷ V_E) × (r_I − r_B)
cards.mnemonic: Asset return plus leverage times the spread over funding.

cards.front: How is the leverage embedded in a futures position measured, and what capital does each of the other leverage tools actually require?
cards.back:
• Notional value = current value of the underlying × the multiplier (quantity of the underlying controlled by one contract)
• Margin = the deposit required to control that notional amount
The ratio measures exposure obtained IN EXCESS of the cash posted. Classic error: computing Notional ÷ Margin, which overstates the leverage by exactly 1×.

Capital required by the other methods:
• Swaps — only the collateral required by the counterparties or the clearinghouse; an interest rate swap is economically a long–short bond portfolio (the fixed-rate receiver is long a fixed-rate bond and short a floater)
• Repurchase agreements — the haircut. Dollar interest = Principal amount × Repo rate × (Term in days ÷ 360); the dealer repurchases at that higher price. Haircuts run about 1%–3% for high-quality government bonds and more for volatile collateral; the haircut protects the lender AND caps the borrower's net leverage capacity
• Securities lending — collateral of cash or highly rated bonds, often about 102% of the loaned securities' value; Rebate rate = Collateral earnings rate − Security lending rate (negative when the security is hard to borrow)
cards.formula: Leverage_Futures = (Notional value − Margin) ÷ Margin
cards.mnemonic: Subtract the margin before you divide by it.

cards.front: List the methods available for leveraging a fixed-income portfolio and the specific risks that leverage creates (beyond "bigger losses").
cards.back:
Methods
• Futures contracts — large exposure for a modest margin deposit
• Swap agreements — interest rate and total return swaps; only collateral is posted, increasingly through central clearinghouses
• Repurchase agreements — effectively collateralized loans; bilateral (usually security-driven) or tri-party (usually cash-driven against general collateral); overnight repos are commonly rolled to create longer funding
• Securities lending — collateralized lending, chiefly to facilitate short sales but also for financing; open-ended and recallable by either side, unlike a repo with a fixed term
• Structured financial instruments — an implicit form of leverage

Risks
• Magnified losses — a heavily levered portfolio can suffer significant losses on only moderate declines in asset values
• Forced liquidation — falling portfolio value shrinks equity and RAISES leverage; assets must be sold to pay down borrowing, potentially as "fire sales" below fair value, and declining prices, deleveraging and forced selling can spiral into further price declines and lost market liquidity
• Financing/rollover and counterparty risk — in a crisis, counterparties to credit lines, repos and securities lending agreements reassess counterparty risk and withdraw financing, forcing investors to cut exposure at exactly the worst time, when prices are depressed
cards.mnemonic: Futures, Swaps, Repo, Sec-lending, Structured — and the risks are magnify, forced sale, funding pulled.

cards.front: An analyst claims taxable investors should always sell overvalued bonds before fairly valued ones, and should never intentionally realize capital losses. What is wrong, and what is the correct rule for taxable versus tax-exempt portfolios?
cards.back:
Both statements are wrong.
• Taxable: defer realizing GAINS (deferral raises the present value of the investment) and realize LOSSES early — tax-loss harvesting. Losses offset current or future capital gains (carried forward, in some countries carried back) but generally cannot offset other income. So the manager may liquidate a slightly UNDERVALUED position carrying an embedded capital loss instead of the overvalued one carrying a gain, because the realized loss reduces the net gain distributed to clients.
• Tax-exempt (pension, foundation, endowment): taxation of gains and losses is irrelevant; sell the OVERVALUED bond — investment views alone drive the trade. The objective is simply the highest risk-adjusted return net of fees and transaction costs.

Other rules for taxable portfolios: coupon interest is taxed at ordinary income rates while capital gains are often taxed at a lower effective rate, and short-term gains are frequently taxed higher than long-term, so be judicious about realizing short-term gains; control turnover, since lower turnover defers gains longer; weigh income against capital gains.
Vehicle matters: with pass-through treatment (US mutual funds) realized fund gains are taxed to investors in the year they arise; without it (UK) gains raise NAV and are taxed only when shares are sold; in a separately managed account the investor is taxed on gains as the manager realizes them.
cards.mnemonic: Defer gains, harvest losses — unless the client pays no tax at all.

cards.front: In LDI, how are liabilities classified by certainty of amount and timing? Give the four types with an example of each and the duration measure each requires — and state the difference between LDI and ADL.
cards.back:
• Type I — amount KNOWN, timing KNOWN: traditional fixed-rate bond with no embedded options; fixed-rate government bond. Macaulay, modified and money duration and PVBP all apply.
• Type II — amount known, timing UNCERTAIN: callable and putable bonds; a term life insurance policy (timing of death); demand and time deposits redeemable early.
• Type III — amount UNCERTAIN, timing known: floating-rate note (payments depend on future rates); inflation-protected securities.
• Type IV — amount and timing BOTH uncertain: property and casualty insurance, defined benefit pension liabilities, contingent convertible bonds, prepayable residential mortgages.

Types II, III and IV require EFFECTIVE duration: start from an assumption about the yield curve, model the uncertain cash flows, then shift the curve up and down by the same amount to revalue the liability.

LDI vs ADL (both are special cases of ALM): under LDI — much the more common — the LIABILITIES are given and the assets are managed (life insurer, DB pension). Under ADL the ASSETS are given and the liability structure is chosen to reduce interest rate risk (a leasing company with short-term contracts funding itself with short-term debt).
cards.mnemonic: I = both known; II = timing unknown; III = amount unknown; IV = neither. Anything but Type I needs effective duration.

cards.front: How is a cash flow matching portfolio constructed, what constraint governs it, and what is its main weakness?
cards.back:
Construction
• Buy a DEDICATED (held-to-maturity) portfolio of high-quality zero-coupon or fixed-income bonds whose coupon and principal inflows match the amount and timing of each scheduled liability outflow.
• Work BACKWARD: fund the final liability first with a bond maturing on or just before that date; the coupons that bond pays in earlier years then reduce every earlier liability; step back one liability at a time to the nearest one, sizing each bond's par value net of the coupons already received from longer bonds. Round up to the minimum denomination and let small surpluses carry forward.

Governing constraint
• The cash-in-advance constraint: securities are NOT sold to meet obligations — sufficient funds must be available on or before each liability payment date.

Why do it rather than simply retire the debt
• Buying back the bonds is difficult and costly when they are held by buy-and-hold investors and are illiquid, so open-market purchases drive up the price; dedicating assets achieves the same economics, can improve the credit rating, and may permit accounting (in-substance) defeasance, removing both the dedicated assets and the debt from the balance sheet.

Weakness
• Traditional bonds pay fixed coupons and redeem principal at maturity, which mismatches a level-payment annuity liability stream: large cash balances accumulate between payment dates, creating cash flow REINVESTMENT risk — most painful when short-term high-quality yields are low or negative.
cards.mnemonic: Build the ladder of liabilities from the back to the front; never sell to pay.

cards.front: For equal-duration bullet, ladder and barbell portfolios, which equation drives the convexity ranking, what is that ranking, and what else does a ladder buy or cost the investor?
cards.back:
• MacDur = portfolio Macaulay duration; Dispersion = weighted variance of the times to receipt of cash flows around the duration; cash flow yield = internal rate of return on the portfolio's aggregate cash flows.
• Holding duration and cash flow yield equal, convexity rises with DISPERSION, so the ranking is barbell (highest) > ladder > bullet (lowest). Classic error: naming the ladder the most convex structure — it is only relatively high, and the barbell wins.

Ladder construction: bond maturities and par values spread EVENLY along the yield curve (a bullet concentrates at one point; a barbell sits at the short and long ends). Each can share the same duration and roughly the same response to a parallel shift — it is twists and non-parallel shifts that separate them.

Benefits
• Diversification across the curve, so protection from shifts and twists
• Balances the two sources of interest rate risk — cash flow reinvestment risk against market price risk; maturing bonds are reinvested at the long end, typically at higher rates, which also maintains portfolio duration (like dollar cost averaging across rate environments)
• High convexity with far less cash flow reinvestment risk than a barbell
• Liquidity management, the most prized feature in practice: there is always a soon-to-mature, low-duration bond whose price is stable and which is high-quality collateral for a personal loan or a repo

Limitations
• Less diversification of default risk and a much higher cost of acquisition than a bond mutual fund, which can also be liquidated faster and at a better price. Fixed-maturity corporate bond ETFs are an alternative way to build the rungs.
cards.formula: Immunized Portfolio Convexity = (MacDur² + MacDur + Dispersion) ÷ (1 + Cash flow yield)²
cards.mnemonic: Spread the cash flows, gain the convexity: barbell > ladder > bullet.

cards.front: In the asset allocation framework, what four functional roles can an asset class play, and which alternatives are perceived to fill each?
cards.back:
• Capital growth — public and private equity; top priority for long-horizon, high-return-target portfolios
• Income generation — fixed income and real estate (steady cash flow); private credit/direct lending
• Risk diversification — for an equity-dominated portfolio, real assets and several hedge fund strategies diversify the dominant equity risk; for fixed-income investors, private credit diversifies pure yield-curve risk
• Safety — safe haven when risky assets suffer: government bonds, gold
Exhibit 3 detail: private real assets (timber) rate high (H) for growth, income AND diversification; both public and private real estate are rated M/H/M — moderate growth, high income, moderate diversification. Separately, within real estate, core strategies (fully occupied properties collecting rents) are income-oriented while opportunistic strategies (ground-up development, distressed rehabilitation) rely on capital appreciation.
Trap: a named allocation must actually deliver its assigned role — long-biased strategies are relabelled equity risk, not diversification.
cards.mnemonic: GIDS: Growth, Income, Diversification, Safety

cards.front: Where do the main hedge fund styles sit on the risk-reducing vs return-enhancing spectrum, and what global equity betas did they exhibit over 1997-2017?
cards.back:
• Long/short ("equity hedged") — equity-like returns with less than full exposure to the equity premium, plus alpha from shorting individual stocks; beta about 0.5
• Short-biased — lowers the portfolio's overall equity beta while producing some alpha; but upside is capped and downside unlimited (mirror image of long-only)
• Arbitrage and event-driven — exploit small public-market inefficiencies with low to no correlation to traditional assets; carry "short volatility" risk, so reported volatility looks muted unless the sample includes a stress period
• Opportunistic (global macro, managed futures) — very volatile standalone but give exposures unavailable in stocks/bonds; macro and equity market-neutral betas as low as 0.1
• Hedge funds in aggregate: beta about 0.4
• Private equity is the return enhancer (illiquidity premium), NOT a diversifier — its global equity beta is similar to public equity, and reported PE volatility is understated because holdings are not traded (proxy it: microcap tech for early-stage VC; a large-cap index adjusted for leverage for buyout).

cards.front: Bonds vs alternatives as mitigators of a long equity position: which wins over a short horizon and which over a long horizon, and with what numbers?
cards.back:
• Short horizon, risk = volatility -> BONDS win. Equities volatility about 17%; of all 70% equity/30% other blends the lowest volatility is 11.1% with government bonds, driven by their −0.6 correlation with equities (30% cash gives 11.9% = 0.70 × 17%)
• Long horizon, risk = failing the return target -> ALTERNATIVES win. 70/30 government bonds expects 5.7% vs a 7.1% nominal target (under 50% chance); 70/30 private equity expects 7.2% (just over 50%); hedge funds sit between
• Why the gap widens: return accumulates proportionally with time, volatility scales with the square root of time, so a low-returning portfolio cannot catch up
• Bond caveat: the negative equity-bond correlation is regime-dependent — it was POSITIVE in the 1970s-1990s when inflation was high, so bonds' hedge erodes if inflation returns; also low yields mean low expected return
• Alternatives caveat: hedge funds are levered, highly actively managed, and individual funds can suffer significant PERMANENT losses in turbulent times; drawdowns still need managing.

cards.front: An endowment must earn a 5% real return with 2% expected inflation. What nominal return must the asset allocation deliver, and how is it computed?
cards.back:
Symbols: real return target = spending rate plus any real principal growth (e.g. 4% spend + 1% growth); inflation = expected rate; result is a geometric (compound) annual nominal return.
• Compute: 1.05 × 1.02 − 1 = 7.1%
• Use it to convert a real spending/purchasing-power objective into the nominal hurdle each candidate allocation's MEDIAN (50th percentile) expected return must clear
• Classic errors: (1) adding 5% + 2% = 7.0% instead of compounding; (2) comparing the hurdle to an arithmetic mean — portfolio expected geometric return is approximately arithmetic return minus half the variance, and is NOT the weighted average of the asset classes' geometric returns, because portfolio variance benefits from diversification.
cards.formula: Nominal return target = (1 + real return target) × (1 + expected inflation) − 1

cards.front: Contrast the traditional (asset-class) and risk-based (factor) approaches to defining the opportunity set: two strengths and the key limitations of each.
cards.back:
Traditional — strengths:
• Easy to communicate; intuitive to decision makers; supports macro scenario analysis
• Relevant for liquidity management and operations — public and private mandates have vastly different liquidity profiles, and manager mandates are hired by asset class
Traditional — limitations:
• Over-estimates diversification (a false sense of it: many classes, same underlying risks)
• Obscures the primary drivers of risk (government and high-yield bonds both sit in "fixed income")
Risk-based — benefits:
• Identifies common risk factors across every holding, public or private, passive or active
• Supports an integrated risk framework and more reliable portfolio-level risk quantification
Risk-based — limitations:
• Factor sensitivities are sensitive to the look-back period (commodities' inflation beta is unstable; a bond portfolio's duration is stable)
• Implementation hurdles converting factor targets into mandates (liquidity planning, manager selection, rebalancing)
• Subjectivity — which factors, and how measured (Pastor-Stambaugh liquidity or something else?)

cards.front: Name the eight risk factors used to extend the risk-based (factor) asset allocation framework to alternatives, and what does the R-squared evidence say about describing alternatives with them?
cards.back:
• Equity market return (the proxy for "growth"); Size (small minus large); Value (value minus growth; negative loading = growth bias); Liquidity (Pastor-Stambaugh); Nominal duration (sensitivity to 10-year government yield changes); Inflation (sensitivity to 10-year breakeven inflation); Credit spread (sensitivity to high-yield spread changes); Currency (domestic vs a basket)
• Fit: traditional public asset classes R-squared 0.8-1.0; ALTERNATIVES only 0.3-0.7 — a large unexplained residual from appraisal-based valuation, portfolio-company idiosyncratic risk, and hedge fund active management/alpha
• More factors improves fit but becomes unwieldy; Level III Hedge Fund Strategies uses just four (equity, credit, currency, volatility), all realizable through liquid instruments
• Sign convention: duration and credit-spread sensitivities are sign-flipped — broad fixed income's 4.2 means about a 4.2% decline per 100 bp rise in nominal rates
• Payoff: two portfolios with identical asset-class weights can have radically different factor risk (Portfolio A's total risk is almost entirely explained by the equity factor, while about 70% of Portfolio B's comes from the equity factor).

cards.front: Beyond risk, return and correlation, what seven practical considerations must be settled before committing to an allocation to an alternative asset class?
cards.back:
• Properly defining risk characteristics
• Establishing return expectations
• Selecting the appropriate investment vehicle
• Operational liquidity issues
• Expense and fee considerations
• Tax considerations (taxable entities)
• Build vs. buy
Key supporting points:
• Risk: MVO's standard deviation is a poor descriptor of illiquid, subjectively valued, "chunky", option-like payoffs — practitioners compensate by assigning a HIGHER standard deviation than history implies
• Return: use a building-blocks approach — risk-free rate + returns on the relevant factor exposures (credit spread, curve, equity, leverage, liquidity) + assumed manager alpha − fees − taxes
• Allocation models assume the class is always fully invested; with call-down funds it rarely is, so aggregate exposures must be monitored continually
• Build vs. buy turns on access to capacity-constrained top-tier managers, access for effective due diligence, and in-house skill vs cost (small investors are generally pushed to a fund of funds).

cards.front: Why do "2 and 20" gross returns understate the real fee drag in alternatives — and what extra bite do call-down funds take?
cards.back:
• Typical terms: management fees 0.5%-2.5% of assets, incentive fees 10%-20% of returns
• Curriculum example: a 3% gross QUARTERLY return (12.6% annualized), after a 2% management and 20% incentive fee accrued quarterly, nets just 8.2% at year-end
• Call-down structures are worse: the management fee is charged on COMMITTED capital, not invested capital — slow deployment produces a pronounced J-curve (negative IRRs in the early years) that is hard to overcome ("it takes a 100% return to recover from a 50% loss")
• Pass-through expenses on top: legal, custody, audit, administration, accounting — roughly 0.5% at small funds but only 0.05%-0.20% at large funds; plus deal due-diligence costs and brokerage; some (capitalized organizational costs) have a limited life
• Fix: read the offering documents for the all-in cost, and use net-of-fee returns in the allocation exercise. Tax treatment affects those return assumptions the same way.

cards.front: What minimum investment horizon should an investor generally have before committing to private real estate, private real assets or private equity funds, and what three other investor attributes decide suitability?
cards.back:
• HORIZON: investors with less than a 15-year horizon should generally avoid private real estate, private real assets and private equity funds. A private program takes 5-7 years to fully develop and another 10-12 years to unwind (assuming no new investments after year 7); even 10 years may be too short. Public-equity and managed-futures hedge funds have much shorter lock-ups (months or none); secondaries can shorten entry/exit.
• EXPERTISE: must understand the strategies and what drives their success or failure; LP-GP information asymmetry never disappears. A pension without full-time staff, or an individual without an adviser with a dedicated alternatives team, is unlikely to succeed. The investment PHILOSOPHY must fit too — a believer in efficient markets will struggle with strategies predicated on active management.
• GOVERNANCE: clear long- and short-term objectives; decision rights held by those with the knowledge, capacity and time; a formal investment policy; a reporting framework tracking progress.
• TRANSPARENCY: must accept less than 100% look-through — a blind pool in RE/PE/real assets, delayed reporting (real estate reported a quarter in arrears, audited annual reports possibly in Q2), non-standardized risk reports. Insist on an independent administrator and an annual audit by a respected firm.

cards.front: Write the unsmoothing formula for an appraisal-based return series, and state what it does to measured risk.
cards.back:
