Symbols: r(t,reported) = the reported (appraisal-based) return for period t; s = the estimated serial (auto)correlation of that reported series; output is the unsmoothed return for the same period and frequency (typically quarterly).
• Use it whenever a test shows statistically significant serial correlation — appraisal parameters change slowly, so reported returns lag and look artificially calm
• Effect (Exhibit 20, quarterly 1997-2017): private real estate serial correlation 0.85, reported volatility 4.6% -> unsmoothed 13.8% (about 3×); private equity 0.38, 10.7% -> 15.7%; HF distressed 0.36, 8.9% -> 13.0%; high-yield credit 0.34, 10.0% -> 14.3%. Public equities (0.03) barely move.
• Correlations rise too — smoothing dampens measured co-movement with volatile public assets
• Classic errors: feeding smoothed volatilities/correlations into an optimizer (it then over-allocates to private assets), and scaling by the square root of time, which assumes serially uncorrelated returns in the first place.
cards.formula: r(t,unsmoothed) = [r(t,reported) − s × r(t−1,reported)] ÷ (1 − s)

cards.front: What three approaches are used for the alternatives iteration of the asset allocation exercise, and what three steps make the process statistically sound?
cards.back:
Three approaches (complements, not substitutes):
• Monte Carlo simulation — generate return scenarios that relax normality (e.g. mix a low-volatility and a high-volatility regime) and assess multi-period outcomes vs the objective
• Optimization techniques — MVO with minimum/maximum constraints, or optimizations that incorporate downside risk (mean-CVaR) or skew
• Risk factor-based approaches — optimize factor exposures, then implement with asset classes
The sound process:
1. Unsmooth the observed return series if autocorrelation is significant
2. Judge whether normality is a reasonable assumption — if yes, MVO is appropriate
3. If the series shows fat tails and skew with downside beyond the normal case, choose an optimization that accounts for tail risk
Tested details: unconstrained MVO is dominated by cash and fixed income at the low-risk end and by PRIVATE EQUITY at the high-risk end, and small input changes swing the weights; constraints used were PE and hedge funds 30% each, private real estate 15%, major public classes 50%, and the constrained frontier necessarily lies BELOW the unconstrained one. At a 6.8% return target, mean-CVaR cut a 22% combined real estate allocation to 0% (public/private real estate 99% CVaR −40.2%/−27.9%), accepting higher volatility (12.1% vs 11.5%) for a far better 99% CVaR (−15.6% vs −20.7%).

cards.front: Write the capital contribution (capital call) formula in the Takahashi-Alexander cash-flow model, and apply it to a 100 million commitment called at 25% then 50% of the remainder.
cards.back:
Symbols: C(t) = capital contributed (called) in year t; RC(t) = assumed rate of contribution for year t; CC = total capital commitment; PIC(t) = paid-in capital to date. In words: contribution = rate of contribution × (commitment − paid-in capital).
• Year 1: 100 × 25% = 25
• Year 2: (100 − 25) × 50% = 37.5
• Year 3: (100 − 25 − 37.5) × 50% = 18.75, and so on — calls decay as PIC rises
• Conventions: the investment period is usually limited (3-5 years per the PPM; calls typically over 3-4 years), the GP often never calls the FULL commitment, and the LP must normally fund a call within about 30 days or risk forfeiting its entire investment
• Classic errors: treating committed capital as invested capital, and parking all uncalled capital in cash. Because of the opportunity cost, uncalled capital is usually held in a proxy — public equities for private equity, high yield for private credit, REITs for private real estate, energy stocks or commodity futures for private real assets.
cards.formula: C(t) = RC(t) × (CC − PIC(t))

cards.front: Write the distribution and NAV equations of the private-fund cash-flow model, then compute year-end 2022 NAV for a fully called fund whose NAV was 30 million at year-end 2020, with a 20% distribution paid at end-2021 and a 12% expected growth rate.
cards.back:
Symbols: D(t) = distribution in year t; RD(t) = rate of distribution; NAV(t) = net asset value at end of year t; G = assumed annual growth rate (equals the fund's IRR if it develops as expected); C(t) = capital contribution; L = the fund's contractual life (e.g. 12 years); B = the "bow" parameter controlling how back-loaded distributions are.
• Grow FIRST, then distribute, then add calls: distribution is taken on NAV(t−1) × (1 + G)
• Worked (Example 8): distribution end-2021 = (30 × 1.12) × 20% = 6.72m. NAV end-2022 = (30 × 1.12) × (1 − 0.20) × 1.12 = 30,105,600
• Bow effect: B = 2.5 gives gradually rising rates (year 5 about 11%, year 12 = 100%); B = 5.0 keeps early rates near zero (year 5 about 1%), letting NAV build higher but keeping cumulative net cash flow negative for longer — contributions are unaffected
• Classic errors: applying RD to last year's NAV before growing it, and forgetting to re-grow the post-distribution NAV in the next year.
cards.formula: D(t) = RD(t) × [NAV(t−1) × (1 + G)], where RD(t) = (t/L)^B; NAV(t) = [NAV(t−1) × (1 + G)] + C(t) − D(t)

cards.front: How do you size the commitments needed to reach a private-asset target, and why spread them across vintages? (1bn portfolio, 20% PE target, 6% portfolio growth, NAV peaks in 5 years.)
cards.back:
Symbols: target % = strategic allocation; g = assumed growth of the TOTAL portfolio (net contributions plus returns); n = years until the private NAV peaks; NAV per unit of commitment comes from the cash-flow/pacing model.
• Worked: portfolio in 5 years = 1bn × 1.06^5 = about 1.338bn, so target PE NAV = 20% × 1.338bn = about 268m. A 100m commitment peaks at about 110m of NAV, so about 243m of commitments are required.
• But do NOT commit it in one vintage: commit about 70m per year over four years. This gives a more stable NAV, diversifies vintage years (private returns are highly vintage-sensitive), and lets distributions from older funds help fund newer calls. A single vintage peaks then declines; ongoing commitments are needed to hold 20%, though at a slower pace once the program is established.
• Classic errors: sizing against today's portfolio value instead of its projected future value; and failing to stress the plan — in a bear market GPs call capital FASTER, distribute SLOWER, and extend the fund's life, which is how 2008-09 investors ended up cutting distributions, selling on the secondary market at severe discounts, or walking away from commitments and forfeiting earlier investments.
cards.formula: Commitment needed = [target % × current portfolio × (1 + g)^n] ÷ (projected peak NAV per 1 of commitment)

cards.front: Beyond returns, what seven firm- and process-level items must an alternatives program monitor, and why does this matter more than for public managers?
cards.back:
Why: the manager cannot be terminated easily and the assets moved to someone else, so problems must be caught early.
• Key person risk — fund documents name key persons and give LPs rights if one leaves; also probe COO/CCO departures; quantitative strategies carry less key-person risk
• Alignment of interests — has the GP withdrawn her own capital? Is a new fund distracting the team or outgrowing the opportunity set? Shared ownership of an asset across two funds creates incentive-fee conflicts
• Style drift — confirm investments still sit where the manager has a real edge
• Risk management — understand and periodically verify the philosophy and process, essential where leverage is used
• Client/asset turnover — a big inflow can force larger or more numerous investments than is optimal; heavy redemptions force selling what they CAN, not what they should
• Client profile — other LPs' behavior can trigger gates or an untimely liquidation (as in 2008-09)
• Service providers — verify independent administrators, custodians and auditors are intact; investigate any change
Also monitor the program against the GOALS set for it (e.g. real estate replacing part of fixed income), not just against a benchmark, and confirm the original market thesis still holds.

cards.front: Why can a private fund's reported IRR and its peer-group ranking both mislead, and what measure or context is used to offset each?
cards.back:
• IRR is money-weighted and highly sensitive to the TIMING of calls and distributions — two managers with similar portfolios can post very different IRRs, and managers can bias the figure. Public managers report time-weighted returns, so the two are not comparable.
• Offset: MOIC = (current value of the underlying companies + distributions received) ÷ total invested capital. If capital came back fast (inflating IRR), weight MOIC more; if it came back slower than expected, weight IRR more. Even weak MOIC and weak IRR need vintage-peer context — poor across the vintage suggests a bad climate, not a bad manager.
• Peer groups: providers differ on strategy definitions, weighting (asset vs equal), survivorship-bias treatment and inclusion rules. An event-driven fund earning 6% over five years looks strong against Credit Suisse (3.7%) and weak against Eurekahedge (7.2%); a ranking also moves with what OTHER managers do. Custom proxies (e.g. MSCI World + 3%) frame expectations but will not match realized risk, return or liquidity.
• Stale pricing distorts betas, correlations and Sharpe ratios; and a small residual portfolio prints meaningless percentages (a $2,000 stake revalued to $3,000 = +50%). Reserve judgment on illiquid funds until most investments are monetized, and back the numbers with qualitative tracking of the manager's thesis, value-add plan and exit strategy.

cards.front: Define the four measures of an individual's wealth the curriculum distinguishes — aggregate wealth, net worth, investable net worth, economic net worth — and say what each one adds or leaves out.
cards.back:
• Aggregate wealth = total value of ALL assets owned: personal property + financial assets + real assets + rights (patents, trademarks, copyrights, mineral rights). Excludes human capital
• Net worth = assets whose value is relatively easy to measure (publicly traded and privately held investments, real estate) − debts. Excludes hard-to-value intangibles (copyrights, digital rights)
• Investable net worth = liquid savings and investment accounts − short-term liabilities (e.g. credit card debt). Wealth managers prioritize investable/liquid wealth over total wealth as the first read on a client's service needs
• Economic net worth = net worth EXTENDED to include claims on future consumption: human capital and pension benefits (only the VESTED pension value counts)
• Related terms: real wealth (tangible: real estate, commodities); productive wealth (a directly owned business — the largest slice for many wealthy clients); liquid/cash wealth
• Wealth creation vs transfer: entrepreneurship, asset price appreciation and sudden fame CREATE wealth; inheritance, gifts, lottery/gambling wins and legal settlements only TRANSFER existing wealth
cards.mnemonic: Aggregate = everything owned; Economic = everything owned plus everything you will earn.

cards.front: State the curriculum's human capital equation and say what makes one worker's human capital worth less than another's with identical pay.
cards.back:
• HC_0 = human capital today = the mortality-weighted net present value of expected future LABOR income
• p(s_t) = actuarial probability of surviving to year (age) t, from mortality tables
• w_(t−1) = employment income in the prior period; g_t = annual wage growth rate
• r_f = nominal risk-free rate; y = risk premium for occupational income volatility; N = length of working life in years
• The discount rate is r_f + y, so identical pay gives LOWER human capital when income is riskier: an entrepreneur, investment banker or race-car driver carries a high y; a government worker or teacher a low y. y also prices the chance of interruption from job loss, disability or death
• Units: keep growth and discount rate both nominal. Curriculum example: 1.5% real growth with 2% inflation gives g = (1.015)(1.02) − 1 = 3.53%
• Classic errors: dropping p(s_t) entirely; discounting at r_f alone and ignoring y; mixing a real growth rate with a nominal discount rate
cards.formula: HC_0 = SUM over t = 1 to N of [ p(s_t) × w_(t−1) × (1 + g_t) ] ÷ (1 + r_f + y)^t

cards.front: List the seven financial stages of life in order. At which stage does total wealth reach its maximum, and at which does longevity risk arise?
cards.back:
• Education (0–25) — financially dependent, little financial capital or saving
• Early career (25–35) — marriage, young children, debt to buy a home, start saving for education
• Career development (35–50) — skill building and income growth, but family and housing costs limit saving; human capital is a LARGE share of total wealth
• Peak accumulation (50–60) — maximum earnings and greatest opportunity to accumulate; focus on retirement income planning and minimizing taxes
• Pre-retirement (60–65) — maximum career income and the HIGHEST point of wealth accumulation (total wealth peaks HERE, not in peak accumulation)
• Early retirement (65–75) — most active period, fewest cognitive/mobility limits; still take an appropriate level of investment risk to keep assets growing
• Late retirement (75+) — unknown duration = LONGEVITY RISK (outliving financial resources), plus cognitive decline and long-term care needs
• Through all of it: financial wealth is accumulated as human capital declines, and consumption is increasingly met from accumulated financial, real and personal assets

cards.front: In the accumulation phase, contrast the appropriate equity vs fixed-income tilt for a stable-salary government employee and for an entrepreneur — and give the reason.
cards.back:
• Principle: the investment portfolio is the only piece the client controls, so allocate it to DIVERSIFY the income and risk already embedded in human capital
• Stable salary (government worker, teacher) = bond-like human capital, low occupational risk premium → tilt the financial portfolio TOWARD EQUITIES, the higher allocation being balanced by the stability of the salary
• Entrepreneur or commission income = equity-like human capital, volatile and concentrated in one industry → tilt TOWARD FIXED INCOME, and favor industries LESS correlated with the business
• Why the entrepreneur is doubly exposed: if the business does poorly it hits both the value of the business AND the owner's earnings; business asset values also correlate with the household's other financial assets
• Same logic extends to a private employer's pension (company-specific risk, plan termination) and to employer stock
• Decumulation follow-through: the retired EMPLOYEE leans on pension wealth, so the portfolio must generate income and maintain purchasing power; for the wealthy retired ENTREPRENEUR pension wealth is a small share, so focus shifts to philanthropy, wealth transfer and other long-term goals

cards.front: Distinguish risk tolerance, risk capacity, and risk perception. Which one explains an investor with low risk aversion and ample means choosing the LOWEST-risk of three portfolios that all have the same Sharpe ratio?
cards.back:
• Risk tolerance = the level of risk an individual is WILLING and able to bear — an attitude; the flip side of risk aversion
• Risk capacity = the ABILITY to bear financial risk — objective, set by wealth, income, time horizon and liquidity needs. Greater capacity = can absorb losses without compromising current or future consumption goals
• Risk perception = the SUBJECTIVE assessment of how risky a decision or the investment climate is; depends on circumstances, varies widely across people, and the wealth manager CAN shape it through education
• Answer: risk PERCEPTION. Capacity was sufficient for the riskiest portfolio and low risk aversion means high tolerance, so only a subjective view that the higher-risk portfolios are unattractive explains the choice
• Risk tolerance can differ ACROSS goals for the same client — low tolerance on a specific, near-term, must-hit goal; higher tolerance on a flexible long-term goal
• Questionnaire limits: highly subjective, question order and wording change answers, losses framed in percent vs currency get different responses, and they may not predict behavior — supplement with a risk tolerance conversation

cards.front: Write the future value accumulation factor for a return taxed annually, and its inflation-adjusted version. When do you use each, and what is the ordering error candidates make?
cards.back:
• R = pre-tax annual return; t_x = the ACCRUAL tax rate (levied each period, usually annually); T = years; infl = annual inflation rate
• Accrual taxes apply to interest, dividends and, in the same way, an annual wealth tax; the model assumes after-tax returns are reinvested at R
• Curriculum example: EUR100,000 at R = 7%, t_x = 20%, T = 20 gives 100,000 × (1.056)^20 = EUR297,357, against EUR386,968 with no tax
• Add 3% inflation: 100,000 × (1.056 ÷ 1.03)^20 = EUR164,500 in real terms; with no tax the real figure is EUR214,110, so tax cost about EUR49,600 of purchasing power
• Use it to compare an annually taxed vehicle with a deferred or sheltered one, and to state wealth in real, after-tax terms
• Classic error: SUBTRACTING inflation from the after-tax return instead of dividing by (1 + infl) — and applying the inflation adjustment before tax. Tax is levied on the NOMINAL amount, so deflate only AFTER tax
cards.formula: FVIF_accrual = [1 + R(1 − t_x)]^T  and  FVIF_accrual,infl = [ (1 + R(1 − t_x)) ÷ (1 + infl) ]^T

cards.front: Pitfall: candidates assume the share of investment growth consumed by tax equals the tax rate. When is that true, when is it false, and what follows for choosing between a lower tax rate and deferral?
cards.back:
• Tax drag = (no-tax FV − after-tax FV) ÷ the pre-tax GAIN — divide by the gain, not by the amount invested
• ACCRUAL (annual) taxation: drag EXCEEDS the tax rate and COMPOUNDS. EUR100,000 at 7% for 20 years taxed 20% annually: EUR89,611 ÷ EUR286,968 = 31% drag versus a 20% rate
• Drag rises with BOTH the return and the horizon, and the two effects are multiplicative — worst for high-return assets held a long time, and for fixed income whose return is almost all annually taxed
• DEFERRED capital gain: drag EQUALS the tax rate exactly — 20% here — regardless of return or horizon, because deferral removes the compounding of the drag. Same facts, deferred: FV = EUR329,576, about EUR32,218 more
• Consequence: a deferred investment can beat an annually taxed one at the SAME rate, and deferral value can outweigh a LOWER annually applied rate over a long horizon
• The counter-case: enough pre-tax alpha (buying sufficiently below intrinsic value) on an accrual-taxed investment can overcome tax drag
• Low basis compounds the problem: FVIF = (1 + R)^T(1 − t_CG) + t_CG × B, where B = cost basis ÷ current market value — a low B means a larger embedded tax liability today

cards.front: Name the main sections of a private-client IPS, and list everything that belongs in the Investment Parameters section.
cards.back:
• Sections: Background | Investment objectives | Investment parameters | Portfolio management | Duties and responsibilities | Appendix
• Background: name, age, family and its values, source of wealth, market value and TAX STATUS of each account, significant assets NOT managed by the adviser, relevant tax jurisdictions
• Investment objectives: return and risk objectives, quantified wherever possible, with primary vs secondary priority, plus expected future contributions and large inflows/outflows
• INVESTMENT PARAMETERS contains: risk tolerance (ability and willingness); investment time horizon (e.g. "exceeds 15 years", one per goal when goals are parallel); asset class preferences; liquidity preferences (a stated minimum cash balance); other investment preferences (legacy/employer holdings, ESG or SRI, turnover policy, active vs passive, special tax or legal issues); constraints (e.g. a position with large embedded capital gains); portfolio asset allocation (target plus lower and upper rebalancing limits)
• Portfolio management: degree of discretionary authority (full, less than full, non-discretionary), rebalancing method (time-based vs threshold-based), tactical changes, implementation
• Duties and responsibilities: the manager's obligations and IPS review — at least annually, and sooner when circumstances or markets change
• Appendix: modeled portfolio behavior (distribution of returns by percentile, downside risk) and capital market expectations
cards.mnemonic: BOP-PDA: Background, Objectives, Parameters — Portfolio management, Duties, Appendix.

cards.front: Name the five defining characteristics institutional investors share as a group, and the key nuance attached to each.
cards.back:
• Scale (asset size) — drives access to strategies, liquidity, trading costs. Small funds (e.g., under USD25 million) cannot meet private-market minimums and outsource to external managers/consultants; the very largest face DIS-economies: capacity-constrained strategies (VC, small cap) are too small to matter, and market impact on trades.
• Long-term investment horizon — usually set by a liability stream (pension benefits, endowment spending policy). Net payouts are typically about 5% or less of AUM, so liquidity needs are low and alternatives are feasible. Exception: frozen DB plans in de-risking mode have HIGHER liquidity needs.
• Regulatory frameworks — multiple, jurisdiction-specific and evolving (ERISA, PPA, UPMIFA, IORP II, Solvency II, Basel III); they set the rules for tax-exempt or reduced-tax status.
• Governance framework — board/trustees plus an investment committee set policy and strategic asset allocation and delegate; an investment office (CIO plus staff) implements, in-house or outsourced.
• Principal-agent issues — agents (committee members, staff, external managers, brokers, consultants) decide for beneficiaries; classic example is a high base fee payable regardless of performance. Managed via strong governance, accountability, and a clear IPS.
cards.mnemonic: S-H-R-G-P: Scale, Horizon, Regulation, Governance, Principal-agent

cards.front: Name the four common institutional investment approaches, and for each give the defining feature plus its main pro and con.
cards.back:
• Norway model (GPFG) — traditional 60/40 public equity and fixed income, few alternatives, largely passive, tight tracking-error limits. Pro: low cost, transparent, scalable, low manager-selection risk, easy for a board to understand. Con: limited value-added potential.
• Endowment model (Yale) — high allocation to alternatives, significant active management, EXTERNALLY managed. Pro: high value-added potential. Con: expensive; hard for small investors (no access to top managers) and for very large ones (footprint). Suits a long horizon, high risk tolerance, relatively small liquidity needs, and skill in sourcing alternatives.
• Canada model (CPPIB) — high alternatives and active management but INSOURCED; features are (a) reference portfolio, (b) total portfolio approach, (c) active management. Pro: value-added plus internal capability. Con: potentially expensive and hard to manage.
• LDI model — objective is returns sufficient to cover liabilities; focus shifts from asset-only to maximizing expected surplus return and managing surplus volatility. Other than for banks and insurers, LDI portfolios typically hold significant long-duration fixed income; in SOME implementations the portfolio is separated into a hedging portfolio (hedges interest-rate risk in the liabilities — long-duration fixed income, interest-rate swaps to extend duration) and a return-generating portfolio (public equities, alternatives). Pro: explicit recognition of liabilities. Con: longevity and inflation risk may remain unhedged.
• Reference portfolio = a passive, PUBLIC-ONLY mix of equities, fixed income and cash that is a cheap, risk-equivalent benchmark; it may differ from the strategic asset allocation, which can include privates.

cards.front: Rank the five sovereign wealth fund types by horizon and liquidity need, and state the typical portfolio of each.
cards.back:
• Budget stabilization fund — insulates the fiscal budget from commodity-price/revenue shocks. SHORTEST horizon, HIGHEST liquidity; objective is capital preservation. Mostly cash and high-grade, very liquid fixed income; avoids assets correlated with the main revenue commodity.
• Development fund — supports national economic development/infrastructure. LOW liquidity needs (projects are long-dated); allocation often dictated by mandate (e.g., 100% domestic or 100% offshore).
• Savings fund — intergenerational wealth transfer. VERY LONG horizon, LOW liquidity, comparable to endowments and foundations; invests heavily in equities, alternatives and illiquid assets. Liquidity needs can rise once the natural resource is depleted and the government starts withdrawing.
• Reserve investment fund — earns more than the yield paid on the central bank's monetary stabilization bonds, offsetting the negative carry of FX reserves. Liquidity need is LOWER than a stabilization fund but HIGHER than a savings fund; typically 50%-70% in equity or equity-equivalents with the rest in liquid fixed income.
• Pension reserve fund — prefunds government pension/health liabilities. Long horizon in accumulation (equities and relatively illiquid assets), shifting gradually to liquid, high-quality fixed income in decumulation.
• Trap: horizon and liquidity come from the fund's TYPE and mission, not from the "sovereign" label.

cards.front: Write the single formula that covers all three endowment spending rules, and state what w = 1, w = 0 and 0 < w < 1 each produce.
cards.back:
• w = weight placed on the prior year's spending amount; Spending(t) = last year's payout; Inflation rate = HEPI for US endowments, otherwise a general CPI, possibly plus a spread; Spending rate = headline payout percentage, typically 4%-6%; Average AUM = a smoothed 3- to 5-year moving average of asset values.
• w = 1 → Constant growth rule: a fixed, inflation-adjusted amount. Weakness: spending ignores the endowment's value, so the payout percentage can drift very high or low; commonly capped and floored at roughly 4%-6% of 1- or 3-year average AUM.
• w = 0 → Market value rule: rate × moving-average AUM. Most common among US endowments. Weakness: PRO-CYCLICAL, payout rises and falls with markets.
• 0 < w < 1 → Hybrid, the "Yale" spending rule; weights commonly 30%-70%; used by many larger endowments; balances the two weaknesses.
• Use: compute the payout and judge whether spending is smoothed. Foundations use similar smoothing, but the constant growth and hybrid rules are rarely used by them.
• Classic errors: applying the spending rate to the CURRENT market value rather than the moving average, and forgetting to inflate the prior year's spending term.
cards.formula: Spending(t+1) = w × [Spending(t) × (1 + Inflation rate)] + (1 − w) × Spending rate × Average AUM

cards.front: US private foundation vs US university endowment: contrast spending obligation, net spending, liquidity needs, and revenue dependence.
cards.back:
• Spending obligation — Foundation: legally mandated 5% of assets (trailing 12-month basis) PLUS investment expenses PLUS 100% of donations received in the year (flow-through). Endowment: flexible spending rule, headline rate 4%-6% of assets, with smoothing.
• Net spending — Foundation: at least 5% of assets. Endowment: typically only 2%-4% of assets after alumni gifts and donations.
• Liquidity — Foundation HIGHER: the mandated payout, multi-year (two- to five-year) grant installments, plus capital calls on privates and margin/collateral on derivatives. Endowment LOWER.
• Horizon — Both very long-term/perpetual, and both are high risk tolerance. Exception: limited-life foundations (e.g., spend-down mandates); as the horizon shortens, liquidity needs RISE and risk tolerance FALLS.
• Revenue dependence — Foundations rely almost exclusively on the investment portfolio, so they are on average more conservative and more liquid. Universities also have tuition, research grants and ongoing fundraising, and can often issue debt.
• Cost structure — A foundation's operating costs count inside the 5% payout (investment office is a cost center), so its investment staff is smaller than a same-size endowment's and outsourced-CIO use is common.

cards.front: Life insurer vs P&C insurer: contrast liability duration and predictability, liquidity needs, and the key rate-driven risk. How is the general account segmented?
cards.back:
• Life — long-duration liability stream; portfolio return objectives historically set over 20- to 40-year horizons. Claims are fairly predictable (term life highly so via actuarial analysis of large policy pools; annuities have a shorter, ongoing payout subject to longevity risk). Emphasis is close asset/liability matching; liquidity needs are moderate. Key rate risk: DISINTERMEDIATION — in periods of rising/high interest rates, policyholders surrender policies chasing higher yields, causing significant net cash outflow.
• P&C — shorter-duration liability stream and horizon; low-probability, high-cost events (hurricanes, other catastrophes) make claims highly volatile and uncertain in both amount and timing. Requires ample liquidity: high proportions of cash, cash substitutes and short-term fixed income. Results also swing with the underwriting cycle.
• General account segmentation (both): a RESERVE portfolio, typically sized by statute, managed conservatively in highly liquid, low-risk assets to ensure policy liabilities are met; and a SURPLUS portfolio, aimed at higher expected return, where more liquidity risk and alternatives (private equity, hedge funds) are acceptable.
• Life insurers also run SEPARATE accounts for variable life and variable annuities, where the POLICYHOLDER bears investment risk; whole/term life, universal life and fixed annuities sit in the general account, where the company bears the risk.

cards.front: Match each institutional type to the primary focus of its legal/regulatory constraints and its tax treatment.
cards.back:
• DB pension — funding standards, vesting, payouts, fiduciary code of conduct and disclosure (ERISA and the PBGC, Pension Protection Act minimum funding, IORP II in the EU). Accounting drives behavior: ASC 715 puts an over/underfunded plan on the sponsor's balance sheet, which pushed corporates toward LDI. Tax: contributions and investment earnings usually tax-deferred/exempt, benefits taxed as ordinary income; watch double taxation and treaty access when investing offshore.
• Endowment/foundation — prudence and MPT-based diversification (UPMIFA in the US, Trustee Act 2000 in the UK), plus a duty of care. Tax-exempt on income and gains, gifts deductible to the donor. US private foundations must distribute 5% of assets or face a 30% tax on undistributed income, and most pay a 2% excise tax on net investment income.
• Sovereign wealth fund — national enabling legislation covering mission, contributions, withdrawal rules and governance; political independence and transparency (Santiago Principles/GAPP via the IFSWF). Generally tax-free, but often cannot reclaim withholding taxes or credits available to taxable investors.
• Bank/insurer — capital adequacy, liquidity (LCR: liquid assets above 100% of highly probable near-term outflows; NSFR: stable funding relative to assets), asset quality and diversification, leverage, systemic (SIFI) rules; Basel III for banks, Solvency II in the EU and state/NAIC regulation in the US for insurers. Three accounting regimes apply: GAAP/IFRS, statutory, and economic (mark-to-market). Taxable.

cards.front: State the funded-ratio and surplus formulas, what each input is, and the two directional conclusions the exam wants from them.
cards.back:
• Fair value of plan assets = market value of the pension fund; PV of defined benefit obligations = expected benefits discounted at the plan's discount rate (government/swap yields, corporate bond yields, or an actuarial rate). Expressed as a ratio or percent; also called the vested benefit index (VBI) in some countries.
• Below 100% = underfunded; in some countries the sponsor must raise contributions until the ratio exceeds 100%. An improving ratio can turn the pension from a liability into an ASSET on the sponsor's balance sheet.
• Directional rules: higher surplus/funded status implies greater risk tolerance, all else equal; and a larger sponsor relative to plan size implies greater risk tolerance.
• Classic errors: treating the liability as fixed — it is discount-rate sensitive, so the ratio moves with rates as much as with asset returns; and assuming underfunded automatically means de-risk (the curriculum allows an underfunded plan to take MORE risk to return to fully funded status).
cards.formula: Funded ratio = Fair value of plan assets ÷ PV of defined benefit obligations ; Surplus = Plan assets − PV(liabilities)

cards.front: List the five risk considerations of a private DB plan, and give the direction each pushes risk tolerance.
cards.back:
1. Plan funded status — surplus supports more risk. Three sponsor responses: (a) match assets to liabilities in quantity, timing and risk via LDI/duration-gap or cash-flow matching (suits plans at or near fully funded); (b) grow assets faster than liabilities by taking MORE investment risk (suits underfunded plans seeking full funding, or funded plans wanting lower contributions and willing to accept funded-status volatility); (c) hold defensive, low-volatility assets (suits a sponsor willing to contribute more for less funded-status variability). Adequately funded sponsors may transfer risk via lump sums to beneficiaries or an insurer buyout.
2. Sponsor financial strength — weak sponsors may fail to contribute, and in bankruptcy an underfunded plan queues with other creditors. Lower debt ratios and higher expected profitability imply more risk tolerance; a plan that is LARGE relative to the sponsor's balance sheet or market cap implies LESS.
3. Sponsor/fund interaction — the lower the correlation of plan asset returns with sponsor operating results, the greater the risk tolerance.
4. Plan design — the benefit formula must balance adequacy against sustainability. Early-retirement and lump-sum provisions SHORTEN liability duration, implying LOWER risk tolerance.
5. Workforce characteristics — younger workforce and a higher proportion of active vs retired lives means longer liability duration, more risk tolerance, and more capacity for liquidity risk. Older/retired-heavy means shorter duration and a need to hold liquidity. High turnover means fewer benefits vest; rising average tenure means more vesting and a worse funded status. Longevity risk is pooled, but rising life expectancy still raises total liabilities.

cards.front: A cyclical manufacturer's DB plan holds no sponsor stock but is spread across 40 industrial companies. Why is this still the classic DB error, and what does the curriculum actually require?
cards.back:
• The error: diversifying out of the sponsor's OWN shares while retaining exposure to the sponsor's INDUSTRY. The curriculum says it is prudent to diversify away from the sponsor company's stock AND from companies operating in the same industry, because their risk and return are expected to be highly correlated with the sponsor's.
• Why it matters: if the sponsor's business deteriorates, plan assets fall at the same moment the sponsor is least able to make additional contributions — funded status and contribution capacity are hit together.
• Decision rule: the lower the correlation between the sponsor's operating results and pension asset returns, the greater the risk tolerance, all else equal. It is desirable for plan assets to have LOW correlation with the sponsor's operating assets.
• Extension: if the sponsor's revenues are highly cyclical, the allocation should be modified so that funded status does not deteriorate exactly when the core business suffers a cyclical downturn.

cards.front: What must an institutional IPS contain, how often is it reviewed versus revised, and what is the first test when evaluating one?
cards.back:
• Contents: mission; investment objectives (return target and risk tolerance); constraints affecting asset allocation (legal, regulatory, tax, accounting); asset allocation policy with ranges and asset-class benchmarks; rebalancing policy; guidelines for implementing the allocation; reporting requirements.
• Cadence: REVIEW annually, but REVISE infrequently — only on material change in the investor's circumstances or the market environment, since the IPS is the foundation of the program. The asset allocation policy and investment guidelines sit in an APPENDIX so they can be modified more easily.
• Purpose: a well-crafted IPS reduces principal-agent problems by giving clear day-to-day guidance.
• Objectives flow from the mission and must be tied to the valuation of liabilities — the discount rate for a DB plan, the spending rate for an endowment; for banks and insurers the objective is to maximize net present value by balancing expected asset returns, the expected cost of liabilities, the risks of both, and the economic relationships between them. If the target is stated in real terms, the inflation index must be defined (e.g., HEPI, or G3 inflation).
• Evaluation test: internal consistency — do the return objective, risk tolerance and constraints fit the institution's liabilities, horizon and liquidity needs? Flag, for example, a perpetual endowment with an all-bond policy, or an underfunded plan with a weak sponsor running an aggressive equity policy.

cards.front: What return must a perpetual endowment earn, and how do you use it to judge whether its portfolio is appropriate?
cards.back:
• Spending rate = annual payout as a percent of (average) assets, headline 4%-6%; expected inflation measured by HEPI for US endowments or a general CPI. Because intergenerational equity requires preserving purchasing power, endowments target a REAL return at least equal to the spending rate — typically 5%-5.5% real over the long term.
• Curriculum example (MIT): inflation around 3% plus a spending rate around 5% means roughly 8% nominal is needed just to hold purchasing power.
• Use: test the proposed allocation against the objective. Curriculum case — 80% US Treasuries at 2% plus 20% US equities at 7% gives 0.8 × 2% + 0.2 × 7% = 3% nominal; with 2% inflation that is only 1% real against a 5% real objective, so purchasing power erodes. Fix by changing the asset mix (add non-US equity, privates), or by changing the spending policy.
• Related check: an endowment supporting a SMALL share of the university's operating budget can tolerate more market, credit and liquidity risk than one funding 40%-50% of it.
• Classic error: comparing a NOMINAL expected return with the spending rate and forgetting inflation.
cards.formula: Nominal required return ≈ Spending rate + Expected inflation  (equivalently: target real return ≥ spending rate)

cards.front: Write the curriculum's equation for the duration of a financial institution's equity capital, define every term, and show how a bank lowers it.
cards.back:
• D*E = modified duration of shareholders' equity capital; D*A and D*L = modified durations of assets and liabilities; A ÷ E = leverage (the inverse of the equity-to-assets ratio); Δi ÷ Δy = sensitivity of liability yields to asset yields. Percent change in equity value ≈ −D*E × Δy.
• Worked example: equity capital ratio 9% → A ÷ E = 1 ÷ 0.09 = 11.11 and (A ÷ E) − 1 = 10.11; with D*A = 2.0, D*L = 1.5 and Δi ÷ Δy = 0.85, D*E = (11.11 × 2) − (10.11 × 1.5 × 0.85) = 9.33. A 50 bp rise in asset yields costs 0.5% × 9.33 = 4.67% of equity value.
• Two levers: raise the equity ratio to 10% (A ÷ E = 10) → D*E = 8.53; then also shorten asset duration to 1.75 → D*E = 6.03. Less leverage and a narrower duration gap both cut equity duration.
• Units: durations in years, yields in decimal form; the equity ratio is for financial assets.
• Classic errors: using (A ÷ E) instead of (A ÷ E − 1) on the liability term, and setting Δi ÷ Δy = 1 when the question says liability yields move only, say, 85% or 90% as much as asset yields.
cards.formula: D*E = (A ÷ E) × D*A − (A ÷ E − 1) × D*L × (Δi ÷ Δy)

cards.front: "Banks profit by funding long-duration loans and securities with short-duration deposits." Why does the curriculum flag this as a misconception, and what do banks actually do?
cards.back:
• The curriculum states it is often MISTAKENLY thought that banks — and to a lesser degree insurers — climb the yield curve this way. Combined with leverage, a large asset/liability duration mismatch produces an extreme duration for equity capital.
• Curriculum illustration: with equity/assets = 10% and liability duration near zero (demand deposits, overnight borrowing), an asset portfolio duration of only 2.5 years drives the duration of shareholders' equity to about 25 — roughly a 26-year zero-coupon bond. A ±100 bp move in asset yields would swing equity value ±25%, a loss potential no depositor, creditor, shareholder or regulator would accept.
• What banks actually do — shorten asset duration: hold cash, central bank deposits, FX reserves and other near-zero-duration liquid assets; make floating-rate business loans tied to market reference rates; tie credit card and many real estate loans to variable-rate indexes; securitize and sell fixed-rate mortgages. And lengthen liability duration: issue intermediate and long-term debt, deeply subordinated capital securities, perpetual preferred stock. Futures and interest-rate swaps close the remaining mismatch.
• Since the 2007-2009 crisis many large international banks have run asset duration SHORTER than liability duration, so earnings are positioned to benefit from rising rates — the opposite of "borrow short, lend long."

cards.front: How does the curriculum split trading costs into explicit and implicit, and what are the four sources of implicit cost?
cards.back:
• Explicit = the direct costs of trading — "costs for which a trader could receive a receipt": broker commissions, transaction taxes, stamp duties, exchange fees
• Implicit = indirect costs caused by the market impact of trading; no receipt exists but they are real
• Four sources of implicit cost:
  − Bid−ask spread: traders wanting immediacy buy at higher (ask) and sell at lower (bid) prices than those willing to wait
  − Market (price) impact: filling a large order requires price concessions to encourage others to trade
  − Delay costs (slippage): inability to complete the trade immediately, so price moves before the fill
  − Opportunity cost (unrealized profit/loss): the order never fills and the price moves as expected
• Small market orders usually have small impact (they fill at the quotes); larger orders walk the book, so impact rises with order size and falls with available liquidity
• Keep these VARIABLE costs separate from the buy side's FIXED costs (employing traders, systems and data, trading rooms)
cards.mnemonic: Explicit = you get a receipt; implicit = you only get a worse price.

cards.front: Given a limit order book with several dealers, how do you compute the inside spread, the midquote, and the average fill price of a market order larger than the top-of-book size?
cards.back:
• Best bid (inside bid) = highest bid price; best ask (best offer / inside ask) = lowest ask price; the market or inside spread is best ask − best bid, quoted in currency per share
• The inside spread is normally TIGHTER than any single dealer's own spread, because the highest bidder is usually not also the lowest offeror
• Midquote = (best bid + best ask) ÷ 2 — this is the benchmark price used for the effective spread
• A market order fills from the top of the book down: take all size at the best price, then the next-best, and so on; the average fill is the size-weighted average of those prices
• Curriculum example: a buy for 1,000 shares takes 200 at 100.49 (all of Dealer C's size) then 800 at 100.51 from Dealer A — the second part costs 0.02 more per share, which is price impact
• Classic error: comparing a single dealer's quoted spread with the market spread, or using quotes prevailing after the trade rather than at order entry
cards.formula: Market (inside) spread = best ask − best bid; Midquote = (best bid + best ask) ÷ 2; Average fill = Σ(price × size filled) ÷ total size filled

cards.front: State the effective spread for a buy and for a sell, and the transaction cost estimate built from it. Why is the deviation doubled?
cards.back:
• Midquote = (bid + ask) ÷ 2 AT THE TIME THE ORDER WAS ENTERED — not at the fill, not after the trade
• One-side cost estimate = trade size × (trade price − midquote) for buys, trade size × (midquote − trade price) for sells; currency per share × shares
• Doubling makes it comparable with the QUOTED bid−ask spread: it is the spread traders would have observed if the quoted ask (buy) or bid (sell) equalled the trade price
• A buy filled exactly at the ask gives half-spread cost per share, so effective spread = quoted spread
• Worked: buy at 25.20 with market 25.17 / 25.20 → midquote 25.185 → 2 × (25.20 − 25.185) = 0.03
• Classic errors: forgetting the × 2; using the post-trade midquote; reversing the sign convention on sells (for a sell, subtract the TRADE PRICE from the midquote — a fill above the midquote gives a negative estimate, i.e. a gain)
• Careful with wording: the curriculum reserves "price improvement" for a fill better than the QUOTE (a sell above the bid, a buy below the ask), which can still leave a POSITIVE effective spread — e.g. the sell at C$10.15 against a C$10.12 bid and a C$10.18 midquote received price improvement yet had an effective spread of C$0.06
cards.formula: Effective spread (buy) = 2 × (trade price − midquote at order entry); Effective spread (sell) = 2 × (midquote at order entry − trade price); cost estimate = trade size × (one-side deviation)

cards.front: Effective spread versus quoted spread: what does it mean when the effective spread comes out smaller than, equal to, or larger than the quoted spread?
cards.back:
• SMALLER → price improvement: the order filled better than the quote (a buy below the ask, a sell above the bid); typical of small orders
• EQUAL → the order filled exactly at the quoted price, with no price improvement and no impact beyond trading at the quote
• LARGER → the fill was outside the quoted spread: the order size exceeded the displayed size and "walked" the limit order book (up for a buy, down for a sell), so the order had market impact
• Curriculum sell example: quoted spreads C$0.12, C$0.11, C$0.14 against effective spreads C$0.06, C$0.11, C$0.22 — order 1 got price improvement, order 2 sold at the bid, order 3 walked down the book
• Read the comparison as a diagnostic of IMPACT, not of the trader's skill

cards.front: Write the VWAP benchmark and the VWAP transaction cost estimate. Which trades go into the benchmark, and how is the sign read?
cards.back:
• VWAP benchmark = total currency value ÷ total quantity of the benchmark trades; analysts normally use ALL market trades from the start of the order until it was completed ("interval VWAP")
• Trade VWAP = volume-weighted average of the manager's OWN fills only
• Positive estimate = a cost; negative = you beat the market's average price over the interval
• Interpretation it answers: did you get a better or worse average price than all traders trading while you were trading?
• Worked (sell): day's trades total C$131,230 on 13,000 shares → VWAP C$10.0946; the fund's 10,000 shares averaged C$10.0680 → cost = 10,000 × (10.0946 − 10.0680) = C$266.15
• Classic errors: flipping the buy/sell sign; weighting by number of trades rather than by volume; forgetting the benchmark includes the trader's own prints
cards.formula: VWAP = Σ(price × volume) ÷ Σ(volume); VWAP cost estimate = trade size × (trade VWAP − VWAP benchmark) for buys, trade size × (VWAP benchmark − trade VWAP) for sells

cards.front: Why can a VWAP transaction cost estimate report near-zero cost on a trade that badly moved the market?
cards.back:
• VWAP is biased toward ZERO when the evaluated trades are a substantial fraction of all trades in the benchmark interval, or when the trader traded at about the same rate as the rest of the market
• In both cases trade VWAP ≈ VWAP benchmark, so the estimate ≈ 0 no matter how large the true price impact
• Extreme case from the curriculum: if a large trader was the ONLY buyer in the interval, the VWAP cost estimate is exactly zero regardless of market impact
• This bias helps explain the measure's popularity — managers like showing sponsors estimates suggesting trading was not expensive
• Consequence: VWAP tends to produce LOWER cost estimates than implementation shortfall because it often does not measure market impact well

cards.front: Define implementation shortfall: what two portfolios are compared, what is the benchmark price called, and which costs does it capture?
cards.back:
• Compares the value of the ACTUAL portfolio with a PAPER portfolio built on the assumption that trades could be arranged at the prices prevailing when the decision to trade was made
• Implementation shortfall = the excess of the paper value over the actual value (paper return − actual return)
• Benchmark = the prevailing price, also called the DECISION price, the ARRIVAL price, or the STRIKE price; generally taken as the midquote at the time of the trade decision
• It measures the TOTAL cost of implementing an investment decision, capturing all explicit and implicit costs: commissions and fees, market impact, delay (slippage), and opportunity cost
• Its appeal is that it views trading from an investment management perspective — it prices the decision, not just the fills
• Opportunity cost is the hardest piece: estimates are sensitive to the arbitrary measurement horizon and to the assumed price at which the unfilled portion could have traded

cards.front: Decompose implementation shortfall in currency terms for a buy order, and convert it to basis points.
cards.back:
• filled = shares executed; unfilled = shares cancelled; decision price = midquote when the decision was made; arrival = price when the order reached the market; exec = average fill price; end price = price when the balance was cancelled
• Terminology warning: this reading uses "the prevailing price — also called the decision price, the arrival price, or the strike price" as one and the same benchmark (the midquote at the trade decision). In the decomposition below, "arrival" means the market price at the moment the order actually reached the market; if the order is routed immediately, arrival = decision and the delay bucket is zero
• Delay (slippage) bucket = filled × (arrival − decision); trading/impact bucket = filled × (exec − arrival); together they are the execution cost
• Opportunity cost = unfilled × (end − decision) — the whole point of IS, the piece VWAP and the effective spread ignore
• Denominator for the percentage is the PAPER investment = full order size × decision price
• Worked: decide to buy 10,000 at 100.00; arrival 100.05; 7,000 fill at 100.15; 3,000 cancel at 100.30; fee 0.02/share → delay 350 + impact 700 + opportunity 900 + fees 140 = 2,090; 2,090 ÷ 1,000,000 = 20.9 bps
• Classic errors: applying opportunity cost to the filled shares, dividing by the executed value instead of the full paper investment, and failing to reverse every sign for a sell order
cards.formula: IS = execution cost + opportunity cost + fees; execution = filled × (exec price − decision price) = [filled × (arrival − decision)] + [filled × (exec − arrival)]; opportunity = unfilled × (end/cancel price − decision price); IS(%) = IS ÷ (total order shares × decision price)

cards.front: Contrast implementation shortfall with the effective spread and with VWAP: what does each miss, and which reports the lowest cost?
cards.back:
• Effective spread: only measures deviation from the midquote at order entry. It is a POOR estimate when a large order is split into many trades over time — each child trade is priced against a midquote the trader's own earlier trades already moved — and when small orders receive price improvement. It captures no delay cost and no cost of unfilled shares
• VWAP: compares average fill price to the market's average price around the trade; it often does not measure market impact well, so it TENDS TO PRODUCE LOWER cost estimates than implementation shortfall
• Implementation shortfall: includes market impact, delay, opportunity cost on shares never filled, and explicit costs — the all-in cost of the decision, and the most rigorous of the three
• Benchmark timing view: effective spread uses the midquote prevailing AT ORDER ENTRY (the module's overview labels this "the midquote at the time of the trade," but every worked calculation uses the quotes at order entry), IS uses the midquote at the trade decision / order submission, VWAP uses an average price around the trade

cards.front: What advantages let electronic order-matching systems displace floor-based trading, and what happened to transaction costs as a result?
cards.back:
• Cheap to operate once built: server rooms need less space than floors, and no exchange officials are needed to record and report prices
• They do exactly what they are programmed to do — precise enforcement of order precedence and pricing rules without error or exception
• Perfect audit trails, so investigators can reconstruct the exact sequence and timing of events
• Hidden orders stay perfectly hidden — computers never inadvertently or fraudulently reveal a client's hidden order, unlike floor brokers
• Near-continuous around-the-clock operation, and they keep running when bad weather or other events would keep workers off a floor
• Computers themselves: infinite attention span and wide scope, extraordinarily fast responses, perfect discipline, perfect memory
• Result: bid−ask spreads fell substantially and buy-side costs dropped — competition forced dealers and arbitrageurs to pass technology savings on as narrower spreads quoted for larger size, and order management systems let fewer buy-side traders handle more orders
• Exception to know: corporate and municipal bond markets have changed little — most public investors still trade over the counter with dealers

cards.front: Define market fragmentation, state why it creates a problem, and name the two algorithmic tools used to cope with it.
cards.back:
• Market fragmentation = trading the same instrument in multiple venues; available liquidity at any one venue is only a small fraction of the aggregate liquidity for that instrument
• Problem: it increases the potential for price and liquidity disparities across venues, because buyers and sellers often are not in the same venue at the same time
• Scale: US exchange-listed equity order flow is divided among 11 exchanges, 40 alternative trading systems and numerous dealers, versus three primary exchanges plus a few regionals in the late 20th century
• ATSs — also called ECNs or MTFs — function like exchanges but exercise no regulatory authority over subscribers except over conduct within their own trading systems
• Coping tools: LIQUIDITY AGGREGATORS create "super books" showing market depth across all venues; SMART ORDER-ROUTING algorithms send orders to the markets displaying the best quoted prices and sizes
• Behavioral response: traders filling large orders now search for liquidity across multiple venues AND across time to control market impact

cards.front: Electronic front runners versus electronic quote matchers: whose orders does each trade ahead of, and what is the quote matcher's main risk?
cards.back:
• Both are PARASITIC traders — speculators who predict prices from information about orders other traders intend, or will soon intend, to fill
• Front runners trade in front of traders who DEMAND liquidity: artificial-intelligence order-anticipation detects one large trader, or many small traders, working the same side, then they buy ahead of the buying and sell ahead of the selling
• Quote matchers trade in front of traders who SUPPLY liquidity: they "lean on" standing limit orders to exploit their option value — buying when they can rely on a standing bid to exit, selling when they can rely on a standing offer
• Quote matcher example: buy while a slow trader bids 20; if price rises they profit, if it falls they sell to the 20 bid and cap the loss
• Quote matcher's main risk: the standing order is unavailable when needed — it was filled by another trader or cancelled
• Exam triggers: "a repeating pattern of trades suggests someone is working a large order in pieces" = front running; "leaning on a standing limit order to limit losses" = quote matching

cards.front: Name the major types of electronic traders, and state what actually separates high-frequency traders from low-latency traders.
cards.back:
• Electronic dealers — post bids and offers, profiting on round trips at favorable net spreads; they run thin inventories, stop quoting a side at their inventory limit, and cancel quotes ahead of scheduled news to avoid supplying liquidity to faster traders
• Electronic news traders — subscribe to high-speed news feeds, parse releases against a stored consensus, and send marketable orders to execute against STALE orders; they can profit while being right only occasionally
• Electronic arbitrageurs — buy an undervalued instrument and sell a similar overvalued one; the two positions are the legs of the arbitrage portfolio
• Parasitic traders — front runners and quote matchers
• Buy-side traders — use order management systems and broker-supplied algorithms to work large orders; non-broker/dealers reach exchanges through brokers providing SPONSORED ACCESS
• HFT versus low-latency: the distinction is how OFTEN they trade. HFTs complete a round trip within a minute, often milliseconds, and may trade in and out over a thousand times a day in small size; low-latency traders (news traders, certain parasitic traders) may hold positions for a day or longer. The distinction is new, and many commentators call all fast traders HFTs

cards.front: You hide a large limit order to conceal your intentions. How can other electronic traders still find it, and exactly what do they learn?
cards.back:
• PINGING: submit a small immediate-or-cancel (IOC) limit order for only a few shares at the price being probed; if the ping trades, a hidden order is present at that price
• The IOC limit order is by far the most common order type in electronic markets precisely because it cancels instantly if it finds nothing, so it reveals no trade intentions
• A successful ping reveals the EXISTENCE of hidden liquidity but not its full size — size can only be discovered by trading with it
• Everyone subscribing to a complete trade feed that includes odd lots can see the result of someone else's ping; at almost all exchanges, however, only the pinger knows which SIDE the hidden liquidity is on
• Related leakage effects: flickering quotes (exposed limit orders submitted then cancelled within a second, so others see willingness to trade without the order standing) and leapfrog (when spreads are wide, a dealer instantly out-quotes an improved buy-side price, forcing the buy-side trader to improve again)
• Defense: randomize submission times and sizes, but note that sophisticated traders can still infer large orders from the inevitable price−volume relation they create

cards.front: Distinguish an advanced order, a trading tactic, and an algorithm, and give the curriculum's example of each.
cards.back:
• ADVANCED ORDER — generally a limit order whose limit price changes as market conditions change. Example: a pegged (floating) limit order keeping a bid two ticks below the current ask; the exchange or broker cancels and replaces it as the ask moves. It demands very low latency — too slow and it executes at an unfavorable price when prices drop, or loses queue position when prices rise
• TRADING TACTIC — a plan for executing one simple function that generally involves submitting MULTIPLE orders; the line between advanced orders and tactics is arbitrary. Example: sweeping every venue with IOC limit orders priced at the 20.01 midpoint (best bid 20.00, best offer 20.02) to uncover hidden limit orders, discretionary limit orders, and midspread orders resting in dark pools
• ALGORITHM — a programmed strategy for filling orders, combining simple, advanced and multiple orders. Example: a VWAP algorithm targeting the interval VWAP by participating in an equal fraction of volume throughout, trading more in historically high-volume periods (around the open and close) and less in quiet periods
• Algorithms break large orders into pieces submitted at randomized times, in randomized sizes, and sometimes to randomly chosen exchanges, to hide their common origin from front runners

cards.front: What are the three situations in which speed is valuable to an electronic trader, and how is low latency actually engineered?
cards.back:
• TAKING — reach an attractive trading opportunity before other traders; often only the first trader to arrive benefits
• MAKING — be first to post a better-priced quote so as to acquire TIME PRECEDENCE at that price, letting you trade sooner or at better prices
• CANCELLING — pull orders you no longer want filled once market events raise their option value (for example, large trades at your price on other exchanges)
• Latency = elapsed time between an event and a subsequent action that depends on it; the latency of a linear multi-step process is the SUM of its steps — learn of the event, decide, then send the instruction and have the exchange receive it
• Fast communications: collocation (servers in the exchange's own server room, with equal-length lines for fairness), line-of-sight microwave (just below light speed) in preference to fibre and copper (about two-thirds as fast), the fewest routers and switches, premium direct data feeds
• Fast computation: overclocked liquid-cooled processors, all data in memory rather than on disk, specialized processors, simple operating systems, hot routines written in assembler, and precomputed contingency tables of prearranged responses
• The key idea: little inherent value comes from being fast — the value lies in being FASTER than competitors
cards.mnemonic: Three needs for speed: Take, Make, Cancel.

cards.front: Name the four ways excessive orders from electronic traders create systemic risk, and the controls used against them.
cards.back:
• RUNAWAY ALGORITHMS — streams of unintended orders from programming mistakes; Knight Capital, 1 August 2012, sent millions of orders in 45 minutes when it intended to fill 212, producing 4 million executions in 397 stocks and a $400 million loss
• FAT FINGER ERRORS — a manual trader submits a larger order than intended; worse in electronic systems because of speed and no clerk to catch it
• OVERLARGE ORDERS — demanding more liquidity than the market can provide; the 6 May 2010 Flash Crash came from selling $4.1 billion of E-mini S&P 500 futures with an algorithm set to a fixed 9% of volume, which SPED UP as its own selling raised volume
• MALEVOLENT ORDER STREAMS — created deliberately to disrupt markets, by manipulators, aggrieved employees, or terrorists, including denial-of-service attacks on competitors' systems
• Controls: thorough software testing (exchanges run mock trading sessions); market access controls; developer access controls with all code read and vouched for by a second developer; real-time surveillance of order flow against preset volume/size parameters with automatic shut-off; broker surveillance of client orders and a ban on SPONSORED NAKED ACCESS; exchange price limits and trade halts; converting market orders into marketable limit orders
• Post-crash rule: a 5-minute halt if a stock moves more than 10% (large stocks) or 20% (smaller stocks), plus rules for when trades will be broken

cards.front: Which improper market ACTIVITIES and which manipulation STRATEGIES does real-time surveillance target, and what identifies each?
cards.back:
• FRONT RUNNING — buying ahead of anticipated purchases and selling ahead of anticipated sales. Illegal where the order information was improperly obtained (a tip from a broker handling a large order); LEGAL if properly obtained, for example by watching a market data feed. It raises costs for the front-run trader by taking liquidity they would have taken
• Improper activities: trading for market impact (deliberately moving prices, accepting big costs to change others' perceptions of value); rumormongering (spreading false information about values or others' intentions); wash trading (trades among COMMONLY CONTROLLED ACCOUNTS to fake activity and liquidity); spoofing, also called layering (EXPOSED STANDING LIMIT ORDERS placed to mislead, cancelled once the real hidden order fills)
• Strategies: bluffing (submitting orders and arranging trades to shift perceptions of value — the pump-and-dump preying on momentum traders, with "short and distort" as its mirror image); gunning the market (selling aggressively to push price down to a cluster of stop-loss sell orders, triggering them, then repurchasing lower); squeezing and cornering (gaining control of the resources needed to settle contracts, then withdrawing them so shorts must buy at exceptionally high prices)
• Exam triggers: exposed standing limit orders = spoofing; commonly controlled accounts = wash trading; neither, but orders and trades luring momentum traders = bluffing
• Enforcement is hard because prosecutors generally must prove SCIENTER — intent or knowledge of wrongdoing

cards.front: What ratio does a long-term institutional investor monitor against internal bands to control illiquidity, and what must be in the numerator?
cards.back:
• Invested capital = capital already drawn and at work in illiquid funds/assets (NAV); Uncalled commitments = capital committed but not yet called (drawn down at the GP's discretion on an unknown schedule); Total assets = fund AUM. Expressed as a percentage.
• When to use: step 1 of liquidity management, setting liquidity risk parameters. Investors set guidelines/bands on this sum, held internally or in a board-approved IPS, alongside rules on what percentage of assets must be liquid daily or monthly.
• Attached to it are automatic or semiautomatic escalation triggers: once the ratio hits a set level, reduce new commitments to illiquid asset classes or actively seek secondary sales.
• Classic error: tracking invested capital only. Ignoring uncalled commitments understates true illiquidity and leaves capital calls unfunded, since calls arrive exactly when markets are stressed.
• Committing too much creates severe liquidity risk; committing too little means never reaching the target allocation and falling short of return expectations.
cards.formula: Illiquidity exposure = (Invested capital + Uncalled commitments) ÷ Total assets
cards.mnemonic: Count the money you promised, not just the money you sent.

cards.front: State the denominator effect as a relationship, and explain why an unchanged private portfolio can breach an illiquidity limit without a single transaction.
cards.back:
• Illiquid asset NAV = appraisal-based/stale carrying value of private equity, private real estate, infrastructure; Total AUM = whole portfolio, marked mostly at live public prices.
• Denominator effect: in a downturn total AUM falls by a LARGER amount than the repricing of the illiquid asset classes, so the ratio soars even though the private book was never touched.
• Driver: illiquid assets carry stale pricing, appraisal-based valuations and a lagged response to public markets, so the numerator is slow and the denominator is fast.
• Consequences: breach of illiquidity guidelines, forced secondary sales at a significant price concession, and inability to rebalance or meet capital calls.
• Classic error: treating stale appraisal marks as current value, so the fund over-commits in good markets. Set the policy limit with a buffer below the maximum tolerable level.
cards.formula: Illiquid allocation % = Illiquid asset NAV ÷ Total AUM
cards.mnemonic: The numerator sleeps; the denominator crashes.

cards.front: Observed private equity returns show lower standard deviation and lower beta to public equity than public equity itself. Why is feeding those returns into a mean-variance optimizer a trap, and what are the fixes?
cards.back:
• Cause: illiquid asset classes are subject to stale pricing, appraisal-based valuations and a lagged response to public markets, so reported returns are SMOOTHED. This understates true volatility and understates correlation/beta with public markets.
• The trap: smoothed returns make observed Sharpe ratios of private classes look superior to public ones, so MVO systematically OVER-ALLOCATES to private assets. Appealing-looking numbers, not real risk reduction.
• Fix 1: use public market proxies in place of the private class (e.g., small-cap public equities as a proxy for private equity).
• Fix 2: unsmooth the observed returns to remove serial correlation. Geltner (1993) removes first-order serial correlation only; Okunev-White (2003) extends to higher-order; Getmansky, Lo and Makarov (2004) GLM assumes observed returns follow a moving-average process. After unsmoothing, volatility is HIGHER and beta to public equity is HIGHER.
• Residual problem: even with unsmoothed inputs, single-period MVO still fails, because it implicitly assumes weights are rebalanced perfectly and costlessly and it ignores the drawdown structure and cash flow uncertainty of illiquids. No widely accepted alternative exists, so most investors simply constrain the illiquid allocation in the optimization.
cards.mnemonic: Smooth returns, sharp mistake.

cards.front: Distinguish physical from transition climate risk: what drives each, how each hits an institutional portfolio, and what single tool the TCFD recommends for both?
cards.back:
PHYSICAL
• Acute: storms, floods, hurricanes, wildfires. Chronic: sea-level rise, drought, sustained extreme heat.
• Portfolio impact: permanent impairment of asset valuations, lower rents and yields on prime coastal real estate, accelerated depreciation of roads and rail from prolonged heat and so more frequent replacement cost, large drawdowns in asset value, and assets that become difficult or expensive to insure (most global flood losses are uninsured).
TRANSITION
• Drivers: carbon restrictions and carbon pricing, new technology, changed consumer behavior, policy such as the EU sustainable finance taxonomy. Anchors: to stay under 2 degrees C, energy-related CO2 must fall 25% by 2030 and reach net zero by 2070; the IEA says half of all cars must be electric by 2030 for 2050 carbon neutrality.
• Portfolio impact: massive disruption in electricity generation (renewables now cost-competitive with coal) and autos (ICE to EV), producing stranded assets. The PRI's Inevitable Policy Response forecasts a response by 2025 that is forceful, abrupt and disorderly because action was delayed, and argues markets have inefficiently priced this risk.
BOTH
• Tool: climate-related scenario analysis (e.g., a 2, 3 or 4 degree warmer world), which the TCFD recommends for banks, asset managers and asset owners; IEA and IPCC scenarios are widely used.
• Trap: the damage concentrates in what you cannot divest — real assets (real estate, infrastructure) and private equity.
cards.mnemonic: Physical = the weather hits you; Transition = the policy hits you.

cards.front: What is a "universal owner," and why can such an investor NOT diversify away negative environmental and social externalities?
cards.back:
• Universal owner: a large institutional investor (SWF, public pension fund) whose portfolio is so large, diversified and long-term that it effectively owns a slice of the whole economy, so it manages TOTAL market exposure rather than a subset of issuers.
• An externality is an impact a person's or corporation's activity has on a third party. Because the universal owner holds both sides, costs externalized by one portfolio company reduce the profitability of ANOTHER portfolio company, hurting overall portfolio return. Curriculum example: a plastics manufacturer saves treatment cost by releasing waste into a river; resulting water toxicity cuts productivity at downstream agricultural operations the same fund owns.
• Per the PRI, environmental costs reach portfolios through insurance premiums, taxes, inflated input prices, and the physical costs of weather-related disasters. Strengthening environmental regulation also brings fines and penalties on the polluter itself.
• Remediating environmental damage typically costs far more than preventing it, so the universal owner should internalize the price of externalities rather than assume diversification protects it.
• Scale of the systemic risk: the Grantham Institute/Vivid Economics study projected climate change could cut the value of global financial assets by as much as $24 trillion, far eclipsing the permanent damage of the 2007-09 crisis.
• Social issues (community relations, health and safety, data privacy, modern slavery in the supply chain, inequality) are harder than environmental issues to quantify and put into DCF models, because reported data are largely qualitative policies rather than performance metrics.
cards.mnemonic: If you own the whole economy, you also own the pollution.

cards.front: Three years in, a SWF's US$25 million (0.05% of assets) 35% stake in a frontier-market beverage maker faces: regional recession plus expected currency devaluation; import tariffs cut from 100% to 20%; a two-year statutory notice period blocking the planned 40-50% headcount cut; waste dumped into a biodiverse river; and shortened breaks with soap removed from restrooms. Which exposure dominates, and why does the tiny position size not make it immaterial?
cards.back:
• Reputational risk dominates. The financial loss cannot move the needle for the fund, but even a small investment can have an outsized negative impact if the risk is not managed. Headline risk is heightened precisely because the owner is a state fund: "Government of Ruritania Cuts Jobs in XYZ during a Recession." A conventional PE house can cut jobs for purely financial reasons; a SWF cannot.
• The non-financial exposures map to named issues: occupational health and safety (soap removed), labor standards (breaks halved, firings during a recession), and environmental waste management/biodiversity (river dumping, habitat of a rare reptile).
• The risks are not independent, they CHAIN: recession plus devaluation plus loss of the tariff advantage cut profits, management then cuts corners on waste and labor to protect margin, and that produces the environmental and social breaches that create the reputational damage.
• Why it cannot simply be sold: a 35% minority stake in an unlisted company is illiquid and control is limited, unlike a public-equity holding that can be exited within the hour. Influence must run through the two board seats and the incentive structure.
• Evaluation point: social and reputational risks are generally difficult to manage even once identified, because they resist quantification and integration into financial models, and best practice requires considering the interests of all stakeholders.
cards.mnemonic: Small ticket, big headline.

cards.front: List the methods available to manage the risks of a large, long-horizon DIRECT investment, in the order they should be applied.
cards.back:
• BEFORE investing (the most important stage, because exit is slow): quantify each identified risk with scenario analysis presenting base, optimistic and pessimistic cases (the airport's 15% base-case IRR fell to roughly 10-11% on the low-traffic case and about 13% under cost overruns and delays), and agree a conditional action plan plus the hedging tools to be used if bad outcomes materialize.
• Structure and contract: fixed-price construction contract passing delay and quality penalties down to the contractor; non-recourse project finance debt; concession agreement with quality/performance standards, default and termination terms, and break clauses; a debt-service reserve to absorb a revenue stoppage.
• Hedge: hedge the interest rate exposure on borrowings against higher-than-forecast rates; manage frontier currency risk by contracting in USD (airport charges collected in USD via IATA, commercial pricing set in USD, debt denominated in USD) since frontier currencies are costly or impossible to hedge.
• Active ownership: take board seats, monitor closely, and reset management incentives away from pure profit so they stop cutting corners; engage to end harmful practices and educate the local community.
• Adaptation, not mitigation, for physical climate risk: a small nation cannot move the global needle, so design for 1-in-50 and 1-in-100 year flood scenarios, upgrade drainage, and support a government-led storm-surge barrier. Do not be seen dodging a climate tax.
• Negotiate with government where regulation is the binding constraint (e.g., rigid labor law risking the whole business).
• Plan an exit path with a deadline: engage, lobby, allow about a year, then seek an exit or hand the asset to a team suited to distressed situations. R-SWF ultimately sold its 35% stake for $27 million to an international beverage exporter, for which local production was a natural FX hedge.
cards.mnemonic: Model it, contract it, hedge it, sit on the board, adapt, then exit.

cards.front: Evaluate the ERM process of a SWF whose investment committee devoted a full meeting to the risks of two small direct deals, identified many risk factors, and voted: name the strength, the weaknesses, and the recommended improvements.
cards.back:
STRENGTH
• The fund dedicated an entire internal investment committee meeting to identifying and discussing the potential risks of two relatively SMALL opportunities.
• Ample time was given for senior management to voice concerns and debate mitigation strategies; a range of risk factors was surfaced and a formal vote was taken on each investment.
WEAKNESSES
• Too little effort went into QUANTIFYING the various risks. Identification without measurement.
• No agreement on the specific ACTIONS to be taken if those risks materialized.
• Scenario analysis was thin: the team, supported by the Head of Risk, should have presented a base case, an optimistic case and a pessimistic case for BOTH investments.
• No risk-mitigation action plan or hedging toolkit was settled before the money went in.
• Because both deals were small and carried limited financial and liquidity implications for the fund, too little consideration was given to reputational and ESG risks, which is exactly where the damage later came from.
RECOMMENDATIONS
• Run full three-case scenario analysis on each investment pre-commitment.
• Pre-agree a conditional action plan and hedging tools triggered by defined bad outcomes.
• Extend risk identification and assessment explicitly to reputational and ESG exposures, regardless of position size.
cards.mnemonic: They named the risks but never priced them, planned for them, or looked past the money.

cards.front: Performance evaluation has three components. Name each, the question it answers, and how they build on one another.
cards.back:
