• Performance MEASUREMENT — what was the portfolio's performance? Calculates portfolio and benchmark returns (absolute return, and excess return vs the benchmark) and the risk taken, both ex post (e.g., standard deviation of past returns) and ex ante (e.g., VaR).
• Performance ATTRIBUTION — how was the performance achieved? Decomposes absolute or relative return (and risk) into the active decisions that produced it.
• Performance APPRAISAL — was it skill or luck? Uses the risk, return and attribution results to judge the quality of performance; if superior results come from skill, they are more likely to repeat.
• They build in sequence: measurement is the foundation, attribution explains it, appraisal draws on both — a key feedback loop into the investment process.
• Exam trap: "measures excess performance" = measurement, not attribution; "distinguishes skill from luck" = appraisal, not attribution.

cards.front: List the four things an effective performance attribution process must do.
cards.back:
• Account for ALL of the portfolio's return or risk exposure — it must reconcile to the total; an unexplained residual makes the attribution incomplete at best and suspect at worst.
• Reflect the investment decision-making process.
• Quantify the active decisions of the portfolio manager.
• Provide a complete understanding of the excess return/risk of the portfolio.
• Curriculum illustration: for a genuine bottom-up stock picker who ignores sector benchmark weights, measuring sector allocation effects measures nothing he decided — sector effects are merely a byproduct.
• Note: intraday transaction data improves attribution but is NOT required; a returns- or holdings-based analysis can still be effective.

cards.front: Contrast return attribution with risk attribution, and macro with micro return attribution — what does each decompose, and at whose level?
cards.back:
Return vs risk:
• Return attribution — the impact of active decisions on RETURN (in practice "performance attribution" usually means this).
• Risk attribution — the RISK consequences of those same decisions. Absolute mandates: sources of portfolio volatility. Benchmark-relative mandates: sources of tracking risk. It may be run on an absolute OR a relative basis, and it captures no return impact.
Macro vs micro:
• Macro — the fund sponsor's / asset owner's decisions: tactical deviation from the strategic asset allocation and manager selection, including "gaps" where the sum of managers' benchmarks differs from the benchmark index.
• Micro — the individual portfolio manager's allocation and selection decisions and their impact on total fund performance.
• Trap: analysis "at the portfolio level" is not automatically micro — what defines it is whose decisions are being evaluated.

cards.front: Rank returns-based, holdings-based and transactions-based attribution by data required and accuracy, and state when each is used.
cards.back:
• RETURNS-BASED — uses only total portfolio returns to identify return-generating components. Easiest to implement, LEAST accurate, most vulnerable to data manipulation. Use when holdings are not available at sufficient frequency/detail (e.g., hedge funds).
• HOLDINGS-BASED — uses beginning-of-period holdings (monthly, weekly or daily; shorter intervals improve accuracy, longer periods are linked). Misses transactions made during the period, so it may NOT reconcile to the actual return; that residual is a timing or trading effect. Best for low-turnover/passive strategies; improved by pricing the portfolio with the same prices used for the index.
• TRANSACTIONS-BASED — uses holdings AND all purchases and sales, including transaction costs. MOST accurate but the most difficult and time-consuming; the entire excess return is explained, the return reconciles to what the client is shown, and it doubles as an error-diagnostic tool.
• Choice depends on data availability and quality, client reporting requirements, and complexity of the decision-making process.

cards.front: State the three Brinson-Hood-Beebower (BHB) sector attribution formulas, and what each effect measures.
cards.back:
• w_i = portfolio weight in sector i; W_i = benchmark weight in sector i; R_i = portfolio return in sector i; B_i = benchmark return in sector i. Weights are percentages summing to 100% (leverage/shorts enter as negative weights); single period, single currency.
• A_i = allocation: value added by weighting a sector differently from the benchmark. S_i = selection: value added by holding different securities within the sector. I_i = interaction: the combined effect of the two decisions.
• Summed across sectors, A + S + I = the arithmetic excess return (R − B). Curriculum example: −1.4% + 3.2% + 0.1% = 1.9% = 10.1% − 8.2%.
• Use when the manager's process really is sector allocation plus within-sector selection.
• Classic errors: using the PORTFOLIO weight in the selection term (it must be the BENCHMARK weight W_i), and dropping interaction so the effects fail to reconcile to the excess return.
cards.formula: A_i = (w_i − W_i) × B_i ; S_i = W_i × (R_i − B_i) ; I_i = (w_i − W_i) × (R_i − B_i)

cards.front: How does the Brinson-Fachler allocation term differ from BHB, and what defect does it repair?
cards.back:
• B = the TOTAL benchmark return; all other symbols as in BHB. Only the allocation term changes — selection and interaction are identical, and the total portfolio allocation effect is unchanged (it still equals B_S − B).
• Defect in BHB: overweighting any sector with a positive return produces a positive allocation effect even when that sector LAGS the overall benchmark (B_i < B), and overweighting a negative-return sector always scores negative even when it beat the overall benchmark.
• BF fix: an overweight is rewarded only if the sector beat the total benchmark; an underweight is rewarded only if the sector lagged it.
• Curriculum numbers (B = 8.2%): health care (30% − 20%) × (−2.0% − 8.2%) = −1.02% (BHB gave only −0.2%); financials (20% − 30%) × (12% − 8.2%) = −0.38% (BHB gave −1.2%); both total −1.4%.
• Classic error: multiplying by the portfolio weight w_i instead of the ACTIVE weight (w_i − W_i).
cards.formula: A_i (Brinson-Fachler) = (w_i − W_i) × (B_i − B)

cards.front: The same portfolio and period give one report showing good country allocation with poor selection, and another showing poor sector allocation with strong selection. What is happening, and what is the lesson?
cards.back:
• Nothing is wrong with the arithmetic — both decompositions reconcile to the same excess return. Curriculum eurozone example: portfolio 8.3% vs benchmark 7.45% (+0.85%). Country framework: allocation +1.20%, selection + interaction −0.35%. Sector framework: allocation −2.30%, selection + interaction +3.15%.
• The split between "allocation" and "selection" is an artifact of the decomposition you choose, not a fact about the manager.
• Lesson: build the attribution around the manager's actual decision-making process (country-allocation process → country level; sector process → sector level; pure stock picker → security level, where "allocation" measures security weighting and the selection term captures transaction costs and timing).
• Reading effects from a framework the manager does not use produces a confident but wrong verdict on skill.

cards.front: Reading an exposure-decomposition fixed-income attribution: which effects are reported, and what does the sign of each tell you?
cards.back:
• DURATION effect — return from an aggregate duration different from the benchmark's. Curriculum: −62 bps, because the portfolio ran 8.17 duration vs the benchmark's 7.19 while yields rose.
• CURVE effect — where along the curve the duration bets were placed. +52 bps with an overweight to the long end implies the yield curve FLATTENED.
• Total interest rate allocation = duration + curve (−10 bps).
• SECTOR allocation — −23 bps from overweighting corporates (60% vs 45%) while credit spreads widened (benchmark corporate returns below government returns in every duration bucket).
• BOND SELECTION — +13 bps from holding non-benchmark bonds.
• Effects sum to the −20 bps total (−5.03% portfolio vs −4.83% benchmark).
• In the duration-based yield-curve decomposition the columns are yield, roll, shift, slope, curvature, spread, specific and RESIDUAL; the residual exists because duration and convexity only approximate the true price change, and it grows with large yield moves.
• Candidates must INTERPRET, not calculate, fixed-income attribution.

cards.front: How do you select a risk attribution approach? State the two questions and the prescribed method for each combination.
cards.back:
Ask: (1) is risk measured relative to a benchmark or in absolute terms? (2) is the decision process bottom up, top down, or factor based?
• Bottom up + RELATIVE → each position's marginal contribution to tracking risk (× its active weight = that position's contribution to TR).
• Bottom up + ABSOLUTE → each position's marginal contribution to total risk (the change in portfolio standard deviation from a slight increase in the holding).
• Top down + RELATIVE → attribute tracking risk to the relative allocation and selection decisions.
• Factor based + RELATIVE → each factor's marginal contribution to tracking risk and active specific risk.
• Factor based or top down + ABSOLUTE → each factor's marginal contribution to total risk and specific risk (the curriculum applies this to a top-down sector-timing manager hedging market risk with a T-bills + 300 bps target).
• Overriding principle: risk attribution must mirror the investment decision-making process, and it only says WHERE risk was introduced — pair it with return attribution to judge whether the risk was rewarded.

cards.front: In a multi-level attribution of a pension fund, which results belong to the asset owner (fund sponsor) and which to the investment manager?
cards.back:
• ASSET OWNER (macro attribution): the strategic asset allocation, tactical deviations from it, and the decision of which managers to hire. In the BF framework run at the sponsor level, ALLOCATION = the sponsor's over/underweight vs its own strategic benchmark, and SELECTION + INTERACTION = did the hired managers beat their assigned benchmarks.
• MANAGER (micro attribution): the allocation and selection decisions taken inside the mandate, measured against the manager's own benchmark.
• Curriculum computation: allocation = (78% − 75%)[0.32 − (−0.03)] = 0.01 for overweighting value; selection + interaction = 75%(0.99 − 0.32) + (78% − 75%)(0.99 − 0.32) = 0.52. Total fund +0.98, of which +0.94 came from selection and only +0.04 from allocation — the hired managers, not the sponsor's tilts, drove the result.
• The two verdicts can diverge: in the fund-of-funds case both products roughly matched their benchmarks (A −16 bps, B +39 bps) while the strategist's allocation caused the shortfall — the right action was to replace the strategist, not the managers.

cards.front: What is a liability-based benchmark, when is it used, and why is a cap-weighted bond index usually wrong for a DB pension plan?
cards.back:
• It focuses on the CASH FLOWS the assets must generate rather than on a market's return. Used most often when assets must fund a specific future liability (defined benefit pension), so the sponsor can track progress to fully funded status, or once fully funded, track assets against changes in liabilities. A portfolio can beat a market index and still fail to meet its liabilities.
• A cap-weighted index is typically unsuitable: its duration is usually SHORTER than plan liabilities, and it is often heavily weighted to short-maturity corporates, carrying more credit risk than the plan wants.
• Alternatives: a well-diversified portfolio of individual bonds that minimizes idiosyncratic risk, or LDI indexes (e.g., the Bloomberg Barclays LDI Index Series of six investible indexes) — though a benchmark built for the specific plan describes its liability structure better.
• Liability drivers to check: average years to retirement, % of workforce retired, life expectancy, inflation indexing, early-retirement option, sponsor's ability to raise contributions, correlation of plan assets with the sponsor's operating assets (lower is better), and going-concern status. Younger workforce → more equities; more inflation indexing → more real-return bonds.

cards.front: Name the seven types of asset-based benchmarks and the defining feature of each.
cards.back:
• ABSOLUTE (target) return — a minimum return to beat: a stated rate, a spread over an index or risk-free rate, or an actuarial rate. Typical for market-neutral long-short funds (e.g., 3-month T-bill plus a spread) and private equity.
• BROAD MARKET INDEX — asset-class performance (MSCI World, JP Morgan EMBI); well known, readily available, widely reported.
• STYLE INDEX — a segment within an asset class (Russell 1000 Growth, Russell 2000 Value).
• FACTOR-MODEL-BASED — portfolio returns regressed on chosen factors; suits a manager who times exposures to systematic risks.
• RETURNS-BASED (Sharpe style analysis) — an optimization on style-index returns with sensitivities constrained to be non-negative and to sum to 1; treats style as a continuum (e.g., 60% small value / 40% small growth).
• MANAGER UNIVERSE (peer group) — median-manager comparison; not truly a benchmark: members are not substitutable, rankings move on other managers' actions, and it encourages herding around the median.
• CUSTOM SECURITY-BASED (strategy) — built with the manager to mirror the real process and client restrictions, rebalanced periodically; best when no index fits, but costly to build and maintain.

cards.front: List the seven properties of a valid benchmark (Bailey and Tierney) with a one-line test for each.
cards.back:
• UNAMBIGUOUS — the individual securities and their weights are clearly identifiable.
• INVESTABLE — you could replicate and hold it passively to earn its return (at least gross of expenses); the sponsor must have a real passive alternative. A frequently rebalanced cap-weighted bond index often FAILS this.
• MEASURABLE — its return can be calculated on a reasonably frequent and timely basis (e.g., published daily).
• APPROPRIATE — consistent with the manager's style or area of expertise. A benchmark holding foreign bonds for a domestic-only fund, or one ignoring client cap/liquidity constraints, fails here.
• REFLECTIVE OF CURRENT INVESTMENT OPINIONS — the manager knows the constituents and their factor exposures and can form views on them; not a mandate of obscure securities.
• SPECIFIED IN ADVANCE — constructed before the evaluation period, never after the fact.
• ACCOUNTABLE — the manager accepts ownership of the benchmark and agrees to be held to it; the sponsor then owns any gap between the fund's target portfolio and the benchmark.
cards.mnemonic: SAMURAI — Specified in advance, Appropriate, Measurable, Unambiguous, Reflective of current investment opinions, Accountable, Investable

cards.front: Decompose portfolio return into market, style and active components, and give the two empirical correlation tests of benchmark quality.
cards.back:
• P = portfolio return, B = benchmark return, M = broad market index return. S = style return (benchmark minus market); A = active management return (portfolio minus benchmark); E = P − M, the portfolio's return relative to the market.
• Worked: P 5.6%, B 5.1%, M 3.2% → S = 1.9%, A = 0.5%. And P 18.9%, B 21.7%, M 25.2% → S = −3.5% (value out of favor), A = −2.8% (weak within style).
• Test 1 — no systematic bias: the correlation between A and S should NOT be statistically different from zero. A non-zero correlation says the manager's active decisions simply track whichever style the market currently favors.
• Test 2 — style captured: the correlation between S and E should be statistically significant and POSITIVE, since when the manager's style is in (out of) favor both the benchmark and the account should beat (lag) the market.
• Classic error: benchmarking to a broad market index, which forces S to be assumed zero — any real style return is then dumped into measured A, obscuring true value added.
• Related point (a different Bailey et al. quality test): for hedge funds, both broad market indexes and risk-free-plus-a-spread are weakly correlated or uncorrelated with fund returns, so they fail the test that portfolio and benchmark factor sensitivities be similar.
cards.formula: P = M + S + A, where S = B − M (style) and A = P − B (active); also E = P − M

cards.front: Define true and misfit active return, then compute both for: manager 18.0%, investor's benchmark (MSCI Pacific) 20.0%, normal portfolio (MSCI Japan) 9.0%.
cards.back:
• The NORMAL PORTFOLIO is the portfolio that most closely represents the manager's typical positions in his investment universe.
• True active = 18.0 − 9.0 = +9.0%. Misfit active = 9.0 − 20.0 = −11.0%. Measured active = 18.0 − 20.0 = −2.0% = 9.0 + (−11.0).
• Read: the manager genuinely beat his own universe by 900 bps, yet appears to have lost 200 bps because the sponsor benchmarked a Japan manager against a five-market Pacific index.
• Reverse case: manager 15%, Russell 3000 10%, normal portfolio 18% — looks like +5% of value added but is really −3%.
• Why it matters: misspecification corrupts BOTH analyses — attribution would labor to explain an underperformance that never happened, and appraisal misjudges skill. Using a broad market index typically misses the manager's style and creates the misfit (style bias).
• Also unethical in practice: underperforming managers switching benchmarks to improve measured excess return; and peer-group benchmarks push managers to herd around the median.
cards.formula: True active return = Manager return − Normal portfolio return ; Misfit active return = Normal portfolio return − Investor's benchmark return ; Investor's (measured) active return = True + Misfit

cards.front: Why are alternative investments hard to benchmark? Give the general causes, then the specific limitations of hedge fund peer universes.
cards.back:
General causes: no high-quality investible market indexes; frequent use of leverage; limited liquidity and no readily available market values; and the use of internal rates of return instead of time-weighted returns.
Hedge funds: strategies vary enormously, the investment universe can be unlimited, allocations shift over time, and funds use leverage, shorts and derivatives — so no single standard fits, and broad market indexes are unsuitable. Risk-free plus a 3%–6% spread is sometimes used for arbitrage strategies, but most such funds retain systematic risk (magnified by leverage), so the spread should be raised. Both broad indexes and the risk-free rate are weakly or uncorrelated with hedge fund returns, failing the quality test that portfolio and benchmark factor sensitivities be similar.
Peer universe limits: (1) a strategy peer group is unlikely to represent any single fund's approach; (2) survivorship AND backfill bias (the provider imports a new member's entire history); (3) data are self-reported and unverified, and illiquid holdings are appraised or stale-priced, so standard deviations are biased DOWNWARD and correlations are unstable — which can lead to oversized allocations.
Other classes: real estate — appraisal-based, smoothed, lagging values, mixed leverage, open-end funds use TWR while closed-end funds use IRR. Private equity — IRRs swayed by an early win or loss and by differing valuation methods; PME methodologies (Long-Nickels, PME+, Kaplan-Schoar, Direct Alpha) compare them with public indexes. Commodities — futures-based, and cap weighting is impossible because every long position has a matching short.

cards.front: State the Sortino ratio and its denominator, and say when it beats the Sharpe ratio.
cards.back:
• MAR (r_T) = minimum acceptable return, also called the target return — the lowest return at which the investor will invest. It is investor-specific (it may be set to expected inflation for real capital preservation, or to the benchmark return), which makes cross-sectional comparison of Sortino ratios difficult.
• σ_D = target semideviation (target semi-standard deviation): square only the shortfalls below the MAR, but divide by N, the TOTAL number of periods — not by the number of shortfall periods. That is the classic error.
• Worked: MAR 4%, mean return 6% over 10 years, Σ of squared shortfalls = 0.0094 → σ_D = (0.0094 ÷ 10)^0.5 = 3.07%, Sortino = 2.0 ÷ 3.07 ≈ 0.65.
• Use it when returns are not symmetric — the Sharpe ratio penalizes upside and downside volatility equally and cannot separate positively skewed strategies (trend following) from negatively skewed ones (option writing) — or when capital preservation is a primary objective.
• It is not a risk premium; it is return above what is minimally acceptable to the investor.
• Exam move: invert it to back out the denominator, e.g., target semideviation = (8.20% − 5.00%) ÷ 0.87 = 3.68%.
cards.formula: Sortino = (mean R_p − MAR) ÷ σ_D , where σ_D = square root of [ Σ min(r_t − MAR, 0)^2 ÷ N ]

cards.front: State the appraisal ratio, what its denominator is, and which risk measure sits in the denominator of each rival ratio.
cards.back:
• AR (Treynor-Black ratio) = annualized alpha ÷ annualized RESIDUAL (non-systematic) risk, both taken from a factor regression; σ_ε is the standard error of the regression. It measures the reward of active management per unit of the risk of active management.
• Worked: R_p 9%, σ_p 20%, R_M 8%, σ_M 12%, β 1.40, r_f 3% → α = 9 − [3 + 1.40(8 − 3)] = −1.0%; σ_ε^2 = 0.20^2 − 1.40^2(0.12^2) = 0.011776 → σ_ε = 10.85%; AR = −0.01 ÷ 0.1085 ≈ −0.0922.
• Denominators to keep straight: Sharpe = TOTAL risk (σ_p), and it can be compared across funds without choosing a market benchmark; Treynor = SYSTEMATIC risk (β), meaningful mainly when the fund is one sleeve of a fully diversified portfolio; Information ratio = TRACKING risk, IR = [E(r_p) − E(r_B)] ÷ σ(r_p − r_B); Appraisal ratio = RESIDUAL risk.
• Classic errors: dividing alpha by total risk or by tracking error, and forgetting that Treynor and AR both need an appropriate market benchmark, so benchmark misspecification flows straight through.
cards.formula: AR = α ÷ σ_ε , with α = R_p − [r_f + β_p(R_M − r_f)] and σ_ε^2 = σ_p^2 − (β_p^2 × σ_M^2)

cards.front: Give the upside, downside and overall capture ratio formulas, and say what each level signals.
cards.back:
• R(m,t) = manager return, R(B,t) = benchmark return; the up and down periods are split by the sign of the BENCHMARK return, and the captures are computed from the GEOMETRIC average return over each set of periods.
• Upside capture above (below) 100% generally suggests outperformance (underperformance); downside capture below (above) 100% generally suggests outperformance (underperformance).
• CR > 1 = positive asymmetry, a CONVEX return profile (analogous to bond convexity or option gamma); CR < 1 = negative asymmetry, a concave profile.
• Worked: UC = 0.51% ÷ 0.70% = 72.8%, DC = −0.70% ÷ −1.17% = 59.8%, CR = 121.7% — note an upside capture BELOW 100% can still give an attractive capture ratio. Also 0.66 ÷ 0.50 = 1.32 → convex.
• Profile table: long only 100/100 = 1.0; positive asymmetry 75/25 = 3.0; low beta 50/50 = 1.0; negative asymmetry 25/75 = 0.3.
• Trap: when manager and benchmark returns have OPPOSITE signs the ratio turns negative — a manager at +1% while the benchmark is −1% has a downside capture of −100%.
• Caution: convexity from rolling out-of-the-money puts is a property of the strategy, not evidence of skill.
cards.formula: UC = R(m,t) ÷ R(B,t) when R(B,t) ≥ 0 ; DC = R(m,t) ÷ R(B,t) when R(B,t) < 0 ; CR = UC ÷ DC

cards.front: Define maximum drawdown and drawdown duration, and explain why drawdowns matter more than symmetric volatility.
cards.back:
• Drawdown = the cumulative peak-to-trough loss during a continuous period of negative returns; maximum drawdown is the deepest such loss.
• Drawdown DURATION = the total time from the start of the drawdown until the cumulative drawdown recovers to zero, split into the drawdown phase (start to trough) and the recovery phase (trough back to zero).
• Curriculum S&P 500 example: drawdown begins January 2020 (−0.04%), reaches a maximum of −19.6% in March 2020, recovers by July 2020 → 7 months total duration with a 4-month recovery.
• Why it matters: percentage gains are computed on a smaller base, so losses need proportionally larger gains to reverse — a −50% decline requires +100% to get back. Limiting drawdowns can deliver better absolute AND risk-adjusted results (the 50% low-beta profile fell only 18.8% vs 42.5% long-only over Jan 2000–Sep 2002).
• Suitability: investors with shorter horizons, lower risk capacity or a tendency to overreact should favor shallower, shorter drawdowns; drawdowns are also stress tests of the manager's process, construction and risk management.
• Trap: a −24% maximum drawdown with a 4-month duration over 10 years means the portfolio recovered QUICKLY — it is not an average loss.
cards.formula: Maximum DD(m,t) = min( [V(m,t) − V(m,t*)] ÷ V(m,t*) , 0 ), where V(m,t*) is the prior peak value and t > t*

cards.front: A manager posts the highest Sharpe ratio in her peer group over three years. Why is that alone not evidence of skill?
cards.back:
• Appraisal measures are returns-based and backward-looking, built on limited data that is subject to error; a short record cannot separate skill from luck, and a long track record is needed for any statistical confidence.
• The Sharpe ratio assumes symmetric, normally distributed returns and penalizes upside and downside volatility equally, so it cannot distinguish a positively skewed strategy (trend following) from a negatively skewed one (option writing).
• Smoothed, stale or appraisal-based pricing (typical of alternatives) biases standard deviations DOWNWARD and flatters any volatility-based ratio.
• Ratios that need a market benchmark (Treynor, appraisal ratio) or a strategy benchmark (information ratio) inherit any benchmark misspecification; Sharpe at least needs no market benchmark choice.
• Each ratio answers a different question — Treynor is informative only if the fund will sit inside a fully diversified portfolio — so the measure must match the investor's risk tolerance, horizon and the investment process.
• Paradox of skill: as aggregate manager skill rises, performance differentials narrow and a greater share of what remains is luck.
• Conclusion: no single ratio suffices — use several tools that agree, plus qualitative work on process, goals and fees.

cards.front: Set out the steps for judging whether outperformance reflects skill, using the case of Manager A (9.42% vs a 9.25% benchmark over five years).
cards.back:
1. Define skill: the ability to add value on a RISK-ADJUSTED basis through investment analysis and insight — not a high raw return.
2. Run attribution to see HOW the 17 bps arose: allocation −43 bps (overweighting Australia cost 24 bps because it lagged the total benchmark, 4.10% vs 9.25%; underweighting Japan cost 21 bps because it beat it, 12.40% vs 9.25%) against selection + interaction of +59 bps (Japan +47, Australia +31, Hong Kong SAR −18). Verdict so far: a good stock picker, a poor country allocator.
3. Run appraisal ratios against peers with the SAME benchmark over the SAME period: Manager A's Sharpe (0.68) trails the benchmark (0.73) and Manager B (0.76) because her volatility is higher (10.83 vs 9.76), but she has the best Treynor (0.35) and information ratio (0.43), plus a Sortino of 0.82.
4. Test consistency with the stated process: are country allocations an intended part of her approach or a byproduct of stock selection? Penalize only the decisions the process actually claims to make (the same logic applies to a factor tilt — a value tilt that pays off is skill only if the process calls for it).
5. Qualify the conclusion: five years is a small sample of possible outcomes. Add risk attribution and ex ante analysis, plus qualitative work (interviews, goals, fees). Use multiple tools that agree, and state conclusions with prudence — here, skill worthy of further analysis, not proof.

cards.front: A manager search and selection process has three broad components. Name them, say what the qualitative component splits into, and list the key aspects under each half.
cards.back:
• UNIVERSE — the feasible set of managers that fit the portfolio need: suitability for the IPS, style, active vs passive
• QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS — the performance track record: attribution and appraisal, capture ratio, drawdown
• QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS — two halves:
  – Investment due diligence: philosophy, process, people, portfolio
  – Operational due diligence: process and procedures, firm, investment vehicle, terms, monitoring
• Underlying assumption: a consistent, robust process generates a similar return distribution relative to risk factors through time
• Quantitative tells you what happened; investment DD asks whether it is repeatable; operational DD asks whether the back office safeguards assets and issues accurate, timely reports and whether the firm will stay in business
• Exam trap: philosophy and people belong to INVESTMENT due diligence, while procedures, back office, key-employee compensation, vehicle and terms belong to OPERATIONAL due diligence
cards.mnemonic: U-Q-Q: Universe, Quantitative, Qualitative (= investment DD + operational DD)

cards.front: How is the manager universe defined, and what are the four ways a manager can be assigned to a benchmark or strategy category?
cards.back:
Objective: reduce the universe to a size your time and resources can evaluate — balancing too narrow a search (excludes interesting managers) against too broad a search (little gain in narrowing the list).
• THIRD-PARTY CATEGORIZATION — database, software provider or consultant sector assignment; easy and efficient, but the provider's definition may differ from the desired portfolio role, so understand their criteria
• RETURNS-BASED STYLE ANALYSIS — exposures from the actual return series; objective, but adds computational effort and carries the limits of returns-based analysis
• HOLDINGS-BASED STYLE ANALYSIS — estimates CURRENT factor exposures; more effort and depends on the timing and amount of transparency
• MANAGER EXPERIENCE — judgment built from observing the manager's portfolios and returns over time
• A HYBRID is recommended: build the initial universe from third-party categories, then refine with quantitative methods and experience
• The screening at this stage should AVOID performance — focus on the risk profile and the role the manager will fill
• The IPS and the reason for the search (new strategy, added capacity, replacement) set both the universe and the benchmark; the universe is not static

cards.front: With the null hypothesis that the manager is NOT skillful, define Type I and Type II errors in hiring and continuation decisions, and give the cost of each.
cards.back:
• TYPE I (false positive — rejecting a true null): hiring or retaining a manager who SUBSEQUENTLY UNDERPERFORMS expectations → an explicit cost (fees paid for no value added)
• TYPE II (false negative — failing to reject a false null): NOT hiring, or FIRING, a manager who subsequently outperforms or performs IN LINE WITH expectations → an opportunity cost
• Grid: Hire/Retain × below expectations = Type I; Not hire/Fire × at or above expectations = Type II; the other two cells are correct decisions
• Both errors can occur at any hiring or firing decision; the decision maker must choose which error they prefer given the expected benefits and costs of changing managers
• Expected cost of the errors depends on the size, shape, mean and dispersion of the skilled and unskilled return distributions: the SMALLER the difference in means and the WIDER the dispersion, the SMALLER the expected cost — so more efficient markets imply a lower cost of hiring an unskilled manager and a lower opportunity cost of missing a skilled one
cards.mnemonic: Type I = I hired the wrong one; Type II = the one that got away

cards.front: Decision makers systematically worry more about Type I than Type II errors. Give the three reasons why — and the monitoring remedy for a pattern of Type II errors.
cards.back:
Why Type I dominates attention:
• REGRET — Type I errors create explicit costs, Type II errors only opportunity costs, and people put less weight on opportunity costs, so Type I is psychologically more painful
• MEASURABILITY — Type I errors are straightforward to measure and are often linked directly to the decision maker's compensation; the cost of a manager not hired is rarely measured, so its link to pay is weak
• TRANSPARENCY — Type I errors are visible to investors and must be explained; firing or passing on a skilled manager is invisible unless the investor tracks fired managers or evaluates the universe themselves
The trap: fear of Type I drives decisions based on short-term performance (trend following) and reveals behavioral biases such as regret and loss aversion.
Remedy: monitor not only managers currently held but also managers EVALUATED AND NOT HIRED and managers FIRED — ask what factors differentiate them, whether those factors are consistent with your own investment philosophy and process, and what value the retain/fire decisions added.
• Evidence: plan-sponsor products receiving contributions subsequently underperformed those experiencing withdrawals (over $170 billion lost in the period studied)

cards.front: Contrast returns-based (RBSA) and holdings-based (HBSA) style analysis on approach, data, accuracy, and the weakness of each.
cards.back:
• RBSA — TOP-DOWN: estimates the portfolio's sensitivities to security market indexes representing distinct factors, from the return series
  – Advantages: data are easy to acquire (returns only); comparable across managers and through time; OBJECTIVE and not subject to window dressing; estimable even for complicated strategies; available as soon as returns are
  – Weakness: an IMPRECISE tool — it attributes performance to an UNCHANGING AVERAGE portfolio over the period, so it cannot capture dynamic decisions and may not reflect current or future exposures
• HBSA — BOTTOM-UP: estimates risk exposures from the actual securities held at a point in time
  – Advantages: gives CURRENT factor exposures, accurate, identifies the important return and risk drivers, comparable across managers and through time
  – Weaknesses: a point-in-time SNAPSHOT (poor for high-turnover strategies); potentially subject to WINDOW DRESSING; needs position-level transparency, which hedge funds, PE and VC may not give; effort rises with strategy complexity; easiest for equities and ETFs
• Common to both: stale pricing of illiquid holdings UNDERSTATES risk exposure, and timeliness is set by the securities that take longest to price
• Use: style analysis is most useful for strategies holding publicly traded, frequently priced securities; track results over time — exposures out of line with the stated style signal STYLE DRIFT, and results inconsistent with the stated philosophy and process suggest the process is not repeatable or is inconsistently implemented

cards.front: State the capture ratio and interpret upside capture, downside capture, and the ratio itself.
cards.back:
• UC (upside capture) = capture measured over periods when the BENCHMARK return is POSITIVE; UC greater than 100% suggests outperformance relative to the benchmark
• DC (downside capture) = capture measured when the BENCHMARK return is NEGATIVE; DC less than 100% generally suggests outperformance
• CR = UC ÷ DC measures the ASYMMETRY of return; CR greater than 1 indicates greater participation in rising than in falling markets
• Units: captures are percentages of the benchmark's move; CR is a pure number
• Curriculum profiles: long only 100%/100% = 1.0; low beta 50%/50% = 1.0; positive asymmetry 75%/25% = 3.0; negative asymmetry 25%/75% = 0.3
• Use: assess suitability against the IPS, especially the investor's time horizon and risk tolerance — a manager whose relative performance is worse in downturns has CR less than 1
• Classic errors: reading a high upside capture alone as skill (UC 75% with DC 125% means the manager underperforms whether the benchmark is up OR down), and treating equal CRs as equal managers — long only and low beta both score 1.0 with very different risk
cards.formula: CR = UC ÷ DC, where UC = upside capture and DC = downside capture

cards.front: Define drawdown and drawdown duration, and explain what a drawdown reveals about a manager.
cards.back:
• DRAWDOWN = the cumulative PEAK-TO-TROUGH loss during a particular continuous period; maximum drawdown is the largest such loss
• DRAWDOWN DURATION = the total time from the START of the drawdown until the cumulative drawdown RECOVERS TO ZERO — not merely the time to the trough
• Why they matter: large losses require proportionally greater gains to reverse or offset
• Drawdowns are STRESS TESTS of the investment process — they expose flawed or inconsistently implemented processes, inadequate risk controls and operational issues
• Questions to ask: was the stated process applied consistently? What lessons were learned and how was the process adapted? If the manager deviated, why? In a large or long drawdown, did the manager start worrying about BUSINESS risk rather than investment risk and act in their own interest?
• Suitability: investors closer to the end of their horizon, with lower risk capacity, or prone to overreacting to losses are better served by managers with SHALLOWER and SHORTER expected drawdowns
• If investment policy has not changed and the manager remains suitable, resist the temptation to exit — selling into a drawdown risks crystallizing losses and missing the reversal (the quantitative long-short funds of August 2007 sold, locked in losses, then faced redemptions or closure as the market recovered)

cards.front: A manager shows consistent positive asymmetry — high upside capture, low downside capture. Why is it a mistake to book that as skill?
cards.back:
• The profile may come from the INHERENT CONVEXITY of the strategy rather than from manager skill, so you must determine which
• Curriculum example: a hedge implemented by rolling forward out-of-the-money put options produces many small losses (most options expire worthless) punctuated by an occasional large gain in a big downturn — consistent positive asymmetry with no skill involved
• Second trap in the same exhibits: positive asymmetry (75%/25%) LAGS in up markets, yet beat long only over 2000-2013 because lower participation in down markets more than offset the lag — limiting drawdowns can deliver better absolute AND risk-adjusted returns
• Third trap: full-period comparisons hide the path — the low-beta profile led long only for most of the period (declining 18.8% vs 42.5% from January 2000 to September 2002); long only's full-period win came from the strong up market of 2013 alone
• So: separate strategy design from skill, and read capture and drawdown together rather than comparing a single cumulative return

cards.front: Contrast behavioral and structural inefficiencies in a manager's investment philosophy, and state the capacity questions that decide whether exploiting one is worthwhile.
cards.back:
• BEHAVIORAL inefficiency — a perceived mispricing created by the ACTIONS of other market participants, usually tied to biases such as trend following or loss aversion; TEMPORARY, lasting only long enough for the manager to exploit it before market price and perceived intrinsic value CONVERGE
• STRUCTURAL inefficiency — a perceived mispricing created by external or internal RULES AND REGULATIONS; can be LONG LIVED and assumes the rules CONTINUE rather than that prices converge
• Index-based strategies instead assume markets are sufficiently efficient that active management cannot add value after costs, and harvest systematic risk premiums (equity, duration, credit) or alternative ones (liquidity, natural disaster, volatility)
Capacity — the level, repeatability and sustainability of return the inefficiency can support:
• Does it offer sufficient frequency of opportunity and level of return to cover transaction costs and fees, and does that require leverage?
• Is the return repeatable by a single process, or is each opportunity unique and needing a different skill set?
• Is it sustainable — at what asset level does the realized return become unacceptably low? The more well known an inefficiency, the more likely it is arbitraged away
Philosophy checks: can the manager articulate the philosophy clearly and consistently; are the assumptions credible and consistent with the process; has the philosophy stayed stable, with any change a reasoned response to market conditions rather than an ad hoc reaction to performance or investor flows?

cards.front: What are the four elements of a manager's investment decision-making process, and what three properties must the information behind a signal have?
cards.back:
• 1 SIGNAL CREATION (idea generation) — a data point or fact observable early enough to be implemented as a position
• 2 SIGNAL CAPTURE (idea implementation) — how an idea becomes a position; is the process repeatable and consistent with the strategy's assumptions, and who approves a position?
• 3 PORTFOLIO CONSTRUCTION — how positions are sized and adjusted; conviction, risk management, hedging, long/short expression, liquidity
• 4 MONITORING THE PORTFOLIO — a feedback loop over EXTERNAL considerations (economy, markets: can the targeted inefficiency still be exploited?) and INTERNAL ones (performance, risk profile, construction: any sign of style drift?)
To exploit an inefficiency, information must be:
• UNIQUE, • TIMELY, • INTERPRETED DIFFERENTLY (interpretation is where most managers claim their edge; beware a vague 'secret sauce' claim)
Construction details worth knowing:
• Turnover should agree with the frequency of signals, the payoff horizon of the signals, and security liquidity — turnover greater than signal frequency is a red flag
• Stop-losses: HARD = positions sold automatically at the loss threshold; SOFT = positions evaluated at the threshold
• A market-neutral book must be BETA neutral, not merely dollar (local-currency) neutral, for long and short exposures to net to zero; hedges that are too small are ineffective and too large let beta swamp alpha

cards.front: Name the three behavioral biases that most damage investment TEAM decision making, and the structural techniques that mitigate them.
cards.back:
• GROUPTHINK — the team minimizes conflict and dissent to reach and keep a consensus; symptoms are closed-mindedness and confirmation bias, with members withholding information and perspectives
• AUTHORITY BIAS — deferring to a subject-matter expert or the senior-most member, which destroys the very reason for a team: a synthesis of diverse perspectives and skills
• AVERSION TO COMPLEXITY — Parkinson's law of triviality, or 'bike-shedding': disproportionate attention to trivial, familiar items at the expense of important but harder or contested topics (surveyed investment committees spent heavy time on items they themselves rated unimportant, at the expense of asset allocation, capital market expectations and manager selection)
Mitigating techniques to ask a manager about:
• TEAM SIZE — research suggests three to five is optimal; larger teams add coordination problems and raise the odds of groupthink
• DECISION METHOD — a secret ballot, though awkward, beats open deliberation because it reduces groupthink and authority bias
• MEETING CONDUCT — agendas agreed IN ADVANCE with the most important topics first and given the longest time, countering complexity aversion and availability bias
• DIVERSITY — social and cognitive diversity reduces groupthink and errors (analogous to combining uncorrelated assets) and members of diverse teams may work harder, being less focused on fitting in
Context: 64% of US active mutual funds were team-managed in 2021, and evidence on team vs individual performance is MIXED — there is nothing magical about a team, so structure and culture are what matter
cards.mnemonic: G-A-C: Groupthink, Authority bias, Complexity aversion

cards.front: List the advantages of a separately managed account over a pooled vehicle, and the costs and risks that come with it.
cards.back:
Advantages of an SMA:
• OWNERSHIP — the investor owns the individual securities directly, so manager decisions are not driven by other investors' redemption or liquidity demands, and legal ownership is clear for recovering assets after bankruptcy or mismanagement
• CUSTOMIZATION — individual constraints and preferences can be expressed, addressing the investor's objectives more closely
• TAX EFFICIENCY — in jurisdictions such as the US where tax is paid only on REALIZED gains, tax-efficient investing and trading become possible
• TRANSPARENCY — real-time, position-level detail and accurate attribution; a pooled vehicle's position detail, if provided at all, comes with a delay
Costs and risks of an SMA:
• COST — an additional operational burden per account; SMAs do not scale as pooled vehicles do (once a pool's fixed costs are paid, each new investor is largely incremental), and transaction costs rise when trades cannot be aggregated
• TRACKING RISK — customization creates tracking risk versus the benchmark and confuses attribution, because performance reflects investor constraints rather than manager decisions
• INVESTOR BEHAVIOR — transparency plus control invites micromanagement, negating the point of hiring the manager: performance chasing, familiarity bias, loss aversion
• A pooled or commingled vehicle holds many investors' money as a single portfolio with no customization: open-end and closed-end funds, ETFs, ETNs, hedge funds
• Favor pooled when the investor is COST SENSITIVE or TAX EXEMPT; favor an SMA for direct ownership, customization, tax control and real-time transparency — provided the benefits justify the extra cost and the manager has the infrastructure to run it

cards.front: The contract with a manager (prospectus, private placement memorandum, or LP agreement) turns on liquidity and fees. Rank the vehicles by liquidity and state the four liquidity features of a hedge fund.
cards.back:
Liquidity ranking:
• MOST liquid — closed-end funds and ETFs: listed, tradable intra-day, though price is uncertain for less liquid funds or large orders
• Open-end funds — slightly less liquid: daily liquidity WITH price certainty, bought and sold at end-of-day NAV
• Limited partnerships such as hedge funds — money committed for longer periods
• LEAST liquid — private equity and venture capital: investors are contractually obliged to meet capital calls during a typical 5-year investment phase, then receive distributions as investments are harvested; typical fund life 10 years, extendable by two 1-year periods
Hedge fund liquidity has four basic features:
• REDEMPTION FREQUENCY — how often capital may be withdrawn
• NOTIFICATION PERIOD — how far in advance the intent to redeem must be given
• LOCKUP — the initial period when no redemption is allowed; a HARD lock permits no redemptions, a SOFT lock charges a fee PAID INTO THE FUND (a mutual fund redemption fee is the equivalent)
• GATES — a limit on the fund assets, or an investor's assets, redeemable at any one redemption date
Trade-off: limited liquidity reduces flexibility to rebalance or meet unexpected needs, but lets the fund take long-term views and hold illiquid assets without forced selling into redemptions — and it imposes that horizon on investors, reducing their ability to overreact (visible in 2008)
• An SMA's liquidity is simply the liquidity of the securities it holds, since they may be sold at any time
cards.mnemonic: Hedge fund liquidity = R-N-L-G: Redemption frequency, Notification, Lockup, Gates

cards.front: State the three basic forms of performance-based fees, then compute the fee for a base of 1.50% plus 20% sharing of return net of the base fee when the gross return is 15%.
cards.back:
• FORM 1 — SYMMETRICAL: the manager is fully exposed to BOTH downside and upside (fee = base plus sharing of performance, positive or negative)
• FORM 2 — BONUS: the manager is NOT fully exposed to the downside but IS fully exposed to the upside (fee = higher of base, or base plus sharing of POSITIVE performance)
• FORM 3 — BONUS WITH A LIMIT: not fully exposed to either downside or upside — as form 2, but capped at a maximum annual fee
• 'Performance' may be TOTAL return or ACTIVE return, and the share may be of return NET OF the base fee — the schedule states which, so read it before computing
• Computation: 1.50% + [20% × (15% − 1.50%)] = 1.50% + 2.70% = 4.20%
• Cap example (sharing on ACTIVE return, base 0.50%, sharing 20%, maximum 2.50%): gross 14% less a 2% benchmark return = 12% active return, so the uncapped fee is 0.50% + 20% × 12% = 2.90%, and the 2.50% maximum is billed instead
• HIGH-WATER MARK (clawback): sharing is charged only to the extent prior losses have been recouped, so the investor does not pay twice for the same recovery; it bites in the first PROFITABLE year FOLLOWING a loss year — never in the loss year itself, which already earns only the base under a bonus structure
• Classic errors: applying the sharing rate to the full gross return rather than return net of the base fee; charging sharing in a negative year under a bonus structure (fee = base only); and forgetting that symmetrical structures, though best for aligning risk and effort, are unpopular with managers because of bankruptcy risk
cards.formula: 1 Symmetrical: Fee = Base + Sharing × Performance | 2 Bonus: Fee = higher of [Base] or [Base + Sharing × positive performance] | 3 Bonus with a limit: Fee = higher of [Base] or [Base + Sharing × performance], up to a maximum

cards.front: A schedule reads: standard fee 0.50%, base fee 0.25%, sharing 20% on active return beyond the base fee, maximum annual fee 0.75%. Compute the billed fee for active returns of 0.25%, 1.00%, 2.00% and 3.00%.
cards.back:
• Base fee = the floor below which the computed fee can never fall; sharing applies only to active return IN EXCESS of the base fee; the maximum annual fee is the cap
• Active return ≤ 0.25% → 0.25% (base only, no sharing)
• Active return 1.00% → 0.25% + 0.20 × (1.00 − 0.25) = 0.25% + 0.15% = 0.40%
• Active return 2.00% → 0.25% + 0.20 × 1.75 = 0.60%
• Active return 3.00% → 0.25% + 0.20 × 2.75 = 0.80% → billed at the 0.75% CAP (the cap binds from an active return of 2.75%)
• Design logic: the schedule is symmetric around the commonplace 0.50% standard fee — 25 bps of protection below (the base) matched by 25 bps of upside above (the maximum)
• Units: annual percentages of assets; performance fees are normally paid annually or less often
• Payoff shape: base fee, PLUS a long call on active return struck at the minimum (base) fee, MINUS a less valuable call struck at the maximum fee — higher volatility raises option value, which is why bonus-style fees encourage risk taking and why the investor must pick benchmarks carefully and monitor risk
• Classic error: multiplying the sharing rate by the WHOLE active return (0.20 × 2.00 = 0.40, giving 0.65%) instead of the active return beyond the base fee
cards.formula: Billed fee = Base fee + Sharing % × (Active return − Base fee), floored at the base fee and capped at the maximum annual fee

cards.front: On a performance-fee schedule, what is the 'breakeven active return', and what net active return does the client keep at, below, and above it?
cards.back:
• BREAKEVEN ACTIVE RETURN = the active return at which the performance-based BILLED FEE exactly equals the STANDARD (flat) fee — below it the client pays LESS than under the flat fee, above it MORE
• Net active return = gross active return − the TOTAL billed fee (base plus any sharing), not just the sharing component
• Sample schedule (standard 0.50%, base 0.25%, sharing 20% beyond the base, maximum 0.75%, breakeven 1.50%):
  – Active return ≤ 0.25% → billed 0.25% → net ≤ 0.00%
  – 1.00% → billed 0.40% → net 0.60%
  – 1.50% (breakeven) → billed 0.50% = the standard fee → net 1.00%
  – 2.00% → billed 0.60% → net 1.40%
  – ≥ 2.75% → billed 0.75% (cap) → net ≥ 2.00%
• Second schedule (base 0.20%, sharing 25% on active return beyond the base): active return 0.75% → billed 0.20 + 0.25 × 0.55 = 0.3375% → net 0.41%; active return 1.75% → billed 0.20 + 0.25 × 1.55 = 0.5875% → net 1.16%
• Interpretation: at or below the base fee the client's net active return is zero or negative, so performance fees favour the client when active returns are LOW; they also convert a symmetric gross distribution into an asymmetric net one, cutting upside variability but not downside, which UNDERSTATES downside risk if a single standard deviation is computed on the net series
• Classic error: subtracting only the sharing element, or only the base, from gross active return instead of the full billed fee
cards.formula: Net active return = Gross active return − Billed fee; at the breakeven active return, Billed fee = Standard fee

cards.front: List the five stated objectives of the GIPS standards, and state what a firm must do when the GIPS standards conflict with local law or regulation.
cards.back:
Five objectives:
• Promote investor interests and instill investor confidence
• Ensure accurate and consistent data
• Obtain worldwide acceptance of a single standard for calculating and presenting performance
• Promote fair, global competition among investment firms
• Promote industry self-regulation on a global basis
Underlying principle: fair representation and full disclosure of the firm's performance history; the standards are voluntary, ethical standards.
Provisions are split into REQUIREMENTS (must be met to claim compliance) and RECOMMENDATIONS (best practice, optional). Firms must also follow Guidance Statements, interpretations and Q&As issued by CFA Institute and the GIPS governing bodies.
Conflict with law/regulation: comply with the LAW or regulation and DISCLOSE the conflict in the GIPS Report — the firm does not get to claim an exemption from GIPS on that basis.
cards.mnemonic: Objectives = Confidence, Consistent data, Common standard, Competition, self-regulation

cards.front: Who may and may not claim compliance with the GIPS Standards for Firms, and what exactly does a firm's claim of compliance signify?
cards.back:
May claim: investment management firms and asset owners that manage assets on a DISCRETIONARY basis AND COMPETE FOR BUSINESS.
• An asset owner that manages assets for participants, beneficiaries, or itself and does NOT compete for business complies with the GIPS Standards for Asset Owners instead.
May NOT claim: consultants, software houses, and third-party performance measurement providers such as custodians.
Compliance is FIRM-WIDE ONLY — it cannot be claimed for only some products, nor for a specific composite, pooled fund, or portfolio.
A claim of compliance signifies:
• performance data inputs, processes, and return calculation methodology conform to the prescribed guidelines
• ALL the firm's actual fee-paying discretionary segregated accounts are assigned to at least one composite
• all limited distribution pooled funds meeting a composite definition are in the appropriate composites
Benefits: to clients — confidence in the record and comparability across firms; to firms — credibility (especially if verified), RFP/manager-search eligibility, a "passport to the international marketplace," and stronger internal controls.
Trap: "Our large-cap composite is GIPS-compliant" is a violation.

cards.front: How must the "firm" be defined for GIPS purposes, what does that definition determine, and what is included in / excluded from total firm assets?
cards.back:
Definition: an investment firm, subsidiary, or division HELD OUT TO THE PUBLIC as a DISTINCT BUSINESS ENTITY.
Distinct business entity = a unit, division, department or office that is organizationally and functionally SEGREGATED from others, RETAINS DISCRETION over the assets it manages, and should have AUTONOMY over the investment decision-making process. Possible criteria: it is a legal entity; it has a distinct market or client type; it uses a separate and distinct investment process.
Why it matters: the firm definition is the foundation for firm-wide compliance — it sets the scope of implementation and the boundaries for TOTAL FIRM ASSETS.
Total firm assets = aggregate FAIR VALUE of all assets for which the firm has investment management responsibility, whether or not discretionary and whether or not fee-paying.
• INCLUDES assets managed by sub-advisors the firm has authority to select
• EXCLUDES advisory-only assets and uncalled committed capital
Hard rule: changes in corporate structure must NOT alter historical performance — apart from correcting errors, historical performance is never altered.
Trap: a division that shares the parent's investment process/approved list, or whose strategy or security selection can be dictated by another division, lacks autonomy and cannot be the "firm."

cards.front: Write the GIPS-required time-weighted return calculation for a period containing a large external cash flow, and state the valuation frequency rules.
cards.back:
Symbols: r_twr = TWR for the whole period; r_t,i = sub-period returns in decimal form; V0 = beginning fair value INCLUDING cash and accrued income; V1 = ending fair value including cash and accrued income.
When to use: TWR is REQUIRED for all portfolios except those qualifying for a money-weighted return. It negates the effect of external cash flows (client-controlled), isolating the manager's decisions.
Conventions:
• Portfolios must be valued at least MONTHLY and TWR calculated at least monthly as of calendar month end / last business day (private market investment portfolios: QUARTERLY)
• If returns are not calculated daily and an intra-month LARGE cash flow occurs, the portfolio must be valued and a sub-period return calculated on the flow date
• "Large cash flow" is defined by the FIRM, composite by composite (absolute amount or % of assets), documented and followed without exception
• Sub-period returns must be GEOMETRICALLY linked — returns compound, so they are multiplicative, not additive
Worked: V0 = 100,000 on 31 May; 5 June value 109,000 including a 10,000 contribution; 30 June value 110,550.
r1 = (99,000 − 100,000) ÷ 100,000 = −1.00%; r2 = (110,550 − 109,000) ÷ 109,000 = 1.42%; TWR = (0.99)(1.0142) − 1 = 0.41%.
Classic error: adding sub-period returns, or leaving the contribution in sub-period 1's ending value — sub-period 1 ends EXCLUDING the flow (99,000); sub-period 2 begins INCLUDING it (109,000).

cards.front: Write the Modified Dietz formula and its cash-flow weight, and state precisely when GIPS permits its use.
cards.back:
Symbols: V1 = ending fair value; V0 = beginning fair value; CF = Σ CFi = net external cash flows (inflows +, outflows −); wi = fraction of the period cash flow i was in the portfolio; CD = total calendar days in the period; Di = calendar days from the START of the period to the date of CFi.
When to use: if a cash flow is NOT a large cash flow and the firm does not calculate daily performance, GIPS requires a method that adjusts for DAILY WEIGHTED cash flows — Modified Dietz or Modified IRR are the named acceptable approaches. Both estimate, not replicate, the true TWR. The formula assumes the portfolio is NOT revalued on the flow date.
Conventions: as written it assumes flows occur at END of day; under a beginning-of-day convention wi = (CD − Di + 1) ÷ CD. The firm must establish one policy per composite/pooled fund and apply it consistently.
Worked: V0 = 100,000; +10,000 on 5 June (CD = 30, Di = 5, w = 25/30 = 0.83); V1 = 110,550.
Numerator = 110,550 − 100,000 − 10,000 = 550; denominator = 100,000 + 10,000(0.83) = 108,333; return = 0.51%.
Classic errors: using it when a LARGE cash flow required revaluation; weighting by Di ÷ CD instead of (CD − Di) ÷ CD; assuming the estimate equals the true TWR — here true TWR was 0.41% vs 0.51%, and in VOLATILE markets the gap widens materially (Modified IRR gives the same 0.51%).
cards.formula: r_ModDietz = (V1 − V0 − CF) ÷ [V0 + Σ(CFi × wi)], with wi = (CD − Di) ÷ CD

cards.front: GIPS requires time-weighted returns — under exactly what conditions may a firm present a money-weighted return instead, and what extra rules then apply?
cards.back:
TWR (default, required):
• Required for all portfolios not qualifying for MWR
• Removes the effect of external cash flows, which the client controls
• Value monthly and at large cash flows; calculate at least monthly; link sub-periods geometrically
MWR (permitted only if BOTH conditions hold):
1. the firm has CONTROL over the external cash flows into the portfolios/pooled fund, AND
2. at least ONE of: the portfolios (or fund) are closed-end; fixed life; fixed commitment; or illiquid investments are a significant part of the investment strategy
MWR rules when used:
• Annualized SINCE-INCEPTION MWR, calculated at least annually
• Daily external cash flows must be used for periods beginning with the 2020 edition effective date (quarterly for earlier periods)
• Portfolios valued at least annually and as of the period end for which performance is calculated (private market investment portfolios: quarterly)
Trap: illiquidity ALONE does not qualify a portfolio for MWR — the firm must also control the external cash flows.

cards.front: A firm annualizes a strong 8-month return, omits the custodian-managed cash sleeve from the portfolio return, and treats per-transaction custody fees as transaction costs. Which GIPS return-calculation rules are broken?
cards.back:
All three are violations:
• Returns for periods of LESS THAN ONE YEAR must NOT be annualized — that would be a prediction about the rest of the year
• Returns from CASH and CASH EQUIVALENTS must be included in ALL total return calculations — even when the cash is managed by another firm or the client's custodian, because the manager's cash weighting affects results
• Returns must be after deduction of TRANSACTION COSTS: brokerage commissions, exchange fees/taxes, and spreads from internal OR external brokers. CUSTODY FEES ARE NOT transaction costs, even when charged per transaction
Related rules:
• Transaction costs may be ESTIMATED only if actual costs are not known
• Bundled fees (any mix of management, transaction, custody and administrative fees): if transaction costs cannot be identified and segregated from the bundle, composites for institutional investors must reduce the GROSS-of-fees return by the ENTIRE bundled fee, or by the portion containing the transaction costs
• Gross-of-fees = before management and custodial fees but AFTER all trading expenses

cards.front: State the GIPS definition of fair value and rank the valuation hierarchy from most to least preferred.
cards.back:
Fair value = the amount at which an investment COULD BE SOLD in an orderly, arm's-length transaction between willing parties. It must include accrued income on fixed-income securities and all other interest-earning investments (income on cash and cash equivalents may be recognized on a cash basis).
REQUIRED top rung: the objective, observable, UNADJUSTED quoted market price for an IDENTICAL investment in an ACTIVE market on the measurement date — if available, it MUST be used.
If that is not available, the RECOMMENDED hierarchy, in declining order of preference:
1. Quoted prices for SIMILAR investments in ACTIVE markets
2. Quoted prices for identical or similar investments in markets that are NOT ACTIVE (few transactions, stale prices, or quotes varying substantially over time or between market makers)
3. Market-based inputs, OTHER than quoted prices, that are OBSERVABLE for the investment
4. SUBJECTIVE, UNOBSERVABLE inputs
Firms must document valuation policies, procedures, methodologies and hierarchies, follow them consistently, and make them available to prospective clients on request; composite- or pooled-fund-specific hierarchies are RECOMMENDED.
Trap: the top rung is a requirement while levels 1–4 are only recommended — and "similar in an ACTIVE market" outranks "identical in an INACTIVE market."

cards.front: Write the composite return under the beginning-of-period asset-weighting method and state how often composite returns must be computed.
cards.back:
Symbols: r_C = composite return; r_pi = return of individual portfolio i for the period; V0,pi = beginning fair value of portfolio i; Σ V0,pi = total beginning fair value of all portfolios in the composite. Each weight = portfolio's beginning value ÷ total beginning assets.
When to use: it is the simplest of the three permitted methods for a composite TIME-WEIGHTED return, appropriate when external cash flows are not being weighted into the base.
Conventions: composite TWRs must be calculated at least MONTHLY (except private market investment composites) — less frequent asset-weighting makes the composite return a poorer reflection of constituent performance.
Worked (four-portfolio composite, June): weights 23.00%, 22.40%, 25.97%, 28.63% with returns 0.51%, 0.28%, 0.32%, 1.36% →
r_C = 0.0051(0.23) + 0.0028(0.224) + 0.0032(0.2597) + 0.0136(0.2863) = 0.65%
Classic error: EQUAL-weighting the member portfolio returns — the composite return is always the ASSET-weighted average of the portfolios in the composite.
cards.formula: r_C = Σ [ r_pi × V0,pi ÷ Σ V0,pi ]

cards.front: Name the three permitted methods of calculating a composite time-weighted return, and write the formula for the beginning-assets-plus-weighted-cash-flows method.
cards.back:
Three permitted methods:
1. Asset-weight the individual portfolio returns using BEGINNING-OF-PERIOD values
2. Use a method reflecting beginning-of-period values AND EXTERNAL CASH FLOWS (the formula above)
3. The AGGREGATE RETURN method — combine all composite assets and external cash flows and compute the return as if the composite were a single portfolio (e.g., apply Modified Dietz to the totals)
Symbols: Vp = portfolio i's beginning value plus its weighted external cash flows; V0 = beginning fair value; CFi = external cash flow i; wi = (CD − Di) ÷ CD, the same weight used in Modified Dietz. Note Vp is exactly the DENOMINATOR of the Modified Dietz formula.
Worked (same four-portfolio composite): weights become 24.56%, 24.41%, 25.61%, 25.42% → r_C = 0.62%, versus 0.65% under beginning assets only.
Aggregate Return method on the composite totals, using Modified Dietz: net CF = +25 − 15 − 5 − 6.5 − 6.5 = −8; numerator = V1 − V0 − CF = 429.55 − 434.81 − (−8) = 2.74; denominator = V0 + Σ(CFi × wi) = 440.97; r_C = 2.74 ÷ 440.97 = 0.62% — the same answer. Note the numerator SUBTRACTS net cash flow, so net outflows ADD to it.
Classic error: mixing conventions across periods; the method chosen must be applied consistently, and all three are asset-weighted (never equal-weighted).
cards.formula: Vp = V0 + Σ(CFi × wi); r_C = Σ [ r_pi × Vpi ÷ Σ Vpi ]

cards.front: A client's IPS bans derivatives and screens out tobacco stocks. Does that automatically make the portfolio non-discretionary and therefore excluded from all composites?
cards.back:
NO. No client-imposed constraint — ESG screens, bans on selling company stock, statutory bans on non-domestic securities, derivative prohibitions — automatically renders a portfolio non-discretionary.
The test: do the constraints MATERIALLY affect the manager's ability to execute the intended investment strategy?
• Not material → include the portfolio in a composite alongside unconstrained portfolios
• Material → either place it in a composite of SIMILARLY CONSTRAINED portfolios, or classify it non-discretionary and exclude it from ALL composites
Example: a derivatives ban is irrelevant to a long-only mid-cap stock strategy that simply buys, holds and sells common stock, but may be fatal where derivatives are central to implementing the mandate.
Other discretion killers: unsellable legacy holdings with a low cost basis (alternatively strip out the restricted assets and composite the remainder); a pattern of frequent large client withdrawals forcing an abnormally high cash level; a portfolio below the composite's documented minimum asset level (non-discretionary with respect to THAT composite).
Rules: the firm must have a clear, WRITTEN definition of discretion, consistently applied, and may set a materiality threshold (e.g., portfolio is discretionary if non-discretionary assets are under x% of assets). Both discretionary and non-discretionary portfolios count toward TOTAL FIRM ASSETS; only discretionary ones may be in composites.

cards.front: On what basis must composites be defined, which portfolios must and must not be in them, and what goes wrong with too few or too many composites?
cards.back:
Basis: composites must be defined according to investment MANDATE, OBJECTIVE, or STRATEGY. A composite must include ALL portfolios meeting the composite definition, and the definition — including the detailed criteria for assigning portfolios — must be documented in the firm's policies and procedures. Portfolios with DIFFERENT mandates/objectives/strategies may never share a composite.
A possible definitional hierarchy, broad to narrow: investment mandate → asset class → style or strategy → benchmarks → risk/return characteristics. Benchmark-based definitions are acceptable if the benchmark reflects the strategy and no other composite shares those characteristics.
Membership rules:
• All actual, FEE-PAYING, DISCRETIONARY segregated accounts must be in at least one composite
• Discretionary NON-fee-paying accounts MAY be included (additional disclosures may be required — e.g., waived-fee charity accounts or seed money)
• NON-discretionary accounts must NOT be in any composite
• MODEL, hypothetical, backtested or simulated portfolios must NOT be in any composite, and theoretical performance may NEVER be linked to actual performance (supplemental information only)
• A firm must create composites for strategies managed for or offered as a segregated account; none is required for a strategy offered ONLY as a pooled fund — but if offered both ways, the pooled fund must be in that strategy's composite
Too FEW composites: significant strategy differences overlooked, overly broad grouping, wide return dispersion. Too MANY: unnecessary cost, groupings too much alike, too few portfolios or assets to be useful, client-confidentiality risk.

cards.front: State the GIPS timing rules for adding a new portfolio, removing a terminated portfolio, and switching a portfolio between composites.
cards.back:
New portfolios: include on a TIMELY and CONSISTENT basis after the portfolio comes under management, per a documented, composite-specific policy. Common practice is the beginning of the next full measurement period after funding — funded 20 May with monthly composite returns → include from 1 June. Firms have some latitude where assets need redeploying (funding in kind, illiquid/emerging markets), but the policy must be applied consistently to all new portfolios.
Terminated portfolios: keep in the composite's historical performance through the LAST FULL measurement period in which the firm had DISCRETION to manage to the strategy. Notified 20 May of a 31 May termination and told to stop trading, with monthly returns → include only through 30 APRIL. The historical performance stays in the composite.
Switching: portfolios must NOT move between composites unless (1) there are DOCUMENTED changes to the portfolio's investment mandate, objective, or strategy, or (2) the composite is REDEFINED. The portfolio's HISTORICAL performance must REMAIN with the ORIGINAL composite. Redefining an existing composite should be highly unusual — a changed strategy normally calls for a NEW composite.
Significant cash flow: a client-directed flow large enough to temporarily prevent implementing the strategy; defined EX ANTE and composite-specific. The portfolio may be temporarily removed from the composite, or the flow parked in a TEMPORARY ACCOUNT (in no composite) until invested, then transferred in and treated as an external cash flow.
Minimum asset level: permitted; the firm must document how portfolios falling below are treated (e.g., add at $1m, remove only below $900,000); changes to the minimum must NOT be applied retroactively; a removed portfolio's prior performance stays in the composite and the firm must check whether it fits another composite.
Why: unrestricted switching would let a firm re-populate composites with whichever portfolios performed best.

cards.front: State the minimum performance record required on first compliance and list the core required elements of a GIPS Composite Report presenting time-weighted returns.
cards.back:
Minimum record: at least FIVE years of annual performance (or since inception if the composite has existed less than five years), then extend the record by one year each year until at least TEN years of GIPS-compliant performance are presented.
Core required elements:
• Composite AND benchmark annual returns for all years
• The number of portfolios in the composite at each period end — required only IF SIX OR MORE
• The amount of assets in the composite
• Total firm assets at the end of each period
• A measure of INTERNAL DISPERSION of individual portfolio returns for each annual period — required only if the composite contains SIX OR MORE portfolios for the FULL year
• Where monthly composite returns are available, the THREE-YEAR ANNUALIZED EX POST STANDARD DEVIATION of both the composite and the benchmark as of each annual period end
Distribution: the firm must make every reasonable effort to provide a GIPS Report to ALL prospective clients and limited distribution pooled fund investors, and it must be the report representing the STRATEGY BEING MARKETED to that prospect. Two report types: GIPS Composite Report and GIPS Pooled Fund Report.
Trap: the six-portfolio threshold governs BOTH the portfolio count and the dispersion measure — with fewer, "n/a" is correct, not a violation.

cards.front: Write the equal-weighted and asset-weighted standard deviation measures of a composite's internal dispersion, and state which portfolios enter the calculation.
cards.back:
Symbols: ri = the full-year return of individual portfolio i; r̄c = equal-weighted (arithmetic) mean return of the composite's portfolios; n = number of portfolios; wi = portfolio i's beginning value ÷ total beginning value of all n portfolios (weights sum to 1); r̄proxy = the asset-weighted mean return.
When to use: to satisfy the annual internal-dispersion disclosure. GIPS does not mandate one method — acceptable measures include high/low, the range, and the equal-weighted or asset-weighted standard deviation; the method chosen must fairly represent the range of returns for the year and the firm must disclose which it uses.
Convention: ONLY portfolios in the composite for the ENTIRE year are included.
Worked (14-portfolio German equity composite): high 2.66%, low 1.93%, high/low range 0.73% = 73 bps; equal-weighted mean 2.32% with Sc = 22 bps; asset-weighted Sc,aw = 21 bps. Under normality about two-thirds of portfolios fall between 2.10% and 2.54%.
Classic errors: including portfolios that joined or left mid-year; letting one outlier drive a high/low disclosure that misrepresents the distribution; confusing this cross-sectional statistic with the three-year ex post standard deviation of monthly returns.
cards.formula: Sc = sqrt[ Σ(ri − r̄c)² ÷ n ]; Sc,aw = sqrt[ Σ (ri − r̄proxy)² × wi ], with wi = V0,i ÷ V0,Total and r̄proxy = Σ(wi × ri)

cards.front: Contrast internal dispersion with the three-year annualized ex post standard deviation in a GIPS Composite Report.
cards.back:
Internal dispersion:
• Measures the spread of ANNUAL returns of INDIVIDUAL PORTFOLIOS WITHIN the composite — cross-sectional, across accounts, for one year
• Required for EACH annual period, when the composite holds six or more portfolios for the full year
• Only full-year portfolios count
• Acceptable measures: high/low, range, equal-weighted or asset-weighted standard deviation of portfolio returns
• Purpose: shows how CONSISTENTLY the strategy was implemented across accounts; a wide spread suggests the composite may be defined too broadly
Three-year annualized ex post standard deviation:
• Measures the variability of the composite's MONTHLY returns — and the BENCHMARK's — over the preceding 36 months; a time-series risk measure
• Presented as of EACH annual period end, required where monthly composite returns are available
• Purpose: gives prospects a comparable indication of the strategy's historical RISK, based on historical experience rather than subjective inputs
One sentence: dispersion is spread ACROSS portfolios in a year; the three-year standard deviation is volatility OVER time.

cards.front: State the four conditions for LINKING a past firm's or affiliation's performance to a new or acquiring firm, and what is permitted if only some are met.
cards.back:
All four must hold, applied on a COMPOSITE-SPECIFIC basis:
1. Substantially ALL the investment decision makers are employed by the new or acquiring firm
2. The decision-making PROCESS remains substantially INTACT and INDEPENDENT within the new or acquiring firm
3. The new or acquiring firm has RECORDS that document and support the reported performance
4. There is NO BREAK in the track record between the past firm/affiliation and the new or acquiring firm
If the first three tests are met but there IS a break: the past performance may be USED TO REPRESENT the new or acquiring firm's historical performance, but the two records may NOT be LINKED.
Acquisition grace period: a GIPS-compliant firm that acquires another firm or affiliation has ONE YEAR to bring any non-compliant assets into compliance for future reporting periods.
Disclosure: the report must state that performance before the transition occurred while the team was affiliated with another firm, that the team has managed the composite since inception, that the process has not changed, and that the history has been linked.
Trap: "used to represent" is NOT the same as "linked" — a break in the record costs the firm linkage, not necessarily the whole history.
cards.mnemonic: Port the record: People, Process, Papers, no Pause

cards.front: How do verification and a performance examination differ in scope, and what assurance does verification explicitly NOT provide?
cards.back:
Verification:
• Performed by a QUALIFIED, INDEPENDENT third party, following the GIPS Standards for Verifiers
• FIRM-WIDE only — a single verification report is issued with respect to the WHOLE firm; verification cannot be carried out on a single composite or pooled fund
• Provides assurance that the firm's policies and procedures for composite and pooled fund maintenance, and for the CALCULATION, PRESENTATION and DISTRIBUTION of performance, have been DESIGNED in compliance with GIPS and IMPLEMENTED on a firm-wide basis
• RECOMMENDED, not required
• Process: the verifier learns the firm's structure, policies and valuation/return methodologies, then SAMPLES portfolios (sample size reflects composite/portfolio counts, AUM, internal controls, years verified, systems, calculation method, use of external providers); tests discretionary vs non-discretionary classification, composite assignment and timing, switching, input-data treatment, third-party documentation, recalculated returns, and a sample of GIPS Reports and advertisements. Errors or weak records call for a larger sample
Performance examination:
