• Optional and composite- or pooled-fund SPECIFIC; a firm may state a composite has been examined only if an examination REPORT has been issued for that composite
• Available only to a firm that has ALSO been verified firm-wide
Explicitly NOT provided: verification gives NO assurance on the ACCURACY of any specific composite or pooled fund presentation.
Trap: "our large-cap composite is GIPS verified" — impossible without firm-wide verification plus a performance examination.

cards.front: State put-call parity and put-call-forward parity, and name the two portfolios each equates.
cards.back:
• S0 = current underlying price; c0, p0 = call and put premiums (SAME underlying, strike X, expiration T); X/(1+r)^T = PV of a risk-free bond paying X at T
• Left side = protective put (long asset + long put); right side = fiduciary call (long call + risk-free bond)
• Put-call-forward parity replaces S0 with the PV of the forward price, where F0(T) = S0(1+r)^T; long forward + long put = synthetic protective put
• Use: price one leg off the others, build synthetics, or change exposure without trading the underlying
• Classic error: using X rather than PV(X), or combining options with different strikes/expirations

cards.front: Give the four position equivalencies the curriculum uses to replicate an asset's returns with options.
cards.back:
• Long call + short put (same strike, same expiry) = synthetic LONG forward/stock
• Short call + long put (same strike, same expiry) = synthetic SHORT forward/stock
• Short stock + long call, call strike = price at which stock was shorted = synthetic LONG PUT
• Long stock + long put, put strike = price at which stock was bought = synthetic LONG CALL (this is the protective put)
• Uses: market makers hedging a sold forward, banks hedging structured-product exposure, arbitraging a mispriced leg
• Watch: replicating a short stock position with American options carries early-assignment risk

cards.front: For a covered call (long stock + short call), write max gain, max loss, breakeven, value at expiration, and profit.
cards.back:
• S0 = stock price when the position is opened; ST = stock price at expiration; X = strike; c0 = call premium received
• Max gain = (X − S0) + c0 — appreciation up to the strike plus the premium
• Max loss = S0 − c0 (stock goes to zero, writer keeps premium); numerically the SAME number as the breakeven
• Breakeven = S0 − c0
• Value at expiration = ST − Max(ST − X, 0); Profit = ST − Max(ST − X, 0) + c0 − S0
• Example: S0 = 15.84, write the 17 call at 1.44 → max gain 2.60, max loss = BE = 14.40
• Classic error: using ST or X in place of S0 in the gain/breakeven formulas
cards.formula: Max gain = (X − S0) + c0 ; Max loss = Breakeven = S0 − c0 ; VT = ST − Max(ST − X, 0)

cards.front: Name the three investment objectives for writing covered calls in the curriculum, and the volatility view the writer is implicitly expressing.
cards.back:
• Yield enhancement / cash generation — the most common motive; premium is kept regardless of outcome, in anticipation of limited upside
• Reducing a position at a favorable price — write an in-the-money call; if exercised the effective sale price is X + c0 (write the 15 call at 1.64 with stock at 15.84 → 16.64, a 0.80 or 5.05% improvement)
• Target price realization — write near-term calls struck at the research target price; if unexercised, roll to the next expiration
• Implicit view: realized volatility of the underlying will be LOWER than the call's implied volatility
• Not free money: opportunity loss if the shares rise sharply, and the writer must keep holding the stock (100 shares per contract)

cards.front: You write an IN-THE-MONEY covered call. Why does plugging into "max gain = appreciation to the strike plus premium" trip candidates up?
cards.back:
• When X < S0 there is DEPRECIATION to the strike, so (X − S0) is negative and is subtracted, not added
• Curriculum case: stock at 50, write the 45-strike call for 7 → max gain = (45 − 50) + 7 = 2, not 12
• Breakeven and max loss are unaffected by moneyness: both remain S0 − c0 = 50 − 7 = 43
• Same formula throughout — do not switch signs by hand; just let (X − S0) carry its own sign
• Related trap: an ITM call is far more likely to be exercised, so the shares are very likely called away
cards.formula: Max gain = (X − S0) + c0, with (X − S0) < 0 when the call is written in the money

cards.front: For a protective put (long stock + long put), write max loss, max gain, breakeven, value at expiration, and profit.
cards.back:
• S0 = stock price when the position is opened; ST = price at expiration; X = put strike; p0 = put premium paid
• Max loss = S0 − X + p0 — the "deductible" plus the cost of the insurance
• Max gain = ST − S0 − p0 = theoretically UNLIMITED (stock can rise to any level)
• Breakeven = S0 + p0 (the stock must rise by the premium paid)
• Value at expiration = ST + Max(X − ST, 0); Profit = ST + Max(X − ST, 0) − S0 − p0
• Example: S0 = 37.41, buy the 35 put at 1.81 → max loss 4.22, breakeven 39.22
• Classic errors: subtracting p0 in the max loss, or adding p0 to X instead of to S0 for the breakeven
cards.formula: Max loss = S0 − X + p0 ; Breakeven = S0 + p0 ; VT = ST + Max(X − ST, 0)

cards.front: Explain the protective put as an insurance policy: what plays the role of coverage and deductible, and what does the curriculum say about buying puts continuously?
cards.back:
• Put strike X = the coverage amount; deductible = S0 − X (current price minus strike)
• LOWER strike = larger deductible = cheaper premium but greater price exposure before protection kicks in
• Like term insurance, the cover lasts only to expiration — the put must not expire before the feared event
• Longer-dated puts cost more but decay more slowly (NOV 15 put theta −0.009/day vs SEP 15 put −0.015/day), and the price is not linear in time
• Continuous put buying lowers portfolio volatility but is expensive enough to wipe out most of the long-run gain; OCCASIONAL purchase against a specific short-term risk is the sensible use
• Once the event passes, sell the put to recover part of the premium (a price shock can also raise implied volatility and the put's value)

cards.front: Compare the position delta of an at-the-money covered call, an ATM protective put, and long stock hedged with a short forward.
cards.back:
• Long 100 shares = +100; ATM call delta ≈ +0.5, ATM put delta ≈ −0.5; long forward/futures delta = +1, short = −1
• Covered call: +100 (stock) − 50 (short ATM call) = +50
• Protective put: +100 (stock) − 50 (long ATM put) = +50
• Long 100 shares + short forward on 50 shares: +100 − 50 = +50
• All three have position delta 50, so for SMALL moves in the underlying they show very similar gains and losses
• Beyond small moves the payoff shapes diverge sharply (the forward hedge is linear; the option positions are not), and a covered call is short gamma while a protective put is long gamma
• Useful check: Call delta − Put delta = 1 for the same underlying and model inputs

cards.front: Against a SHORT underlying position, contrast buying a call with writing a put — on maximum loss, delta, vega, and theta.
cards.back:
Short stock at 15.84, plus:
• BUY the 16 call at 0.97 → loss on a rally is CAPPED at 1.13 [(15.84 − S) + (S − 16) − 0.97]; position delta −1 + 0.516 = −0.484; LONG vega (+0.018); theta NEGATIVE (−0.018/day)
• WRITE the 15 put at 0.65 → no upside protection, loss on a rally is potentially UNLIMITED, cushioned only by the 0.65 premium; gain on a decline is capped at 1.49; position delta −1 + 0.335 = −0.665; SHORT vega (−0.017); theta POSITIVE (+0.015/day)
• Both remain net bearish (negative delta); only the long call converts the symmetric short into a protected, asymmetric payoff
• Choose the call to hedge upside risk, the short put to earn income when a quiet, mildly falling market is expected

cards.front: For a bull CALL spread (buy strike XL, write strike XH), give value at expiration, max profit, max loss, and breakeven.
cards.back:
• cL, cH = premiums of the lower- and higher-strike calls; cL > cH, so the position is a DEBIT spread with net premium (cL − cH)
• VT = Max(0, ST − XL) − Max(0, ST − XH)
• Max profit = (XH − XL) − (cL − cH), earned at ST ≥ XH
• Max loss = cL − cH, at ST ≤ XL
• Breakeven ST* = XL + (cL − cH) — the LOWER strike plus the cost of the spread
• Example: buy the SEP 15 call at 1.64, write the SEP 17 call at 0.51 → debit 1.13, max profit 0.87, max loss 1.13, breakeven 16.13
• Classic error: subtracting the net premium from XH for the breakeven; also remember a spread caps BOTH gain and loss
cards.formula: Max profit = (XH − XL) − (cL − cH) ; Max loss = cL − cH ; Breakeven = XL + (cL − cH)

cards.front: For a bear PUT spread (buy strike XH, write strike XL), give value at expiration, max gain, max loss, and breakeven.
cards.back:
• pH, pL = premiums of the higher- and lower-strike puts; pH > pL, so the put bear spread is a DEBIT spread (a bear spread built with calls would be a credit spread)
• VT = Max(0, XH − ST) − Max(0, XL − ST)
• Max gain = (XH − XL) − (pH − pL), at ST ≤ XL
• Max loss = pH − pL, at ST ≥ XH
• Breakeven ST* = XH − (pH − pL) — the HIGHER strike minus the cost of the spread
• Example: buy the NOV 16 put at 1.96, write the NOV 15 put at 1.46 → debit 0.50, max gain 0.50, max loss 0.50, breakeven 15.50
• Classic error: anchoring the breakeven to the lower strike (that is the bull-spread rule)
cards.formula: Max gain = (XH − XL) − (pH − pL) ; Max loss = pH − pL ; Breakeven = XH − (pH − pL)

cards.front: For a long straddle (buy a call and a put at the same strike and expiry), give value at expiration, both breakevens, max loss, and max profit on each side.
cards.back:
• X = common strike; c0 + p0 = total premium paid
• VT = Max(0, ST − X) + Max(0, X − ST)
• Lower breakeven = X − (c0 + p0); upper breakeven = X + (c0 + p0)
• Max loss = c0 + p0, occurring exactly at ST = X (the worst outcome — both options expire worthless)
• Max profit is unlimited on the upside, but capped on the downside at X − (c0 + p0), because the stock can fall no further than zero
• Example: stock 50, call 2.29 + put 2.28 = 4.57 → breakevens 45.43 and 54.57; downside max profit 45.43
• Greeks at inception: delta ≈ 0 (+0.069), gamma high (+0.139), vega positive (+0.114), theta negative (−0.075) — a LONG-volatility trade
• Classic error: calling the downside profit unlimited too
cards.formula: Breakevens = X ± (c0 + p0) ; Max loss = c0 + p0 at ST = X

cards.front: Describe a collar's structure, its profit in each of the three price ranges, and what happens to its delta and to its risk profile.
cards.back:
• Structure: long shares + long put struck at X1 below spot + short call struck at X2 above spot (also called a fence or hedge wrapper); usually OTC so the call strike can be set for a ZERO-COST collar
• Profit if ST ≤ X1: X1 − S0 − p0 + c0 (floor); if X1 < ST < X2: ST − S0 − p0 + c0; if ST ≥ X2: X2 − S0 − p0 + c0 (cap)
• Example: shares bought at 12, buy the NOV 15 put at 1.46, write the NOV 17 call at 1.44 → minimum profit 2.98, maximum profit 4.98
• Delta falls from +1 to +0.166 (= 1 − 0.359 − 0.475) and gamma is near zero; outside both strikes the position delta approaches 0
• Risk profile: sells the right tail (large gains) to remove the left tail (large losses) — risk reducing, return limiting
• As the strikes converge, the payoff converges on a risk-free return; a collar sits economically BETWEEN equity and fixed income

cards.front: How is a long calendar spread built, what is its source of profit, and what is its main risk?
cards.back:
• Build: SELL the near-dated option and BUY the longer-dated option — same type, same strike, same underlying (short calendar = the reverse)
• Source of profit: the near-dated ATM option's time value decays faster (SEP 45 call theta −0.029/day vs JAN 45 call −0.014/day → net position theta +0.015)
• Profile: delta near zero (+0.041) and LONG vega, because the longer-dated option has the greater vega
• Maximum profit: the short option expires worthless with the underlying near the strike, then implied volatility rises, lifting the remaining long option
• When to use: near-term flat/range-bound view combined with a longer-term directional view; implement in a LOW implied-volatility market
• Main risk: gamma — the underlying moves too far, too fast, away from the strike. A big move or falling implied volatility helps the SHORT calendar
• Nuance: for in-the-money calls the theta relationship reverses (SEP 40 −0.007 vs OCT 40 −0.011), which can motivate a short calendar

cards.front: Distinguish volatility skew from volatility smile, say which is more common in equity index options, and state how skew is measured.
cards.back:
• SKEW: implied volatility INCREASES for OTM puts and DECREASES for OTM calls as the strike moves away from spot — a downward-sloping IV-versus-strike line. The more common shape; driven by universal demand for OTM puts as portfolio insurance against fat-tailed sell-offs (little skew existed before the 1987 crash)
• SMILE: implied volatility of BOTH OTM puts AND OTM calls trades above ATM — a U-shape
• Measurement: skew = IV(90% moneyness put, X/S = 90%) − IV(110% moneyness call); e.g., S&P 500 three-month 17.7 − 9.4 = 8.3 volatility points
• Reading it: a sharp rise in skew with a jump in the absolute IV level signals bearish sentiment; elevated OTM CALL IV signals bullish demand for upside
• Term structure is usually in contango and inverts under stress; the volatility SURFACE plots expiry, strike and IV together, showing skew and term structure at once
• Trap: calling it a smile when only put IV is elevated — that is a skew

cards.front: Give the curriculum's direction-by-implied-volatility grid for choosing an option strategy (bearish / neutral / bullish across falling, unchanged, and rising implied volatility).
cards.back:
Implied volatility expected to DECREASE:
• Bearish → write calls • Neutral → write a straddle • Bullish → write puts
Implied volatility expected to REMAIN UNCHANGED:
• Bearish → write calls and buy puts (a collar against a long position) • Neutral → calendar spread • Bullish → buy calls and write puts (long risk reversal)
Implied volatility expected to INCREASE:
• Bearish → buy puts • Neutral → buy a straddle • Bullish → buy calls
Also:
• Bull call spread / bear put spread when the direction view is right but the market is not clearly trending — and to cut cost
• A skewed IV curve makes the bear PUT spread cheaper still (the richer, more OTM low-strike put is the one sold)
• Getting direction right but volatility wrong still loses money through vega and theta

cards.front: When options at several strikes fit a targeted equity exposure, how does the curriculum choose between them?
cards.back:
• Step 1: compute each strike's breakeven and discard any whose breakeven lies beyond the expected target price (the 70-strike call's breakeven of 70.40 fails a 70 target)
• Step 2: rank by profit per unit of premium paid at the target price. Long calls: 60-strike (70 − 63)/3 = 2.3 beats 58-strike (70 − 62)/4 = 2.0. Protective puts: 42.50-strike (40.78 − 37.80)/1.72 = 1.73 beats 45.00-strike 1.08
• The cheaper, nearer-the-money choice has the LOWER delta but the LARGER gamma, so it gains more if the expected large move actually happens
• Writing puts at the target buy price gives an effective purchase price of X − p0 (165 − 5.30 = 159.70); a covered call gives an effective sale price of X + c0
• Hedging a fixed cash need: premium income must cover it — 50 contracts × 100 × 6.45 = $32,250
• Close the hedge once the event passes and recover the remaining premium

cards.front: You correctly foresee a known event that will move the stock sharply, and buy a straddle. Why can the trade still be a bad one?
cards.back:
• Everyone else sees the same event, so implied volatility — and both premiums — rise BEFORE the announcement, widening the breakevens
• MNZA case: the 170 straddle initially cost 6.45 + 7.69 = 14.14, with breakevens 155.86 and 184.14, needing roughly a 10% move — achievable on her forecast
• After the news of the unveiling, IV rose from about 30% to about 45%; the straddle cost 10.20 + 10.89 = 21.09, so the stock now had to move more than 12%. She declined the trade
• Vega check: straddle vega +0.468 × 15 volatility points = 7.02, close to the actual 6.95 price increase
• Lesson: to profit from a long straddle you must be right that TRUE volatility exceeds the market's already-elevated implied volatility — a directional view on the event is not enough

cards.front: Using bond futures to move a portfolio to a target duration, what is the basis point value hedge ratio (number of contracts), and how do you get the BPV of the futures?
cards.back:
• BPV_T = target BPV; BPV_P = portfolio BPV; both from BPV = MDUR × 0.01% × market value (0.01% = 0.0001)
• BPV_CTD = MDUR_CTD × 0.01% × MV_CTD, where MV_CTD = (CTD price ÷ 100) × futures contract size
• BPV_F = BPV_CTD ÷ CF, so dividing by BPV_CTD and multiplying by CF is the same thing
• Sign is the instruction: positive = BUY futures (add duration); negative = SELL futures (cut duration); complete hedge sets BPV_T = 0
• Worked: MV 49,531,000, MDUR 9.50 → BPV_P = 47,054.45; CTD price 98.14, MDUR 8.623, CF 0.619489 → BPV_CTD = 84.63; full hedge = (0 − 47,054.45)/84.63 × 0.619489 = −344.4 → sell 344
• Classic errors: using portfolio PRINCIPAL instead of MARKET value; dividing by CF instead of multiplying; forgetting BPV is per 1 bp (0.0001), not 1%
cards.formula: BPVHR = [(BPV_T − BPV_P) ÷ BPV_CTD] × CF, with BPV = MDUR × 0.01% × MV and BPV_F = BPV_CTD ÷ CF
cards.mnemonic: Gap over CTD, times CF.

cards.front: What notional interest rate swap hits a target modified duration, and which side of the swap carries positive duration?
cards.back:
• MDUR_T = target modified duration; MDUR_P = portfolio's; MV_P = portfolio market value; MDUR_S = the swap's modified duration FROM THE SIDE BEING ENTERED
• Swap duration = the NET of the modified durations of the equivalent fixed- and floating-rate bond positions, signed by the side taken: for the PAY-fixed, receive-floating party it is MDUR(floating bond) − MDUR(fixed bond), and floating duration ≈ 0, so the net is negative
• PAY-fixed, receive-floating = NEGATIVE duration (short the fixed bond) → cuts duration and gains as rates rise
• RECEIVE-fixed, pay-floating = POSITIVE duration → adds duration
• Worked: €50m portfolio, MDUR 5.5 → target 4.5, two-year pay-fixed swap MDUR_S = −2.00 → N_S = [(4.50 − 5.50) ÷ (−2.00)] × €50m = €25m notional
• Classic error: dropping the minus sign on MDUR_S for a pay-fixed swap (gives a negative notional) or inverting the numerator to MDUR_P − MDUR_T
cards.formula: N_S = [(MDUR_T − MDUR_P) ÷ MDUR_S] × MV_P

cards.front: Which deliverable bond becomes the cheapest-to-deliver, and what three real-world factors make a bond futures hedge imperfect?
cards.back:
• The futures SELLER has the obligation to deliver and the right to choose the bond; he picks the one with the greatest profit / smallest loss = principal invoice amount − dirty purchase price
• Principal invoice amount = (futures settlement price ÷ 100) × CF × contract size
• CTD tends to be a LOW-coupon, LONG-maturity, LONG-duration bond when market yield is ABOVE the contract's notional yield (high-coupon, short, short-duration when yield is below)
• Because futures price sensitivity tracks the CTD, the futures' duration and BPV come from the CTD adjusted by its conversion factor
• Basis = spot cash price − (futures price × CF); must be zero at delivery (physical delivery forces convergence). Negative basis → buy the basis (buy bond, short futures); positive → sell the basis
• Hedge imperfections: (1) the CTD can CHANGE over the holding period, changing the futures' duration; (2) convexity — the price/yield relation is not linear; (3) the yield curve often moves NON-parallel

cards.front: A firm needs foreign-currency funding but borrows more cheaply at home. How does a cross-currency basis swap solve this, and what exactly is "the basis"?
cards.back:
• Borrow in the local currency at the better rate, then swap: exchange notionals at inception at spot S0, make floating interest payments in the borrowed foreign currency and receive floating in the local currency, re-exchange the SAME notionals at the SAME S0 at maturity
• Because S0 is fixed for inception, all coupons, and maturity, the FX risk is eliminated — a local-currency loan converted into a foreign-currency loan
• Mostly floating-for-floating; notional exchange is usual but optional (skip it if only interest cash flows are being hedged)
• The basis is quoted on the NON-USD leg and exists because covered interest rate parity generally does NOT hold; it is driven by credit, liquidity, and supply/demand for cross-currency financing
• Paying the basis = borrowing the other currency vs lending USD; receiving the basis = lending the other currency vs borrowing USD
• Worked: Canadian firm borrows CAD at reference + 65 bps, swap quoted at −15 bps → effective spread 80 bps, versus 100 bps on a direct USD loan
• Same logic lets an investor buy a foreign bond and swap back for a synthetic domestic yield that beats the domestic asset when the basis is favorable

cards.front: Currency forwards vs currency futures for hedging FX exposure: which suits whom, and how many futures hedge a known foreign-currency inflow?
cards.back:
• FORWARDS: OTC, customizable to the exact amount and date, no daily settlement, bilateral counterparty risk — favored by corporations hedging specific foreign cash flows
• FUTURES: exchange-traded and standardized, guaranteed by a clearinghouse so counterparty risk is virtually zero, liquid and best suited to dealers and portfolio managers — but standard sizes and expiries force rounding and date mismatch
• A future foreign-currency INFLOW is hedged by SELLING the foreign currency: short futures with the closest expiry to the inflow
• With a hedge ratio of 1, N = FC exposure ÷ contract size. Worked: CAD50,000,000 ÷ CAD100,000 = 500 contracts SOLD
• Fully effective only if futures and spot prices move equally; basis = futures price(t) − spot price(t) can widen or narrow between initiation and liquidation → basis risk
• Longer-dated or interest-plus-principal FX exposure is better handled by a currency (cross-currency) swap than by rolling short-dated contracts

cards.front: How many equity index futures move a stock portfolio from its current beta to a target beta?
cards.back:
• β_T = target beta, β_S = current portfolio beta, β_f = beta of the futures, S = market value of the stock portfolio
• F = VALUE PER CONTRACT = quoted futures price × multiplier (e.g., S&P 500 at 2,700 × $250 = $675,000)
• β_T > β_S → N_f positive → BUY futures (add market risk); β_T < β_S → negative → SELL futures
• Complete hedge sets β_T = 0, reducing to N_f = −(β_S ÷ β_f)(S ÷ F), always a sell
• Worked: £40m portfolio, β_S 0.85 → β_T 1.10, β_f 1.00, FTSE futures 7,300 × £10 = £73,000 → (0.25/1.00) × (40,000,000/73,000) = 136.99 ≈ BUY 137; the combined position returned 2.2% when the market rose 2%, an effective beta of 1.10
• Classic errors: plugging in the index LEVEL instead of level × multiplier; omitting β_f in the denominator; applying the target beta to the futures value (a futures position is worth zero after each mark to market)
cards.formula: N_f = [(β_T − β_S) ÷ β_f] × (S ÷ F), where F = futures price × multiplier

cards.front: Name the three main types of equity swap, what a total return swap adds, and the trade-offs of synthetic equity exposure versus owning the shares.
cards.back:
• Three types: (1) receive-equity return, pay-FIXED; (2) receive-equity return, pay-FLOATING; (3) receive-equity return, pay-ANOTHER equity return
• A total return swap is a modified equity swap that also passes through DIVIDENDS paid by the underlying stock or index over the swap's life
• Preferred over share ownership when market access is restricted, when taxes apply to holding physical stock but not to swaps (e.g., stamp duty), when custodian fees are high, or when monitoring the position (corporate actions) is costly
• Drawbacks: collateral must be posted, contracts are relatively ILLIQUID, they confer NO VOTING RIGHTS, and each side bears counterparty credit risk
• Concentrated low-basis holding: pay the stock's TOTAL return (price move plus dividends) and receive a floating reference rate — value is protected, no sale is made, and ownership/votes are kept
• Single-stock swaps settle physically (receive the shares, pay the notional) or in cash (receive the appreciation in cash); either way the economics match
• Tenor must be matched to the period over which protection is wanted

cards.front: What is the settlement amount on a variance swap, and how do you convert a vega notional quote into the variance notional?
cards.back:
• Trades are quoted in VEGA notional and the strike X is quoted as annualized VOLATILITY; the payoff is computed in VARIANCE, so square the volatilities
• Variance notional = vega notional ÷ (2 × strike), with the strike in volatility POINTS (20, not 0.20)
• Realized variance = 252 × Σ R_i² ÷ (N − 1), with R_i = ln(P_i+1 ÷ P_i)
• Long pays off when realized variance EXCEEDS the strike variance; if the amount is positive the seller pays the buyer, if negative the buyer pays the seller. No cash changes hands at inception or during the life
• Worked: $50,000 vega notional, strike 20% → variance notional = 50,000 ÷ (2 × 20) = 1,250; realized vol 18% → 1,250 × (18² − 20²) = 1,250 × (324 − 400) = −$95,000, so the short receives $95,000
• Classic error: treating the vega-notional rule of thumb (about $50,000 of P&L per 1 volatility point) as the exact payoff — it is only an approximation because the payoff is CONVEX in volatility
• The strike itself is set off the implied volatility skew, by rule of thumb the implied vol of the 90%-moneyness put
cards.formula: Settlement = variance notional × (realized variance − strike variance); variance notional = vega notional ÷ (2 × strike)

cards.front: A manager buys and continuously rolls VIX futures as a tail hedge. Why can the hedge bleed money even when spot VIX ends where it started?
cards.back:
• VIX futures converge to spot VIX at expiration, so with volatility expectations unchanged the futures price is PULLED toward spot
• In CONTANGO (upward-sloping curve) that pull is downward → a long roll incurs roll-down LOSSES (negative carry); in BACKWARDATION the long earns positive roll return
• Daily roll = (front-month VIX futures price − VIX spot) ÷ business days to settlement; assume the basis declines linearly to settlement
• Costs are highest when the SHORT end of the curve is much steeper than the long end; long VIX positions can be very expensive to maintain over time
• Volatility ETPs/ETNs rebalance daily (sell shorter-dated, buy longer-dated) to hold constant average maturity, so in contango they suffer negative carry and UNDERPERFORM the VIX move
• Second trap: longer-maturity contracts are less sensitive to short-term VIX spikes, so the futures may not track a spike; and for a long VIX hedge to protect the equity book, implied vol must rise by MORE than the consensus already priced in before the sell-off
• Mirror image: the systematic short-volatility seller collects the risk premium in calm markets but faces large losses when volatility jumps

cards.front: Walk through equitizing an unintended cash balance with index futures: the objective, the sizing step, and the resulting return.
cards.back:
• Objective: remove the cash drag and minimize tracking error versus the fund's index without actually investing the cash, exploiting futures liquidity
• Step 1 — identify the cash to equitize; it has β_S = 0, so the general beta formula collapses to N_f = (β_T ÷ β_f) × (S ÷ F)
• Step 2 — S = the cash amount, F = futures price × multiplier; for full index replication β_T = β_f = 1.0
• Step 3 — BUY that many contracts (round to whole contracts; rounding leaves small residual tracking error)
• Worked: £20,000,000 of cash, FTSE 100 futures at 7,900 with £10 per point (£79,000 per contract) → 20,000,000 ÷ 79,000 = 253.16 ≈ BUY 253
• Outcome: cash keeps earning the floating rate WHILE the futures deliver the index return; with the index up 5% the fund returned 5.0% instead of roughly 4.6% unequitized
• Alternative synthetic: buy calls and sell puts on the underlying with the same strike and expiry
• Reverse the trade (sell the futures) once the cash is deployed or no longer held

cards.front: From a fed funds futures price, how do you infer the expected policy rate and the probability of a 25 bp hike — and what distorts that probability?
cards.back:
• Fed funds futures price = 100 − expected FFE rate; the contract cash settles to the simple average OVERNIGHT EFFECTIVE federal funds rate for the delivery month, not the Fed's target rate
• Probability of a hike = (FFE rate implied by the futures − current fed funds rate) ÷ (fed funds rate assuming a hike − current fed funds rate), using the MIDPOINTS of the 25 bp target ranges
• Worked: price 97.90 → implied 2.10%; current range 1.75%–2.00% (mid 1.875%), post-hike range 2.00%–2.25% (mid 2.125%) → (2.10 − 1.875) ÷ (2.125 − 1.875) = 90%
• Distortion: end-of-month activity by large banks dips the EFFE rate — a price of 98.05 implies 1.95% and the probability collapses to (1.95 − 1.875) ÷ 0.25 = 30%; data providers SMOOTH these EOM dips using a forward rate structure
• Probabilities of hike, cut, and no change at a given meeting sum to 1
• These are current market EXPECTATIONS, not forecasts of what will happen; they can diverge from the Fed's forward guidance and dot plot and have weak predictive power at longer horizons
• Companion inferences: CPI (inflation) swaps for expected inflation, VIX futures for expected volatility

cards.front: Write the domestic-currency return on a foreign asset, and compute it for a local asset return of 8% when the foreign currency appreciates 3%.
cards.back:
• R_DC = return measured in the investor's home (reporting) currency
• R_FC = foreign-currency (local) return on the asset itself
• R_FX = % change in the FOREIGN currency against the domestic currency — the domestic currency must be the PRICE currency in the quote
• Multiplicative, not additive: expanded, R_DC = R_FC + R_FX + (R_FC × R_FX)
• Answer: (1.08)(1.03) − 1 = 11.24%, not 11% — the extra 0.24% is the cross-product
• Multi-asset: R_DC = Σ ω(i)(1 + R_FC,i)(1 + R_FX,i) − 1, weights measured in the domestic currency and summing to 1 (short positions may be negative)
• R_DC ≈ R_FC + R_FX is only an approximation for small returns — it is the basis for the variance formula, never the exact return answer
• Classic error: summing the two returns and dropping the cross-product

cards.front: Write the risk (variance) of the domestic-currency return on a single foreign asset, and solve for σ(R_FC) = 3%, σ(R_FX) = 2%, ρ = +0.50.
cards.back:
• σ²(R_FC) = variance of the local asset return; σ²(R_FX) = variance of the currency return; ρ = correlation between them
• Units: decimals or percents consistently (3% = 0.03); the output is a VARIANCE — take the square root for risk
• Solve: 0.03² + 0.02² + 2(0.03)(0.02)(0.50) = 0.0019 → σ(R_DC) ≈ 4.36%
• Rests on the approximation R_DC ≈ R_FC + R_FX, so it is valid for small returns
• Because all three terms add, currency exposure generally RAISES risk above σ(R_FC); the effect is indeterminate only when ρ is negative
• A perfect, costless hedge sets R_FX = 0, so σ(R_DC) = σ(R_FC) — this is the pure risk-reduction case for hedging
• Classic errors: omitting the 2ρ cross term, or reporting the variance as if it were the standard deviation
cards.formula: σ²(R_DC) ≈ σ²(R_FC) + σ²(R_FX) + 2 × σ(R_FC) × σ(R_FX) × ρ(R_FC,R_FX)

cards.front: A eurozone investor holds a Canadian asset and is given CAD/EUR moving from 1.4500 to 1.4700. Why does plugging +1.38% into R_DC give the wrong answer?
cards.back:
• R_FX is defined as the change in the DIRECTLY quoted rate — the investor's home currency must be the PRICE currency
• CAD/EUR prices the EUR in CAD, so for a eurozone investor the home currency is the BASE — the quote must be inverted first
• Canadian investor: R_FX = (1.4700 ÷ 1.4500) − 1 = +1.38%
• Eurozone investor: R_FX = [(1 ÷ 1.4700) ÷ (1 ÷ 1.4500)] − 1 = −1.364%
• Same market move, opposite sign — the sign of the currency contribution flips with the investor's domicile
• Market-standard P/B conventions (EUR always base, then GBP, then AUD/NZD, then USD) are NOT always direct quotes, so convert before taking percentage changes
• Same trap on the exam: deciding whether the hedge means buying or selling the BASE currency
cards.mnemonic: Home currency on top (price side) before any % change.

cards.front: Which is hedged more in practice — the currency risk of a foreign BOND portfolio or a foreign EQUITY portfolio — and what drives the difference?
cards.back:
• Bonds: ρ(R_FC, R_FX) is generally HIGHER, because both bond prices and currencies react strongly to interest rates
• → currency offers little diversification benefit to fixed income → hedge it; Campbell, Serfaty-de Medeiros & Viceira found no diversification benefit and recommended FULL hedging; joint optimal hedge ratios for international bonds are almost always near 100%
• Equities: returns are driven more by expected earnings → lower correlation with currency → a better case for CARRYING currency exposure
• Optimal equity hedge ratios vary widely with the investor's domestic currency and the foreign market — some near 0%, some near 100% (Campbell 2010)
• Evidence is mixed, not absolute (Darnell 2004 found the fixed-income hedging advantage is not always large or consistent)
• Safe havens (USD, JPY, CHF) appreciate in stress, so keeping some exposure — a hedge ratio away from 100% — can offset losses on risky assets, especially in equity portfolios
• Bottom line: currency hedging is still more common for fixed-income than for equity portfolios

cards.front: What five items does the currency risk management policy inside an IPS specify?
cards.back:
• Target proportion of currency exposure to be PASSIVELY hedged (the benchmark/strategic hedge ratio)
• Latitude for ACTIVE currency management around that target (the discretionary band)
• Frequency of hedge REBALANCING
• The currency hedge performance BENCHMARK to be used
• The hedging TOOLS permitted (which forwards, options, exotics; limits on leverage and short positions)
• This is a strategic decision belonging to the beneficial owners, not a tactical one
• Hedging costs alone usually dictate a RANGE of permissible exposures rather than a single point — the range acts like an insurance deductible
• Example band: hedge ratio kept within 95%–105%, or exposures allowed ±20% of the EUR market value

cards.front: List the conditions that bias the strategic currency program toward being MORE fully hedged.
cards.back:
Bias toward a fully hedged program the more:
• SHORT-TERM the portfolio's investment objectives are
• RISK AVERSE the beneficial owners are (and impervious to ex post regret over missed opportunities)
• IMMEDIATE the portfolio's income and/or liquidity needs are
• FIXED-INCOME assets are held in the foreign-currency portfolio
• CHEAPLY the hedging program can be implemented
• VOLATILE (risky) financial markets are — though this also raises option premiums
• SKEPTICAL the owners/oversight committee are of the benefits of active currency management
Relaxing any one creates latitude for a more proactive posture: wider discretionary bands, or currency overlay run as a separate asset class — the more the overlay's alpha is uncorrelated with other portfolio alpha sources, the more of it is allowed

cards.front: Name the four active currency trading styles and the core bet each one places.
cards.back:
• ECONOMIC FUNDAMENTALS — estimate fair value; the long-run equilibrium REAL exchange rate (PPP/fair-value model) is the anchor and spot converges to it; buy undervalued, sell overvalued currencies
• TECHNICAL ANALYSIS — ignores economics; assumes historical price patterns repeat because they reflect market psychology; identifies trends, overbought/oversold conditions, and support/resistance (e.g., the 200-day moving average); asks where prices WILL trade, not where they SHOULD; least useful in a trendless market
• CARRY TRADE — borrow/sell the LOW-yield currency, invest in/buy the HIGH-yield currency; an explicit bet AGAINST uncovered interest rate parity, which fails persistently in the short to medium term
• VOLATILITY TRADING — use delta-hedged FX options to express a view on future implied VOLATILITY, not on direction
Carry earns steadily then loses sharply: funding currencies are safe havens (EUR, CHF, JPY) and investment currencies are riskier/EM, so a flight to safety forces a leveraged, panicked unwind — a pronounced NEGATIVE SKEW, "picking up nickels in front of a steamroller"

cards.front: How does a trader isolate a pure volatility view in FX options, and what is the cheapest structure for "much more volatile, no directional view"?
cards.back:
• Delta = sensitivity of the premium to the spot rate (price risk); Vega = sensitivity to implied volatility (volatility risk)
• DELTA HEDGE first: offset with spot (delta = 1) or forwards, sized as delta × notional, to set net delta to zero — a long EUR1m call with delta +0.5 is hedged by a EUR0.5m short forward
• What remains is a pure vega position — a view on future implied volatility, not direction
• Long STRADDLE = long ATM put (delta −0.5) + long ATM call (+0.5); delta neutral, profits on a large move either way; the most expensive
• Long STRANGLE = long OTM put + OTM call, same expiry and same delta (e.g., 25-delta); cheaper, more moderate risk–reward, pays only past the OTM strikes
• Cheapest "vol up" expression = long OTM strangle (e.g., 25-delta) rather than a straddle; writing a near-ATM strangle (40-delta) would LOSE if the view is right
• FX options are quoted by delta — ATM, 25-delta, 10-delta; the 10-delta is deeper OTM and cheaper
• Speculative vol traders usually want to be net SHORT volatility (most options expire OTM; the premium is the risk premium for absorbing vol risk); hedgers are usually net LONG volatility and pay time decay (theta)

cards.front: In the curriculum's fundamentals framework, what four upward movements should cause the BASE currency's real exchange rate to appreciate?
cards.back:
All else equal, the base currency's real exchange rate should appreciate with an upward movement in:
• Its LONG-RUN EQUILIBRIUM real exchange rate
• Its own REAL or NOMINAL interest rates — attracts foreign capital (recall r = i − expected inflation)
• EXPECTED FOREIGN inflation — depreciates the foreign currency
• The FOREIGN risk premium — makes foreign assets less attractive than the base country's
It should also rise if it is currently BELOW its long-run equilibrium value
• Structure: the long-run equilibrium real rate is the anchor (PPP/fair value); short- to medium-term real-rate, inflation, and risk-premium DIFFERENTIALS shape the timing and path, and can overshoot or undershoot it
• Tactical use: an unexpected policy tightening not yet priced in raises real rates → that currency appreciates; a rise in a country's expected inflation cuts its real rate and depreciates it
• Watch the quote: an appreciation of the PRICE currency shows up as a DECLINE in the P/B rate

cards.front: Give the magnitude of roll yield on a currency hedge and the rule for its sign. Which currency is expensive to hedge?
cards.back:
• F and S are the all-in forward and spot rates for the same P/B pair; the result is a return over the contract's term (not annualized unless stated)
• Sign is POSITIVE when you BUY the base currency at a forward DISCOUNT or SELL it at a forward PREMIUM — "buy low, sell high"; otherwise negative (a cost)
• Covered interest rate parity fixes which is which: the LOWER-yield currency trades at a forward PREMIUM, the HIGHER-yield currency at a forward DISCOUNT
• Hedging a long foreign exposure means SELLING that currency forward → positive roll yield if it is the LOW-yield (forward-PREMIUM) currency, and a COST if it is the HIGH-yield (forward-DISCOUNT) currency. So the expensive currency to hedge is the HIGH-yield one (curriculum example: long ZAR, HKD/ZAR at a 2.5% forward discount → selling ZAR forward costs about 2.5%)
• The three equivalent rows: implementing the carry trade = buy high-yield / sell low-yield; trading the forward rate bias = buy forward-discount / sell forward-premium; earning positive roll yield = the same pairing. Negative roll yield = trading AGAINST the forward rate bias = a negative carry trade
• Decision rule: weigh expected roll yield against the expected spot move — if the hedge costs 6% to avoid an expected 4% depreciation, a risk-NEUTRAL manager drops the hedge; a risk-AVERSE manager may still hedge because the realized loss could exceed 6%
• Classic error: treating a forward hedge as costless because no premium is paid up front
cards.formula: Roll yield magnitude = |(F(P/B) − S(P/B)) ÷ S(P/B)|

cards.front: A CHF-based investor hedged a EUR1,000,000 exposure with a short one-month CHF/EUR forward. One month later the assets are worth EUR950,000. Walk through rolling and rebalancing the hedge.
cards.back:
• Roll with an FX SWAP = simultaneous spot and offsetting forward transaction (the two "legs")
• NEAR leg: buy EUR1,000,000 spot to settle the maturing short forward — the EUR amounts net to zero, but a CHF cash gain or loss is realized (a hedge cuts mark-to-market volatility while ADDING cash-account volatility)
• FAR leg: sell EUR950,000 forward for one month → legs are unequal, so this is a MISMATCHED swap; the size adjustment is reflected in the spot rate quoted (bid or offer by the net direction), with forward points still taken from the side matching the forward trade
• If the asset value were unchanged and the manager had no view: a MATCHED swap (equal legs), priced conventionally off the MID-market spot rate
• If the original forward has NOT yet matured (curriculum's variant: it was a three-month contract, now one month in), no swap is needed — leave it outstanding and BUY EUR50,000 forward to that same settlement date, so the net EUR delivered is the desired EUR950,000
• Drift rule: a RISING foreign asset leaves a static hedge UNDER-hedged (sell more forward); a FALLING asset leaves it OVER-hedged (buy some back)
• More frequent rebalancing tracks the target ratio more tightly but adds transaction costs — higher risk aversion means more frequent rebalancing; more active discretion means letting the ratio drift

cards.front: A manager is LONG the base currency and must SELL it to hedge. What is the "core" hedge, and what is the menu of ways to cut its cost?
cards.back:
• CORE hedge: a short forward (no premium, but zero upside and possible negative roll yield) or a long PUT (protective put; ATM is the most expensive and the most complete)
• Buy an OTM put (25- or 10-delta) — cheaper, but accepts a "deductible" of unprotected loss
• SHORT RISK REVERSAL (collar) — buy an OTM put, WRITE an OTM call; the premium received funds the put, upside is capped at the call strike. (In FX, long call + short put = a LONG risk reversal, so the hedger's collar is the SHORT one.)
• PUT SPREAD — buy an OTM put, write a deeper-OTM put; protection exists only BETWEEN the two strikes and disappears below the lower one
• SEAGULL — the put spread plus a written call: at least three options, with the "wings" on the opposite side of the market from the "body"; lets the long put be ATM for fuller protection
• EXOTICS — knock-in/knock-out options exist only under barrier conditions, so they are cheaper; digital/binary options pay a fixed amount and cost MORE than a vanilla at the same strike — a speculative tool, not a hedging one
• Zero-cost structures are built by adjusting strikes and/or notional sizes
• Universal rule: every cost reduction buys some combination of LESS downside protection and/or LESS upside potential — lower insurance premiums mean lower insurance

cards.front: Give the minimum-variance hedge ratio, when it should be used, and solve it for ρ = 0.20, σ(R_DC) = 4.4%, σ(R_FX) = 2.7% on a USD10 million holding.
cards.back:
• It is the OLS regression slope (beta) of the asset's DOMESTIC-currency return on the % change in the spot rate (R_FX = %ΔS with the domestic currency as the price currency)
• It minimizes σ²(R_DC) — the all-in domestic-currency variance — not just currency variance, so it also hedges the part of asset risk correlated with the currency
• Units: both standard deviations in the same units; h* is expressed as a fraction of the exposure to sell forward
• Solve: 0.20 × (4.4 ÷ 2.7) = 0.33 → short about USD3.3 million forward against the USD10 million position
• h* can EXCEED 1 (a Swiss equity example regressed to β = 1.35 → hedge CHF1,350,000 of a CHF1,000,000 exposure) or be NEGATIVE
• Use it only for INDIRECT hedges — cross hedges, macro hedges, or a joint R_FC-and-R_FX optimization for a SINGLE foreign asset. For a direct spot-versus-its-own-forward hedge the regression gives ≈1, so running it is superfluous
• Classic errors: inverting the ratio (σ_FX ÷ σ_DC), using ρ alone as the hedge ratio, and forgetting the beta is a backward-looking estimate — an unstable beta IS basis risk and must be re-estimated and rebalanced
cards.formula: h* = ρ(R_DC, R_FX) × [σ(R_DC) ÷ σ(R_FX)]

cards.front: Non-deliverable forward vs an ordinary deliverable forward: settlement, credit risk, and pricing — and what makes EM currency exposure hard to manage in the first place?
cards.back:
NDF vs deliverable forward:
• NDF is used where capital controls or convertibility limits block delivery (CNY, KRW, RUB, INR, BRL); it is CASH SETTLED in the non-controlled currency (usually USD) — the controlled currency is never delivered
• A vanilla forward exchanges both principal amounts physically
• Credit risk is LOWER on an NDF because the principal sums never move — only the small net difference changes hands
• Pricing: with capital controls the cross-border arbitrage enforcing covered interest rate parity does not function, so NDF pricing reflects OFFSHORE supply, demand and risk premia and need not match CIP or the onshore rate; participants are largely offshore hedge funds and prop traders making directional bets
EM challenges:
• Higher trading costs and thin liquidity; crosses (e.g., CLP/THB) route through the USD, paying TWO bid–offer spreads, with time-zone liquidity gaps
• Fat tails and pronounced negative skew — VaR and the Sharpe ratio, built on normality, understate the true risk after long calm periods
• Contagion: in a crisis currencies trade in baskets (havens vs commodity currencies), so a "diversified" EM book doubles up exactly when it matters
• Crowded carry trades are easy to enter and impossible to exit; volatility spikes make rolling option protection far more expensive
• Central banks defending a falling currency HIKE rates, deepening its forward discount — selling it forward then inflicts worse negative roll yield
• Government involvement (intervention, controls, pegs) creates artificial calm punctuated by sudden breaks

cards.front: Name the four sources from which a CFA Institute professional conduct investigation can arise.
cards.back:
• Self-disclosure on the annual Professional Conduct Statement — civil litigation, criminal investigation, being subject of a written complaint
• Written complaints received by Professional Conduct (PC) staff
• Public sources — media, regulatory notices, other public information
• CFA Institute's own exam surveillance — testing-center reports, post-exam analysis of scores and exam materials, monitoring of online and social media for disclosure of confidential exam information
Trap: exam answers that say inquiries are NOT initiated from media reports are wrong — media is an explicit source.
cards.mnemonic: Self, Complaint, Public, Surveillance

cards.front: Walk the disciplinary review process from the moment a PC inquiry is opened to a final outcome.
cards.back:
1. PC staff investigate: request a written explanation from the member/candidate; interview the member/candidate, complaining parties, and third parties; collect relevant documents and records.
2. On review, PC staff may (a) conclude with no disciplinary sanction, (b) issue a cautionary letter, or (c) continue proceedings to discipline.
3. If staff believe a violation occurred, the member/candidate may accept or reject the charges and proposed sanction.
4. If rejected, the matter goes to a hearing panel of DRC members, which weighs materials and presentations from both PC staff and the member/candidate and decides violation and sanction.
5. DRC panels also review accepted (agreed) matters to confirm the findings are reasonable.

cards.front: Who enforces the Code and Standards, and what sanctions can be imposed on a member versus a candidate?
cards.back:
Structure: the CFA Institute Board of Governors oversees the Professional Conduct (PC) group; PC staff investigate; the Disciplinary Review Committee (DRC) — a volunteer committee of CFA charterholders — serves on hearing panels, imposes sanctions, and partners with PC staff on professional conduct policy. The Bylaws and Rules of Procedure form the basic enforcement structure.
Sanctions on members: • public censure • suspension of membership and use of the CFA designation • revocation of membership and the right to use the CFA designation.
Candidates: may be suspended or prohibited from further participation in the CFA Program.
Scope: applies to CFA Institute members and to candidates for the CFA and CIPM designations.

cards.front: List the seven Standards of Professional Conduct and their subsections.
cards.back:
I Professionalism: A Knowledge of the Law; B Independence and Objectivity; C Misrepresentation; D Misconduct; E Competence
II Integrity of Capital Markets: A Material Nonpublic Information; B Market Manipulation
III Duties to Clients: A Loyalty, Prudence, and Care; B Fair Dealing; C Suitability; D Performance Presentation; E Preservation of Confidentiality
IV Duties to Employers: A Loyalty; B Additional Compensation Arrangements; C Responsibilities of Supervisors
V Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions: A Diligence and Reasonable Basis; B Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients; C Record Retention
VI Conflicts of Interest: A Avoid or Disclose Conflicts; B Priority of Transactions; C Referral Fees
VII Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate: A Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs; B Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
cards.mnemonic: I profession, II markets, III clients, IV employers, V the work, VI divided loyalties, VII the program

cards.front: What three changes did the CFA Institute Board of Governors approve to the Standards in 2023?
cards.back:
• New Standard I(E) Competence — members and candidates must act with and maintain the competence necessary to fulfill their professional responsibilities. It reinforces a Code principle; it does NOT mandate any specific continuing-education or professional development program, and the required competence varies with the nature and complexity of the role.
• Revised Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients — new item 1 requires disclosure of the nature of the services provided plus information about the costs to the client of those services (filling the gap on financial impact).
• Renamed and revised Standard VI(A), now "Avoid or Disclose Conflicts" — members must avoid conflicts or make full and fair disclosure; previously the standard's language mentioned only disclosure. Disclosures must be prominent, in plain language, and communicate the information effectively.
cards.mnemonic: One new (I-E), one expanded (V-B), one renamed (VI-A)

cards.front: A portfolio manager is offered a gift. When does Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity govern versus Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements?
cards.back:
I(B) Independence and Objectivity — the harm is to professional judgment. Must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity, and must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity. No consent cures it — the prohibited item stays prohibited.
IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements — the harm is to the employer. Must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that compete with, or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with, the employer's interest UNLESS written consent is obtained from all parties involved.
Traps: consent under IV(B) must be written and from all parties — not the employer only, and not oral; and an offered gift can still fail I(B) even with employer consent.

cards.front: Under Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, whose information is protected and what are the only three exceptions?
cards.back:
Protected: information about current, former, AND prospective clients — the duty survives the end of the relationship and begins before it formally starts.
Disclosure permitted only if:
1. The information concerns illegal activities on the part of the client or prospective client
2. Disclosure is required by law
3. The client or prospective client permits disclosure
Trap: there is no "reasonable and adequate basis" judgment call to make on confidentiality — that criterion belongs to Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis.

cards.front: A manager runs a fund to a stated aggressive-growth mandate. Must the manager confirm the mandate is suitable before each investment action? What does Standard III(C) actually require?
cards.back:
No — that is the classic misread.
• Managing to a specific mandate, strategy, or style: make only recommendations and take only actions consistent with the stated objectives and constraints of the PORTFOLIO. Whether the mandate suits any particular investor is not the manager's concern here.
• Advisory relationship with a client: (a) make reasonable inquiry into investment experience, risk and return objectives, and financial constraints BEFORE any recommendation or action, and reassess and update regularly; (b) determine the investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints; (c) judge suitability in the context of the client's TOTAL portfolio.
Other traps: "document constraints after the initial action" is wrong (inquiry comes first); "place client interests before own" is III(A), not III(C).

cards.front: Standard I(A): a member lives in one country, does business in another, and the Code and Standards also apply. Which rules govern — and what if applicable law says "the law of the locality where business is conducted (or the client's home country) governs"?
cards.back:
• Rule: comply with the STRICTER of (i) applicable law/regulation and (ii) the Code and Standards
• "More strict" = imposes greater restrictions on the member, or calls for greater action to protect client interests
• No applicable law, or law LESS strict than the Code → follow the Code and Standards
• Law STRICTER than the Code → follow that law (e.g., local ban on adviser IPO participation binds a US citizen registered there)
• If applicable law defers to the locality or the client's home country, run the same strictness test on THAT law: stricter → follow it; less strict or absent → follow the Code
• Complying with law is only the minimum threshold — conduct that is legal may still violate the Code
cards.mnemonic: Stricter wins; silence defaults to the Code.

cards.front: You have reasonable grounds to believe a colleague's or employer's ongoing activity is illegal or unethical. What sequence does Standard I(A) require — and must you report it to the regulator?
cards.back:
• Step 1: attempt to stop the behavior through direct discussion with the person involved
• Step 2: if unsuccessful, bring it to the employer — the supervisor or the compliance department (seek legal/compliance advice)
• Step 3: if it is not remedied, dissociate — remove your name from reports or recommendations, ask for a different assignment, refuse to accept a new client or continue advising a current one
• Extreme cases: dissociation may require leaving the employment
• Document the violation when dissociating
• Reporting to a government or regulatory body is NOT required by the Code unless mandatory under applicable law (voluntary reporting = whistle-blowing) — CFA Institute strongly encourages reporting members/candidates to the Professional Conduct Program
• Trap: inaction plus continued association with the wrongdoers can itself be construed as participation or assistance; relying on counsel's opinion that the regulator "could not prove" involvement does not absolve you

cards.front: Standard I(B): how does a gift from a CLIENT differ from a gift from a party seeking to influence you, and what is required in each case?
cards.back:
• From a client: the client already has a compensation arrangement with you or your firm, so the gift is treated as supplementary compensation and is deemed less likely to impair objectivity — it may be accepted, but must be DISCLOSED to the employer, preferably before acceptance; if prior notice is impossible, disclose after
• Purpose of disclosure: lets the employer independently judge the effect on independence and guard against favoring the gift-giving client over other fee-paying clients (e.g., a larger IPO allocation)
• From others (issuers, underwriters, brokers, managers seeking a mandate): must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise your own OR another's independence and objectivity
• Example violation: World Cup tickets, resort nights, meals, and limo service from a broker receiving your commission business
• The OFFERING side violates too: contributions to a hiring representative's reelection campaign or to a charity they name ("pay-to-play"), and lavish entertainment of a key decision maker

cards.front: Recommend the Standard I(B) procedures covering research pressure, travel funding, gifts, and issuer-paid research.
cards.back:
• Research pressure: comply with firm policies protecting research integrity; maintain a RESTRICTED list of companies with investment banking or other relationships and issue only factual information on them; analysts may decline coverage rather than shade a view; never change a rating to win business — not even by one increment
• Travel: pay for commercial transportation and hotel yourself or through your firm; no corporate issuer should reimburse air transportation; modestly arranged sponsored travel is acceptable only when commercial transport is unavailable (e.g., a mine or property tour) and hospitality is not lavish
• Gifts: limit acceptance to token items even if the employer has no gift policy; customary, ordinary business-related entertainment is permitted if its purpose is not to influence or reward
• Issuer-paid research: negotiate only a FLAT fee, agreed before writing and not linked to conclusions, recommendations, or investor uptake (no bonuses, warrants, or equity); fully disclose the compensation arrangement and the relationship; conduct thorough, independent analysis distinguishing fact from opinion
• Rating agencies / performance analysts: firewalls between business lines; never alter composite construction or exclude accounts under internal pressure

cards.front: Under Standard I(C), what counts as a misrepresentation, what does "knowingly" mean, and what are the recurring forms tested?
cards.back:
• Definition: any untrue statement, any OMISSION of a fact, or any otherwise false or misleading statement relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities — written, electronic (email, website, social media), or verbal
• "Knowingly" = knows or should have known the statement was false or that the omitted information could alter the investment decision
• Communications must be accurate, timely, complete, and in plain language
• Recurring forms: guaranteeing a return or preservation of capital (only guarantees built into the product's structure, or covered by an institution, may be called guaranteed); overstating firm services or personal credentials; cherry-picking accounts or omitting underperformers from composites; technically true but misleading track records; non-comparable benchmarks (disclose why a reference index is used); shopping valuations for higher prices; distributing stale fact sheets or out-of-date performance; presenting model output as fact or omitting negative scenarios; overstated ESG claims (promising engagement and proxy voting, then not doing it); passing off third-party or repackaged research as your own work
• Unintentional error (typo) is not a violation, but once discovered you must stop distribution and inform recipients

cards.front: Standard I(C) plagiarism: which uses of another's work violate the Standard, which are permitted, and what procedures prevent a violation?
cards.back:
Violations:
• Copying or using material in substantially the same form without naming the author and publisher — verbatim excerpts, slight rewording, paraphrases, summaries, even plain-language descriptions of general concepts
• Charts and graphs without sources; quotes attributed only to "leading analysts"; others' forecasts cited without their qualifying caveats; copying proprietary spreadsheets or algorithms without authorization
• Testing and slightly modifying someone else's model and announcing it as your own discovery — credit for the innovative idea belongs to the originator
• Repackaging outsourced research while implying you are the author
Permitted:
• Quoting recognized financial and statistical reporting services without attribution
• Using research and models developed within your own firm — the firm owns the work and may reissue it without crediting departed analysts; but you must never reissue a previously released report solely under your own name
• Distributing third-party research when you do not claim authorship and disclose the source (repackaging can add value if clients are told what they are paying for)
Procedures: maintain copies of all source material relied on; attribute direct quotations, tables, statistics, and new methodologies; attribute paraphrases and summaries; cite the original study rather than the media conduit (best practice is to obtain and review the original)

cards.front: Pitfall — candidates stretch Standard I(D) Misconduct to cover any bad behavior. What conduct does I(D) actually reach, and what falls outside it?
cards.back:
• Reaches PROFESSIONAL conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit, or any act reflecting adversely on professional reputation, integrity, or COMPETENCE
• "Professional activity" includes: workplace or academic interactions with colleagues, employees, and clients; anything explicitly or implicitly using the CFA charter, CFA Institute membership, or candidacy; unpaid volunteer work for CFA Institute or a local society; attending industry meetings or conferences; writing about investments outside work (blogs, message boards, books); communicating with regulators within your professional scope
• Inside: intoxication during business hours (impairs competence); altering health-insurance reimbursement forms; taking a kickback on purchases for a charity board joined as a charterholder; harassment while instructing a society exam review course; publishing fabricated statistics signed as a CFA charterholder; a malicious blog attack on a company with no basis
• Outside: generally, legal transgressions from acts of civil disobedience supporting personal beliefs; personal bankruptcy not involving fraudulent or deceitful business conduct; dishonesty untethered to professional activity (e.g., filing false papers for a disabled parking permit) — deplorable, but not professional conduct
• Separate caution (not itself labeled an I(D) violation): individuals sometimes try to abuse the Professional Conduct Program by seeking enforcement of I(D) to settle personal, political, or other disputes unrelated to professional ethics — CFA Institute has disciplinary policies, procedures, and enforcement mechanisms in place to address that misuse

cards.front: What does Standard I(E) Competence require, and when does a bad outcome NOT prove incompetence?
cards.back:
• Must act with AND maintain the knowledge, skills, and abilities needed to fulfill professional responsibilities — a continuing duty, not a one-time threshold
• Knowledge = the body of information applied to performing the function; Skills = capabilities to perform role-specific tasks; Abilities = capabilities and attitudes producing observable outcomes
• Role-specific and facts-and-circumstances based: education alone is not competence, and passing a licensing exam without learning the material is not competence
• When responsibilities change or expand, acquire the new competence FIRST — promotion to supervisor requires learning management and compliance-for-subordinates duties; buying a cryptocurrency product you do not understand to avoid seeming out of touch violates I(E)
• Lack of competence is not shown by an unsuccessful or negative outcome: an unprofitable decision, a wrong forecast, or thorough due diligence that failed to uncover an issuer's hidden fraud is not by itself a violation
• No particular continuing education program is mandated — CE programs, certifications, conferences and webinars, employer training, self-study, and expert groups all satisfy it

cards.front: Under Standard II(A), when is information "material"? Name the four attributes the curriculum says drive that judgment, and the two conditions that make information LESS material.
cards.back:
Material if: • its disclosure is likely to have an impact on the security's price, OR • reasonable investors would want to know it before making an investment decision — i.e., it would significantly alter the total mix of information available.

Four key factors: • specificity of the information • extent of its difference from public information • its nature • its reliability (source).

Less material when: • the effect on price is ambiguous (unclear whether/how much price moves) • enough time has passed that once-important information is now stale.

Curriculum examples: earnings; M&A / tender offers / JVs; changes in assets or asset quality; new products, trials, discoveries; licenses, patents, regulatory approval or rejection; gain or loss of a major customer/supplier contract; management changes; auditor change or withdrawn opinion; securities events (defaults, calls, splits, dividend changes, new issues); bankruptcies; significant legal disputes; government economic reports; large orders before execution; new or changed third-party equity/debt ratings.

Scope trap: the ban is not just on the stock — derivatives, mutual funds, and alternatives are all covered.

cards.front: When does information stop being "nonpublic"? Does a briefing to a room full of analysts count — and what is the one legitimate use of insider information the curriculum permits?
cards.back:
Nonpublic until disseminated or available to the marketplace IN GENERAL (not a select group). "Disseminated" = made known: posted broadly, press release, or accompanying filing.
• Test: a reasonable expectation that people have received it — but you need NOT wait for the slowest method of delivery.
• A select-group forum is NOT public: an analyst briefing/conference call, or a meeting with the 10 largest shareholders, leaves the information nonpublic.
• Company "guidance" or interpretation of published filings can itself be selective MNPI — stay alert.
• Social media: content behind group-membership walls may not be public; verify it is obtainable from a genuinely public source first.

Permitted use: insider information supplied legitimately by the source company for due diligence under a business agreement — M&A, loan underwriting, credit ratings, offering engagements — is not a violation when used FOR THAT PURPOSE. Using it for any other purpose, especially to trade or entice others to trade, violates II(A).

cards.front: State the mosaic theory: what two ingredient types may an analyst combine, why is the resulting conclusion safe even if it is material, and what single practice protects the analyst?
cards.back:
• Ingredients: PUBLIC information + NONMATERIAL NONPUBLIC information.
• The analyst may use significant conclusions drawn from that mix as the basis for recommendations and decisions — even if the same conclusion would have been material inside information had a company insider communicated it directly.
• Rationale: the conclusion is the product of the analyst's own work and expertise, not of privileged access; this analysis enhances market efficiency.
• Protection: save and document ALL research. Evidence of the public and nonmaterial nonpublic inputs supports the assertion that the conclusion came from appropriate methods.
• Flip side (Investment Research Reports): a well-known analyst's pending report or rating change can itself be material — anyone given advance notice (e.g., the journalist about to interview the analyst) who trades on it, or relays it, violates II(A). Yet the analyst is not required to publish the work to the general public; non-clients can do the work themselves or become clients.

cards.front: Classic trap: candidates flag every tip as MNPI and freeze trading. When does an unreleased tip FAIL the materiality test — and when does an identical-sounding tip pass it?
cards.back:
Fails materiality (trading allowed) when the SOURCE is unreliable or the content is conjecture:
• A doctor who "casually follows the markets" predicting a takeover — unreliable source, so not material.
• A text from another firm's trader guessing at strong earnings — market noise / whisper numbers; no reason to suspect MNPI unless you know the trader has an ongoing business relationship with the issuer.
• Educated conjecture about drug trials by subject experts NOT connected to the trials.

Passes materiality (do not trade):
• Factual information from a corporate insider about a significant new contract.
• Trial results from qualified personnel actually involved in the trials — e.g., the scientist leading the semiconductor tests voicing disappointment.
• A CFO's remark on the golf course that the quarter will beat estimates by ~10% — and buying a retail ETF containing that issuer is still a violation; going indirect does not cure it.

Also trapping: "He's a senior executive, he knows the law" is no defense, and losing money on the trade does not absolve you. You must determine materiality yourself BEFORE acting.

cards.front: Standard II(B): distinguish information-based from transaction-based market manipulation, with the curriculum's examples of each.
cards.back:
Information-based — disseminating false or misleading information:
• Spreading false rumors to induce trading (chatroom rumors of a big new contract).
• "Pump and dump": issuing misleading positive information or overly optimistic valuations, then selling once the price is artificially high.
• Promotional "independent research" paid for in stock and cash by the issuer.
• Exaggerating an earnings estimate to force a company comment and fuel a quick gain.

Transaction-based — trades where the member knows or should know the action could distort price:
• Trades that artificially affect price or volume to give the impression of activity or price movement.
• Securing a controlling, dominant position in an instrument to manipulate the price of a related derivative and/or the underlying.
• Trading a thin stock back and forth between two funds you manage to lift volume and price — a violation even if the funds' participants would benefit.

Note both can stack: dividing holdings across accounts, running a blog rumor campaign, AND cross-trading to fake liquidity violates II(B) on both fronts.

cards.front: Aggressive trading moved a thin stock's price sharply. What single element decides whether that is a II(B) violation, and which red flags signal manipulation?
cards.back:
The hinge is INTENT — specifically intent to mislead market participants by distorting prices or artificially inflating volume.
• II(B) is NOT intended to preclude transactions on legitimate trading strategies based on perceived market inefficiencies.
• Legitimate activity may LOOK abusive, especially in illiquid or volatile markets — appearance alone is not the test.

Indicators that may signal manipulation (nonexhaustive):
• Orders entered for an unusually short time period
• Orders above market price
• Orders resulting in no change in beneficial ownership
• Orders intended to move the bid or offer, canceled before execution
• Orders on both sides of the trade using different platforms
• Coordinated action by two or more traders in a market with few participants

Worked case: a bank president placing a personal buy order of four times average weekly volume to lift the price and pull a merger buyer to the table violates II(B) — but issuing a press release announcing the search for a merger partner, or reaffirming prior earnings guidance after confirming with the CFO, does not.

cards.front: You come into possession of material nonpublic information. Walk the required sequence of actions under the II(A) compliance guidance.
cards.back:
1. Make reasonable efforts to achieve PUBLIC DISSEMINATION — usually by encouraging the issuing company to make it public (and to issue a press release promptly if it slipped out first in an analyst meeting or call).
2. If public dissemination is not possible: communicate the information ONLY to designated supervisory and compliance personnel within your firm.
3. Take NO investment action and do NOT alter current investment recommendations based on it.
4. Add the security to the firm's restricted list — the recommended step when the firm has or may have MNPI.
5. Never knowingly engage in conduct that may induce company insiders to disclose MNPI privately.
6. Comply with all employer procedures: review of employee and proprietary trading, review of recommendations, supervision of interdepartmental communications, and reporting suspected misuse.

Wrong answers the exam offers: waiting until tomorrow "so it becomes public" (negotiations may drag on or fail — you must wait for actual dissemination), and telling all the firm's PMs "so no client is disadvantaged" (that spreads the MNPI). Preventively: encourage companies you follow to issue press releases before analyst meetings and to script those calls.

cards.front: A multiservice firm's investment banking arm holds MNPI. What is the best structural remedy, what are its four elements, and what happens to a research analyst who helps on the deal?
cards.back:
Best policy: establish physical and informational barriers — a FIREWALL — between investment banking and brokerage/research. (Permanently banning recommendations on banking clients is inferior: coverage may properly resume once the information is public. Merely MONITORING the exchange of information is wrong — no exchange should be occurring.)

Four elements:
• Substantial control of interdepartmental communications, preferably through a clearance area in compliance or legal
• Review of employee trading via "watch," "restricted," and "rumor" lists
• Documentation of the procedures limiting information flow and of enforcement actions taken
• Heightened review or restriction of PROPRIETARY trading while the firm holds MNPI

Staffing rules: no overlap of personnel between investment banking/corporate finance and sales/research (or between commercial lending and trust/research); an employee must be on only ONE side of the wall at a time. An analyst who assists the bankers is treated as a banker and must remain on the banking side until what he learned is publicly disclosed — he may not use it for research or share it with the research department. Public disclosure, not compliance approval, is what releases him.

Separate procedure — "looking over the wall": when someone behind the wall believes he must share confidential information with someone on the other side, he consults a designated compliance officer, who determines whether sharing is necessary and how much, then coordinates the exchange so the barrier's integrity is preserved.

Personal trading: firm monitoring, periodic reports of personal transactions, restricted and watch lists.

cards.front: Under Standard III(A), to whom is the duty of loyalty, prudence, and care owed when you manage (a) a pension plan or trust, (b) a fund run to an index or stated mandate, and (c) an execution-only brokerage account?
cards.back:
• Pension plan / trust: the ultimate BENEFICIARIES — not the sponsor, the company management, or the shareholders who hired you; sponsor wishes never override beneficiary interests
• Index / mandate fund: no individual client exists — the duty is to invest consistently with the stated mandate; the fund manager is NOT responsible for any single investor's profile (that duty sits with whoever has the advisory relationship with that investor)
• Execution-only broker: duty is skill and diligence in execution — seek best execution on the most favorable terms, within the client's own instructions on quantity, price, and timing; the Code imposes no fiduciary duty in that role
• III(A) is a minimum benchmark for every member regardless of job title; it does not make all members fiduciaries, but a legally imposed fiduciary duty still binds (follow the strictest requirement)
• "Custody" = any direct or indirect access to client funds → heightened responsibility; manage per the governing documents (trust deed, IMA)
cards.mnemonic: Follow the money to the beneficiary, not to the signature on the contract.

cards.front: A manager uses client brokerage commissions to cover her firm's rent, five vacation days tacked onto a research trip, and her own CFA Program fees — and the fund prospectus fully discloses the soft dollar policy. What is wrong, and what MAY client brokerage buy?
cards.back:
• Client brokerage is an ASSET OF THE CLIENT, usable only for goods and services that benefit that client — disclosure does not cure misuse
• Permitted: research services that directly assist the investment decision-making process, with commissions commensurate with the value of the brokerage and research received
• Not permitted: the manager's or firm's operating expenses (rent, overhead); personal education — CFA Program fees are a personal/firm expense, not research; the non-research days of a trip
• Paying a higher commission than you would normally pay, without corresponding benefit to the client, violates the duty of loyalty
• Unless directed by the client, you must seek best price and best execution
• Directed brokerage (client names the broker) does NOT violate III(A): confirm the goods/services will benefit the account beneficiaries, and disclose that the client may not be getting best execution
• Steering other clients' trades to a broker as a reward for referrals requires best price and execution AND disclosure to those accounts

cards.front: Standard III(B) says deal "fairly," not "equally." Which differences in client treatment are permitted, and what turns a difference into a violation?
cards.back:
Permitted:
