• More personal, specialized, or in-depth service to clients who pay for premium service
• Personal follow-up with selected clients AFTER a recommendation has been widely disseminated
• Choosing which clients receive an initial recommendation based on suitability and known interest — never on preferred or favored status
Required of any differentiated service: disclosed to all clients and prospects, and available to everyone — never offered selectively
Violation once a difference disadvantages or negatively affects other clients:
• Advance word to favored clients (pre-release lunch, a post to a subset of social-media followers, a "whisper" number given only to large clients)
• Distributing recommendations to institutional clients before individual accounts (discriminates by size and asset class)
• Filling a commingled or discretionary fund ahead of other accounts
Benchmark test: email the recommendation to all clients, then phone the three largest to discuss = fine; discuss with those three first = violation
Client consent can never legitimize a patently unfair allocation, and disclosing an inequitable method does not relieve the obligation

cards.front: Recommend the trade-allocation procedures a firm should adopt for block trades and new issues to comply with Standard III(B).
cards.back:
• Document and time-stamp all orders, modifications, and cancellations; process and execute first-in, first-out, bundling orders where efficient
• Give every client account in a block trade the SAME execution price and the SAME commission
• Partial fills: allocate pro rata on the basis of order size, but not below an established minimum lot size (e.g., bonds); allocate on a round-lot basis to avoid odd lots
• New issues: obtain advance indications of interest, allocate BY CLIENT (not by portfolio manager), and provide a stated method for calculating allocations
• Oversubscribed issues: prorate to all suitable accounts and forgo sales to yourself and immediate family to free up shares — but family accounts managed as regular fee-paying client accounts must NOT be excluded
• Allocate before executing the order, or by a systematic method as soon as practical afterward — never after seeing which fills were profitable
• Disclose the allocation procedures to clients and prospects; have supervisors review accounts systematically for preferential treatment
• Maintain a list of all clients and their holdings so every holder can be notified of a recommendation change

cards.front: Contrast the two suitability regimes under Standard III(C): an advisory relationship versus managing a portfolio to a specific mandate, strategy, or style.
cards.back:
Advisory relationship — must:
• Make reasonable inquiry into the client's investment experience, risk and return objectives, and financial constraints BEFORE any recommendation or action, and reassess and update that information regularly
• Determine the investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's WRITTEN objectives, mandates, and constraints
• Judge suitability in the context of the client's TOTAL portfolio — a holding that is risky standing alone can be suitable within the whole, and a risk-averse client's portfolio can accommodate covered calls if properly explained
Managing to a mandate, strategy, or style — must:
• Make only recommendations and take only actions consistent with the portfolio's stated objectives and constraints (a high-income fund buying a zero-dividend stock violates III(C); an IPS requiring liquid assets bars a private-equity fund with a lockup, however small the position)
• NOT determine whether the fund suits the individuals buying its shares — the suitability duty can be conferred only on someone with an advisory relationship
Trap: suitability is assessed only on the information the client actually provided — encourage clients to disclose the whole portfolio, including assets you do not manage
cards.mnemonic: Advisory = know the person; mandate = keep the promise.

cards.front: A client makes an unsolicited trade request that you know is unsuitable under his IPS. What is the required sequence of actions under Standard III(C)?
cards.back:
• Refrain from making the trade until you have discussed your concerns with the client
• Educate the client on how the request deviates from the current investment policy statement
• Require the client to acknowledge the discussion — including that the trade is against your advice because it is unsuitable for the portfolio
• If the request is expected to have a MATERIAL impact on the portfolio, use the occasion to update the IPS so the client understands the effect on his goals and risk level
• If the client declines to modify the IPS yet insists on the trade, evaluate the effectiveness of your services and determine whether to continue the advisory arrangement
Related timing rules: review each client's IPS at least annually, and again before any material change in recommendations or decisions — more often if business conditions or a major market change dictate; a large inheritance or other change in circumstances triggers a review of both ability and willingness to take risk

cards.front: A firm does not claim GIPS compliance. Recommend the practices that still let it satisfy Standard III(D)'s "fair, accurate, and complete" requirement.
cards.back:
• Consider the knowledge and sophistication of the audience and tailor the information accordingly
• Present a COMPOSITE of similar portfolios rather than a single representative account
• Include terminated accounts in the composite performance history
• Include disclosures that fully explain the results: state when results are simulated or model-derived; clearly indicate when the record is that of a prior entity (and your specific role if a team achieved it); disclose whether returns are gross of fees, net of fees, or after tax
• Maintain the data and records used to calculate the performance presented
Boundaries:
• GIPS compliance is the BEST method, not a requirement — but a false claim of compliance is itself the violation, even when the underlying data are not misused
• Brief presentations: make the supporting detail available on request and note the limited nature of what is shown
• Changing attribution methodology, mixing time-weighted and money-weighted returns unlabeled, or deviating from the firm's own stated composite policy to capture a gain all fail III(D)

cards.front: Whose information does Standard III(E) protect, what three conditions permit disclosure, and what does the standard NOT prohibit?
cards.back:
• Protects information about CURRENT, FORMER, and PROSPECTIVE clients — the duty survives the end of the relationship
• Disclosure permitted only if: (1) the information concerns illegal activities on the part of the client, (2) disclosure is required by law, or (3) the client or prospective client permits disclosure
• If applicable law requires confidentiality even as to the client's illegal acts, follow the law; consult compliance or legal counsel before disclosing
• Does NOT prevent cooperating with a CFA Institute Professional Conduct investigation — members must cooperate with investigations into their own and others' conduct unless prevented by law
• Vulnerable investors: contacting a secondary contact the client named at account opening, about documented concerns of diminished capacity, does not violate III(E); best practice is to request that contact when every account is established and to document all such conversations
• Sudden or unexpected client decisions are not by themselves evidence of lost capacity — a family member's demand does not authorize disclosing or freezing the account
• Traps: disclosure that would "benefit" the client still needs permission; confirming details you learned in the confidential relationship to a third party is a breach
cards.mnemonic: Three gates: Illegal, Law, Permission.

cards.front: Under Standard IV(A), what may a departing employee take to a new firm, and what must be returned or erased?
cards.back:
Test = skill vs. employer property.
• LEAVES with the employee: skills, experience, and knowledge gained while employed — not "confidential" or "privileged"; simple knowledge of the names and existence of former clients is generally not confidential unless an agreement or law says so.
• STAYS (employer property, absent WRITTEN permission to keep): client lists with contact details, client account statements, marketing presentations/performance records, recommended-security lists, computer models, spreadsheets — even ones the member personally built.
• Medium is irrelevant: hard copy, or electronic files on a personal phone, tablet, or laptop kept "for convenience," must be returned or erased.
• Firm-approved, business-related social media accounts are firm assets — transfer or delete as firm policy directs.
• Classic trap: "I created it, so it's mine" — taking any employer record, even one you prepared, violates IV(A).

cards.front: A member wants to run an independent business for compensation while still employed. What exactly must happen before the first client is served?
cards.back:
Independent practice is NOT prohibited, but providing a service your employer offers requires employer consent first.
1. Notify the employer.
2. Describe: the types of services to be rendered to prospective independent clients, the expected duration of the services, and the compensation for the services.
3. Receive the employer's consent to ALL terms of the arrangement.
4. Only then render services.
• Preparing to enter an independent business is permitted, so long as you do not solicit or serve clients or otherwise harm the employer.
• Also check firm policy — it may set an approval process or flatly prohibit outside services.

cards.front: Pitfall: a manager who has already handed in her resignation tells her clients where she is going, gives them her new contact details, and describes the new firm's services. Which part violates IV(A) — and what may she do after leaving?
State Standard IV(B)'s trigger and its precise cure, including what the disclosure must contain.
cards.back:
Trigger: accepting gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with — or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with — the employer's interest.
Cure: written consent from ALL parties involved, obtained BEFORE accepting. "Written consent" includes any documentable communication (e.g., a retrievable email).
Disclose to the employer via supervisor or compliance officer, stating:
• the nature of the compensation;
• the approximate amount;
• the duration of the agreement.
The party offering the additional compensation should acknowledge and confirm the details.
• Covers direct client compensation (a client's performance bonus) and indirect third-party benefits.
• Trap: NONMONETARY benefits count — free family gym memberships for board service create a conflict just as cash would.
• Trap: the answer is never "refuse it"; a client performance-fee arrangement is permissible once disclosed in writing and approved in advance.

cards.front: Permissible preparation vs. impermissible competition before leaving: contrast registering a competing company with the regulators against responding to an RFP that your employer is also bidding on.
cards.back:
Both happen pre-departure; only one is allowed.
• PERMISSIBLE — registering the new investment company with regulatory authorities, arranging financing, general preparations: no violation if done on the member's own time outside the office, with no client solicitation and no operation of the new entity until employment ends. Employer notice is not required for mere preparation.
• VIOLATION — a departing group responding to an RFP that their employer is also bidding on: this puts the employees in DIRECT competition with the employer, so it breaches IV(A) unless the employer grants permission.
Dividing line: preparing to compete is fine; actually competing for, soliciting, or taking business while still employed is not.

cards.front: A supervisor learns an employee may have violated the law or acted unethically. What is the required response, and what responses are explicitly NOT enough?
What must a member do when the firm's compliance system is inadequate, and when is a supervisor NOT in violation of IV(C) despite a violation occurring on the watch?
cards.back:
Inadequate system:
• bring it to the attention of the firm's senior managers and recommend corrective action; and
• if supervisory responsibilities clearly cannot be discharged because the system is absent or inadequate, DECLINE to accept supervisory responsibility until the firm adopts reasonable procedures.
Standard of liability — reasonable efforts, not omniscience:
• procedures must be established, documented, communicated to covered personnel, monitored, and enforced, and must be in place BEFORE a violation occurs;
• if reasonable procedures and an effective program were instituted, failing to detect a violation may NOT be a IV(C) violation;
• but the occurrence may itself indicate the procedures are inadequate, and the supervisor IS in violation if he knows or should know the compliance procedures are not being followed.
• Delegation spreads the work, not the responsibility: subordinates given supervisory duties must be instructed on preventing and detecting violations. Supervisory authority exists over anyone under your control or influence, member or not.

cards.front: Code of ethics vs. compliance policies and procedures: how does the curriculum say each should be written, and what mistake does it say to avoid?
cards.back:
CODE OF ETHICS
• Fundamental, principle-based ethical concepts applying to all employees.
• Plain language, general, accessible and easily understandable; unencumbered by detailed procedures or boilerplate legal terminology.
• Should be provided to clients — it signals commitment to acting in clients' interests.
COMPLIANCE POLICIES AND PROCEDURES
• Detailed, firm-wide implementation of those principles in day-to-day operations. Adequate procedures should: be a clearly written, accessible resource tailored to the firm's operations; be easy to understand; designate a compliance officer with clearly defined authority, responsibility, and resources to implement procedures and investigate; describe the supervision hierarchy and assign duties; implement checks and balances; describe scope; document monitoring and testing; detail permissible conduct; and delineate reporting of violations and sanctions.
• Trap: mingling compliance procedures into the code of ethics — it defeats the goal of conveying ethical obligations simply.
• Once in place, supervisors should disseminate, periodically update, continually educate, issue reminders, include professional-conduct evaluation in performance reviews, monitor employee actions, and enforce after a violation. Incentives should reward HOW outcomes are achieved, not just revenue generated.

cards.front: Standard V(A) imposes which two duties, and what three factors determine how much diligence is "enough" in a given situation?
cards.back:
Two duties:
• Exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness in analyzing investments, making recommendations, and taking investment actions
• Have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by appropriate research and investigation, for any analysis, recommendation, or action

Level required depends on:
• The investment philosophy the member/firm follows
• The member's role in the investment decision-making process
• The support and resources provided by the employer

Also: make reasonable inquiries into the sources and accuracy of all data — blogs, independent research-aggregation websites, and social media require a GREATER level of review than established research organizations.
cards.mnemonic: Philosophy - Role - Resources

cards.front: Secondary vs third-party research: define each, and list the criteria for deciding whether either is "sound" enough to rely on.
cards.back:
• Secondary research = research conducted by someone else INSIDE the member's own firm
• Third-party research = research conducted by entities OUTSIDE the firm (brokerage, bank, research firm)
• Same duty for both: may rely only after reasonable and diligent efforts to determine the research is sound

Criteria for soundness (not exhaustive):
• Assumptions used
• Rigor of the analysis performed
• Date/timeliness of the research
• Evaluation of the objectivity and independence of the recommendations

Key limits:
• If there is reason to suspect the source is biased, unreliable, or otherwise deficient, the member must NOT rely on it
• A member MAY rely in good faith on colleagues' determination of soundness (e.g., senior management picked the data vendor after due diligence) unless there is reason to question its validity

cards.front: What does V(A) demand of a member who uses (or builds) a quantitative model — backtests, screens, derivative pricing, portfolio construction?
cards.back:
• Understand the parameters, assumptions, and limitations of the model and how its results are used — not required to be an expert in every technical aspect, but black-box reliance fails V(A)
• Test the output of models and preprogrammed tools BEFORE incorporating them into methods, models, or analyses
• Creators of new models owe a HIGHER level of diligence than end users, and must understand the technical aspects; thorough testing must be completed prior to product distribution
• Incorporate a broad enough range of assumptions to capture the investment's underlying characteristics, including negative market events and risk levels outside the norm
• Consider the source and time horizon of input data; databases may not span both positive and negative cycles, so test with volatility/performance scenarios outside the observable data
• Test components as an INTEGRATED whole, not only individually (validated parts can work at cross-purposes in extreme conditions)

Applies even to a modeler who never trades or faces clients — the model gives recommendations, and its author is accountable for their quality.

cards.front: Your firm will allocate a mandate to an external adviser/subadviser. What selection procedure satisfies V(A), and what are the two classic shortcuts that violate it?
cards.back:
Review external advisers as diligently as you review individual investment opportunities. Use consistent, objective criteria, including:
• Reviewing the adviser's established code of ethics
• Understanding the adviser's compliance and internal control procedures
• Assessing the quality of the published return information
• Reviewing the adviser's investment process and adherence to its stated strategy

Supporting policy: adopt a consistent, objective criteria set that states how often and on what basis the allocation to the external adviser will be reviewed.

Adherence to recognized industry standards is one evaluation factor — CFA Institute Asset Manager Code, GIPS standards, and the Model Request for Proposal (equity, credit, or real estate managers).

Classic violations: choosing the firm with the LOWEST FEES alone, or the HIGHEST RETURNS plus a claim of GIPS compliance alone. Selection must rest on a full review of services, performance history, and cost structure.

cards.front: List the five things Standard V(B) requires a member to do when communicating with clients and prospective clients.
cards.back:
1. Disclose the nature of the services provided, along with information about the costs to the client of those services
2. Disclose the basic format and general principles of the investment process used to analyze investments, select securities, and construct portfolios — and promptly disclose any changes that might materially affect those processes
3. Disclose significant limitations and risks associated with the investment process
4. Use reasonable judgment in identifying which factors are important to analyses/recommendations/actions, and include them in client communications
5. Distinguish between fact and opinion

Scope notes:
• Communication is medium-neutral: in-person, electronic, social media, broadcasts; from one word ("buy") to a 100-page report
• Leverage in general constitutes a significant risk and must be disclosed; also disclose limitations such as liquidity (ability to liquidate timely at reasonable cost) and capacity (the amount beyond which new investments hurt returns)
• Disclosures are ongoing, need not give specific dollar amounts, and must cover costs charged by affiliates, related entities, and third parties — client sophistication is never an excuse to omit them
• Best practice: written, at the outset of the engagement. The standard generally binds only client-facing members.

cards.front: Standard V(C): what records must be kept, who owns them, and for how long?
cards.back:
Requirement: develop and maintain appropriate records supporting investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and other investment-related communications — including reviews that led to NO change in position.

Examples of supporting documentation:
• Personal notes from meetings with the covered company; press releases/presentations issued by it
• Computer-based model outputs AND model input parameters
• Risk analyses of securities' impact on a portfolio
• Selection criteria for external advisers; notes from client meetings; outside research reports
• Electronic formats count: emails, text messages, blog posts, social media posts

Ownership and period:
• Records created in professional activity for an employer are the FIRM's property — cannot be taken to a new employer without express consent; work from a previous firm cannot be used if the supporting documentation is unavailable, and records must be recreated at the new firm. Those new records cannot be recreated from sources obtained at the previous employer WITHOUT THAT EMPLOYER'S PERMISSION
• Follow local regulator and firm retention time frames; doing so satisfies V(C). Absent regulation or firm policy, CFA Institute recommends at least SEVEN YEARS
• Responsibility to maintain records generally rests with the firm, but members should archive their own supporting notes anyway

cards.front: Two fact patterns that LOOK like V(A) violations but are not — a recommendation that loses 60%, and a group report whose conclusion you reject. Why is each compliant?
cards.back:
1. Loss after sound due diligence: a reasonable basis does NOT guarantee no downside risk. Decisions can rest only on facts known at the time. If the adviser analyzed track record, principals, fees, and risk profile against an aggressive-risk IPS, a later 60% loss is not a violation — but the adviser should discuss the analysis process and remind the client that past performance does not guarantee future gains.

2. Group/committee research: the report represents the consensus, not necessarily the member's own view. A member need NOT dissociate — and may leave their name on it — if they believe the consensus has a reasonable and adequate basis and is independent and objective. They MAY ask to have their name removed, but are not required to.

The trap runs the other way too: changing a recommendation because you overheard a respected analyst's contrary opinion IS a V(A) violation — another's opinion is not an adequate basis. It is only a valid trigger for further research that might then justify the change.

cards.front: Where exactly does the fact/opinion line fall under V(B), and what phrasing trips the violation?
cards.back:
Rule: opinions must be separated from facts — failure to separate the PAST from the FUTURE is the violation. Earnings estimates, changes in the dividend outlook, and future price levels are opinions subject to future circumstances.

Classic violating phrasings:
• "Based on the fact that the company has 500,000 ounces of gold, I recommend a strong buy" — a reserve estimate computed from core samples is a quantitative OPINION, not a fact
• "We expect the price to rise US$8 because the dividend WILL increase by US$1.50" — the increase is contingent on pending legislation; stating it as fact violates V(B). (It is NOT a mosaic/inside-information violation, and it IS acceptable to base a recommendation partly on uncertain future events — as long as they read as opinion.)

Also required:
• In complex quantitative work, separate fact from statistical conjecture and identify the analysis's known limitations
• Do not promote the perceived accuracy of a model — output is an estimate, not a certainty (e.g., "our VaR has never been exceeded" must be paired with how inputs were chosen and the model's limitations)
• Support quantitative advice with readily available reference material and disclose changes in methodology

cards.front: Standard VI(A): what is the required order of remedies for a conflict of interest, and what three qualities must any disclosure have?
cards.back:
Order of remedies:
• Best practice = AVOID the actual conflict and the appearance of one
• If avoidance is not reasonable = full and complete DISCLOSURE to clients, prospective clients, and employer
• Also mitigate the conflict where possible and disclose how it was mitigated
Disclosure must be:
• Prominent
• In plain language
• Communicated in a manner that effectively conveys the information
Scope: any matter that could reasonably be expected to impair independence and objectivity or interfere with duties to clients, prospects, or employer.
Update trigger: when the nature of the conflict changes materially (e.g., bonus shifts from annual to quarterly profits); err on the side of caution.

cards.front: Under Standard VI(A), when do you "beneficially own" a security, and what is the single most prevalent conflict requiring disclosure?
cards.back:
Beneficial ownership exists if you:
• Have a direct or indirect pecuniary interest in the security/investment, OR
• Have power to vote or direct the voting of the shares, OR
• Have power to dispose or direct the disposition of the investment
Most prevalent conflict under VI(A): members' and candidates' ownership of stock in companies they recommend to clients or that clients hold.
• Simplest cure = prohibit ownership of such securities, but that is often overly burdensome and too restrictive
• Required minimum = disclose any beneficial ownership interest in investments you recommend
Note: it also covers ownership by the FIRM, and by a spouse (e.g., inherited stock) — not just your own brokerage account.

cards.front: Standard VI(A): name the three basic conflicts created by serving as a board member/director, and the recommended structural safeguard.
cards.back:
Three basic conflicts:
1. Duties owed to clients may conflict with duties owed to the company's shareholders
2. Director compensation in securities or options could bias trading actions that raise the value of those securities
3. Board service creates the opportunity to receive material nonpublic information — and the perception that MNPI flows to the director's firm
Safeguard: members/candidates who provide investment services while serving as directors should be isolated from those making investment decisions by firewalls or similar restrictions.
Also report outside board membership promptly to the employer; many employers prohibit it outright to avoid even the appearance of conflict.

cards.front: Standard VI(C) Referral Fees: what must be disclosed, to whom, by when, and what two things does the disclosure let the client evaluate?
cards.back:
What: any compensation, consideration, or benefit RECEIVED FROM or PAID TO others for the recommendation of products or services.
• Consideration includes fees paid in cash, in soft dollars, or in kind
• Includes internal, interdepartmental referral payments within one firm — VI(C) does not distinguish third-party from internal payments
To whom: employer, clients, and prospective clients.
When: BEFORE entry into any formal agreement for services.
Content: nature of the benefit (flat fee vs percentage, one-time vs continuing, performance-based, research or other noncash) plus the estimated dollar value.
Two stated purposes — the client can evaluate:
1. Any partiality shown in the recommendation of products/services
2. The full cost of the services

cards.front: Distinguish Standards VI(A), VI(B), and VI(C) — the core duty of each in one line.
cards.back:
VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts — avoid, or make full and fair disclosure of, all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair independence and objectivity or interfere with duties to clients, prospects, and employer. Disclosure must be prominent, plain-language, effective.
VI(B) Priority of Transactions — client and employer transactions must have PRIORITY over transactions in which the member/candidate is a beneficial owner. It is an ordering rule, not a disclosure rule.
VI(C) Referral Fees — disclose to employer, clients, and prospects any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for recommending products or services, before any formal agreement.
Exam cue: ownership/board seat/banking relationship = VI(A); front-running or taking the hot issue first = VI(B); payment for sending or receiving clients = VI(C).

cards.front: List the basic personal-investing procedures a firm should adopt to comply with Standard VI(B).
cards.back:
• Limited participation in equity IPOs — participation can look like taking an attractive opportunity from clients, or like an incentive bestowed to influence future decisions; avoid entirely, or preclear even where no conflict appears
• Restrictions on private placements — same conflict issues as IPOs; never take transactions that could be perceived as favors/gifts influencing future judgment or rewarding past business
• Blackout/restricted periods — investment personnel in the decision-making process must observe them so they cannot front-run client trades (trading personally ahead of client accounts)
• Reporting requirements — disclose holdings with beneficial interest (at hire and periodically), provide duplicate trade confirmations to the employer, and follow preclearance procedures
• Disclosure of policies — on request, fully disclose the firm's personal-investing policies to investors; not boilerplate such as "personnel are subject to policies regarding personal trading"
Duplicate confirmations serve two purposes: they signal independent verification (deterrence) and they let the flow of personal investments be verified, which holdings alone cannot show.

cards.front: A manager allocates every IPO to all other clients first and only puts the remainder in her parents' fee-paying account at the firm, so no one can accuse her of favoritism. Why is this a violation?
cards.back:
It violates Standard VI(B) — by DISADVANTAGING the parents she breaches her duty to them.
• Family accounts that are ordinary fee-paying CLIENT accounts are client accounts: treated like any other firm account, neither favored nor disadvantaged because of the family relationship
• The trap: candidates assume "family = always last" is the safe answer; VI(B) subordinates only accounts in which the member/candidate is a BENEFICIAL OWNER
• If she does have beneficial ownership in the account and the firm has preclearance/reporting rules, she may have to preclear the trades and report them
Contrast: routing hot issues to a spouse's outside account while clients cannot participate violates VI(B) and must be disclosed to the employer.

cards.front: Your firm just upgraded a stock to "strong buy" and you need to sell your personal holding to pay tuition. What does Standard VI(B) actually permit?
cards.back:
You may sell. VI(B) sets PRIORITY, not prohibition.
• Members may need to enter a personal transaction that runs counter to current client recommendations (e.g., a sale for personal financial reasons) and may be justified in doing so
• Requirement: clients and the employer must first have had adequate opportunity to act on the recommendation; the sale must not disadvantage clients; comply with firm preclearance/reporting rules
Common wrong answers:
• "Cannot sell because you would profit from the firm's own recommendation" — wrong
• "Can sell only when a client places an offsetting buy order" — wrong; the Standard does not require matching personal and client trades
Nothing is inherently unethical about personal investment profit when (1) the client is not disadvantaged, (2) you do not benefit personally from trades done for clients, and (3) you comply with applicable regulatory requirements.

cards.front: Standard VII(A): state the standard, and list the categories of prohibited conduct the guidance enumerates.
cards.back:
Standard: must not engage in conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation, or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs.
• Giving or receiving assistance (cheating) on any CFA Institute exam
• Violating the rules, regulations, and testing policies of CFA Institute programs
• Providing confidential program or exam information to candidates or the public
• Disregarding or circumventing exam security measures
• Improperly using an association with CFA Institute for personal or professional goals
• Misrepresenting information to CFA Institute regarding any program
Notes: list is "includes but is not limited to." Applies to ALL CFA Institute programs, not just the CFA Program. Non-member/non-candidate program participants are not thereby made subject to the Code and Standards.
cards.mnemonic: Cheat, Rules, Confidential, Security, Association, Misrepresent — "CRC SAM"

cards.front: After sitting an exam, what may a candidate say publicly versus what violates Standard VII(A)?
cards.back:
Permitted (opinion):
• How difficult, fair, or well-constructed the exam was; how well they think they did
• Disagreement with CFA Institute policies, procedures, or advocacy positions
• Discussing NONconfidential material with others or in study groups
Prohibited (content):
• Specific details of questions appearing on an exam
• Broad topical areas and formulas tested — OR NOT TESTED — on an exam
Key points: "not tested" is just as confidential as "tested" (Rossi: "no questions at all about IPO allocations" violated). Confidential until CFA Institute elects to release publicly — no expiry at exam day. Applies in any medium; CFA Institute polices blogs, forums, and social networking groups.

cards.front: Pitfall: a member on a CFA Institute committee or exam-grading panel tells clients her role helps them. Where exactly is the line under Standard VII(A)?
cards.back:
Line: may factually state involvement with the committee/program; must NOT infer or imply any special advantage to clients from that participation.
Volunteers must not offer, solicit, or disclose confidential material gained while volunteering to unauthorized people, including:
• Questions appearing on an exam or under consideration
• Deliberations related to an exam process
• Information related to the scoring of questions
Also a violation: using a volunteer post to steer business to oneself or one's clients (society program chair scheduling only his own clients to present).
Trap: "weeks after grading ended" does not decontaminate it — naming the question graded, the guideline answer, and that few scored well was still a violation.

cards.front: Under Standard VII(B), what two conditions must both hold for a person to call themselves a candidate for the CFA designation?
cards.back:
Both required:
1. CFA Institute has accepted the person's application to be a candidate, evidenced by issuance of a notice of acceptance; AND
2. The person is enrolled to sit for a specified examination, OR has sat for a specified exam but results have not yet been received.
• Declining to sit an exam already enrolled for ends candidacy; candidacy RESUMES once enrolled for a future exam.
• References must clearly state the person is a candidate for the CFA designation — e.g. "I am a 20XX Level III candidate for the CFA designation."
• Permitted alternative: factually state levels completed, e.g. "I passed the Level II CFA exam" or that one participates in the CFA Program having completed Levels I and II.

cards.front: What must a charterholder do each year to keep the right to use the CFA designation, and what happens the moment a requirement is missed?
cards.back:
Annual membership requirements (all three, every year):
• Complete a CFA Institute Membership Agreement
• Remit a completed Professional Conduct Statement (renews the commitment to the Code and Standards and the Professional Conduct Program)
• Pay applicable CFA Institute membership dues
On failure: the individual is no longer a member and FORFEITS the right to use the designation. Until membership is reestablished they must not present themselves as a member or charterholder and must remove all references to CFA Institute membership and the designation from social media profiles, business communications, reports, and everywhere else.
• Still allowed: stating they WERE a member/charterholder in the past, or the years in which requirements were met.
• Lapsing is not cured by intent or by leaving the industry — retired status exists but must be applied for (reclassification plus reduced dues).

cards.front: List the reference forms Standard VII(B) treats as improper, and the underlying rules that make them so.
cards.back:
Improper forms (per Exhibit 1):
• "CFA, Level II" — implies a partial designation
• "CFA, Expected 20XX" — candidates must not cite an expected completion date
• "John Smith, Charter Pending"
• "CFA charterholders achieve better performance results"
• "As a CFA charterholder, I am the most qualified to manage client investments" / "provides the best value in trade execution"
• "Enrolling as a candidate ensures one of becoming better at valuing debt securities"
Rules behind them: no partial designation may be stated or implied; no expected charter date (final award requires meeting requirements and CFA Institute Board of Governors approval); no statement overstating competency or asserting/implying superior performance.
Also improper: tagging a pseudonym or anonymous online profile with the designation ("Expert, CFA").
Proper: rigor-of-the-program and commitment-to-ethics statements; relative-merit claims when stated as the speaker's opinion; all non-opinion statements must be supported by facts. Applies to every medium — letterhead, business cards, bios, directory listings, ads, LinkedIn, email signatures, websites, resumes, and oral statements.

cards.front: "I passed all three exams in three consecutive sittings" versus "I consistently received the highest possible scores in ethics" — which complies and why?
cards.back:
Consecutive sittings: COMPLIANT — a statement of fact; Standard VII(B) does not prohibit communicating factual information about completing the program in three consecutive years. Violates only once linked to superior ability or performance ("among the elite, having passed all three in three consecutive attempts"; an ad tying first-attempt passes to the firm's superior fund performance).
Highest possible scores: VIOLATION — candidates do not receive actual scores. Results are pass/fail, with topic and subtopic results grouped into three broad categories; a candidate may see a topical result "above 70%" but cannot factually claim the highest possible score because that information is not reported.
Rule of thumb: the fact is fine; the inference drawn from it, or a "fact" the reporting system never produced, is not.

cards.front: What procedures does the curriculum recommend to prevent Standard VII(B) violations in firm communications?
cards.back:
• Disseminate written information about Standard VII(B) and the accompanying guidance to the firm's legal, compliance, public relations, and MARKETING departments — marketing is the one candidates most often forget to list.
• Encourage the firm to create TEMPLATES, consistent with Standard VII(B), for any materials referring to employees' affiliation with CFA Institute — promoting consistent, accurate references to membership, the designation, and candidacy.
Related preventive habits from the VII(A) guidance: study groups may use nonconfidential material freely; keep exam content off blogs, forums, and social networks (CFA Institute actively polices them); consult the program rules, regulations, and testing policies posted on cfainstitute.org, since violating any testing policy is itself a VII(A) violation; report suspected violations to CFA Institute.

cards.front: What are the four components of the CFA Institute framework for ethical decision making, what belongs under each, and must they be done in order?
cards.back:
• Identify: relevant facts, stakeholders and duties owed, ethical principles, conflicts of interest
• Consider: situational influences, additional guidance, alternative actions
• Decide and act
• Reflect: was the outcome as anticipated? why or why not?
• Order is NOT fixed — the components need not be addressed in the sequence shown — but a review of the outcome should conclude the process
• The reflection step is what provides insight for improved decision making in the future; skipping it is the common omission
cards.mnemonic: I-C-D-R: Identify, Consider, Decide and act, Reflect.

cards.front: In an advisory relationship, what three duties does Standard III(C) Suitability impose before any recommendation, how often must the IPS be revisited, and does a client's own trade request cure unsuitability?
cards.back:
• Make a reasonable inquiry into the client's investment experience, risk and return objectives, and financial constraints BEFORE any recommendation or action — and reassess and update regularly
• Determine the investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with written objectives, mandates, and constraints
• Judge suitability in the context of the client's TOTAL portfolio
• IPS cadence: review at least annually and also prior to material changes to specific recommendations or decisions (an IPS left untouched for five years violates III(C))
• Managing to a specific mandate, strategy, or style: take only actions consistent with it — so promising to maximize return for a fund with a dual socioeconomic-plus-return mandate violates III(C), and buying high-beta names for conservative long-term accounts to earn a quarterly bonus violates it too
• A client's unsolicited request does NOT cure unsuitability: make reasonable efforts to balance the trading request against the agreed IPS, and update the IPS when the trade would materially affect the portfolio

cards.front: Presenting a composite to a prospect: which of these violates Standard III(D) and which are acceptable — (1) excluding terminated accounts, (2) quoting a simple average of fund returns to a novice, (3) showing only discretionary accounts of similar size?
cards.back:
• VIOLATION — excluding terminated accounts. The composite must include terminated AND current similar discretionary accounts
• ACCEPTABLE — a simple average presented to an unsophisticated investor: III(D) obligations may be met by considering the knowledge and sophistication of the audience addressed
• ACCEPTABLE — presenting the weighted composite of similar portfolios rather than a single representative account; nondiscretionary accounts need not be included because those clients make their own investment decisions
• ACCEPTABLE — quoting returns gross of fees, provided the basis is disclosed (gross of fees, net of fees, or after tax), along with disclosures such as flagging simulated/model results or a prior entity's record
• Test to apply: performance information must be fair, accurate, and complete

cards.front: Pitfall: a partner invests personally in a deal after studying it but before his fund invests; the fund is not disadvantaged in any way and gets its full allocation. Is there still a violation, and under which standard?
cards.back:
• Yes — Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions: investment transactions for clients and employer must have priority over transactions for personal benefit
• This is front-running — trading in advance for one's personal account ahead of client accounts for economic advantage
• The violation stands EVEN IF the personal investment does not disadvantage the fund at all; harm is not an element
• Cure: wait until the client/employer transaction is completed before investing personally
• Trap to avoid: citing VI(A) conflicts instead. Simply co-investing in the same security as your employer or clients is not necessarily a conflict of interest — disclosing such co-investing is only best practice

cards.front: Standard VII(B): what may a charterholder who has stopped paying CFA Institute dues say about herself, and what may a Level I passer put on a business card?
cards.back:
Lapsed charterholder:
• The charter is NOT like a university degree — the right to use the designation also requires satisfying CFA Institute membership requirements, including paying dues and submitting a Professional Conduct Statement annually
• Unpaid dues means lapsed membership: she must not use the CFA designation or present herself as a charterholder until membership is reactivated
• She may state that she was previously a CFA Institute member
Candidate:
• May refer to participation in the CFA Program, but must clearly state she is a candidate
• Must not imply any partial designation — "CFA, Level I" on a card violates VII(B)
• Must NEVER cite an expected completion date for earning the charter
• Having actually passed Level I is irrelevant to the analysis

cards.front: Which standard fires for (a) a bonus your EMPLOYER pays you for moving clients over or for client IPO participation, versus (b) a bonus a CLIENT promises you for processing his transfers quickly — and what cures each?
cards.back:
• (a) Employer-paid signing or year-end bonus is NOT additional compensation under IV(B): IV(B) addresses conflicts with the EMPLOYER's interest, and this money flows employer-to-employee. It does create a conflict with CLIENTS → Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts. Cure: avoid it (firm stops compensating that way) or make full and fair disclosure to all clients — prominent, plain language, effectively communicated
• (b) Client-promised bonus → Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements: must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably create a conflict with the employer's interest unless written consent is obtained from all parties; at minimum it must be disclosed to the employer
• Neither is a referral fee — VI(C) covers compensation received from or paid to OTHERS for recommending products or services; an internal fee split rewarding colleagues for building a client relationship they did not refer is likewise not a referral fee
• A benefit that creates no conflict with the employer at all (talk-show sponsor gift bags for unpaid media appearances) violates neither IV(B) nor I(B)
cards.mnemonic: Who is on the other side of the conflict? Employer → IV(B) (written consent); client → VI(A) (avoid or disclose).

cards.front: A supervisor learns an employee may have violated the law or the Code. What must she do, and which two common responses fall short of Standard IV(C)?
cards.back:
• Required: promptly initiate an assessment/investigation to determine the extent of the wrongdoing — Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires reasonable efforts to ensure anyone subject to her supervision or authority complies with laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards
• NOT enough: raising the concern with the employee and relying on his statements about the extent of the violation or his assurances it will not recur
• NOT enough: reporting the concern up the chain to the director of compliance
• Contrast that with compliant conduct: on receiving a written client complaint, calling the adviser in immediately, reviewing the account and IPS, and sitting in on the client meeting IS a prompt investigation — no violation
• Redirecting a subordinate's concern to people without firsthand knowledge of the transaction does not discharge the duty; the supervisor should have arranged the meeting that would confirm the source and purpose of the funds
• Delegating supervision to an assistant manager does not by itself violate IV(C) — failing to ensure procedures are enforced does

cards.front: Your supervisor makes a false statement to a prospective client in front of you and you stay silent. Have you violated anything, and what is the required sequence of actions afterward?
cards.back:
• Yes — Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law prohibits knowingly participating or assisting in the violations of others and requires dissociation from unethical or illegal conduct
• Silence and acquiescence while false information is given to an investor who could be harmed constitutes assisting the violation, even though you took no active step
• Sequence: (1) address the person directly and ask them to correct the statement or cure the underlying defect; (2) if they refuse, bring the conduct to the firm's compliance department or legal counsel; (3) dissociate — for example, stop participating in sales meetings with that person
• Same ladder when a supervisor brushes off your suspicion of illegal activity in a client account: the FIRST next step is the firm's compliance department or legal counsel, not the regulator. The Code does not compel reporting to governmental or regulatory bodies unless disclosure is mandatory under applicable law, though it may be prudent
cards.mnemonic: Confront → Compliance → Cut ties (dissociate).

cards.front: Name the three categories of index-based factor ("smart beta") strategies, and give the curriculum's example strategies for each.
cards.back:
• Return-oriented — dividend yield (e.g., S&P 1500 High Yield Dividend Aristocrats: firms raising dividends 20 straight years, then weighted by yield), momentum (e.g., MSCI momentum uses 12-month and 6-month price performance), and fundamentally weighted strategies
• Risk-oriented — volatility weighting (hold all constituents, weight by the INVERSE of relative price volatility; measured as SD of returns over 252 trading days or 156 weeks); minimum variance (needs a mean-variance optimizer; constraints on sector/country/single-stock concentration)
• Diversification-oriented — equal weighting (1/n, low single-stock risk); maximum diversification (maximize the diversification ratio = weighted-average volatilities ÷ portfolio volatility)
• Goal of all three: improve on the risk OR return of cap-weighting
cards.mnemonic: Return, Risk, Diversification = R-R-D

cards.front: Compared with broad market-cap weighting, how do index-based factor strategies differ in risk exposure, the timing of active decisions, and cost?
cards.back:
• Risk exposure: factor strategies CONCENTRATE risk exposures, leaving the investor vulnerable when the chosen factor is out of favor — even strong factors have long stretches of underperformance (motivates multi-factor approaches). Cap-weighting is a single-factor (CAPM beta) market exposure
• Active decisions: factor strategies are labeled "passive" but decisions on the TIMING and DEGREE of factor exposure are active — per Jacobs and Levy, the active management happens UP FRONT rather than continuously (as in traditional active)
• Cost: higher management fees and trading commissions than broad-market indexing; all else equal this lowers net performance (though still modest vs. active, since rules-based strategies need no constant monitoring)
• Other factor risk: ease of replication by other investors → OVERCROWDING, eroding the advantage
• Factor rotation = changing factor exposures as market conditions change — an active bet made with index-based vehicles

cards.front: Describe the ETF creation/redemption mechanism, why it makes ETFs more tax-efficient than an equivalent index mutual fund, and the disadvantages of the ETF wrapper.
cards.back:
• Authorized participant (AP) is market maker and intermediary: to CREATE, the AP delivers a basket of underlying stocks to the fund manager and receives ETF shares to sell to the public; to REDEEM, the process reverses (AP delivers ETF shares, receives the stock basket)
• Tax efficiency: a mutual fund must SELL holdings to meet redemptions, realizing gains that pass through to investors (in jurisdictions like the US). An ETF meets redemptions by IN-KIND delivery of stock — no capital gain is recorded — so the gain/loss passed to investors is smaller
• Other ETF advantages: intraday trading, low fees, can be bought on margin and sold short (unlike open-end funds)
• Disadvantages: buy at the offer / sell at the bid, commission costs, and the risk of an illiquid market in the ETF shares; frequent investor trading can negate the ETF's slightly lower expense ratio
• Limitation: far more benchmark indexes exist than ETFs, so not every index has a tracking ETF

cards.front: Write the formula for the number of equity index futures contracts needed to equitize cash to a target allocation, and state the conventions and classic error.
cards.back:
• Contract unit value = futures price × multiplier — the notional value one contract controls
• Cash to equitize × policy weight = the currency amount of index exposure wanted; divide by contract unit value; BUY contracts to gain long exposure
• Curriculum example: USD5,750,000 bonus, 15% US equity policy weight → USD862,500; S&P 500 E-mini at 2,464.29 with multiplier 50 → unit value USD123,214.50; 862,500 ÷ 123,214.50 = 7.00 → buy seven E-mini contracts
• Multipliers are contract-specific: S&P 500 = USD250, S&P 500 E-mini = USD50, Dow mini = USD5, Nikkei 225 = JPY1,000
• Classic errors: using the full-size multiplier when the question specifies the E-mini (or vice versa), forgetting to apply the POLICY WEIGHT to the full cash amount, and selling rather than buying when the goal is to add exposure ahead of a cash inflow
cards.formula: Number of contracts = (Cash to equitize × Policy weight) ÷ (Futures price × Multiplier)

cards.front: Contrast full replication, stratified sampling, and optimization on what they hold, when each is used, and each one's main drawback.
cards.back:
• FULL REPLICATION — hold ALL index constituents at index weights. Requires sufficient mandate asset size, sufficient liquidity, and constituents available for trading. Lowest tracking error, easy to understand; drawback = significant brokerage commissions when the index is large (e.g., MSCI ACWI IMI has 8,000+ names; the S&P 500 can be replicated in accounts as small as USD10 million)
• STRATIFIED SAMPLING — split the index into mutually exclusive and exhaustive strata (GICS sector, style; COUNTRY first for multinational indexes, then industry), hold a sample weighted proportionately to each stratum's index weight. Used when the index has many constituents or AUM is low; technically unsophisticated; drawback = higher tracking error and it ignores covariances
• OPTIMIZATION — minimize tracking error subject to constraints (max number of holdings, minimum market cap, style match, round lots, low rebalancing cost). Lower tracking error than sampling because it explicitly accounts for COVARIANCES (two names from different sectors that co-move: one gets excluded). Drawbacks = needs technical sophistication, is estimated on past data that shift (so must be rerun, at a cost), and per Roll/Jorion, minimizing tracking error can leave the portfolio MEAN-VARIANCE INEFFICIENT with higher risk than the benchmark — fix by adding a constraint on total portfolio volatility
• BLENDED — replicate the liquid large-cap portion, sample/optimize the illiquid small-cap tail

cards.front: A candidate concludes that holding more of an index's constituents always lowers tracking error. Why is that wrong?
cards.back:
• Gross of trading costs, yes — tracking error falls as holdings approach the full index
• But the added names are progressively SMALLER and MORE THINLY TRADED, so trading costs rise: brokerage fees plus upward price pressure from the fund's own buying
• At the least-liquid end transaction costs DOMINATE and tracking error rises again → the relation between tracking error and the number of constituents held is U-SHAPED for an index with illiquid members
• Practical implication: the manager weighs the benefit of a closer match against the cost of the marginal name (Fabozzi et al.: after optimizing on all constituents, managers often DELETE the lowest-weighted stocks, because their marginal transaction costs exceed their marginal diversification benefit)
• Separate but related exam point: across funds, an index with MORE constituents tends to show higher tracking error (EFA, 933 names > SPY, 506 > XIU, 60), since full replication becomes infeasible

cards.front: State the equations for tracking error and excess return, and explain why the two must never be used interchangeably.
cards.back:
• Rp = portfolio return; Rb = benchmark index return
• Tracking error is the STANDARD DEVIATION of the return difference over time — a volatility, always reported as a non-negative number; it measures the manager's ability to track the benchmark
• Excess return is a single-period LEVEL, Rp − Rb, and can be positive or negative; it says how the manager performed relative to the benchmark
• They are distinct: a manager whose cumulative return equals the index (excess return of zero) by lagging and then leading it still has a POSITIVE, non-zero tracking error
• Reported tracking error depends on data frequency (daily vs. less frequent) and fluctuates over time
• Index-fund objective: minimize tracking error subject to realistic constraints AND avoid negative excess return
• Classic error: calling the return gap "tracking error" — that gap is excess return
cards.formula: Tracking error(p) = √Variance(Rp − Rb) ; Excess return(p) = Rp − Rb

cards.front: List the principal causes of tracking error in an indexed equity portfolio and the method that controls each.
cards.back:
• FEES and expenses — always a negative on excess return and a contributor to tracking error → keep fees low; securities-lending income can offset them
• NUMBER OF SECURITIES HELD vs. the index — sampled portfolios report greater tracking error than fully replicated ones → fully replicate where feasible
• INTRA-DAY TRADING — index returns are struck at the CLOSE, so any fill at a different price creates tracking error (effect can be + or −) → trade at the market-on-close (MOC) price, or as near to the close as feasible
• TRADING COMMISSIONS — make excess return more negative → minimize trading costs; net investor inflows against redemptions rather than trading both
• CASH DRAG — equity indexes hold NO cash, so any balance (dividends received, sale proceeds, investor contributions) creates tracking error: negative when the market rises, positive when it falls → EQUITIZE with index futures or ETFs, and hedge accrued dividends (dividend drag) too
• Overall aim: maintain a beta of 1.0 to the benchmark with risk-factor exposures matching the index

cards.front: In a sector attribution analysis, how do you compute each sector's contribution to return and identify the sector primarily responsible for underperformance?
cards.back:
• For each sector: contribution = that sector's weight × that sector's return, computed once with the PORTFOLIO weight and once with the BENCHMARK weight; summed across ALL sectors in the breakdown, these contributions equal the respective total return (the curriculum's full GICS attribution uses eleven sectors; a partial exhibit showing only a few sectors will not sum to the total)
• Difference = portfolio contribution − benchmark contribution; because the sector return is the same in both, this reduces to (wPortfolio − wBenchmark) × sector return
• The sector with the LARGEST NEGATIVE difference is the primary contributor to underperformance
• Curriculum example: information technology returned +10.75% but was underweighted (18.71% vs. 19.06%) → difference of −0.04%, the largest negative, so IT was the primary drag
• Classic error: blaming the worst-returning sector (utilities, −3.92%) — a sector's own return does not matter; only the weight difference times that return does. Underweighting a POSITIVE-return sector hurts; underweighting a NEGATIVE-return sector helps
cards.formula: Contribution to return = Sector weight × Sector return ; Difference = (wPortfolio × R) − (wBenchmark × R)

cards.front: Walk through the securities-lending process for an index fund — parties, collateral, cash flows — and the risks it introduces.
cards.back:
• Lender appoints a LENDING AGENT, usually the custodian bank (sometimes the asset manager). Two documents: a securities lending AUTHORIZATION agreement (lender–agent) and a MASTER securities lending agreement (agent–borrower)
• Agent finds a borrower who posts collateral of typically 102%–105% of the securities' value, revalued DAILY for sufficiency
• If collateral is CASH, the agent invests it in money market instruments and the borrower receives a REBATE partly defraying its lost interest; either way the borrower pays a fee, which the lender splits with the agent
• Borrower takes legal TITLE, receives all cash flows and voting rights, pays an annualized borrow cost of typically 2%–10% (higher for hard-to-borrow names; "easy to borrow" = ETB), and must pay cash in lieu of dividends
• Benefit: income offsets management costs and can make NET expenses negative — the fund then earns a return in excess of the index (iShares Russell 2000 ETF: ~USD63 million of lending income vs. ~USD90.7 million of advisory fees)
• Risks: borrower CREDIT risk, collateral MARKET risk, plus liquidity and operational risk; collateral-REINVESTMENT risk if cash is put into long-term or risky paper (the Sigma Finance default)
• Index funds and pension funds are preferred lenders — long-term holders unlikely to recall shares abruptly

cards.front: Contrast fundamental (discretionary) and quantitative (systematic) active equity management across the six dimensions the curriculum uses.
cards.back:
Decision process: subjective, discretionary vs objective, systematic, non-discretionary
• Forecast focus: individual stock returns, driven by company insight vs factor returns, driven by model quality
• Information used: research on company/industry/economy, including items that cannot be quantified (management quality, reputation) vs data and statistics only
• Focus of analysis: DEPTH — a small group of stocks, high conviction, larger positions vs BREADTH — a selection of factors applied across a very large universe, many small positions
• Orientation to data: forward looking, forecast future corporate parameters vs backward looking, pattern recognition in historical data via back-tests
• Portfolio construction and risk: judgment/conviction within permissible risk limits, risk seen at the company level, holdings monitored continuously and traded at any time vs portfolio optimizer with a risk model, risk seen at the portfolio/factor level, rebalanced at regular intervals (monthly, quarterly)
• Classic trap: "quantitative" does not mean "uses numbers" — fundamental managers also use DCF models, quantitative screens, regressions and commercial risk models (Axioma, MSCI, Northfield, Bloomberg); the difference is whether judgment or a rule makes the ongoing decision
cards.mnemonic: Fundamental = Subjective, Stock, Research, Depth, Forward, Judgment; Quant = Objective, Factor, Data, Breadth, Backward, Optimizer

cards.front: Bottom-up managers buy stocks below intrinsic value. Name the value-oriented sub-styles the curriculum distinguishes, and what defines each.
cards.back:
Relative value — compare the company's P/E or P/B to the average of its industry sector; sector multiples differ widely, so a P/E of 12 is cheap for consumer staples and expensive for real estate
• Contrarian — buy against prevailing sentiment, typically depressed cyclicals with low or negative earnings; differs from other value investors by relying on market sentiment and sharp price moves (52-week highs/lows) rather than fundamental metrics
• High-quality value — valuation plus at least equal weight on consistent earnings power, above-average ROE, financial strength, exemplary management (associated with Buffett; no widely accepted label)
• Income — relatively high dividend yield with positive dividend growth; a secure yield tends to put a floor under the price
• Deep value — extremely low valuation relative to assets (low P/B), often financially distressed; the edge is expertise in reorganizations and the informational inefficiency of neglected names
• Restructuring/distressed — buy the debt or equity of a distressed firm before or during bankruptcy to gain control cheaply and restore intrinsic value; counter-cyclical opportunity set
• Special situations — mispricing around divestitures, spinoffs and mergers; needs industry, company and legal expertise
• Growth side: buy faster-than-industry or faster-than-market revenue/earnings/cash flow growth and tolerate above-average multiples; GARP is the hybrid sub-discipline
• Underlying rationale: mispricing exists at the SECURITY level; parameters analyzed are business model and branding, competitive advantages, and management/corporate governance

cards.front: Write the ratio GARP investors rely on, and use it to rank a stock priced at 50 with 12-month forward EPS of 5 and a 3-year EPS growth forecast of 20%.
cards.back:
P/E = price ÷ forward EPS (the curriculum's example uses 12-month forward EPS)
• Growth rate is entered as the NUMBER OF PERCENTAGE POINTS (20 for 20%), not 0.20
• Worked: P/E = 50 ÷ 5 = 10; PEG = 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5 — the lowest PEG of the four names in the curriculum example, so the GARP pick
• Lower PEG = more expected growth bought per unit of price
• When to use: GARP, a sub-discipline within GROWTH investing (often called a growth/value hybrid) — above-average growth at reasonable multiples
• Classic errors: computing a PEG when growth is negative (it is meaningless — the curriculum's Company C at −5% growth is a deep-value, not a GARP, candidate); entering 0.20 instead of 20 and scaling the answer 100×; treating the ratio as sufficient — GARP investors must still weigh the risk and the duration of the growth
cards.formula: PEG = (P/E) ÷ expected earnings growth rate in percentage points

cards.front: Name the top-down equity decision processes the curriculum lists, and the instruments top-down managers typically use to express them.
cards.back:
Country and geographic allocation — over/underweight regions or countries; may also track aggregate supply and demand for equity (buyback volumes, fund flows, IPO and secondary issuance volumes)
• Sector and industry rotation — globally integrated industries (information technology, energy) suit cross-border sector bets; locally driven ones (real estate, consumer staples) suit within-country bets
• Equity style rotation — allocate to size/value/momentum/quality baskets as each is expected to outperform; classification of stocks into styles is less standardized than sector or country classification
• Volatility-based — for managers who think they can forecast volatility better than option-implied volatility: VIX futures on the CFE, index options, volatility or variance swaps. A long index straddle is a call plus a put, same underlying index, same strike, same expiry; it pays if volatility exceeds what the market implied, loses if the market stays broadly flat, and maximum loss is limited to the premiums paid
• Thematic — macro, demographic, political or disruptive-technology drivers; the key judgment is whether a trend is STRUCTURAL (smartphones, cloud computing) or merely fashionable and short-lived
• Instruments: futures contracts, ETFs, swaps and custom baskets of stocks — fast, cheap macro exposure without picking names
• Related tool: a portfolio overlay is an array of derivative positions managed separately from the securities portfolio — bottom-up managers use one to strip out unintended sector or country bets thrown off by stock selection, or to add uncorrelated active return

cards.front: Describe the hedged portfolio approach to implementing a factor, its five drawbacks, and the two alternatives the curriculum offers.
cards.back:
Construction (Fama and French 1993): choose the factor, rank the investable universe on it, split into quantiles (typically quintiles or deciles), equal-weight or cap-weight within each quantile, then go long the best quantile and short the worst; track the long/short spread over time
• Drawback 1 — the information in the middle quantiles is discarded (in the debt-change example the best returns sat in deciles 3 to 6, which the D1/D10 trade never touches)
• Drawback 2 — it implicitly assumes the factor/return relationship is linear, or at least monotonic
• Drawback 3 — the portfolios are concentrated, and more so when many managers use the same factor
• Drawback 4 — it requires shorting, which may be impossible or too expensive in some markets
• Drawback 5, and most important — it is NOT a pure factor portfolio: it retains significant exposure to other risk factors
• Alternative for long-only mandates: a factor-tilting portfolio tracks the benchmark closely with controlled tracking error while adding the chosen factor exposure — similar to enhanced indexing
• Theoretical ideal: a factor-mimicking portfolio (FMP) is dollar neutral with unit exposure to the chosen factor and no exposure to any other; because it holds almost every stock and ignores short availability and transaction costs it is very expensive to trade, so managers approximate it by adding liquidity and short-availability constraints

cards.front: How is a raw company metric turned into a factor score that can be combined with other factors? Give the equation and standardize a book-to-price of 0.80 when the universe mean is 0.50 and sigma is 0.15.
cards.back:
x = the raw metric for one stock (book-to-price, 12-month momentum, ROE, revenue growth); the mean and standard deviation are computed ACROSS THE UNIVERSE for that period, and recomputed every period
• Output is a standardized exposure — the "factor score" — unitless, with mean 0 and standard deviation 1 across the universe
• Why it matters: metrics measured in different units and scales cannot be added; z-scores can, so several signals aggregate into one composite or multifactor score and stocks become comparable over time
• Worked: z = (0.80 − 0.50) ÷ 0.15 = +2.0
• Where the curriculum uses it: standardizing Russell 3000 fundamentals monthly from 1988 to 2015 to profile activist targets, and calculating and aggregating z-scores for each value and growth variable in MSCI index construction
• Classic errors: standardizing against a single full-sample mean instead of period by period (a look-ahead problem); combining raw, unstandardized metrics; and getting the sign wrong — cheapness must be scored so that a high z means a strong signal (high book-to-price, not high price-to-book)
cards.formula: z = (x − cross-sectional mean) ÷ cross-sectional standard deviation

cards.front: What profile do activist investors screen for, how large a stake do they take, and how does the market react to the announcement?
cards.back:
Target profile (z-scores versus the universe, already visible a year before the campaign and persisting to the event date): slower year-over-year revenue growth and EPS growth than the market; weaker price momentum and weaker ROE than peers; poorer-than-average corporate governance
• Traditionally small and mid-cap listed companies, though large caps are increasingly targeted
• Stake: typically LESS THAN 10% — activists seek change, not a full takeover bid; stakes above jurisdictional thresholds must be disclosed publicly
• Horizon: often shorter than that of buy-and-hold investors, but the whole campaign can run a number of years
• Goal: financial gain (increased shareholder value) or a non-financial cause such as an ESG issue
• Tactics, escalating: seek board representation; write to management, meet privately, or launch a proxy contest; propose corporate changes at the AGM; propose balance-sheet restructuring with buybacks or higher dividends; cut or realign management compensation; litigate for breach of fiduciary duty; coordinate with other shareholders; run a media campaign; break up a conglomerate
• Company defenses: multi-class share structures, poison pills, staggered boards, charter and bylaw provisions
• Market reaction: target stocks rise about 2% on announcement day on average, on top of prior appreciation from stake building or information leakage, with a modest post-announcement drift of about 0.6% over the following month relative to the market
• Aftermath: revenue and earnings growth, profitability and governance indicators generally improve — but financial leverage rises significantly

cards.front: Set out the mechanics of the CNR/CP pairs trade — the entry rule, the exit rule, and the risk that turned the third trade into a loser.
cards.back:
Step 1 — identify two historically highly correlated securities, either with statistical models of stock prices or by fundamental judgment that the two businesses should move together (Canadian National and Canadian Pacific: both operate national rail networks; correlation 69% on daily returns)
• Step 2 — measure the spread, the log price differential ln(price A ÷ price B), against its rolling moving average (130 days in the example) with bands 2 standard deviations above and below
• Step 3 — ENTER when the spread is more than 2 standard deviations from the moving average: go long the underperforming stock and simultaneously short the outperforming one, betting on mean reversion
• Step 4 — EXIT when the spread reaches the moving average again
• Step 5 — apply stop-loss rules to exit at a preset loss limit; risk management is critical to these strategies
• Biggest risk: the divergence is STRUCTURAL rather than temporary — for example one firm develops a technology or product competitors cannot replicate. The third CNR/CP trade was entered on 21 July 2015, CP kept declining while CNR stayed flat, and the loss could have exceeded the first two trades' combined profits if closed before the spring 2016 reversion
• Adjacent strategy: market microstructure arbitrage analyzes the limit order book and TAQ data for order imbalances that spike prices for milliseconds — only high-frequency traders can capture them, and they do so across a portfolio of many stocks

cards.front: List, in order, the seven steps of the fundamental active investment process, and state what triggers a sale.
cards.back:
1. Define the investment universe and the market opportunity — the perceived chance to earn positive risk-adjusted active return net of costs, in line with the mandate. This is the investment thesis: WHAT the opportunity is and WHY it exists
2. Prescreen the universe to a manageable set (a value manager excludes high P/E and high debt-to-equity names; a growth manager excludes names without sufficient historical or forecast EPS growth)
3. Understand the industry and business — industry and competitive analysis plus analysis of the financial reports
4. Forecast company performance, usually cash flows or earnings
5. Convert forecasts to valuations and identify ex ante profitable investments
6. Construct a portfolio with the desired risk profile — overweight upside names, underweight/exclude/short the rest, and decide whether to take active industry and sector exposures or stay sector neutral (with no sector view, in theory be neutral to the benchmark)
7. Rebalance with buy and sell disciplines
• Sell triggers: the price rises past the analyst's target price, so the stock is reclassified from undervalued to overvalued; OR the target price is revised down below the current market price; OR a pre-defined stop-loss point is touched, which caps the loss on any holding and limits behavioral bias
• Nuance: because valuation is imprecise, managers may trim the position rather than sell outright, especially in a relative valuation framework where peer multiples are also moving

cards.front: One stock looks cheap on a low P/E after a sharp fall; another delivered exactly the growth promised yet the share price never moved. Name both traps and explain why each happens.
cards.back:
VALUE TRAP — a stock appears attractively valued on a low P/E (or low P/B or P/CF) because of a significant price fall, but may still be OVERPRICED given worsening future prospects; the company or whole sector faces deterioration and prices can stay low for a long time or fall further. Defence: research thoroughly enough to know WHY it is cheap, and require a catalyst — prices generally need a catalyst or a change in perceptions to advance, and without one there is little chance of reverting to fair value. Curriculum case: HSBC on the HKSE traded above HKD 80 at end-2013 on P/E 10.9x and P/B 0.9x, then fell 48.7% over seven years to below HKD 41 while the Hang Seng Financial Index gained 16.0%
• GROWTH TRAP — loses two different ways: (a) results fall short of the high expectations and the price drops; or (b) the company DELIVERS the above-average growth as expected but the share price still does not rise, because the already high starting multiple had discounted it
• The two assumptions that fail: that current earnings are sustainable — competitors respond and compete away supernormal profits at an industry-specific pace — and that fast growth continues, when growth off a very low base commonly slows sharply after the initial expansion
• These two traps plus behavioral biases are the three pitfalls of fundamental investing. Cognitive errors: confirmation bias ("stock love bias"), illusion of control, availability. Emotional biases: loss aversion, overconfidence, regret aversion

cards.front: How is a factor's predictive power measured in a quantitative back-test, what value counts as strong, and why do practitioners prefer the ranked version?
cards.back:
IC = information coefficient, the cross-sectional correlation between factor exposures and their holding-period returns, computed under the assumption that expected returns are linearly related to factor exposures
• Factor scores are essentially standardized exposures; the return is the NEXT period's return, which is what makes the IC a predictive, not a contemporaneous, measure
• Range: −1 to +1 (−100% to +100%); the higher the IC, the greater the factor's predictive power
• Rule of thumb for US equities: an average MONTHLY IC of 5% to 6% is considered very strong
• Advantage over a quantile approach: the IC aggregates information from ALL securities in the universe, while deciles or quintiles capture only the top and bottom extremes
• Pearson IC is sensitive to outliers. In the curriculum's nine-stock example one stock (highest factor score, worst subsequent return, −8.50%) pushed the Pearson IC to −0.8% while the Spearman rank IC was +40% and the long/short tercile return was a positive 0.56% — so the more robust rank IC is usually preferred
• Classic errors: discarding a genuinely good factor because a single outlier flipped the Pearson IC negative; and expecting IC values close to 1 — an average monthly IC of 0.05 is already excellent
cards.formula: Pearson IC = correlation(factor scores at t, security returns from t to t+1); Spearman rank IC = correlation(rank of factor score, rank of forward return)
