cards.front: A quant back-test produces a spectacular Sharpe ratio. Name the four issues that most often make such a result unrepeatable in live trading, and the fix for each.
cards.back:
SURVIVORSHIP BIAS — testing only companies in business today ignores stocks that left the universe through bankruptcy, delisting or acquisition, so the test assumes the strategy would never have bought a failure; results are overly optimistic. Fix: include dead stocks. Investors know of it but routinely underestimate its significance
• LOOK-AHEAD BIAS — using information unavailable at the decision date, such as accounting data before the company released it, or restated numbers. Fix: original, un-restated, point-in-time data. Satyam case: a simulation dated 31 December 2008 must include Satyam in the Nifty 50 and use the accounts published then, even though they were later proved fraudulent
• DATA MINING AND OVERFITTING — excessive search of past data until a pattern conforms to a pre-determined model. The decisive test is whether the factor MAKES INTUITIVE SENSE; a factor can pass statistical back-testing yet lack any justification, and impressive back-tested performance does not imply future value. Fix: an out-of-sample back-test on data not used to build the model, plus an economic rationale
• TURNOVER, TRANSACTION COSTS AND SHORT AVAILABILITY — back-tests assume an ideal world with no costs, no turnover limits and unlimited shorting. Japanese one-month reversal returned about 12% a year at zero cost, beating price-to-book, but collapsed as the assumption moved to 30 bps per trade, while price-to-book fell only modestly — fast-decaying signals are the most exposed
• Also: crowding. In August 2007 standard quant factors suffered heavy losses as managers running similar trades headed for the exit together (the "quant meltdown")
• Tip: using a well-defined broad index (S&P 500, Russell 3000, MSCI World) as the universe is itself free of look-ahead and survivorship bias, investable and liquid

cards.front: Write the returns-based style analysis regression, define every term and constraint, and say how to read a 0.4 value / 0.6 growth result against current holdings that are 0.85 value.
cards.back:
r(t) = the fund's return in the period ending at time t
• R(s,t) = the return of style index s in the same period, for s = 1 to m styles
• beta(s) = the fund's exposure to style s — the output being solved for
• alpha = a constant, often interpreted as the value added by the fund manager
• epsilon(t) = the residual return the chosen styles cannot explain
• Constraints: the betas sum to 1, and each is positive for a long-only portfolio — a constrained multivariate regression (Sharpe 1992)
• When to use: the manager does not disclose full holdings, so a holdings-based approach is impossible; inputs are just the fund's historical returns and the style index returns
• Critical judgment: WHICH style indexes to include, since stock returns are highly correlated within a sector, across sectors and across global markets; the manager's own description of his or her style is a good starting point
• Reading the example: 60 months of returns giving 0.4 value / 0.6 growth is the AVERAGE style effect over that window, while holdings showing 0.85 value is today's positioning — the gap means the manager was likely running growth for part of the past five years (style rotation or drift), not that either method is wrong
• Classic errors: treating the betas as current holdings, and forgetting that the imposed constraints limit results within boundaries and can hide aggressive positions such as deep value or micro cap
cards.formula: r(t) = alpha + sum over s of [beta(s) × R(s,t)] + epsilon(t), subject to sum of beta(s) = 1 and beta(s) > 0 for a long-only portfolio

cards.front: Holdings-based versus returns-based style analysis: how does each work, and give one strength and one limitation of each.
cards.back:
HOLDINGS-BASED — bottom-up: aggregate the style attributes of the individual stocks held, weighted by the active positions. A stock's value or growth score comes from factors such as price to book, price to earnings, price to sales, price to cash flow, ROE and dividend yield. Morningstar and Lipper assign a stock wholly to one style (attribute 1 or 0); MSCI and FTSE Russell let a stock carry both, so a "value inclusion factor" of 0.6 sends 60% of its market cap to the value index and 40% to growth
• Strength: generally more accurate because it uses actual holdings; it shows every style the portfolio is exposed to, so it supports style allocation decisions and lets a manager see and correct drift holding by holding
• Limitation: needs all portfolio constituents plus each stock's style attributes — and, to track style history, point-in-time databases for both; it is also less effective for funds with substantial derivatives positions, where data are limited
• RETURNS-BASED — regress the fund's returns on style index returns; the coefficients are the style exposures
• Strength: needs returns only, so it can be applied to non-disclosing managers and is more widely applicable and comparable across funds
• Limitation: backward-looking — it reports the average style over the window, and its constraints make aggressive positions such as deep value or micro cap hard to detect
• Best practice: use BOTH (Morningstar studies find holdings-based generally more accurate, with exceptions), and add manager self-identification from the prospectus, which is essential for non-standard styles such as long/short equity, equity market neutral and dedicated short bias
cards.mnemonic: Holdings = what they HOLD now (accurate, data-hungry); Returns = what they EARNED then (easy, backward-looking)

cards.front: Name the four building blocks of active equity portfolio construction and the part of active return each one drives.
cards.back:
• Rewarded factor weightings — over/under/neutral-weight priced factors vs the BENCHMARK's exposures; drives the Σ(βpk − βbk) × Fk term. Most recognized: Market, Size, Value, Momentum.
• Alpha skills — TIMING exposures to rewarded factors, unrewarded factors (sector, country, oil), securities, and other asset classes (cash); also finding/enhancing factors. Drives α.
• Position sizing — balancing conviction against idiosyncratic risk; its most dramatic impact is on ε (same factor beta from 20 or 200 stocks, very different luck).
• Breadth of expertise — the integrating block; confidence in outperformance rises with a larger sample of INDEPENDENT (uncorrelated) decisions.
Static exposure to known rewarded factors is no longer alpha — it is cheap "alternative beta"; only timing it is alpha.
cards.mnemonic: Factors, Alpha, Sizing — held together by Breadth (FAS-B)

cards.front: State the full fundamental law of active management and define every term.
cards.back:
• E(RA) = expected ANNUAL active return (in %).
• IC = expected information coefficient — the extent to which the manager's forecast active returns correspond to realized active returns (skill).
• BR = breadth — the number of TRULY INDEPENDENT decisions made each YEAR, not the number of securities.
• TC = transfer coefficient — the ability to translate insights into positions without constraint; 1.0 if truly unconstrained, well below 1 when long-only/position limits bind (0.25 is representative of a constrained long-only investor).
• σRA = the manager's active risk (tracking error).
Curriculum anchor: σRA 6%, TC 0.25, IC 0.10, BR = 1 → 0.10 × 1 × 6% × 0.25 = 15 bps; about 40 fully independent decisions are needed for 1% active return.
Classic error: counting positions as breadth. Buying the 100 lowest price-to-book names out of 1,000 is nowhere near 100 independent decisions — correlated bets collapse effective breadth and flatter expected IR.
cards.formula: E(RA) = IC × √BR × σRA × TC

cards.front: Contrast systematic and discretionary construction on universe, factor use, concentration, and optimization — and name the second, independent axis.
cards.back:
Systematic:
• Research-based RULES applied across a broad universe; judgment expressed up front in strategy design.
• Seeks balanced exposure to known rewarded factors; little or no factor timing.
• Diversified, small positions to minimize idiosyncratic risk — systematic managers are UNLIKELY to run concentrated portfolios.
• Readily adapted to formal optimization; objectives and constraints explicitly specified.
Discretionary:
• Manager judgment on a SMALLER subset of securities; depth on governance, business model, competitive landscape; better factor proxies; nonfinancial inputs.
• Factor timing is more likely here, especially top-down.
• Generally more concentrated; construction less formal, objectives set implicitly.
Second axis — bottom-up vs top-down: bottom-up starts from security risk/return characteristics (alpha mainly from security selection); top-down starts from the macro environment and projects onto countries, sectors, securities (alpha mainly from FACTOR TIMING, and more likely to raise cash when the Market view is poor).

cards.front: Write the Active Share formula, state its range, and name the only two things that can create it.
cards.back:
• w_portfolio,i and w_benchmark,i are the weights of security i; n = every security in the PORTFOLIO OR the benchmark.
• Range 0 (matches the benchmark) to 1 / 100% (shares no holdings with it). Pure arithmetic from holdings — no statistics, no estimation.
• Two and only two sources: (1) holding securities NOT in the benchmark; (2) holding benchmark securities at DIFFERENT weights.
• 100% − Active Share = the share of capital deployed the same way as the index (Active Share 80% → 20% index-like).
• Use it to check fee reasonableness: at equal fees, a 0.80 Active Share manager gives twice the active management per unit of fee as a 0.40 manager.
Classic errors: forgetting the ½ (or summing only the overweights), and comparing Active Share across DIFFERENT benchmarks — an S&P 500 portfolio's Active Share rises about 12% simply by measuring it against the Russell 1000.
cards.formula: Active Share = ½ × Σ |w_portfolio,i − w_benchmark,i|

cards.front: Active Share vs active risk: what does each measure, what inputs does each need, and which one can the manager fully control?
cards.back:
Active Share:
• Measures the extent to which the NUMBER and SIZING of positions differ from the benchmark — the size of holdings deviations only.
• Needs only portfolio and benchmark weights; ignores variances and cross-correlations, so it says nothing about the efficiency of diversification.
• FULLY controlled by the manager, since he sets the weights.
Active risk (tracking error):
• Standard deviation of the difference between portfolio and benchmark returns.
• Active variance = variance from factor exposures, Σ(βpk − βbk) × Fk, PLUS idiosyncratic active variance (alpha's variance sits inside the idiosyncratic term).
• Realized active risk is historical and easy; construction is forward-looking, so the relevant figure is PREDICTED active risk, which needs forecast variances and correlations (EWMA, GARCH).
• NOT fully controllable — it depends on variances and correlations outside the manager's control, and it rises with market volatility.

cards.front: Two funds have nearly identical Active Share (0.73 vs 0.71) and a similar number of positions, yet active risk is 2.8% vs 6.0%. Explain, and give the general rule.
cards.back:
• Active Share weights every deviation equally: a 0.5% underweight plus a 0.5% overweight counts the same whether the pair is bank/bank or bank/technology. Active RISK does not — it depends on cross-correlation.
• So the higher-active-risk manager is almost certainly making active decisions at the SECTOR/factor level (or size, style, country), not just the security level. Expect his realized outcomes to be far more dispersed around the benchmark in both directions.
• Sapra–Hunjan rules: high net exposure to a risk factor gives high active risk irrespective of idiosyncratic risk; if factor exposure is fully NEUTRALIZED, active risk is attributable entirely to Active Share; that Active-Share-driven active risk shrinks as the number of securities rises or average idiosyncratic risk falls; active risk rises when factor and idiosyncratic volatility rise (2008).
• Map anchors: diversified multi-factor fund, 250+ names — Active Share about 0.70 but tracking error only about ±3%. Concentrated stock picker — Active Share above 0.90 AND active risk 8%–12%+. Closet indexer — low on both. High Active Share alone never implies high active risk, and it certainly does not imply skill.

cards.front: Define risk budgeting and list, in order, the four things an effective risk management process requires of the manager.
cards.back:
Risk budgeting = the process by which the portfolio's TOTAL risk appetite is allocated among the various components of portfolio choice (factors, countries, sectors, securities), so the active-risk budget is spent efficiently.
1. Determine which type of risk measure is appropriate to the strategy — a long/short manager benchmarked to cash-plus prefers ABSOLUTE risk (total volatility); a long-only manager benchmarked to a cap-weighted index prefers RELATIVE risk (active risk).
2. Understand how each aspect of the strategy contributes to overall risk — factors vs country/sector/security allocation, plus the risk created by timing those exposures.
3. Determine the appropriate LEVEL of the risk budget — part principle, largely a policy choice.
4. Properly allocate that risk among individual positions/factors, absolute or relative.
Guiding principle: the risks a manager CHOOSES to take should match his perceived skills — market timers time factor exposure, sector rotators time sectors, multi-factor managers balance factors. All other risk should be diversified away or minimized.

cards.front: A manager benchmarked to the FTSE 100 takes a large cash position. What happens to absolute risk and to active risk — and why do candidates get this backwards?
cards.back:
• Absolute risk FALLS — cash has very low volatility and low correlation with everything.
• Active risk RISES — precisely because cash has a LOW correlation with the equity benchmark.
• The trap: in a relative-risk framework what matters is not an asset's own volatility but its ACTIVE (relative) volatility versus the benchmark. You may not assume a low-risk asset cuts active risk or a high-risk asset raises it.
• Curriculum illustration: benchmark 50/50 in two equity indexes; portfolio 40/40 plus 20% cash. Index A and Index B each carry 5% active risk, cash 12% — and 100% of the portfolio's active variance is attributed to the CASH position, the lowest-absolute-risk asset in the book.
• The mirror image also holds: adding a HIGH-volatility asset can LOWER active risk if it has high covariance with the benchmark. Same logic across countries, sectors, securities, and factors.

cards.front: List the formal (statistical) risk measures used in equity portfolio construction, and define VaR, CVaR, IVaR, and MVaR.
cards.back:
• Volatility — standard deviation of portfolio returns.
• Active risk — standard deviation of portfolio minus benchmark returns (tracking error / tracking risk).
• Skewness — degree of non-normality; negative skew means the mean sits below the median and negative deviations are larger on average.
• Drawdown — the portfolio loss from its high point until it begins to recover.
• VaR — the MINIMUM loss expected a given percentage of the time over a given period under modeled conditions; typically quoted as the minimum loss expected 5% of the time.
• CVaR — the AVERAGE loss incurred if the VaR cutoff is exceeded (expected tail loss / expected shortfall); not technically a VaR measure.
• IVaR — the CHANGE in portfolio VaR from adding a new position (which shrinks existing positions).
• MVaR — the effect of a VERY SMALL change in position size; in a diversified portfolio it gives each asset's contribution to total VaR.
Key distinction: formal measures require the manager to PREDICT risk (heuristic controls do not), and they behave badly for portfolios with few securities, where estimation error is large — VaR suits a multi-asset pension sponsor far better than a 40-stock equity manager. Managers usually state them as soft targets ("targeting 10%–12% volatility").

cards.front: Give four typical heuristic constraints, and state exactly what imposing limits costs the manager and what it buys him.
cards.back:
Typical heuristic constraints (exogenous classification rules based on experience, not empirical evidence):
• Any single position limited to the LESSER of 5× its benchmark weight or 2%.
• Portfolio weighted average capitalization no less than 75% of the index's.
• No position exceeding 2× the average daily trading volume of the past three months.
• Carbon footprint no more than 75% of the benchmark's. Also used: sector/industry/geography concentration, net factor and currency exposures, leverage, illiquidity, turnover.
What limits COST:
• They restrict the manager's ability to fully exploit his return insights → the TRANSFER COEFFICIENT declines → if he still tries to hold active risk constant, the INFORMATION RATIO declines. Hence there is an optimal/maximum level of active risk for a constrained manager: he cannot simply scale active weights up (no shorting → cannot deepen underweights; no leverage → cannot deepen overweights; illiquid names and position caps block the rest).
What limits BUY:
• Control of unknown/unexpected risk, and a safeguard against overconfidence and hubris. Heuristic limits also deliver low active risk as an OUTCOME even with no explicit tracking-error constraint (e.g. ±3% sector deviations plus index weight + 1% security caps) — but they need continuous monitoring, since price moves alone can breach them.
Over-tight, benchmark-anchored limits produce a portfolio that simply mirrors the benchmark.

cards.front: A fund caps positions at 2% of assets and at 10% of a stock's average daily volume. Write the rule that sets the true maximum position, and show how AUM changes which limit binds.
cards.back:
• AUM in dollars; max position weight is the allocation/concentration constraint; ADV is average daily dollar trading volume; the % of ADV cap is the liquidity constraint. The BINDING limit is whichever produces the smaller dollar figure.
• Curriculum example: smallest index name has $2bn cap and trades 1% of cap daily → ADV = $20m. Liquidity limit = 10% × $20m = $2m.
  – $200m fund: allocation limit = 2% × $200m = $4m, so liquidity binds at $2m — the position can be only about 1.0% of assets.
  – $1bn fund: the SAME $2m cap is now just 0.2% of assets — the insight barely moves the portfolio.
  – $5bn fund: a 2% position is $100m, yet only about 35% of Russell 1000 names trade more than $100m a day — the opportunity set collapses.
• Classic error: assuming the stated percentage limit is the operative one. As AUM grows the LIQUIDITY limit binds first, forcing larger, more liquid names, more positions, lower turnover, patient/unlit-venue trading, or closing the fund. A 40-stock small-cap strategy struggles at $100m; small-cap funds with $1bn+ capacity may need 400+ names.
cards.formula: Max position ($) = lesser of [AUM × max position weight] and [ADV × max % of ADV]

cards.front: What four attributes define a well-constructed portfolio, and what are the tie-breakers when two products show similar risk?
cards.back:
Four attributes:
• A clear investment philosophy and a CONSISTENT investment process.
• Risk and structural characteristics as PROMISED to investors.
• A risk-efficient delivery methodology.
• Reasonably low operating costs GIVEN the strategy.
Tie-breakers:
• Comparable factor exposures and similar costs → prefer the product with LOWER absolute volatility and LOWER active risk.
• Similar active risk, similar absolute risk, similar costs, similar alpha skills → prefer the HIGHER Active Share, because it leverages the manager's alpha skills and carries higher expected return (curriculum case: Product B, Active Share 0.80 with about 120 names, beat Product A, Active Share 0.43 with about 320 names, by more than 3.1% annually at the same 4.8%–4.9% active risk).
• Look for risk exposures aligned with investor expectations and LOW unexplained (idiosyncratic) risk relative to total risk.
Judge efficiency against the MANDATE and the investor's total portfolio — a concentrated stock picker should have higher active risk and may have a lower information ratio than a diversified factor investor and still be well-structured.

cards.front: Define net and gross exposure, then give the figures for long-only, 130/30, and a 100/100 market-neutral book.
cards.back:
• Long % and short % are stated as percentages of CAPITAL; the short leg is taken in absolute value. Net exposure signals Market-factor exposure; gross exposure signals leverage.
• Long only 100/0: net 100%, gross 100%.
• 130/30 long extension: net 130 − 30 = 100% (same as long-only), gross 130 + 30 = 160%. The shorts FUND the extra longs.
• Market neutral 100/100: net 0%, gross 200%. Directional 80/40: net 40%, gross 120%.
• Typical equity hedge fund parameters: gross 150%–200%, net 0%–60%. Any net exposure above zero implies positive Market-factor exposure.
• Why 130/30 raises potential alpha: a long-only manager can express a negative view on a 0.25%-weight stock only down to zero — a 0.25% underweight. Shorting lets the underweight be sized to conviction, so positive and negative views are expressed SYMMETRICALLY, raising the transfer coefficient and breadth.
Classic error: treating dollar neutral as market neutral. Equal dollars long and short is not zero beta — the economic drivers of the two sides differ; market neutral means the aggregate targeted BETA is zero (e.g. long $100 at beta 1.0 vs short $80 at beta 1.25).
cards.formula: Net exposure = long % − |short %| ; Gross exposure = long % + |short %|

cards.front: Moving from long-only to a leveraged long/short book: name the added risks and costs, and the two inherent limitations of a market-neutral strategy.
cards.back:
Added risks and costs of shorting:
• A short moves AGAINST the manager as the price rises, and the loss is not limited — versus long-only, where limited liability puts a firm floor (the stock can only fall to zero).
• Leverage is often significant and magnifies both directions.
• Borrow cost can be prohibitive for hard-to-locate names, and borrowed stock can be RECALLED at the worst moment.
• Collateral requirements rise with the relative amount of shorting and as a short moves against you — collateral is quoted as a percentage OF THE SHORT POSITIONS: a book with 20% of capital short may post collateral equal to 40% of the short positions; a book with 100% of capital short, 200% of the short positions. Risky collateral counts at less than full value (a T-bill at 100%, a high-yield bond at only part of market value) — in extremes forcing liquidation of good long positions.
• SHORT SQUEEZE: the shorted stock rises so fast that shorts cannot meet collateral, and their buying pushes it higher still.
• Operational: prime broker plus three-party custodian agreements, counterparty risk if collateral sits in a prime broker's general account (Lehman), regulatory bans on short-selling or naked shorting, and fees that are a multiple of long-only (hedge funds about 2% and 20%).
Two inherent limitations of market neutral:
1. Maintaining a beta of ZERO is no easy task — not all risks hedge efficiently and correlations continually shift.
2. Limited upside in a bull market UNLESS equitized — index the equity exposure and overlay the market-neutral long/short book, restoring market beta on top of the pure alpha.
Net benefit: shorts cut market risk, expand the harvestable risk premiums and alpha, and diversify better — at the cost of giving up part of the market premium, possibly amplifying active risk, and higher cost and complexity.

cards.front: State the three characteristics of a bond portfolio structured to immunize a single (Type I) liability, and explain why matching Macaulay duration to the horizon works.
cards.back:
Conditions:
• Initial market value equals or exceeds the present value of the liability
• Portfolio Macaulay duration matches the liability's due date (the investment horizon)
• Minimizes the portfolio convexity statistic (equivalently, minimizes dispersion of cash flows)
Why it works:
• A rate rise cuts price (loss, measured by money duration) but raises the future value of reinvested coupons; at the Macaulay duration date the two effects exactly offset — same logic for a rate fall
• Immunization is "zero replication": manage coupon bonds so they track the zero-coupon bond maturing at the liability date (MacDur = maturity, no reinvestment risk, zero dispersion)
• The strategy locks in the portfolio's CASH FLOW YIELD (IRR on the aggregate cash flows), not the market value-weighted average of the bonds' yields to maturity
• Not buy-and-hold: duration drifts as time passes and yields change, so rebalance (bonds or a derivatives overlay), trading transaction costs against an allowed duration gap
cards.mnemonic: Value ≥, Duration =, Convexity minimized.

cards.front: Two portfolios immunize a single 10-year liability: A has cash flow yield 7.64%, MacDur 9.98, convexity 107.88; B has 7.65%, 10.01, 129.43. Candidates pick B. Why is that wrong?
cards.back:
• Recommend A — the LOWER-convexity portfolio.
• The trap: "convexity is always desirable" plus "B has the higher yield and a duration closer to 10." A 1 bp yield difference and a 0.03 duration difference are not economically meaningful; the convexity difference is.
• The client's objective is to minimize the variance of the realized return over the horizon, which means minimizing dispersion of cash flows around the Macaulay duration — making the portfolio behave like the perfect zero (dispersion = 0).
• Higher convexity/dispersion = greater STRUCTURAL RISK: under twists and non-parallel shifts, the portfolio's cash flow yield changes differently from the yield on the immunizing zero. Barbell = high dispersion, bullet = low.
• Do not carry this rule across: for MULTIPLE liabilities the asset convexity must be GREATER than the liabilities' (though the lowest available that still exceeds them).

cards.front: Contrast the immunization conditions for a single liability with those for multiple liabilities, and name the alternative implementation that avoids rate risk entirely.
cards.back:
Single liability:
• PV(assets) ≥ PV(liability); asset money/modified duration slightly greater than the liability's
• Portfolio Macaulay duration = the liability due date
• MINIMIZE portfolio convexity and dispersion
Multiple liabilities (duration matching):
• MV(assets) ≥ MV(liabilities)
• Asset BPV = liability BPV (match MONEY durations; the match may be slightly above or below, provided it is the closest available)
• Asset dispersion and convexity GREATER than the liabilities' — but the lowest available that still exceeds them (a portfolio with a near-perfect BPV but convexity below the liabilities' fails the condition)
• Why BPV and not modified duration: the market values and cash flow yields of assets and liabilities differ
Alternative implementation — cash flow matching (dedication): buy bonds (usually governments) whose coupons and principal match the liability dates and amounts; no interest rate risk, no rebalancing, and auditors will normally grant accounting defeasement, but it is the most expensive and most restrictive route. Duration matching with cheaper corporates plus a derivatives overlay costs less but only "effectively defeases" the debt.
cards.mnemonic: Single: minimize convexity. Multiple: more convexity than the liabilities — but the least available.

cards.front: Write the basis point value of a bond portfolio from its Macaulay duration, and say what each input must be.
cards.back:
• MacDur = ANNUALIZED portfolio Macaulay duration computed from the aggregate cash flows discounted at the cash flow yield — not the market value-weighted average of the individual bonds' durations
• Cash flow yield = annualized IRR on the portfolio's aggregate cash flows, semiannual bond basis (periodicity 2); dividing that ANNUAL yield by the periodicity gives the periodic yield, and MacDur ÷ (1 + periodic yield) is the annualized modified duration
• Market value = full market value of the portfolio; 0.0001 = 1 bp
• The bracketed term × market value is money (dollar) duration; BPV = money duration × 0.0001 = the approximate change in market value per 1 bp change in the cash flow yield. Also called PVBP, PV01, or DV01.
• Use it to match assets to liabilities when market values and yields differ (multiple liabilities) and to size a futures or swap overlay.
• Worked: [6.0004 ÷ (1 + 0.037608 ÷ 2)] × 200,052,250 × 0.0001 = EUR117,824
• Classic errors: using weighted-average bond durations and yields instead of portfolio statistics (with an upward-sloping curve this understates duration — 5.8776 vs 6.0004 — and is a source of model risk); forgetting to divide by (1 + periodic yield); treating BPV as exact when it ignores convexity.
cards.formula: BPV = [MacDur ÷ (1 + Cash flow yield ÷ 2)] × Market value × 0.0001

cards.front: How many bond futures contracts close a money duration gap, and how is the futures BPV obtained?
cards.back:
• Derived from: Asset BPV + (Nf × Futures BPV) = Liability portfolio BPV — futures have zero market value (daily mark to market) yet add to or subtract from asset BPV
• Nf positive → BUY (go long) futures, raising asset money duration; Nf negative → SELL (go short)
• Futures BPV is approximated by the cheapest-to-deliver note's BPV per 100,000 par divided by its conversion factor (CF). Conversion factors assume a 6.00% yield to maturity, so when yields are below 6% the CTD is typically the lowest-duration qualifying note — the 10-year T-note contract has effectively behaved like a 6.5-year contract.
• Worked: (117,824 − 18,819) ÷ 69.1377 = 1,432 contracts using the 6.5-year CTD, but ÷ 95.8909 = only 1,032 using the on-the-run 10-year — a 400-contract error.
• Classic errors: using the on-the-run note rather than the CTD; omitting the conversion factor; forgetting the approximation ignores days to expiration, short rates and accrued interest (model risk). Round to whole contracts; the sign tells you long vs short.
cards.formula: Nf = (Liability portfolio BPV − Asset portfolio BPV) ÷ Futures BPV, with Futures BPV ≈ BPV(CTD) ÷ CF(CTD)

cards.front: Describe contingent immunization: what permits it, what the manager may invest in, what forces the switch, and the over-/under-hedge decision rule.
cards.back:
• Requires a SURPLUS — assets' market value minus liabilities' market value — above a designated threshold.
• Hybrid passive-active: while the surplus exceeds the threshold, run the assets as if under a total return mandate, aiming to cut the cost of retiring the liabilities.
• If the actively managed assets perform poorly and the surplus evaporates, the mandate REVERTS to the purely passive strategy: build a duration-matching (BPV-matched) portfolio and manage it on target.
• In principle any asset class is permitted — equity, fixed income, alternatives, out-of-the-money commodity options, CDS — but LIQUIDITY is a key selection criterion because positions must be unwound as the surplus nears the threshold (asset liquidity risk).
• With a futures overlay the active view is expressed as over- or under-hedging versus Nf: deliberately OVER-hedge (more long contracts than Nf) when yields are expected to FALL; UNDER-hedge, or even go short, when yields are expected to RISE.
• Example: Nf = 123.3 but the manager is long 160 contracts → over-hedging → the view is that 10-year yields will fall.

cards.front: A pension plan closes its duration gap with a receive-fixed swap. Give the notional principal equation and the units convention.
cards.back:
• NP = notional principal; Swap BPV is quoted per 100 of notional (effective duration +16.73 → BPV 0.1673 per 100), hence the ÷ 100.
• A receive-fixed swap is long a fixed-rate bond financed by issuing an FRN, so it has POSITIVE duration and raises asset BPV — the right instrument for a plan whose asset BPV is far below liability BPV (equity and alternatives are assumed to have zero effective duration).
• Worked: 594,000 + (NP × 0.1673 ÷ 100) = 2,257,080 → NP ≈ USD994 million for a 100% hedging ratio; multiply by the chosen hedging ratio for a partial hedge (50% ≈ USD497 million).
• Hedging ratio: 0% = no hedge, 100% = full immunization of the duration gap; partial hedges are common because of collateral exhaustion risk, daily cash flows, and stakeholders' reaction to visible derivative losses.
• Classic errors: omitting the ÷ 100 (swap BPV is per 100 of notional, futures BPV is per contract); mixing ABO-based and PBO-based liability BPVs (17.1 vs 8.4 effective duration in the example); solving for the hedged notional and then forgetting to scale it by the hedging ratio.
cards.formula: Asset BPV + (NP × Swap BPV ÷ 100) = Liability BPV

cards.front: Full hedging assumes Asset BPV × ΔAsset yields + Hedge BPV × ΔHedge yields ≈ Liability BPV × ΔLiability yields. Name the risks that break this and give an example of each.
cards.back:
• Model risk — assumptions and approximations: zero effective duration assumed for equity and alternatives; ABO vs PBO choice and the wage, retirement-date and longevity assumptions behind them; futures BPV approximated as BPV(CTD) ÷ CF; portfolio duration estimated as a weighted average of bond durations instead of from the cash flow yield.
• Spread risk — the equation assumes all three yield changes are equal, but assets, hedges and liabilities sit at different curve points and spreads (liabilities discounted at high-quality corporate yields, hedges on Treasuries or swaps). The corporate/swap spread is usually LESS volatile than the corporate/Treasury spread, so swap overlays carry less spread risk than Treasury futures.
• Counterparty credit risk — uncollateralized swaps; a loss requires the JOINT occurrence of the counterparty defaulting AND rates having moved so the swap is valued as an asset to the non-defaulting party (it does not require both parties to default); mitigated by a CSA to the ISDA contract (one-way or two-way, zero or positive threshold, independent amount).
• Collateral exhaustion risk — collateralized swaps and futures margin; large notional hedges generate big daily cash moves, so collateral availability itself limits the feasible hedging ratio.
• Asset liquidity risk — acute under contingent immunization, since active positions must be unwound as the surplus falls; distressed assets become hard to value.
• Structural risk — twists and non-parallel shifts move the portfolio's cash flow yield differently from the immunizing zero's; mitigated by minimizing asset cash flow dispersion.

cards.front: Why is a bond index much harder to replicate than an equity index, and what does the manager match instead of holdings?
cards.back:
Challenges:
• Size and breadth — the Bloomberg Barclays Global Aggregate holds more than 16,000 securities vs about 1,600 in the MSCI World; a US aggregate spans Treasuries, agencies, corporates, MBS, ABS and CMBS.
• Array of characteristics — one issuer has many bonds differing in maturity, currency, coupon, rating, call/put and seniority (Royal Dutch Shell: 57 bonds, 1 common equity), with very different liquidity.
• Issuance and trading patterns — OTC, quote-driven, dealer inventories shrunk by Basel III capital costs; most bonds never trade or trade a few times a year, so illiquid bonds are valued by matrix (evaluated) pricing, itself a source of deviation from index returns.
• Turnover — new issues enter and bonds leave on maturity (under one year), downgrade below investment grade, or call, so bond indexes rebalance MONTHLY rather than semiannually or annually.
So managers target the PRIMARY RISK FACTORS: option-adjusted portfolio duration (plus convexity for large moves); key rate durations for non-parallel shifts; percent in sector and quality; sector and quality spread-duration contribution; sector/coupon/maturity call weights; and issuer exposure.
Success metric: tracking error, the standard deviation of active return (portfolio return − benchmark index return). A 1.25% tracking error means the fund lands within 1.25% of the index in roughly two-thirds of periods.

cards.front: Compare full replication with enhanced indexing for passive bond exposure, and say when a total return swap beats an ETF or mutual fund.
cards.back:
Full replication (pure indexing):
• Buy every constituent in index proportion; minimizes tracking risk in principle, needs no manager analysis
• Must source thinly traded bonds and trade on every index change (new issues, maturities, downgrades, calls) plus fund flows — neither feasible nor cost-effective for broad indexes; practical only for the narrowest ones
Enhanced indexing (stratified sampling / cell approach):
• Map each cell (significant index characteristic), hold a subset of bonds or bond-linked derivatives matching those cells, adjust cells as the index changes
• Fewer securities, lower transaction costs, less need to trade illiquid bonds; accepts some tracking error
• Enhancement levers: lower cost/tighter execution, issue selection, yield curve relative value, sector and quality tilts over the business cycle, call exposure
Indirect vehicles:
• ETFs trade intraday; authorized participants arbitrage price versus NAV, but with thinly traded bonds a discount can persist. Mutual funds transact only at NAV.
• Total return swap: receive the index cash flows plus appreciation against MRR plus a spread. Requires less initial cash outlay than direct investment for similar performance and, being customized OTC, can reach hard-to-access assets such as high-yield and commercial loans — at the cost of counterparty credit risk.

cards.front: What must an index satisfy to serve as a fixed-income benchmark, what investor-specific input drives the choice, and what two dynamics make a bond benchmark unstable?
cards.back:
• Index requirements: clear, transparent rules for security inclusion and weighting; investability; daily valuation with available history of past returns; and acceptable turnover.
• Match the benchmark to the stated goals — return objective, risk tolerance, constraints — settled in the investment policy and asset allocation; benchmark selection is one of the last steps of that process.
• The distinctive fixed-income input is DURATION preference: the investor usually already has fixed-income exposure embedded in its asset/liability profile, so the target duration is effectively the portfolio's "beta" and must be set before choosing the index.
• Two destabilizing dynamics: (1) bonds have finite maturities, so a static portfolio's duration DRIFTS DOWN over time; (2) index composition shifts with the business cycle and issuers' maturity preferences (the US Aggregate's securitized share rose before 2008, government debt after).
• Applications: a highly risk-averse investor or a short-term claims book takes a short-duration, high-credit-quality index (1-3 year sovereign or covered bonds); a long-horizon endowment or a plan with a young workforce takes the longest-duration index. Investors may combine sub-benchmarks (sovereign, agency/ABS, corporate, high yield, bank loans, developed global, emerging debt), and smart beta offers simple, transparent, rules-based excess-return strategies at lower fees than active management.

cards.front: Write the curriculum's expected-return equation for a fixed-income portfolio and name each component.
cards.back:
Five components — coupon income enters positively; the other four carry a +/− sign:
• Coupon income — coupon plus reinvestment income (always an additive contributor)
• +/− Rolldown return — price change as the bond ages along an UNCHANGED curve; computed as (PV1 − PV0) ÷ PV0
• Coupon income + rolldown = "rolling yield" (also called carry-rolldown)
• +/− E(Δ price from the benchmark-yield view) — the duration/convexity term
• +/− E(Δ price from the yield-spread view) — credit/spread strategies
• +/− E(Δ price from the currency view) — only for foreign-currency assets
Units: all terms in % of portfolio value over the stated horizon.
When to use: to project and compare candidate curve positions (bullet vs barbell, etc.) over a fixed horizon.
Classic error: computing rolldown with the NEW curve — rolldown must assume no yield change, and the yield-view term is then measured on the shorter-maturity bond as of the horizon date. Also dropping the currency term on foreign bonds.
cards.formula: E(R) ≈ Coupon income +/− Rolldown return +/− E(Δ Price due to view of benchmark yields) +/− E(Δ Price due to view of yield spreads) +/− E(Δ Price due to view of currency values)

cards.front: State the duration-plus-convexity approximation for the percentage price change of a bond or portfolio, including how it is applied at the portfolio level.
cards.back:
• ModDur = modified duration; Convexity is the "raw" (unscaled) figure, not the trading-screen number divided by 100
• ΔYield in decimal form: 50 bps = 0.0050; the result is the % change in FULL price
• Portfolio version: substitute market-value-weighted averages — AvgModDur = Σ ModDur(j) × [MV(j) ÷ MV] and AvgConvexity = Σ Convexity(j) × [MV(j) ÷ MV]
• The convexity term is positive for a rise OR a fall when convexity is positive: it adds to gains and cushions losses
• Duration is first-order and usually dominates — level changes are roughly 82% of Treasury curve variance — so duration management outranks convexity management
Classic error: using scaled convexity, forgetting to square ΔYield, or applying the formula to a non-parallel move — it assumes a parallel shift.
cards.formula: %ΔPVFull ≈ −(ModDur × ΔYield) + [½ × Convexity × (ΔYield)^2]

cards.front: Name the three primary yield curve risk factors, how each is measured, and the approximate share of US Treasury curve variance each explains.
cards.back:
• LEVEL — a parallel "shift"; all yields move by the same number of basis points. Approximately 82% of variance.
• SLOPE — a "twist": long-maturity YTM minus shorter-maturity YTM (e.g., 2s30s was 127 bps in July 2020: 1.43% − 0.16%). Widening = steepening, narrowing = flattening, negative = inverted curve. Approximately 12%.
• SHAPE / CURVATURE — "butterfly movement": the relationship among short, medium (the "belly"), and long yields. Measured by the butterfly spread = −(short-term yield) + (2 × medium-term yield) − (long-term yield). Positive = humped/concave; negative = "saucer"/convex. Approximately 4%.
Implication: because level dominates, duration is the first exposure to manage; key rate durations and convexity address slope and shape.
cards.mnemonic: 82/12/4 — Level, Slope, Curvature

cards.front: Your rate view coincides with the market and you expect a static, upward-sloping curve. What are the two ways to add excess return versus the index, and what are the cash and derivative strategies for each?
cards.back:
Two ways to generate excess return: add DURATION or add LEVERAGE.
Cash-based:
• Buy-and-hold — buy bonds with duration above the benchmark, no active trading. Income = coupon income.
• Roll down (ride) the curve — buy a maturity beyond the investment horizon and sell it later at a lower YTM. Income = coupon income +/− rolldown return.
• Repo carry trade — buy a long-term bond, finance it at a lower short-term repo rate. Income = (coupon +/− rolldown) − financing cost; the bond is sold and the repo unwound at the end.
Derivatives-based:
• Long bond futures — synthetic duration; return = (Δ price ÷ Δ bond yield) − margin cost; relies on price appreciation only, no coupon.
• Receive-fixed swap — synthetic duration plus "swap carry" (swap rate − MRR) plus swap MTM.
All of it depends on stable rate levels and a stable curve shape; a buy-and-hold in off-the-run bonds also adds liquidity risk.

cards.front: You implemented buy-and-hold with extended duration, a rolldown trade, and a repo carry trade expecting a static curve. Instead the curve INVERTS — short-term yields jump and long-term yields fall. Which position is least likely to lose, and which is hurt worst?
cards.back:
• Buy-and-hold with extra duration is LEAST likely to lose — falling long-term yields produce price appreciation. This is the trap: candidates assume all three static-curve trades fail together.
• Repo carry is hurt worst — the long-short yield difference collapses, so a sharp rise in the short-term financing rate creates NEGATIVE carry.
• Rolldown loses its ride-down price gain (it needs a static, upward-sloping curve), but coupon income can now be reinvested at the higher short-term yields.
Lesson: each "static curve" strategy has a different exposure — buy-and-hold is a level bet, repo carry is a short-rate/financing bet, rolldown is a bet on curve stability. Match the loss to the exposure, not to the label.

cards.front: Contrast a yield curve steepener and a flattener: the bond positions, and the duration-neutral, bear, and bull variants of each.
cards.back:
STEEPENER — expects the long-minus-short spread to WIDEN: LONG the short-dated bond, SHORT the long-dated bond.
• Duration neutral: net zero duration (match position BPVs); gains only from the slope increase.
• Bear steepener: net NEGATIVE duration; gains from slope increase and/or rising yields.
• Bull steepener: net POSITIVE duration; gains from slope increase and/or falling yields (built by increasing the long short-dated leg).
FLATTENER — expects the spread to NARROW: SHORT the short-dated bond, LONG the long-dated bond.
• Duration neutral = net zero; bear flattener = net negative duration; bull flattener = net positive duration.
Downside risk: a steepener loses if the curve flattens, a flattener loses if it steepens — plus level risk whenever the trade is not duration neutral.
Note: the duration-neutral long-short/short-long steepener carries NEGATIVE convexity (−19.34 in the module's 2s/10s example), so a parallel shift of either sign costs a small amount.

cards.front: Distinguish a negative butterfly from a positive butterfly: the yield expectation and the active position for each.
cards.back:
NEGATIVE BUTTERFLY — butterfly spread INCREASES: lower short- and long-term yields, higher medium-term yields.
• Position: SHORT the bullet (the body) and LONG the barbell (long positions in the short- and long-term wings).
POSITIVE BUTTERFLY — butterfly spread DECREASES: higher short- and long-term yields, lower medium-term yields.
• Position: LONG the bullet and SHORT the barbell.
• Both are normally built duration neutral (position BPVs sum to approximately zero) so the trade is a pure shape bet; average duration is then uninformative and convexity/cash flow dispersion becomes the meaningful risk statistic.
Trap: the labels run opposite to intuition — a "positive butterfly" view means a FALL in the butterfly spread, because of the inverse price-yield relationship.

cards.front: You have a view on interest rate volatility. What exactly is the bet, which instruments express each side, and how does each option position change portfolio duration?
cards.back:
The bet is future REALIZED volatility versus the IMPLIED volatility priced into stand-alone options and into bonds with embedded options.
• Expect realized > implied (volatility rising) → be LONG volatility/convexity: buy bond calls/puts, swaptions, or options on bond futures; or own PUTABLE bonds (the investor owns the put).
• Expect realized < implied (static/stable curve) → be SHORT volatility: sell stand-alone options for premium income, or own CALLABLE bonds (an implicit sale of an option to the issuer). You win if rates stay put, the bond is not called, and the options expire worthless.
Duration impact of long option positions:
• INCREASE duration: long bond call, long receiver swaption, long call on a bond future.
• DECREASE duration: long bond put, long payer swaption, long put on a bond future.
Also: stand-alone interest rate puts and calls are struck on the bond's PRICE, not its yield; and effective duration and effective convexity (not modified duration) are the relevant statistics once cash flows are rate-contingent.

cards.front: What do key rate durations reveal that effective duration cannot, what identity must they satisfy, and how do you read a portfolio-versus-benchmark KRD table?
cards.back:
• Key rate (partial) duration = sensitivity of portfolio value to a change in ONE key rate, holding the other key rates fixed: KeyRateDur(k) = −(1 ÷ PV) × (ΔPV ÷ Δr(k)).
• Identity: the key rate durations SUM to effective duration — Σ KeyRateDur(k) = EffDur.
• They identify "shaping risk" — where along the curve the exposure actually sits, which a single duration number hides.
• Read the ACTIVE minus INDEX difference by tenor: in the module's example 2y −0.35, 5y −2.55, 10y +6.76 means less exposure to short rates and far more to the 10-year — a position set for a negative butterfly plus a bull flattening at the long end.
• A short position produces a NEGATIVE key rate duration (short 5y: 4.902 × (−46 ÷ 263) = −0.857).
Trap: two portfolios with the same total duration can have completely different curve exposure — only the KRD profile shows it.

cards.front: Give the domestic-currency return equation for a foreign-currency bond, and state the three risks a cross-currency yield curve trade faces.
cards.back:
• RDC = domestic-currency return; RFC = foreign-currency return on the bond (rolling yield plus price change), in percent; RFX = percentage change in the value of the foreign currency against the domestic currency
• Portfolio form: RDC = Σ ω(i) × (1 + RFC,i) × (1 + RFX,i) − 1, where the weights ω are in domestic-currency terms and sum to 1
• Fully hedging with an FX forward at covered interest rate parity delivers the DOMESTIC risk-free rate; the higher-yielding currency trades at a forward discount, the lower-yielding at a premium
• The cross-currency carry trade — borrow in the low-yield currency, invest in the high-yield currency — exploits divergence from uncovered parity (the forward rate bias); it is unhedged and works best in stable, low-volatility markets
Three risks of an overweight/underweight cross-currency curve trade: (1) curve moves in the overweight currency, (2) curve moves in the underweight currency, (3) exchange rate changes.
Classic error: adding RFC + RFX instead of compounding them, or assuming hedging adds return — it removes the FX bet and the associated yield pickup with it.
cards.formula: RDC = (1 + RFC) × (1 + RFX) − 1

cards.front: Lay out the step-by-step procedure for estimating a curve strategy's expected return over a one-year horizon, and how you then stress-test it.
cards.back:
1. Rolling yield = coupon income + rolldown return, with rolldown = (PV1 − PV0) ÷ PV0 where PV1 is the price in one year assuming NO shift in the curve (for zeros there is no coupon income, so rolling yield is all rolldown).
2. Price change from the rate view = (−EffDur × Δy) + [½ × Convexity × (Δy)^2], using the duration and convexity expected AT the horizon (in one year), not today's figures.
3. Add the spread/credit view, and for a foreign bond compound the currency return: (1 + RFC) × (1 + RFX) − 1.
4. Compare candidate strategies component by component. In the module's AUD bullet-versus-barbell case the barbell won by about 28 bps — roughly 25.5 bps from ROLLDOWN and only about 2.6 bps from the extra convexity.
5. Stress with SCENARIO ANALYSIS: change several assumptions at once (bear steepening, bull flattening, historical episodes, or how far rates must move to trigger a margin call). Duration-matched bullets and barbells behave almost identically in a parallel shift but very differently across slope scenarios.

cards.front: Write the curriculum's equation for a bond's percentage price change caused by a spread move (not a benchmark-rate move), and say what each term measures.
cards.back:
• EffSpreadDur = effective spread duration: price sensitivity to a change in the bond's OWN spread, benchmark curve held fixed; first term alone is called spread duration, or OAS duration when the spread used is OAS
• EffSpreadCon = effective spread convexity; ΔSpread = change in spread (usually ΔOAS), entered in decimal form (+0.20%, not 20)
• EffSpreadDur = (PV−) − (PV+) ÷ [2 × ΔSpread × PV0]; EffSpreadCon = (PV−) + (PV+) − 2(PV0) ÷ [(ΔSpread)² × PV0]
• Portfolio level: substitute market-value-weighted average duration and convexity
• Example: spread duration 5, spread widens 0.50% → about −2.5%
• When to use: first term alone is a fine approximation for small moves and low-spread investment-grade bonds; further down the credit spectrum both EffSpreadDur and ΔSpread may need adjusting
• Classic errors: dropping the minus sign, mixing bp with decimals, and applying an ABSOLUTE bp spread change to low-rated bonds instead of a proportional (DTS) change
cards.formula: %ΔPV(Spread) ≈ −(EffSpreadDur × ΔSpread) + (½ × EffSpreadCon × (ΔSpread)²)

cards.front: Ignoring time value, how do you back an issuer's POD out of one bond's spread, and then price the spread of a more junior claim on the same issuer?
cards.back:
• POD = probability of default, the conditional annual likelihood the borrower fails to pay in full and on time (assuming no prior default)
• LGD = loss given default = loss severity, usually quoted as a percentage of par; RR = recovery rate; EE = expected exposure
• EL = expected loss; CVA = Σ(PV of expected loss), discounted at the risk-free rate
• Use: one claim's spread gives the issuer POD, which then reprices any other claim whose recovery differs by seniority/security
• Curriculum example: first lien loan at 100 bp with RR 64% → POD = 1.00% ÷ (1 − 0.64) = 2.778%; new second lien with RR 29% → spread = 2.778% × (1 − 0.29) = 197 bp
• Recovery ladder (US 1983−2019 averages): first lien loan 64%, senior unsecured bond 35%, junior subordinated 14%
• Classic error: applying this to distressed debt — near default, bonds trade on price approaching the recovery rate, not on a spread basis; the approximation only works close to par
• Also note: raising the assumed recovery rate (lower LGD) RAISES the implied POD for a given spread
cards.formula: Spread ≈ POD × LGD ; POD ≈ Spread ÷ LGD ; LGD = EE × (1 − RR) ; EL = POD × LGD

cards.front: Empirical vs analytical duration for a high-yield bond: how is each estimated, which is larger, and what market behavior explains the gap?
cards.back:
• Analytical duration: computed from the bond's own cash flows (modified/effective duration and convexity); implicitly assumes benchmark yields and credit spreads are independent
• Empirical duration: estimated statistically, by regressing the bond's price returns on changes in a benchmark interest rate
• For high yield, empirical duration is typically LOWER than analytical duration
• Why: in a flight to quality, the macro forces pushing government yields down simultaneously push high-yield spreads WIDER (negative correlation), so the spread move offsets part of the rate-driven price gain
• Curriculum example: analytical 4.234 vs empirical 2.95; for a −50 bp benchmark move, +2.117% vs +1.475% — analytical overstates the gain (about US$339,769 on a $52.9m position)
• Practical rule: use empirical duration to hedge the rate exposure of credit bonds, since it reflects how they actually trade
• Exam trap: high-yield bonds' price sensitivity to INTEREST RATE changes is typically lower, not higher, than investment grade's

cards.front: Why does the curriculum call OAS the most appropriate spread measure for an active credit manager, and what are its two acknowledged drawbacks?
cards.back:
• Definition: OAS is the constant spread over the benchmark zero (spot) curve which, combined with an assumed interest rate volatility, makes the arbitrage-free model value of the bond equal its market price
• It generalizes the Z-spread: for an option-free bond at zero volatility, Z-spread = OAS
• Why best: it gives ONE consistent basis for comparing option-free, callable, putable and structured instruments across the whole curve, so the spread reflects credit and liquidity compensation rather than optionality
• Drawback 1: highly dependent on model assumptions — interest rate volatility, term structure model, and prepayment speed for structured product (a constant CPR assumption can differ greatly from empirical results)
• Drawback 2: it is theoretical — bonds with embedded options are unlikely to actually realize their OAS over time
• Portfolio OAS = market-value-weighted average of each bond's OAS (weights use price PLUS accrued interest)
• Exam trap: of two similar callables, the one more likely to be called is the one with the LOWER OAS; ASW and Z-spread cannot answer this because Z-spread assumes zero volatility

cards.front: Yield spread, G-spread, I-spread, ASW, Z-spread: what benchmark is each measured over, and what is the main disadvantage of each?
cards.back:
• Yield spread (benchmark spread): bond YTM − YTM of the nearest on-the-run government bond. Simple and observable; but maturity mismatch, curve slope bias, and inconsistent over time as the benchmark changes
• G-spread: over an INTERPOLATED government yield (e.g. an 8y rate from the 7y and 10y). Transparent, maturity-matched, default-risk-free; but subject to shifts in government bond demand
• I-spread: bond YTM − interpolated SWAP rate (MRR-based). Market-based measure usable as a hedge and for carry; but only a point estimate of the term structure, and limited to option-free bonds
• ASW: spread over MRR equivalent to the bond's fixed COUPON (not its YTM). A tradable spread; but it is a traded price rather than a spread matching the bond's cash flows, and is option-free only
• Z-spread: constant spread over the government or swap SPOT curve. Accurately captures the term structure; more complex, and option-free only
• CDS basis: bond Z-spread vs same-tenor CDS spread (negative basis = yield spread above the CDS spread)
• Exam trap: yield spread exceeds G-spread when the benchmark used is SHORTER in maturity than the bond and the government curve is upward sloping
• Reconciliation: ASW − I-spread difference mostly reflects the bond's premium or discount to par

cards.front: Walk through the bottom-up credit selection process in the order the curriculum lays it out.
cards.back:
• 1. Define the eligible universe within the mandate
• 2. Group it into sectors/subsectors narrow enough that COMPANY-specific risks, not industry or macro risks, dominate (split global pharma from regional hospitals from multi-industry device makers)
• 3. Analyse each issuer: profitability EBITDA/Total Assets, leverage Debt/Capital, coverage EBITDA/Interest Expense — supplemented by reduced-form and structural models, because ratios are backward-looking and not comparable across industries; managers run their own assessment rather than relying on agency ratings
• 4. Relative value: for two issuers of similar credit risk, take the higher spread; for different risk, compare expected excess returns, E[ExcessSpread] ≈ Spread0 − (EffSpreadDur × ΔSpread) − (POD × LGD); compare issuer spread curves (fitted spread vs maturity) to find rich/cheap tenors
• 5. Adjust for structure and features: callability, seniority in the capital structure, split ratings or negative outlooks, M&A/LBO risk, and liquidity (large recent issues from frequent issuers trade with tighter bid-offer; liquidity decays as the issuer brings new deals)
• 6. Express the view as over/underweights vs the benchmark's sector and spread-duration contributions, which is the basis for measuring excess return going forward
• Note: a long-only benchmark-relative mandate can underweight a disliked name; an absolute-return mandate cannot, so use a long-short CDS pair instead

cards.front: Reduced-form vs structural credit models: what inputs does each use, what does it solve for, and name the curriculum's example of each.
cards.back:
• Reduced form: solves for default intensity (POD over a period) from OBSERVABLE company-specific variables — financial ratios and recovery assumptions — plus macro variables such as economic growth and market volatility
• Example: Altman's Z-score (1968) = 1.2×(Working Capital/TA) + 1.4×(Retained Earnings/TA) + 3.3×(EBIT/TA) + 0.6×(Mkt Value of Equity/Total Liabilities) + 0.999×(Sales/TA); above 3.0 financially sound, 3.0 to 1.8 greater distress risk, below 1.8 likely insolvency
• Structural: uses MARKET-based variables to estimate the market value of the issuer's assets and the volatility of that value; default is defined as asset value falling below liabilities
• Examples: Moody's Analytics EDF and Bloomberg DRSK — both called distance-to-default models; DRSK derives asset value from equity market cap and equity volatility against book liabilities, and outputs a one-year POD plus a model CDS spread to compare against the traded CDS spread
• Exam trap: in a structural model, HIGHER equity volatility RAISES the POD (more likely to breach the default threshold); a higher coverage ratio or lower leverage lowers it

cards.front: State the annualized expected excess return for a spread bond, and the simpler version that ignores default.
cards.back:
• Spread0 = initial spread (usually OAS), earned as carry; for a holding period under a year scale it to Spread0 × (fraction of year)
• ΔSpread = expected change in spread over the horizon; widening is positive, so it subtracts; tightening is negative, so it adds
• POD × LGD = expected credit loss, also prorated for the holding period
• Without defaults (Equation 9): ExcessSpread ≈ Spread0 − (EffSpreadDur × ΔSpread)
• Example: spread 2.75%, six-month hold, spread narrows 50 bp, EffSpreadDur 5, POD 1%, LGD 60% → (2.75% × 0.5) − [(2.25% − 2.75%) × 5] − (0.5 × 1% × 60%) = 3.575%
• Use: the single tool for ranking rating buckets, issuers, or cross-market allocations under a spread scenario — the highest E(excess return) bucket is the one to overweight
• Classic errors: prorating the carry but forgetting to prorate the expected loss, and getting the sign of ΔSpread backwards
cards.formula: E[ExcessSpreadReturn] ≈ Spread0 − (EffSpreadDur × ΔSpread) − (POD × LGD)

cards.front: A portfolio is half A1/A+ and half Ba3/BB−. Why is quoting its average rating on an ordinal scale misleading, and what does a loss-weighted scale give instead?
cards.back:
• Ordinal scale: A1 = 5, Ba3 = 13 → average 9, which maps to Baa2/BBB — looks solidly investment grade
• Moody's loss-weighted factors: A1 = 70, Ba3 = 1,766 → average 918, which sits near Ba1/BB+ — two notches lower
• Why: credit loss and default risk rise far more than proportionally as ratings fall, so equal notch steps are not equal risk steps; averaging notches overstates portfolio quality
• Same logic underlies DTS: wider-spread bonds move proportionally more, so weight by spread, not by rank
• Other rating caveats: ratings LAG market pricing of credit risk; S&P ratings target POD while Moody's target expected loss; short-term and long-term ratings differ
• Which is why active managers often measure average portfolio credit quality with market-value-weighted OAS rather than with ratings at all
cards.mnemonic: Notches are ordinal; losses are exponential.

cards.front: Why are credit markets structurally illiquid, and what are the manager's main tactics for managing that liquidity risk?
cards.back:
• Market structure: bonds trade OTC on a request-for-quote basis, so liquidity sits with individual dealers' inventory and appetite; a single issuer can have dozens of separately traded CUSIPs/ISINs, fragmenting liquidity; dealer inventories shrank after the 2008−09 crisis on higher regulatory capital; many bonds do not trade at all on a given day
• Cost scale: on-the-run developed-market sovereigns trade inside 1 bp bid−offer; small or off-the-run corporates and structured notes can be 10 bp or more and take days to execute
• Measurement: effective spread = trade size × (trade price − bid-ask midpoint) for buys, reversed for sells — inadequate when an order is worked over time or moves the market; matrix (evaluated) pricing for untraded bonds; TRACE prints for ex-post US corporate activity
• Tactic 1: use on-the-run governments and recently issued corporates for short-term TACTICAL positions; reserve illiquid bonds for buy-and-hold/strategic positions, so trading costs do not erode expected return
• Tactic 2: use liquid alternatives — CDS, CDS indexes, and bond ETFs — where bottom-up selection adds little value or markets are moving fast (ETFs neither mature nor suffer duration drift, so portfolio duration stays roughly constant)
• Tactic 3: when liquidating a large illiquid position over time, hedge its benchmark rate risk with a pay-fixed asset swap and unwind the swap PROPORTIONALLY as bonds are sold

cards.front: Candidates cite VaR as the credit tail-risk number. Name the three things VaR fails to do, and the measures that fix each.
cards.back:
• What VaR is: the MINIMUM loss expected over a period at a confidence level — a 5% daily VaR of EUR 8.7m means a loss of at least EUR 8.7m on 5% of trading days (normal assumption: 1.65 SD at 5%, 2.33 SD at 1%)
• Failure 1: it underestimates the frequency and severity of extreme adverse events
• Failure 2: it misses downside correlation and liquidity risk under market stress
• Failure 3: it says nothing about the AVERAGE loss once the threshold is breached
• Fix: CVaR (conditional VaR / expected shortfall) = average loss conditional on exceeding VaR, computed by historical simulation or Monte Carlo
• Related measures: incremental (partial) VaR for the effect of adding or removing ONE position; relative VaR for expected tracking error, computed on active positions minus benchmark holdings
• Assessment methods: parametric (simple, but poor for non-normal or option-based portfolios), historical simulation (real results, no distribution assumed, but tied to the chosen period repeating), Monte Carlo (handles options, but assumption-driven and opaque) — all supplemented by hypothetical scenario analysis
• Manage the tail with position limits and risk budgeting, or buy payer swaptions / credit default swaptions — but the premium erodes excess spread, and hedges bought in an already distressed market cost far more because option volatility is high

cards.front: Give the standard CDS price approximation, say who pays whom at inception, and state the mark-to-market of a spread change.
cards.back:
• Price is per 1 (or per 100) of notional; EffSpreadDurCDS is the contract's effective spread duration, sometimes called CDS DV01; CDS Spread is the issuer's current market spread
• Standard ISDA fixed coupons since 2009: 1% for investment grade, 5% for high yield — the coupon in the formula is this standard coupon, never the market spread
• Upfront: if CDS Spread < Fixed Coupon the contract prices above par and the protection BUYER RECEIVES ((Fixed Coupon − CDS Spread) × EffSpreadDurCDS), because it has agreed to pay an above-market coupon; if CDS Spread > Fixed Coupon the buyer PAYS ((CDS Spread − Fixed Coupon) × EffSpreadDurCDS); equal spreads means no upfront
• Direction: buying protection = SHORT credit risk, gains when spreads widen or a credit event occurs; selling protection = LONG credit risk
• Example: 5-year IG CDS, market spread 0.50%, EffSpreadDurCDS 4.75 → buyer receives 2.375% upfront (price 1.02375, i.e. 102.375); spread rises to 0.60% → new upfront 1.90% (price 1.019) → buyer books a 0.475%-of-notional mark-to-market gain, equal to −(0.10% × 4.75)
• Example: buy EUR 10m protection at 110 bp, EffSpreadDurCDS 4.595, spread widens to 125 bp → gain = −EUR 10,000,000 × (−0.15% × 4.595) = EUR 68,925
• Classic errors: using the market spread in place of the 1%/5% standard coupon, and reversing the sign so the protection buyer appears to lose on widening
• Notional is never exchanged: like a par interest rate swap, a CDS at par has zero net present value
cards.formula: CDS Price ≈ 1 + ((Fixed Coupon − CDS Spread) × EffSpreadDurCDS) ; Δ(CDS Price) ≈ −(Δ(CDS Spread) × EffSpreadDurCDS)

cards.front: How do you size a duration-weighted single-name CDS curve steepener, and how is its P&L computed?
cards.back:
• View: a steepener expects (10-year CDS spread − 5-year CDS spread) to WIDEN — for example, near-term default risk falling on higher profits and stable leverage
• Legs: BUY 10-year protection (short risk at the long end) and SELL 5-year protection (long risk at the short end)
• Size to equal spread BPV: Notional(5y) = Notional(10y) × [EffSpreadDur(10y) ÷ EffSpreadDur(5y)]
• Example: 8.68 ÷ 4.669 = 1.859 × EUR 10,000,000 = EUR 18,590,000; check BPV = notional × EffSpreadDur ÷ 10,000 → both legs EUR 8,680
• P&L per leg = (−Δ(CDS Spread) × EffSpreadDurCDS) × notional, with a bought-protection (short risk) leg carrying a negative notional sign
• Example: 5y +10 bp, 10y +20 bp → 5-year long risk −EUR 86,800, 10-year short risk +EUR 173,600, net gain EUR 86,800 = BPV EUR 8,680 × the 10 bp net steepening
• Same construction for a CDS index or subindex: expecting a slowdown, buy short-tenor protection and sell long-tenor protection on the index for a flattener
• Why duration-weight: without BPV matching the trade carries an unintended outright (level) spread position rather than a pure slope view
• Note: the 5-year tenor is the most frequently traded CDS contract, and standardized contracts remove the duration, liquidity and sourcing frictions of a cash long-short

cards.front: Define DTS, state how it is aggregated at portfolio level, and show how an index spread move translates into an expected portfolio spread move.
cards.back:
• Spread in bp (or %) times effective spread duration in years gives DTS in bp-years; weights wi are market-value weights
• Why DTS rather than spread duration alone: spread changes for lower-rated bonds are consistent on a PROPORTIONAL (ΔSpread ÷ Spread) basis, not in absolute bp — wider-spread bonds move proportionally more
• Procedure: convert the index spread move to a percentage, then multiply portfolio DTS by that percentage to get the portfolio's expected bp spread change
• Example: 50/50 portfolio of an A bond (OAS 100 bp, EffSpreadDur 3.0) and a BB bond (OAS 300 bp, EffSpreadDur 4.0) → DTS = (0.5 × 100 × 3.0) + (0.5 × 300 × 4.0) = 750
• Index OAS 125 bp widening 10 bp = 8% proportional move → expected portfolio widening = 750 × 8% = 60 bp p.a.
• Use: budget and position credit risk by DTS — a tightening view means raising portfolio DTS, a widening view means cutting it
• Classic error: applying the index's absolute 10 bp move to the portfolio regardless of the portfolio's own spread level
cards.formula: DTS ≈ EffSpreadDur × Spread ; Portfolio DTS = Σ wi × (EffSpreadDuri × Spreadi)

cards.front: Under a view that credit curves are fairly priced and will stay stable, what are the two ways to earn excess return — and how do credit curve level and slope evolve from early expansion through contraction?
cards.back:
• Static-curve play 1: lower the portfolio's average credit rating (e.g. A → BBB), raising Spread0 in E[ExcessSpread] ≈ Spread0 − (EffSpreadDur × ΔSpread) − (POD × LGD) while spread, POD and LGD are assumed stable
• Static-curve play 2: add credit spread duration at the same rating — buy-and-hold longer-dated bonds, or carry-and-roll-down the credit curve, which earns the wider coupon PLUS price appreciation as the position rolls to a lower spread point
• Derivative equivalents: sell single-name or index protection at longer maturities or lower quality, or run the same view as a long-short
• Cycle — early expansion (recovery): profits rising but defaults still high, high-yield spreads elevated and well above investment grade, low-rated curves flat to inverted
• Late expansion: lower defaults and rising profits pull short-tenor spreads down, curves STEEPEN for both higher and lower ratings
• Peak: steepening continues amid higher leverage and inflation expectations; spread levels begin to rise
• Contraction/recession: spreads rise to their peak and curves FLATTEN — investment grade flattens, high yield often INVERTS as near-term downgrade and default risk exceeds long-term
• Positioning rule: expect tightening → add credit risk and DTS; expect widening → reduce credit risk, up in quality, shorten spread duration

cards.front: What must a manager consider when extending credit into other developed markets, and what changes when the destination is an emerging market?
cards.back:
• Developed markets — sector composition differs: MBS/ABS is roughly one-third of the US aggregate index, while European and Asian investors reach real-estate cash flows through covered bonds or bank bonds where securitization is less common
• Developed markets — accounting: IFRS vs US GAAP differences (inventory recognition, restricted cash, cash flow definitions) must be adjusted before comparing financial ratios across jurisdictions
• Developed markets — macro: common factors (inflation, monetary policy, growth) but different timing and magnitude of the cycle, showing up in rate differentials, exchange rates and credit spreads — the source of cross-market relative value
• Emerging markets — start with SOVEREIGN risk: both the ability and the WILLINGNESS to repay; ratios are measured against GDP — government debt/GDP and budget deficit/GDP (indebtedness and fiscal stability), external debt/GDP (leverage to foreign lenders), currency reserves/GDP (external LIQUIDITY)
• Exchange-rate regime matters: a freely floating, reserve-held currency permits independent monetary policy; fixed or restrictive regimes blunt policy and magnify crises, with regime change, intervention or devaluation more likely than a small deviation
• Sovereign ceiling: a company is normally rated no higher than its domicile's sovereign, so EM credit clusters in low investment grade and upper high yield
• Concentration and control: sovereign, bank and corporate issuers may all depend on one commodity, giving little diversification, and the state may control nominally private issuers
• Liquidity is thinner (few bonds trade regularly; local volumes can be inflated by interbank and retail activity) and currency volatility higher
• Currency choice: a higher local-currency YTM implies expected depreciation — the unhedged local bond only wins if forward rate bias holds and the currency depreciates less than interest rate parity implies

cards.front: What do structured instruments give a credit portfolio that corporate bonds cannot, and how would you shift across tranches for (a) an expected recovery and (b) a housing-led downturn?
cards.back:
• Instruments: CDOs (diversified debt pool), CLOs (diversified pool of FLOATING-rate leveraged loans), MBS (commercial/residential mortgages), ABS (credit card, auto and other consumer loans), covered bonds (bank senior debt backed by a mortgage or public sector pool)
• Benefit 1: access cash flows unavailable in the corporate bond market — real estate and consumer loans
• Benefit 2: add exposure to interest rate VOLATILITY through prepayment and extension risk (MBS)
• Benefit 3: tranching redistributes default risk — an SPV issues AAA down to unrated tranches; senior tranches are protected by overcollateralization and internal credit enhancement, while successively lower tranches absorb a greater share of defaults, creating risk profiles unavailable in cash bonds
• (a) Recovery / lower-than-expected defaults: move DOWN in tranche, since lower-rated tranches tighten more; a CLO tranche beats a CDO tranche when short rates are rising, because CLO collateral pays MRR plus a spread
• (b) Housing-led slowdown: move UP within MBS (e.g. BBB tranche → A tranche) — this keeps the real-estate cash flow exposure while cutting exposure to the greater spread widening of lower-rated MBS; simply swapping BBB CDOs for A CDOs is a blunt reduction in market risk rather than a targeted underweight
• Covered bonds: DUAL recourse to the issuing bank and to the ring-fenced cover pool, plus substitution of non-performing assets → lower credit risk and a lower yield than ABS/MBS
• Analytics trap: higher benchmark yield volatility RAISES the value of the issuer's embedded call, lowering MBS value versus an otherwise similar option-free bond

cards.front: For a fixed-income portfolio analytics tool, list the key inputs, the key outputs, and the two considerations that govern whether its numbers are usable.
cards.back:
• Position inputs: every long and short cash bond and derivative position, repos, and cash across currencies — securities identified by CUSIP/ISIN carrying payment dates, day count conventions and put/call features; derivative and repo terms include settlement dates, strikes and collateral terms
• Market inputs: real-time vendor feeds via APIs for spot and forward rates, credit curves, implied volatilities and exchange rates; matrix (evaluated) pricing values inactively traded bonds off comparable liquid benchmarks and actively traded bonds of similar maturity, quality and sector
• Other inputs: index subscriptions (fixed-income indexes change constantly with new issuance, maturities, rating changes, calls and prepayment, unlike static equity indexes), credit and ESG ratings, issuer balance sheet data
• User-defined parameters: term structure model, investment horizon, VaR methodology, historical or hypothetical scenarios, user-defined sensitivities, portfolio constraints and filters
• Outputs: portfolio summary vs benchmark by sector, rating and currency; research/construction what-if analysis of incremental positions; risk dashboards showing OAS, effective duration and convexity, key rate durations for both benchmark rates and credit spreads, VaR and expected shortfall, and tracking error; trading, cash and position management — existing cash, anticipated inflows/outflows, liquidity risk
• Consideration 1: accuracy of the model inputs and assumptions (term structure and volatility assumptions drive price and YTM outputs)
• Consideration 2: alignment of outputs with the manager's OBJECTIVE — an index manager minimizes tracking error, an unconstrained active manager maximizes risk-adjusted return with attribution across credit, duration, sector and currency, and a liability-constrained manager models obligations to maximize expected surplus
• Practitioners must recognize the limitations and be able to anticipate and interpret results, not just read them

cards.front: A manager's motivation to trade sets the order's urgency. Name the four motivation categories the curriculum lists and the urgency each implies.
cards.back:
• Profit seeking (alpha) — urgency is set by the rate of ALPHA DECAY: a short-term, event-driven signal (news, earnings overreaction) decays fast, so trade aggressively over a short horizon; a long-term value view (multi-year holding period) has slow decay, so trade patiently, even with no urgency
• Risk management / hedging — trade to restore a target risk level, beta, or duration; often cheapest via liquid futures or ETFs rather than the underlying cash securities, if the mandate permits derivatives
• Cash flow needs — urgency VARIES with the need: collateral or margin calls require close-to-immediate liquidation; a redemption from a longer-term client allocation change does not, and is usually traded at the CLOSE because NAV is struck at closing prices
• Corporate actions / index reconstitutions / margin calls — event-driven and timing set by the event; index changes are predictable and traded at the close to minimize tracking error
High alpha decay → faster trading → more market impact but less alpha loss.
