cards.mnemonic: PRICe: Profit, Risk, Inflows/outflows (cash), Corporate actions

cards.front: Name the four categories of inputs to trading-strategy selection, with the specific items the curriculum lists under each.
cards.back:
• ORDER characteristics — side (buy, sell, cover, short), size, and relative size = order as a % of average daily volume (ADV)
• SECURITY characteristics — security type (underlying, ETF, ADR, GDR), short-term (trade) alpha, price volatility, and the liquidity profile (ADV, bid−ask spread, average trade size)
• MARKET conditions — realized volumes, volatility and spreads at the time of trading, which differ from what was assumed at the decision; liquidity crises cause sudden deviations from normal patterns (volatility and liquidity are negatively related — volatility spikes as liquidity collapses)
• INDIVIDUAL risk aversion — a more risk-averse manager/trader fears market risk and trades with GREATER urgency, accepting more impact
Relative size (% of ADV) is the standardized cross-security measure: the larger the % of ADV, the larger the expected market impact. A 1m-share order is 2% of ADV in a 50m-ADV name but 25% in a 4m-ADV name.
cards.mnemonic: OSMI — Order, Security, Market, Individual

cards.front: An analyst claims: (1) greater trade urgency lowers execution risk; (2) trading a larger order with higher urgency reduces market impact; (3) securities with high alpha decay require less aggressive trading. Which is correct, and why do the others fail?
cards.back:
• (1) CORRECT — trading faster shortens the time the order is exposed to price volatility and changing conditions, so execution risk falls
• (2) WRONG — trading faster and in larger size RAISES market impact; impact is reduced by trading more patiently, in smaller slices, over a longer horizon
• (3) WRONG — high alpha decay demands MORE aggressive, accelerated trading to realize the alpha before other participants act on the same information
The trader's dilemma: "trading too fast results in too much market impact, but trading too slow results in too much market risk."
Key distinction: market impact arises only from TRADING the order; execution risk arises from the passage of time and occurs even if the order is never traded.
cards.mnemonic: Fast = impact up, risk down. Slow = impact down, risk up.

cards.front: Sort the trade-execution reference prices into the curriculum's four categories, and say which kind of manager selects each.
cards.back:
• PRE-TRADE (known before trading starts): decision price, previous close, opening price, arrival price — chosen by managers trading on short-term alpha or a current mispricing who want to transact near current prices
  – previous close: quant managers whose model/optimizer uses it; a proxy for decision price
  – opening price: fundamental managers starting at the open; unlike a prior-day price it carries no overnight risk
  – arrival price: price when the order is RELEASED to the market
• INTRADAY (computed from prices during the trading period): VWAP and TWAP — passive trading over the day, rebalance/two-sided trade lists, no short-term momentum view
• POST-TRADE (set after trading ends): closing price — index funds and mutual funds valued at the close; minimizes tracking error, but the benchmark is unknown until trading is over
• PRICE TARGET (a price to meet or beat): the manager's fair-value price, e.g. buy at $20.50 or better
Trap: do not use the opening (or closing) price as the benchmark if you trade in that auction — your own order helps set the benchmark.

cards.front: VWAP vs TWAP: how is each computed, how does each algorithm slice the order, and when is TWAP deliberately preferred?
cards.back:
• VWAP = volume-weighted average price of all trades over the day/horizon. VWAP algorithms slice on a HISTORICAL intraday volume profile — more at the open and close, less midday, so the schedule is U-shaped
• TWAP = equal-weighted average price of trades over the horizon; volume is ignored. TWAP algorithms send the same number of shares in every time interval
• Choose TWAP to EXCLUDE trade price outliers (e.g. a large buy printed at the day's low or a large sell at the day's high that you could not participate in), and for names with high volume uncertainty or intraday volume spikes
• Both are time-sliced: the advantage is that the specified shares get done in each interval; the disadvantage is that they force trades in thin liquidity and fail to exploit unexpected liquidity
• VWAP's fixed schedule may not complete an order in an illiquid name on a low-volume day — if completing in the day matters more than impact, TWAP is safer than POV.

cards.front: A fund must trade a quarterly index-rebalance list (or raise cash for a redemption paid at NAV). State the reference price, the strategy, and the one fiduciary check the trader must run.
cards.back:
• Reference price: the official CLOSING price — the fund's NAV and the benchmark index are both struck at the close, so executing at the close aligns trade prices with valuation prices and minimizes tracking error (and removes the trader's risk of transacting away from NAV)
• Strategy: market-on-close (MOC) — send orders to the closing auction and receive the auction-guaranteed closing price
• Fiduciary check: confirm the order is not large relative to expected closing-auction volume (e.g. 50% of closing volume). An oversized sell would depress the close, lowering NAV and the client's proceeds — riskless for the fund but a poor execution for the client, which is inappropriate
• Fix when too large: split the order — e.g. send ~90% to the closing auction and work the remaining ~10% VWAP in the market into the close (some brokers automate this as a "close algorithm")
Why not previous close or open? Those are decision-price proxies for quant/fundamental managers, not valuation prices.

cards.front: Name the five classes of execution algorithm and the single condition each is designed for.
cards.back:
• SCHEDULED (POV, VWAP, TWAP) — follow a volume-participation or time schedule; used when there is NO expectation of adverse price movement, the trader tolerates a longer horizon, and minimizing market impact is the priority
• LIQUIDITY-SEEKING / opportunistic — hunt across lit and dark venues and trade fast when liquidity appears at a favorable price ("sweeping the book"); for large orders, thinly traded or episodic-liquidity names, and when displaying size would leak information; uses market orders more than limit orders
• ARRIVAL PRICE — FRONT-LOADED, trading more aggressively early to execute near the arrival price; used when prices are expected to move unfavorably over the horizon, or by a risk-averse trader cutting execution risk
• DARK AGGREGATORS — execute away from lit venues; for orders that are a large % of expected volume, illiquid or wide-spread names, and only when the order need NOT be filled in its entirety (dark fills are uncertain)
• SMART ORDER ROUTERS (SOR) — route SMALL orders: the best-priced venue (NBBO) for marketable orders, the highest fill probability for limit orders
Separate distinction: execution algorithms implement a decision already made; profit-seeking algorithms decide what to buy/sell (market makers, quant funds, HFT).
cards.mnemonic: S-L-A-D-S: Scheduled, Liquidity-seeking, Arrival, Dark, SOR

cards.front: What order-size thresholds does the curriculum attach to scheduled and arrival-price algorithms, and what are the two drawbacks of a POV algorithm?
cards.back:
• Scheduled algorithms suit orders that are relatively small — no more than about 5%–10% of expected volume — in a relatively liquid security, or orders that are part of a risk-balanced basket where trading everything at a common pace preserves the hedge
• Arrival-price algorithms are used when the security is relatively liquid or the order is not outsized — less than about 15% of expected volume — so a participatory strategy will not create significant impact
• POV mechanics: a 10% participation rate executes 1,000 shares for every 10,000 traded in the market, until filled; it automatically trades more when liquidity is ample and less when it is thin
• POV drawback 1 — by FOLLOWING (chasing) volume it keeps buying as prices rise and selling as prices fall, raising cost
• POV drawback 2 — it may not complete the order within the specified period
• Mirror image: VWAP/TWAP time-slicing guarantees the interval quantity but forces trades in insufficient liquidity and cannot exploit a liquidity surge. If completing the order in one day matters most, pick TWAP over POV.

cards.front: For equities, fixed income, exchange-traded derivatives, OTC derivatives and spot FX: state the market structure and the implementation used for a LARGE URGENT vs a LARGE NON-URGENT trade.
cards.back:
• EQUITY — exchanges (lit: pre- and post-trade transparency) plus dark pools/ATS/MTF (post-trade only); most technologically advanced, mostly electronic and algorithmic. Large urgent, especially illiquid small caps → high-touch broker RISK (principal) trade; large non-urgent → algorithms in liquid large caps, high-touch AGENCY in illiquid names; small liquid → electronic
• FIXED INCOME — bilateral, dealer-centric, quote-driven; dealers quote only ON REQUEST (RFQ), not continuously; low transparency and weak price discovery; heterogeneous, and off-the-run bonds are illiquid. Small AND large urgent trades → broker risk trades via RFQ (securities are hard to source otherwise); large non-urgent → high-touch agency. Algorithmic trading is limited to on-the-run US Treasuries and rate futures
• EXCHANGE-TRADED DERIVATIVES — fewer than 1,000 liquid, highly standardized contracts, volume concentrated in FUTURES; high transparency, centrally cleared. Large urgent → sweep the book; large non-urgent → algorithms; small → DMA
• OTC DERIVATIVES — dealer-negotiated and historically opaque; regulation (Dodd–Frank swap data repositories, the G-20 push to central clearing) has raised post-trade transparency. Large urgent → broker risk trade into dealer inventory; large non-urgent → high-touch agency, often needing a strong price concession because contracts are customized
• SPOT FX — entirely OTC, no exchange or central clearing, almost no cross-border regulation, tiered (interbank dealers → mid-size institutions → corporates/retail, each paying a wider spread); over $1 trillion/day yet relatively opaque (quotes only, from some venues). Large urgent → RFQ to multiple competing dealers; large non-urgent → algorithms (e.g. TWAP) or high-touch agency; small → DMA

cards.front: State the three-component implementation shortfall formula, and how IS is converted to basis points.
cards.back:
• S = total order shares (S > 0 buy, S < 0 sell); sj and pj = shares and price of the jth fill; Σ sj = shares actually executed
• Pd = DECISION price (the paper-portfolio price); Pn = the current/final price when the order is completed or cancelled (often the close)
• Term 1 = EXECUTION cost, on shares filled; Term 2 = OPPORTUNITY cost, on the UNFILLED shares marked at Pn; Term 3 = explicit fees (commissions, exchange fees, taxes)
• Equivalent definition: IS = paper-portfolio return − actual portfolio return. A POSITIVE IS is a cost
• Curriculum worked example — buy 100,000 RLK, Pd = $30.00; 80,000 filled for $2,425,000; close Pn = $30.65; commission $0.02/share:
  Execution = $2,425,000 − 80,000 × $30.00 = $25,000
  Opportunity = (100,000 − 80,000)($30.65 − $30.00) = $13,000
  Fees = 80,000 × $0.02 = $1,600
  IS ($) = $25,000 + $13,000 + $1,600 = $39,600
  IS (bps) = $39,600 ÷ (100,000 × $30.00) × 10,000 = 132 bps
• Classic errors: marking unfilled shares at the execution price instead of Pn; putting FILLED shares (or executed value) in the bps denominator instead of total order shares × Pd; omitting fees.
cards.formula: IS = [Σ sj·pj − (Σ sj)·Pd] + (S − Σ sj)(Pn − Pd) + Fees ; IS(bps) = IS($) ÷ (S × Pd) × 10,000

cards.front: Write the EXPANDED implementation shortfall and define the two pieces that execution cost splits into.
cards.back:
• p0 = ARRIVAL price — the price when the order was RELEASED to the market (distinct from Pd, the decision price)
• Bracket 1 = DELAY (slippage) cost — adverse move between the decision and the release, computed on the shares actually EXECUTED
• Bracket 2 = TRADING cost — the prices paid versus arrival, on the shares executed
• Delay + trading = execution cost, so the expanded IS totals exactly the same as the three-part IS
• Curriculum worked example (RLK, Pd = $30.00, released at p0 = $30.10, 80,000 filled for $2,425,000):
  Delay = 80,000 × ($30.10 − $30.00) = $8,000 (20.2% of IS)
  Trading = $2,425,000 − 80,000 × $30.10 = $17,000
  + opportunity $13,000 + fees $1,600 = $39,600
• Diagnosis: delay cost should in theory be mean-zero but in practice is a real cost — it comes from the lag while the trader picks a broker/algorithm, and is cut by having broker performance metrics on hand so the order goes out immediately. Opportunity cost is also not mean-zero (adverse prices and illiquidity) and is cut by sizing the order to what the market can absorb inside the price limit
• Classic error: computing delay cost on the FULL order size — it uses executed shares only.
cards.formula: Expanded IS = [(Σ sj)·p0 − (Σ sj)·Pd] + [Σ sj·pj − (Σ sj)·p0] + (S − Σ sj)(Pn − Pd) + Fees

cards.front: Give the general trade-cost formula in basis points, and state the sign convention that decides whether a number is a cost or a saving.
cards.back:
• P̄ = average execution price of the order; P* = the reference price — arrival price, VWAP, TWAP or the close; Shares = shares executed if you want the dollar version, Cost($) = Side × (P̄ − P*) × Shares
• Sign convention: a POSITIVE value is a COST / underperformance versus the benchmark; a NEGATIVE value is a saving / outperformance. (Some managers multiply by −1 so savings read positive — check the question's convention)
• Evaluate against the benchmark the strategy actually targeted: arrival-price strategy → arrival cost; VWAP strategy → VWAP cost; MOC strategy → closing-price cost. Multiple benchmarks may still be reported for insight (e.g. a post-trade price to detect reversion)
• Examples: buy filled at $30.05 vs arrival $30.00 → +1 × 0.05/30.00 × 10,000 = +16.7 bps cost. Sell filled at $29.50 vs arrival $30.00 → −1 × (−0.50)/30.00 × 10,000 = +166.7 bps, still a COST because the seller received less
• Related metric: Added value (bps) = Arrival cost (bps) − Estimated pre-trade cost (bps); positive means the trade underperformed the pre-trade estimate
• Classic error: dropping Side on a sell order, which flips every cost into a saving.
cards.formula: Cost (bps) = Side × (P̄ − P*) ÷ P* × 10,000 ; Side = +1 for a buy, −1 for a sell

cards.front: How do you strip general market movement out of a trade's arrival cost? Give the formula and the sign logic.
cards.back:
• Purpose: separate the price move the security would have had anyway from the cost caused by the ORDER — buying in a rising market or selling in a falling market inflates raw arrival cost
• β = the security's beta to the chosen index; Index VWAP = volume-weighted index price over the trading horizon (a broad index, a sector index, or a related ETF); the index leg uses the SAME Side as the order
• Worked example: buy at avg $30.50 vs arrival $30.00 → arrival cost 166.7 bps; index arrival $500, index VWAP $505 → index cost +100 bps; β = 1.25 → 166.7 − 125 = 41.7 bps attributable to the order
• Symmetry check: a SELL in a falling market gives the identical answer — Side = −1 makes both the arrival cost (+166.7) and the index cost (+100) positive, so market-adjusted cost is again 41.7 bps
• Classic errors: forgetting Side on the index leg, and subtracting the raw index move without multiplying by β.
cards.formula: Market-adjusted cost (bps) = Arrival cost (bps) − β × Index cost (bps), where Index cost (bps) = Side × (Index VWAP − Index arrival price) ÷ Index arrival price × 10,000

cards.front: A firm's trade policy defines best execution as "the best execution price and the lowest trading cost possible for every transaction." Why is that definition deficient, and what must it contain instead?
cards.back:
• Best execution means terms most favorable to the CLIENT, which is a TRADE-OFF among: execution price, trading costs, speed of execution, likelihood of execution and settlement, order size, and the nature of the trade
• Price-and-cost-only is too narrow: pursuing the lowest cost pushes the trader to be excessively patient, leaving trades unexecuted and generating OPPORTUNITY cost — ruinous for a process with short-horizon, fast-decaying alpha forecasts
• MiFID II: firms must take "all SUFFICIENT steps" to obtain the best possible result — a higher bar than MiFID I's "all reasonable steps"; it also bans bundling commissions with broker research (soft dollars), so the firm pays or a client-funded research payment account does
• The other required trade-policy elements: the meaning of best execution, the factors setting the optimal execution approach (urgency, security characteristics, venue characteristics, strategy objectives, rationale for the trade), treatment of TRADE ERRORS (disclosed to compliance and logged), a list of eligible brokers/venues, and a process to monitor execution arrangements
• Related traps: screening brokers on lowest commission alone, or retaining one broker out of long familiarity — you must show regular, unbiased comparative analysis. A Best Execution Monitoring Committee owns the approved list and the monitoring, and trading records are kept accessible for years (five, in the UK). Partially filled pooled orders are allocated PRO RATA so no account is disadvantaged.

cards.front: Name the four tools an institutional investor uses to manage portfolio liquidity risk, and state the liquidity budget minimums in the curriculum's time-to-cash table.
cards.back:
• Liquidity profiling / time-to-cash tables — bucket every investment bottom-up by expected time to convert to cash without moving the price; aggregate to the portfolio and monitor over time
• Rebalancing and commitment strategies — systematic corridors (wider bands for more volatile classes), automatic adjustment mechanisms (public-market proxy cut when the correlated private allocation rises), and multi-year commitment pacing
• Stress testing — stress assets AND liabilities together (prices, correlations, liquidity terms, plus higher university distributions); historical, statistical, or hypothetical scenarios
• Derivatives — cash-efficient overlays that rebalance exposures, modify the liquidity profile via leverage, or raise short-term cash while leaving external managers untouched
Exhibit 1 liquidity budget: <1 week Highly Liquid at least 10%; <1 quarter Moderately Liquid at least 35%; <1 year Semi-Liquid at least 50%; >1 year Illiquid up to 50% (a maximum, not a minimum)
Case wording of the same kit: cash flow-forecasting and commitment-pacing models, liquidity budgets, stress tests
cards.mnemonic: Profile, Pace, Stress, Derivatives — the last three buckets are floors, illiquid is a ceiling

cards.front: Thompson lists three reasons the endowment's liquidity characteristics deteriorate in severe market stress. What are they, and which commonly cited stress feature is NOT on the list?
cards.back:
• Capital calls exceeding capital distributions — private-market weight rises exactly when cash is scarce; calls are legal obligations and GPs may accelerate them in depressed markets
• Activation of gates — hedge funds and real estate funds refuse withdrawal requests to protect remaining investors, so quarterly/annual liquidity disappears
• The smoothing effect — private marks incorporate valuations with a lag, so private weights rise relatively and liquid weights fall
Key nuance: the smoothing effect does NOT reduce dollar liquidity; it changes the PERCENTAGE of the portfolio available to meet needs
Not one of the three: wider public-bond bid-ask spreads (a general stress feature, a favorite distractor). Adding to private markets during stress is the problem, never a tool
cards.mnemonic: Calls, Gates, Lag

cards.front: State QU's post-2008 geometric smoothing (Yale-type) spending rule and compute this year's spending from prior spending of USD308.9 million and prior year-end market value of USD7,575.1 million.
cards.back:
• Spending(t) = current fiscal year distribution; Spending(t-1) = prior year's actual spending; 5% = long-term desired spending rate; market value is the END of the prior fiscal year; weights 66%/34% are fixed; output in currency units, not a percentage
• Worked: 0.66 × 308.9 + 0.34 × (0.05 × 7,575.1) = 203.9 + 128.8 = USD332.6 million
• Use it when the question asks for the distribution or why distributions are stable: it shields payouts from market-value swings (the pre-crisis rule was simply 5% × beginning-of-year market value)
• Consequence: the effective rate falls below 5% after sustained strong returns and rises above 5% in a protracted weak market — countercyclical, which EXACERBATES liquidity needs in a downturn
• Classic errors: applying 5% to the CURRENT market value, dropping the 5% inside the second term, or calling the smoothed rule non-countercyclical
cards.formula: Spending(t) = 66% × Spending(t-1) + 34% × (5% × Endowment market value at end of year t-1)

cards.front: Why can a long-horizon endowment treat illiquidity as a return source, and which QU-specific facts supported raising private equity 18% → 23% and real assets 13% → 16%?
cards.back:
• The illiquidity premium is compensation for tying up capital for an uncertain period; it is positively correlated with the length of the illiquidity horizon (evidence in private equity and private real estate)
• Higher portfolio efficiency comes from (1) diversification between illiquid assets and the rest of the universe, (2) the higher return from bearing illiquidity risk if adequately priced, or (3) both; in MVO, adding illiquid assets to the eligible universe may shift the efficient frontier UPWARD
• QU supports: positive historical experience with strong realized returns; two decades of gradual build-up so the illiquid portfolios are established, mature, and diversified by manager, strategy, and vintage; alumni-network access to best-in-class managers; illiquid allocation below peers, identified as a cause of post-2008 underperformance
• Funded by cuts to public equities and fixed income, transitioned gradually over two to three years
• Caveats: the premium is hard to isolate and estimates come from broad indexes while an investor holds a small subset (idiosyncratic risk — avoid large allocations to very few funds); use NET-OF-FEES return assumptions; unsmooth illiquid returns before MVO, since stale pricing understates volatility and would push the optimizer into too much illiquidity

cards.front: Proposed vs current SAA: contrast the expected risk-return properties and the liquidity profile, and state the two conditions Thompson must confirm before recommending the change.
cards.back:
Risk-return (Exhibit 10, proposed vs current):
• Nominal return 7.8% vs 7.5%; real 5.3% vs 5.0%; volatility 13.2% vs 12.5%; Sharpe 0.34 vs 0.33
• Probability of 25% purchasing-power erosion over 20 years at a 5% spending rate: 30% vs 35% (i.e., a 70% vs 65% chance of keeping at least 75% of purchasing power)
• 13.2% sits inside the Board's risk tolerance, specified as a long-term volatility range of 12%-14%
Liquidity (Exhibits 13-14, illiquid bucket):
• Current 33% normal / 39% stress / 42% high stress; proposed 39% / 43% / 50% — more illiquid in every state
• Under high stress the proposed SAA temporarily breaches the budget: highly liquid 9% vs a 10% minimum, moderately liquid 19% vs a 35% minimum, illiquid at the 50% ceiling
Two confirmations before recommending: (1) the resulting risk profile (13.2% volatility and the erosion probabilities) is consistent with risk TOLERANCE — willingness and capacity; (2) the allocation remains consistent with the LIQUIDITY BUDGET. Approval is conditional, never "liquidity is not a concern"; a temporary extreme-stress breach is tolerable only with close monitoring and periodic stress testing (and possibly trimming less-liquid commingled public equity funds)

cards.front: Give the corridor test, and apply it to Exhibit 17: international developed equity 11.5% (target 9%, ±2%), fixed income 6.5% (target 9%, ±3%), domestic equity 17.3% (target 15%, ±2.5%).
cards.back:
• Corridor width is in percentage points of the total portfolio, not a percentage of the target; band size should consider the underlying volatility of each investment category (more volatile classes get WIDER bands, to minimize transaction costs), with transaction costs, correlations between asset classes, and investor risk tolerance as the other stated factors (PE 23% ±5%, cash 1% ±1%)
• IntDev: 9% ± 2% = 7%-11%; actual 11.5% exceeds the upper bound by 0.50% → rebalance (to the 11% edge or the 9% target, at the team's discretion)
• Fixed income: 9% ± 3% = 6%-12%; actual 6.5% is below TARGET but inside the corridor → no action required
• Domestic equity: 15% ± 2.5% = 12.5%-17.5%; actual 17.3% → inside, barely
• Other corridors: EM 12% ±2%, real assets 16% ±3%, diversifying 15% ±3%
• Classic error: rebalancing fixed income because 6.5% is under the 9% target — only a corridor breach triggers action
cards.formula: Corridor = SAA target ± corridor width; rebalance only if Actual < lower bound or Actual > upper bound

cards.front: Walk through QUINCO's rebalancing policy from monitoring to execution, and say how it differs for illiquid asset classes.
cards.back:
1. Monitor drift of the actual portfolio versus the SAA MONTHLY
2. Execute at the END OF EACH CALENDAR QUARTER to minimize transaction costs — intra-quarter action only in extraordinary market circumstances
3. For public asset classes, rebalance systematically when the allocation is outside its corridor at quarter end
4. Team has DISCRETION to rebalance back to the target allocation or only to the edge of the corridor
5. For ILLIQUID classes, rebalancing runs through the reinvestment/commitment strategy — alter the pace of new commitments as the allocation approaches a corridor edge — because secondary transaction costs are high and execution is slow
• Example: private equity 19.2% and real assets 13.8% sit near the LOWER edges of their corridors while the team builds toward the new 23%/16% targets; in the very short term these allocations cannot be increased

cards.front: In the GVC manager-selection case, map each individual to the Standards they engage: Winter, Hall, the university president/treasurer, Allen, and Davis.
cards.back:
• Winter (QUINCO CIO) — VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts (main issue: hiring a manager with close university ties) and I(B) Independence and Objectivity (implicit and explicit pressure; also a former-colleague tie to Allen); V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis for not investigating GVC's returns, which exceed third-party databases; must flag a possible III(E) Confidentiality breach since GVC's proposal used non-public trustee information
• Hall (Trustee and GVC managing partner) — IV(A) Loyalty (trustee must act for the university without regard to her own benefit), VI(A), and III(E) if she passed trustee information to GVC; remedy is disclose and RECUSE
• University president and treasurer (QUINCO Board members) — IV(A) Loyalty by letting trustee relations drive hiring, plus VI(A) and I(B), and potentially III(E); disclose and recuse
• Allen (GVC managing director) — I(C) Misrepresentation and III(D) Performance Presentation for returns well above third-party records (inadvertent at best)
• Davis (QUINCO senior PM, spouse is Hall's daughter) — I(B) and at minimum the perception of a conflict under VI(A) for advocating GVC without disclosing the family tie

cards.front: Davis says his family tie to Hall is "common knowledge" and points out he negotiated a management-fee discount from GVC. Why does neither fact resolve the ethical problem?
cards.back:
• "Common knowledge" is never a substitute for disclosure — Davis must make an EXPLICIT disclosure of the potential conflict when making his recommendation; a belief that others already knew does not satisfy VI(A)
• A fee discount is an economic benefit to the client; ethical duties are not offset by economics. Davis's family conflict, Winter's compromised independence, and the confidential-information issue all still require disclosure and recusal
• The committee's concern about GVC scaling from a USD100 million Fund I to a USD300 million Fund II is a diligence point Davis must address in supporting his recommendation, but no Standard prohibits a fund growing in size — and the case flags only I(B) Independence and Objectivity and VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts against Davis. The V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis failure in this case is WINTER's, for not investigating GVC's returns that exceed third-party databases
• The required remedies: (1) identify conflicts (family, business, trustee ties); (2) disclose them explicitly — VI(A); (3) recuse where independence and objectivity are compromised — I(B); (4) institutionalize a due diligence questionnaire/RFP that asks new managers about their own conflicts of interest

cards.front: For a fully funded USD80 million, one-year 1% overweight to the S&P 500, compare ETF, futures, and total return swap: total costs, the largest cost component of each, and replication precision.
cards.back:
Total costs (Exhibit 15, bps): ETF 35.00 < futures 42.00 < TRS 51.00 → choose the ETF
• ETF stack: commission 4 + management fee 9.5 + spread 2.5 + price impact 15 + tracking 4; largest component is PRICE IMPACT (15), management fee second
• Futures stack: commission 2 + spread 2 + price impact 10 + tracking 8 + roll 20; largest is the quarterly ROLL COST (5 bps per quarter, 20 annual), driven by the upward-sloping (contango) curve
• TRS stack: commission 5 + spread 6 + funding 40; dominated by FUNDING COST (40)
Replication: TRS is EXACT — the counterparty is obligated to deliver the index return, so no tracking error. ETF tracking error comes from NAV premiums/discounts, cash drag, and regulatory diversification; futures tracking error from liquidity/supply-demand, dividend forecast errors, and interest rate differentials
Other factors: ETFs and futures are exchange-traded and standardized, the TRS is OTC and customizable but adds counterparty credit risk; futures demand daily margin monitoring and quarterly rolls. Unlevered, the ETF wins on cost, liquidity, tight spreads, and easy early termination if views change

cards.front: At four times leverage, compute the incremental cost for the ETF, futures, and TRS on the USD80 million S&P 500 overweight, and give the new total-cost ranking.
cards.back:
• Leverage 4x means cash supports 25% of notional, so 1 - 1/4 = 75% must be financed; rates: ETF borrows at three-month MRR + 50 bps = 2.5%, futures and TRS at the 2% MRR forgone on the uninvested 75%
• ETF: (80m × 0.75 × 2.5%) ÷ 80m = 1.875% = 187.50 bps
• Futures: (80m × 0.75 × 2%) ÷ 80m = 1.50% = 150.00 bps; TRS: same = 150.00 bps
• Totals = unlevered + incremental: ETF 35 + 187.50 = 222.50; futures 42 + 150 = 192.00; TRS 51 + 150 = 201.00
• The ranking FLIPS: futures 192 < TRS 201 < ETF 222.50, so Thompson implements with futures — accepting daily margin monitoring and the quarterly roll
• Why: ETFs are least cash-efficient (the full notional must be financed; instrument-level margin regulation caps ETF leverage at 2x, so USD80m of exposure ties up at least USD40m of cash)
• Classic errors: applying the rate to the full notional instead of the financed 75%, and using 2% rather than MRR + 50 bps for the ETF
cards.formula: Incremental cost of leverage (bps) = [Notional × (1 - 1/Leverage) × borrowing or funding rate] ÷ Notional

cards.front: International developed equity has breached its corridor. How do you decide between a derivatives overlay and cash-market reallocation for the 0.5% trade versus the 2.5% trade?
cards.back:
Small trade — 0.5% to the corridor edge, one-quarter horizon (Exhibit 18): cash market 30 bps total, driven by ~20 bps CASH DRAG from timing delays and disruption to active manager portfolios; futures (short MSCI EAFE, long fixed income) 24 bps, driven by 17 bps quarterly tracking error — note 17 bps for two instruments vs 8 bps for a single S&P 500 future
→ Costs are similar, so choose DERIVATIVES: small size, fast execution, tactically adjustable, quickly reversible, and the external active managers stay in place
Large trade — 2.5% back to target, one-year horizon (Exhibit 19): cash market 60 bps (cash drag rises to 50 bps with size); futures 82 bps, dominated by 68 bps ANNUAL tracking error (roll cost only 6 bps, since the short equity roll largely offsets the long fixed-income roll)
→ Choose CASH MARKETS: reallocate between the equity and fixed-income managers
Decision drivers: cost; size (larger and more permanent → cash); time horizon (longer → cash, because futures mispricing/tracking risk grows with horizon); speed (faster → derivatives); leaving active managers undisturbed and reversibility (→ derivatives). Context: the Board raised the active risk budget from 100 bps to 250 bps, allowing up to 150 bps for TAA and up to 5% portfolio leverage

cards.front: State the three considerations underpinning QUINCO's responsible investing policy, define its chosen approach, and give QUINCO's stance on divesting Portro Inc.
cards.back:
Three considerations (policy in place seven years):
• ESG factors, alongside traditional financial factors, affect the RISK AND RETURN of investments
• Promotion of greater TRANSPARENCY on material ESG issues affecting QUINCO's investment activities
• Pursuit of long-term SUSTAINABILITY for the companies and markets the endowment invests in
Approach: ESG INTEGRATION — "the explicit and systematic inclusion of ESG factors in investment analysis and investment decisions" — NOT exclusion, which would ban countries, sectors, or companies a priori. Because QUINCO invests through external managers, the policy relies on them to integrate ESG via research, materiality analysis, and active ownership
Portro (a social factor: ILO-documented labor conditions, child-labor allegations, supplier health and safety): DIVESTMENT is a suboptimal risk mitigation strategy, a LAST RESORT. The response is responsible ownership — manager engagement, collective engagement with management through the PRI, and proxy voting for disclosure resolutions
Policy gap and fix: the original policy named principles but not the TOOLS to assess manager ESG implementation; specialist Natalya Long, CFA, added enhanced ESG due diligence in manager selection and monitoring, responsible ownership, portfolio ESG metrics (carbon footprint/intensity, ratings vs peers), and PRI signatory status

cards.front: What is the purpose of the CFA Institute Asset Manager Code, and what benefits can a firm that adopts it expect?
cards.back:
Purpose: a voluntary, firm-level code of ethical and professional responsibilities for asset-management firms — distinct from the Code and Standards, which bind individual members and candidates.
Benefits of adoption: a ready-made framework for meeting regulations that require an adviser's code of ethics; a public signal of ethical culture to clients and prospects; a consistent internal standard across loyalty to clients, the investment process, trading, compliance, performance, and disclosure.
Trap: employing CFA charterholders does not make adoption mandatory; the Code is voluntary and applies to FIRMS, not to individuals acting alone.
cards.mnemonic: Firm-level, voluntary, six-area playbook — not the individual Code and Standards.

cards.front: Name the six General Principles of Conduct of the Asset Manager Code and the ethical responsibility each one captures.
cards.back:
1. Loyalty to Clients — place client interests first; preserve confidentiality; refuse gifts that reasonably could affect independence.
2. Investment Process and Actions — use reasonable care and independent judgment; have a reasonable and adequate basis; fair dealing; suitability.
3. Trading — best execution; fair allocation of trades and opportunities (including IPOs); do not place personal trades ahead of clients.
4. Risk Management, Compliance, and Support — a compliance officer, policies and procedures, a disaster-recovery plan, and adequate resources.
5. Performance and Valuation — fair, accurate, complete, timely, and relevant presentation; fair valuation.
6. Disclosures — timely disclosure of conflicts, fees, risks, and other material facts so clients can make informed decisions.
cards.mnemonic: Loyalty, Process, Trading, Compliance, Performance, Disclosure.

cards.front: A firm allocates the same number of shares of an oversubscribed IPO to every client account, including accounts that never buy IPOs. Does that practice comply with the Asset Manager Code?
cards.back:
No. Equal share counts is not fair dealing. Trading/process principles require fair allocation of investment opportunities given each client's objectives, constraints, and mandate — not a mechanical headcount of shares.
A client who does not participate in IPOs should not be padded into the allocation, and a client for whom the IPO is suitable should not be shorted so that unrelated accounts can be 'treated equally.'
To judge compliance, map the practice to the six principles (here: Loyalty to Clients and Trading / fair allocation) rather than asking whether a rule of thumb 'looks even.'

cards.front: Recommend procedures a firm should put in place so that its practices stay consistent with the Asset Manager Code.
cards.back:
• Adopt the Code at the firm level and name a compliance officer with authority to enforce it.
• Written policies for loyalty/confidentiality, suitability, fair dealing, best execution, trade allocation, personal trading, valuation, and performance presentation.
• Disclose conflicts, fees, and risks to clients in a timely way; record the disclosures.
• Fair, accurate, complete performance reporting (GIPS compliance is supportive, not a substitute).
• Resource the compliance, risk, and disaster-recovery functions; review them.
• Train staff and test adherence (sample allocations, IPO books, personal-trade logs) rather than relying on a one-time policy memo.
cards.mnemonic: Policy, officer, disclose, value fairly, resource, then test.
